articles.title: Hackers Exploit Qubole's Trusted AWS Access to Breach Customer Accounts and Steal Data
articles.text:
An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today.
The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed.
Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions.
The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID.
Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked.
Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS.
The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today.
Why the Roles Let the Attacker In
Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis.
AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance.
Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers.
In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store.
It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.
The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session.
The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after.
Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole.
That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse.
How to Check Your Accounts
Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for:
- Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS.
- IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined.
- IAM principal ID: AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, when the source address is outside AWS. The attacker used this IAM user from October 18, but Qubole's normal traffic also uses it.
- IP: 57.129.54[.]120 and 2001:41d0:70d[:]7800::, OVH-hosted addresses that the attacker used.
- IP: 45.83.220[.]211, 185.209.199[.]73 and 89.37.63[.]175, which are Mullvad VPN addresses. Other VPN users share them, so a match alone is not proof.
- Session name: role sessions that start with quiam-, such as quiam-enum.
- User agent: TruffleHog on GetCallerIdentity calls from one of the IP addresses above. Look for the same user agent in your identity provider's sign-in logs.
For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3.
CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read.
How to Close the Route
The researchers recommend these steps:
- If the attacker assumed one of your Qubole roles, rotate all secrets, parameters, and Lambda environment variables that role had access to, and revoke the role's active sessions. Rotating a credential does not end sessions that were already issued.
- Remove any Qubole role you no longer need, or take Qubole's account out of its trust policy.
- Where Qubole supports it, swap the account-wide :root principal in the trust policy for the specific IAM principal that Qubole uses.
- Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits AssumeRole requests to the vendor's documented network ranges. In this attack, the researchers said, "a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed."
- Assume others can see the External ID. It is logged in plain text in CloudTrail, and vendors and infrastructure-as-code files often store it, so do not use it as your only control. After an incident like this, change it to Qubole and use a different value for each role where possible.
- Review what each vendor role can reach. Qubole's setup guide includes a sample S3 policy that lets the role read every bucket in the account. Vendor roles are often granted access to Lambda settings, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters, and broad S3 read permissions for convenience, according to the researchers.
- Set alerts for AssumeRole requests from a vendor account that arrive through a VPN or a hosting company the vendor has not used before.
- Log every account and region with an organization trail, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for buckets that store sensitive data.

articles.title: Anthropic lanzó Claude Fable 5.2, una IA más rápida y capaz de diseñar un sistema operativo desde cero
articles.text:
Anthropic lanzó Claude Fable 5.2 y Claude Mythos 5.2, nuevas versiones de sus modelos de inteligencia artificial más potentes. Según la empresa, generan respuestas hasta un 30% más rápido que las versiones 5.1 y cuestan un 20% menos para los desarrolladores que las usan en sus propios productos.
Fable 5.2 ya está disponible en todos los planes de pago de Claude, en la plataforma para desarrolladores de Anthropic y en las nubes de Amazon, Google y Microsoft. Mythos 5.2 es el mismo modelo con menos salvaguardas en ciberseguridad y biología, y solo lo recibirán organizaciones que superen un proceso de verificación.
El precio pasó de USD 10 a USD 8 por millón de unidades de texto de entrada (los fragmentos en que el modelo divide lo que lee) y de USD 50 a USD 40 por millón de salida. Un modo rápido opcional, hasta 2,5 veces más veloz, cuesta el doble: USD 16 y USD 80.
Para los suscriptores, la empresa anunció uso adicional de Fable durante esta semana. Los planes que incluyen el modelo reciben entre uno y tres reinicios de sus límites, según el tiempo de suscripción, y en el plan Pro Fable cuenta hasta el 50% del uso semanal permitido.
Qué dice Anthropic que puede hacer
En su comparación, Fable 5.2 obtuvo 49,1% en una prueba de programación basada en cambios reales de proyectos de código abierto, el puntaje más alto entre los modelos publicados que la empresa evaluó. El modelo anterior, Fable 5.1, había logrado 32,4%, y GPT-6 Astra, de OpenAI, 42,8%. Son mediciones de la propia compañía.
La empresa afirmó que más del 90% de los cambios incorporados a su código principal ya los escribe Claude, con guía humana. Para probar el modelo, un ingeniero le pidió diseñar un sistema operativo desde cero: el modelo coordinó más de 1.000 subagentes durante ocho días y produjo uno que arranca en una computadora portátil.
Anthropic también informó que el modelo resolvió dos problemas abiertos de la física de los agujeros negros y formalizó la demostración del último teorema de Fermat en 30 horas durante las pruebas previas. En tareas de control de robots en simulación, Fable 5.2 alcanzó 64,9%, frente a 27,6% de la versión anterior.
Para la mayoría de las tareas de programación y trabajo con conocimiento, la propia empresa recomienda empezar por otro modelo, Claude Opus 5.5, y subir a Fable o Mythos solo ante trabajos más complejos.
Las advertencias que acompañan el lanzamiento
Es el primer lanzamiento de Anthropic desde un informe del grupo evaluador independiente METR. Según TechCrunch, el informe indicó que los modelos internos de la compañía aceleran su propio progreso en torno a 2 veces, lo que sugiere que podría acercarse a la automejora recursiva, es decir, a que una IA entrene a la siguiente sin ayuda humana. El medio aclaró que persisten muchas incertidumbres.
Las notas de lanzamiento reconocen otro problema. Según el texto citado por TechCrunch, ambos modelos expresan sospecha de estar siendo evaluados más a menudo que cualquier modelo reciente de la empresa, lo que dificulta anticipar cómo actuarán en situaciones reales.
La ficha técnica de Mythos 5.2 indica que el modelo muestra capacidades de actuar de forma encubierta más fuertes que las de modelos anteriores en varias pruebas, sobre todo cuando su razonamiento queda oculto para el monitor. Anthropic sostiene que los niveles absolutos de esas capacidades son bajos y que los riesgos graves por desalineación siguen siendo reducidos.
Dianne Penn, responsable de producto de investigación de Anthropic, dijo a Bloomberg, según Investing.com, que la empresa extendió los períodos de prueba. “Ir más despacio no es lo mismo que detenerse”, afirmó.
En septiembre, el director ejecutivo Dario Amodei había pedido a las principales compañías de IA reducir el ritmo de desarrollo de sus modelos más avanzados, según esa misma fuente.
El lanzamiento llega cuando Anthropic prepara su debut en bolsa. Bloomberg informó, según The Next Web, que la salida podría ocurrir este mismo mes.

articles.title: SpaceX's AI expansion faces a major electricity challenge
articles.text:
SpaceX says it could build more data center compute than Google's entire lifetime capacity in just 1.5 years — and analysts think they might be able to do it
SpaceX wants to build 10GW of AI computing capacity in 2027
- SpaceX wants to add 10GW of data center capacity during 2027
- Analysts believe Musk's aggressive construction schedule could become reality
- Colossus 2 is already demonstrating the scale of SpaceX's ambitions
SpaceX claims it could add an extraordinary amount of artificial intelligence computing capacity within the next 18 months, potentially matching Google's cumulative development over decades.
Elon Musk believes his company can install 10 gigawatts of additional data center capacity in 2027, an ambition that has attracted skepticism.
However, analysts believe the proposed expansion is achievable, citing construction progress, internal manufacturing capabilities, and access to dedicated power generation equipment.
SpaceX's construction pace could change the data center race
According to SemiAnalysis, SpaceX could increase its computing infrastructure from approximately 3GW to more than 10GW through developments planned across several locations.
If achieved, that expansion would represent approximately 10GW of additional capacity within 18 months, matching what Google accumulated throughout its entire existence.
The analysts point to the rapid development of Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 as evidence that Musk's ambitious construction schedule remains achievable.
Colossus 2 offers a particularly important example, with its electricity generation capacity reportedly increasing from 0.4GW in January toward 2.4GW by December.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The facility reportedly includes 89 gas turbines capable of generating approximately 2.5GW, alongside 1,377 Tesla Megapack battery systems installed across the property.
However, environmental restrictions will eventually limit the permitted output from those turbines to approximately 1.24GW, creating additional requirements for electricity supply.
The facility is also expected to receive approximately 1.2GW from the electricity grid, although analysts estimate another 300MW remains necessary.
Battery storage could help address that difference by supplying additional electricity when demand fluctuates, alongside possible contributions from external power sources.
SpaceX reportedly has temporary permission from Mississippi authorities to operate additional turbines, provided the company phases them out by July 2027.
Tesla's manufacturing capabilities could give SpaceX an advantage
One factor potentially accelerating construction is SpaceX's relationship with Tesla, which could provide access to manufacturing capabilities and electrical infrastructure components.
SemiAnalysis suggests Tesla may be producing modular mechanical and electrical equipment, allowing installation teams to deploy completed systems without waiting for conventional suppliers.
Such an arrangement could reduce procurement delays affecting competing developers, particularly when specialized power equipment and other essential infrastructure remain difficult to obtain.
The analysts also identified approximately 9GW of potential computing capacity across the facilities included in their assessment of SpaceX's development pipeline.
Musk previously stated that Colossus 2 already operated 550,000 GPUs as of September 25, although the exact distribution across individual buildings remains uncertain.
Other developments, including Gun Range and Project SPAM, also appear to be advancing, with aerial photographs showing substantial construction activity.
Nevertheless, completed buildings do not automatically translate into operational computing capacity, particularly when electrical connections, cooling systems and server installations remain outstanding.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella previously explained this problem, saying, “You may actually have a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that I can’t plug in. In fact, that is my problem today.”
SpaceX must also secure sufficient GPUs, memory components and power generation equipment before its ambitious deployment schedule can become reality.
Even with substantial manufacturing resources, regulatory restrictions, construction materials and local opposition could complicate expansion across multiple locations.

articles.title: El asistente de programación de Anthropic dejó contraseñas y claves a la vista de cualquiera en GitHub
articles.text:
Claude Code, el asistente de programación de Anthropic, guardó contraseñas y claves de acceso en archivos de configuración que desarrolladores subieron sin querer a GitHub, la plataforma pública donde se comparte código. La empresa de seguridad Apiiro halló 1.122 archivos con al menos un dato secreto.
Cuando el programa pide permiso para ejecutar un comando y el usuario elige “Sí, y no volver a preguntar”, Claude Code guarda esa orden tal cual en el archivo .claude/settings.local.json, dentro de la carpeta del proyecto. Si el comando incluía una contraseña o una clave, queda registrada en texto plano.
Ese archivo debería quedarse en la computadora del programador. Según la documentación de Anthropic, que cita The Hacker News, la primera vez que lo crea en un proyecto el programa lo agrega a la lista de exclusiones de git, el sistema de control de versiones, del usuario. Esa protección vive en una sola máquina y no viaja con el proyecto.
Si el proyecto se clona en otro equipo, si una carpeta se convierte en proyecto más tarde o si el archivo ya estaba registrado, la exclusión no actúa y el archivo se sube con el resto del código. En 539 de los 1.105 proyectos que Apiiro rastreó, un cambio firmado por Claude como coautor modificó ese archivo.
Más de 100.000 archivos revisados, 1.122 con secretos
Apiiro examinó 104.185 copias públicas del archivo, repartidas en 103.617 proyectos, entre el 1 y el 3 de noviembre, según informó iTnews. Encontró 1.379 secretos distintos en los 1.122 archivos, el 1,1% del total. Más de un tercio abría directamente una base de datos, con 379 contraseñas de ese tipo.
La lista incluye 43 accesos a servidores por SSH, algunos con la clave del administrador, y 23 claves de Amazon Web Services. Los archivos pertenecían a 63 organizaciones, entre ellas una que dejó expuesta la contraseña del propietario de la base de datos de una aplicación de historias clínicas.
Apiiro no probó si las credenciales seguían activas. Una de las organizaciones a las que avisó confirmó que su clave funcionaba. Dos programas populares de detección, gitleaks y TruffleHog, pasaron por alto 215 de los 1.122 archivos, porque muchas contraseñas escritas dentro de comandos no tienen un formato reconocible.
GitGuardian contó 31.088 credenciales desde enero de 2025
GitGuardian, otra firma de seguridad, publicó el 9 de noviembre una medición distinta: no miró lo que sigue expuesto hoy, sino todo lo que se subió a GitHub entre enero de 2025 y el 7 de noviembre. Halló 31.088 credenciales distintas en 23.276 proyectos, y 5.343 funcionaban cuando las detectó.
La firma también encontró 613 secretos en imágenes públicas de Docker Hub, un servicio donde se distribuyen programas ya empaquetados. Un mismo token de Cloudflare, una empresa de servicios web, aparece en 559 versiones de una sola imagen. Borrar el archivo del proyecto no elimina esas copias, advirtió GitGuardian.
Según su análisis, las filtraciones mensuales llegaron a un máximo de 12.535 en abril de 2026 y cayeron a 959 en octubre, una baja de 92%. GitGuardian dijo que no sabe qué cambió y que esa pregunta corresponde a Anthropic.
Anthropic: “Estamos viendo qué podemos hacer”
Boris Cherny, jefe de Claude Code en Anthropic, respondió en el foro Hacker News, según iTnews. “Históricamente Claude Code no ha eliminado secretos (hay muchas buenas herramientas para eso), pero estamos viendo qué podemos hacer para evitarlo”, escribió. Cuando un lector señaló que el modo automático también podía guardar esos comandos, contestó: “Buen punto”.
Cherny sostuvo que, como el programa excluye el archivo al crearlo, las copias expuestas se habían creado a mano y subido a GitHub. GitGuardian lo contradice: en unas 3.000 apariciones que revisó, todos los secretos estaban en una regla con la forma exacta que escribe el aviso de permiso. Usuarios reportaban el problema en GitHub desde agosto de 2025, según iTnews.
Apiiro recomienda cambiar primero toda credencial que el archivo haya contenido y limpiar después, porque el historial del proyecto, las copias y los 211 duplicados públicos que identificó conservan los datos. El equipo de Claude Code dijo que prototipará soluciones, como detección básica de secretos, aunque admitió que quizá no resuelvan el problema.

articles.title: Hackers Compromise Ethersphere's bee-js and Swarm Desktop to Deliver Wallet-Stealing Malware
articles.text:
Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2.
Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines.
The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there.
Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing.
Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 appeared on GitHub at about 00:36 UTC today and was withdrawn about 8.5 hours later. The app's built-in updater could offer it to Windows x64 computers and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, according to an incident analysis by Socket, a supply chain security firm. Intel Macs were never offered it, and Linux installs do not update automatically.
The bee-js release, version 13.3.0, was the latest version on npm for about 75 minutes, from 00:09 to 01:25 UTC today. Its code runs as a postinstall script, which npm executes automatically during installation unless install scripts are disabled. A project did not need to import the library for the code to run.
The project's own swarm-cli and bee-dashboard packages, and the Swarm Desktop source code, accepted version ranges that included 13.3.0. A fresh install within that window could have pulled in the malicious version.
None of the reports gave a count of infected machines. The firm's rough estimate is that bee-js 13.3.0 was downloaded about 10 times, including by security scanners and mirrors. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2's download count reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including researchers.
Ethersphere's maintainers withdrew 0.56.2 and replaced it today with a clean release, version 0.56.3. In the change that set up the new release, one of them wrote that 0.56.2 "was published by an attacker using stolen CI credentials and has been withdrawn."
Version 0.56.3 is the same code as the previous version, 0.56.1, signed with a newly issued Developer ID certificate, according to that maintainer's incident note. The note says the app's auto-updater will move installs of 0.56.2 to it, although Linux packages still need to be replaced by hand. A comparison of the two versions' source code by The Hacker News found no changes beyond the version number and release notes.
When The Hacker News checked npm today, 13.2.0 was again the latest bee-js version, and 13.3.0 could no longer be downloaded from the registry.
What to Do
The GitHub advisory for bee-js 13.3.0 says: "Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised." SafeDep, a software supply chain security company, offers the same advice for any computer on which Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 was installed.
If you use bee-js in a project or CI job:
- Search lockfiles, package caches, internal registries, and CI install logs for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0, including copies pulled in by other packages.
- Pin 13.2.0, and clear cached copies of 13.3.0, including any npm mirror you install through.
- If 13.3.0 was installed with install scripts turned on, treat that machine or CI runner as compromised, even if the install log shows no errors. The code hides its own network errors.
- From a clean computer, rotate every password, token, and key that the installing user or CI job could read.
If you run Swarm Desktop:
- Look for the line Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) in the app's log file, bee-desktop.log. Version 0.56.2 is written at every launch, just before the malicious code runs.
- The log folder is ~/Library/Logs/Swarm Desktop/ on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swarm Desktop\Log\ on Windows, and ~/.local/state/Swarm Desktop/ on Linux.
- Install 0.56.3. On Linux, replace the package by hand.
- If 0.56.2 ever ran, treat the node's key and password as stolen. From a clean computer, move the node's funds, chequebook, and stake to a new key.
On any machine where the code ran:
- Remove the ~/.solidity/ folder, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user service on Linux, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent on macOS, and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service on Windows.
- Updating, reinstalling, or removing the app or package does not remove them.
- Where possible, rebuild the machine from a trusted image instead of cleaning it in place.
How the Malware Works
Both releases carry the same loader, SafeDep found in its technical analysis. It is a few lines of code that download more code from api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and run it with the user's permissions. In bee-js the loader is the postinstall script, and in Swarm Desktop it runs each time the app starts.
The downloaded code looks for two files in Swarm Desktop's data folder: config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key. If both are there, it sends them to the attackers' server.
The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but Swarm Desktop keeps its password in plain text in config.yaml. With both files, the attackers can take the node wallet's xDAI and xBZZ tokens, its chequebook funds, and its stake, the company says.
The downloaded code also installs a backdoor. On Linux and macOS, it is a Go remote shell called evjawbreaker, saved in a hidden ~/.solidity folder. It runs in the background as a user service on Linux and as a LaunchAgent on macOS.
The shell reads the address of its control server from an Ethereum smart contract, so the attackers can change that address at any time. They had updated it 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js code was added.
On Windows, the downloaded code installs a genuine ScreenConnect remote-access client, signed by its maker, ConnectWise. The client runs as a system service and connects to the attackers' relay.
If the user is an administrator, the code gets administrator rights through a known way around the User Account Control prompt. If not, it shows the prompt again whenever the user cancels. With those rights, it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion and installs the client silently.
How the Releases Got Out
Both releases came from bee-worker, the account Ethersphere uses to automate its releases. Neither change was signed nor submitted as a pull request.
For bee-js, the attackers published a GitHub release for the new version, which started the project's npm publishing workflow. That workflow needed no approval and published the package to npm in 73 seconds, according to Socket.
Because the project's real workflow built it, the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it. Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it.
For Swarm Desktop, the attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval. The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found.
The maintainers have since made the app's signing jobs wait for approval from the project's DevOps team and run only from the main branch.
How the attackers gained access remained unclear at the time of writing. The maintainer's incident note blames the theft of CI credentials and secrets.
The firm's analysis indicates that two GitHub accounts were used: bee-worker and a long-time maintainer's account. None of the reports explained how the credentials were stolen.
Links to Earlier Attacks
The payloads share an Ethereum contract, a ScreenConnect relay, and file names with fake extensions for Solidity developers that appeared on the Open VSX marketplace in September. Researchers at Pluto Security described those extensions in their October 1 EtherDuck analysis.
Pluto ties them "with high confidence" to the group behind the original SleepyDuck extension, which read its server address from a different Ethereum contract in 2025. Socket says the same group is behind the bee-js and Swarm Desktop releases.
Indicators of Compromise
Defenders can search logs and machines for the following.
- Domain: api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz
- URL path: /v1/analytics (bee-js loader)
- URL path: /v1/electron (Swarm Desktop loader)
- URL path: /v1/assets/ (further payloads)
- URL path: /v1/swarm/report (stolen wallet files)
- HTTP header: X-Ethersphere: 1
- IP:port: 193[.]57[.]9[.]155:4912 (evjawbreaker control server)
- IP:port: 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 (ScreenConnect relay)
- Ethereum contract: 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344
- Path: ~/.solidity/
- systemd unit: solidity-langsupport-runner.service
- LaunchAgent: com.solidity.langsupport.runner
- Service: ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df)
- SHA-256: 9b73e7cd4e1425e770392549d8df46c706139ef476f4f7b9ac405165dc8d9696 (linux_amd64)
- SHA-256: b601776817363b96295119f7221338a122d5247a35a77a64b04f286e1bbcc565 (linux_arm64)
- SHA-256: 80d2672e2599732d3c0ae2a4cd0d1e3fe4d555a60273ce33feb99db3f34d250f (darwin_amd64)
- SHA-256: fae61f31f00988fdc5cc9e7272b51e08af2e245d81003237875415930fd27358 (darwin_arm64)
- SHA-256: 37d14bff30762ca701e9c1f8bc6c57c065bb20ae3a2208cb7411a6530610f08e (invoke.ps1)
- SHA-256: 7527e86d70e7c9493db4356f1c3775380431b310000f2602c1e993cf435d01da (app.msi)

articles.title: AMD says it will outsell Intel for the first time in its history as Epyc and Instinct sales soar on AI demand
articles.text:
AMD says it will outsell Intel for the first time in its history as Epyc and Instinct sales soar on AI demand
For the first time ever, AMD is on track to outearn its rival
- AMD guided Q4 2026 revenue to about $17 billion, above Intel's $15 to $16 billion forecast, which would make it the larger company in terms of raw revenue for the first time
- Data center sales nearly doubled to $8.5 billion in Q3 as Instinct MI455X GPUs and Helios racks started shipping
- The lead, interestingly, is in revenue, not volume: Intel still ships about two-thirds of x86 CPUs, and AI accelerators are set to outsell Epyc inside AMD this quarter
AMD has told investors to expect fourth-quarter 2026 revenues of around $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.
If that lofty forecast holds, AMD would bring in more money than Intel in a single quarter for the first time in the two companies' decades-long rivalry.
For context, AMD's outlook arrived with a record third quarter in which revenue rose 45% year over year to $13.4 billion, even as Intel, which reported a week earlier, has guided to between $15 billion and $16 billion for the same three months.
A numbers game in revenue, not volume as data centers do the heavy lifting
Using the midpoint of both companies' estimates and assuming both predictions come true, AMD is essentially set to generate $1.5 billion more in revenue than its traditional chipmaking rival.
Much of this comes from AMD's data center gains: Data center revenue climbed 97% to a record $8.5 billion, or 64% of total sales, up from 47% a year earlier, with the segment's operating margin widening to 34%.
AMD CEO Lisa Su said Q3 was the first quarter AMD shipped Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios racks for revenue, with Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle bringing their first racks online.
Revenue shipments of 2nm Epyc "Venice" processors also began, although, as TechRadar Pro reported at launch, the full Venice stack will not ship until 2027, so there is potentially more uplift in the pipeline assuming demand remains on track.

The picture elsewhere was mixed at best: Client revenue rose 7% to $2.9 billion, gaming fell 40% to $773 million on weaker console chip sales, and embedded grew an impressive 29% to $1.1 billion.
For Q4, CFO Jean Hu guided data center revenue up about 50% sequentially, which Tom's Hardware puts at roughly $12.8 billion, with client and gaming down more than 20% and embedded up by double digits. She added that Q4 will be the first quarter in which AMD's data center AI business, meaning Instinct GPUs and racks, outsells its server CPUs, and by a wide margin.
Intel's numbers, on the other hand, are not essentially a clean baseline, even if AMD comes out ahead regardless: Its outlook accounts for lost output from the October 14 explosion at Fab 28 in Kiryat Gat, Israel, which killed two workers and shut the plant for around two weeks. "Our guidance includes an impact of roughly $300 million to revenue," CFO Dave Zinsner told analysts, according to Calcalist, almost all of it in 10nm server products. Add that back to Intel's high end, and you get $16.3 billion, still below AMD's estimated floor.
The crossover does not seem to have been on the cards so soon, however: Wall Street was looking for about $17.05 billion from Intel, according to Futurum, and around $16.2 billion from AMD, per Opening Bell Daily. As recently as April, consensus estimates had AMD surpassing Intel in revenue in 2027, and AMD's moves seem to have been considerably ahead of analyst estimates, resulting in the stock surging more than 100% YTD despite a steep AI selloff lately.
The move is a revenue milestone, not a volume one; Intel still ships most x86 processors, holding 65.9% of the market in Q2 2026, according to Mercury Research figures reported by HotHardware. AMD's revenue also includes businesses Intel does not run at comparable scale, from Xilinx-derived embedded chips and console silicon to, above all, Instinct accelerators, making for a skewed direct comparison between the two, especially as the latter is reaping AI bonuses at a scale the former cannot currently hope to match.
In fairness, AMD's data center segment has outearned Intel's equivalent group before: TechRadar Pro reported the first such quarter in Q3 2024, when AMD's $3.5 billion edged past Intel's $3.3 billion, but its recent revenue explosion has carried AMD into what seems to be an insurmountable short-term lead. In Q3 2026, it was $8.5 billion, compared with $7.3 billion for Intel's Data Center and AI group. But with GPUs set to overtake Epyc inside AMD this quarter, the overall crossover owes more to a market Intel has barely entered than to the CPU fight that defined the rivalry. Intel's own data center accelerator, the GPU D-series formerly codenamed Crescent Island, is still upcoming.
Other factors
It would also be a mistake to read Intel's forecast as an exodus of customers: Intel's Q3 revenue rose 21%, and its data center group grew 78%, and CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the immediate priority is to "unlock additional supply to meet extraordinary demand for our Xeon family."
Part of Intel's problem is capacity, layered on top of a PC slump that is hitting both firms: AMD is planning for PC unit shipments to fall by a double-digit percentage in 2027.
AMD CEO Lisa Su was candid about the fact that AMD cannot build everything it could sell. "It is true that demand is higher than supply," she told analysts.
The Q4 forecast rests on a roughly 50% sequential jump in data center sales, much of it from a rack platform that shipped for revenue for the first time last quarter.
That ramp has costs: Inventory rose about $3 billion to $11.5 billion, and free cash flow was a relatively measly $554 million. AMD's biggest AI deals also come with customer warrants, which produced a $1.1 billion non-cash charge in Q3 that the company expects to grow. Likewise, revenue is concentrated in a handful of frontier labs and hyperscalers even as circular financing concerns continue to grow.
AMD now expects data center sales to make up more than 80% of revenue in 2027 and server CPU revenue to double. Delivering that depends on partners such as HPE, which became Helios' first major OEM backer and has since said Vultr will deploy the first Helios systems it builds. It also depends on the extra capacity Su has promised for 2027, which TechRadar noted is aimed at AI rather than consumer chips.
If both companies land inside their ranges, AMD will have outearned Intel for the first time. The more telling story is where that money comes from: not a knockout in the old CPU war, but a shift in the industry's revenue toward accelerators and racks that now fill data centers.

articles.title: Bruxelles veut interdire les fausses alertes de stock et neuf autres pièges en ligne
articles.text:
Vous êtes à deux clics de payer, et le site vous répète qu’il ne reste plus que deux exemplaires de l’article. La Commission européenne veut interdire cette fausse alerte de stock et neuf autres pièges des sites et des applications, selon un projet de règlement qu’elle doit présenter mercredi.
Les spécialistes appellent ces astuces des dark patterns. Ce sont des interfaces conçues pour vous faire cliquer, dépenser ou vous abonner sans que vous l’ayez vraiment décidé. Euronews a pu consulter le projet de loi européen sur l’équité numérique, le Digital Fairness Act. Avec ce texte, la Commission remplacerait la directive de 2005 sur les pratiques commerciales déloyales par un règlement, applicable tel quel dans les 27 pays de l’Union. Les dix pratiques de sa liste noire seraient interdites en toutes circonstances, et les autorités n’auraient plus à démontrer, dossier par dossier, que vous avez subi un préjudice.
Dix pièges interdits sur les sites marchands
La Commission interdirait d’abord les mensonges sur la disponibilité ou la popularité d’un produit, puis les alertes de pénurie répétées jusqu’à la dernière étape du paiement. Les options cochées d’avance, qui ajoutent un produit ou une quantité à votre commande, seraient aussi bannies. Les marchands ne pourraient plus vous rendre la résiliation beaucoup plus compliquée que l’inscription, ni cacher un prix ou les conditions d’un renouvellement automatique. Il leur serait interdit de vous faire croire qu’il n’existe aucune autre option, de vous faire passer un refus pour une erreur ou de vous relancer sans cesse pour que vous reveniez sur un choix. La liste comprend aussi les doubles négations, ces questions tournées de façon si confuse que vous acceptez en croyant refuser, et les fausses notifications d’un contact qui n’a jamais eu lieu.
Surtout, la Commission pourrait allonger cette liste sans repasser devant les législateurs européens.
Bruxelles s’attaque aussi aux prix trompeurs. Les frais impossibles à éviter devraient apparaître avant le moment de payer, et une promotion ne pourrait plus se calculer à partir du prix conseillé par le fabricant au lieu du prix réel d’un concurrent. Les vendeurs en dropshipping, qui ne stockent jamais les produits qu’ils vous vendent, n’auraient plus le droit de vous tromper sur leur offre.
Pour vos abonnements, le marchand devrait vous proposer un bouton « résilier le contrat ici », obtenir votre accord explicite avant de transformer un essai gratuit en formule payante, et vous prévenir avant chaque renouvellement automatique. Vous auriez le droit de joindre un conseiller du service client. Pour la première fois en droit européen de la consommation, la Commission encadrerait aussi les assistants d’achat dopés à l’IA. Vous choisiriez les achats à valider vous-même, et l’assistant devrait signaler les suggestions sponsorisées.
D’après l’analyse d’impact de la Commission, les consommateurs européens échapperaient à 88,4 milliards d’euros de pertes financières entre 2025 et 2035, pour un coût de 678 millions d’euros par an à la charge des entreprises. Une société en infraction paierait une amende de 6 % de son chiffre d’affaires mondial au maximum.
Des mécanismes addictifs à désactiver sur les réseaux sociaux et dans les jeux
Selon Bloomberg, qui a lui aussi eu accès au projet, les entreprises devraient permettre aux adultes de désactiver les fonctions qui poussent à une utilisation compulsive. Vous pourriez couper la lecture automatique des vidéos, les notifications sans rapport avec votre activité, les récompenses accordées quand vous vous connectez plusieurs jours de suite, et les chatbots qui simulent une relation personnelle pour vous retenir. Bruxelles pourrait ainsi frapper Meta, Google et TikTok, dont les services fonctionnent en grande partie grâce à ces fonctions. La Commission enquête sur Meta et TikTok pour conception addictive au titre du règlement sur les services numériques (DSA), et reproche aussi à TikTok de mal protéger les comptes des mineurs.
Les enfants font l’objet de règles plus strictes. Les éditeurs de jeux vidéo n’auraient plus le droit de leur vendre des loot boxes ni des avantages de type pay-to-win. Ils devraient afficher la valeur des monnaies virtuelles en argent réel et les désactiver par défaut sur les comptes des mineurs, sauf accord des parents. La publicité fondée sur le profilage des mineurs serait interdite à tous les commerçants, et plus seulement aux grandes plateformes soumises au DSA.
Le Parlement européen et les États membres doivent encore approuver ce règlement, qui s’appliquerait douze mois après son entrée en vigueur. Comme l’explique Michael McGrath, le commissaire européen chargé de la Consommation, il s’agit d’« une initiative à la fois favorable aux consommateurs et aux entreprises », qui allégerait leurs charges administratives. Berlin conteste ce choix. Dans une note officieuse relayée par l’Agence Europe, le gouvernement allemand demande de modifier les directives en vigueur au lieu de créer une nouvelle loi, et estime que la nécessité de passer à un règlement « n’a pas encore été suffisamment démontrée ».

articles.title: Bitter Hackers Deploy New PapRAT Backdoor in Cyberespionage Campaign Targeting South Asia
articles.text:
The South Asian cyber espionage group known as Bitter (aka APT-C-08, APT-Q-37, Hazy Tiger, Orange Yali, T-APT-17, and TA397) has been observed targeting South Asian organizations with a previously unreported remote access trojan called PapRAT.
"PapRAT has both C++ and Rust implementations," Fortinet FortiGuard Labs researcher Cara Lin said. "Its capabilities include command execution, file uploads and downloads, file deletion, directory and drive enumeration, and screenshot capture. The Rust variant adds PowerShell execution and other commands."
The campaign is notable for making use of three different infection chains -
- A Windows Shortcut (LNK) file that abuses the native "ftp.exe" utility to run scripts and create scheduled tasks designed to maintain contact with a command-and-control (C2) server.
- A VHDX disk image containing a LNK file that launches a lure Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, while running an MSI installer in the background to deploy PapRAT.
- A URL shortcut (URL) file that fetches a LNK file via WebDAV, which then leads to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT.
The living-off-the-land (LotL) approach is designed to execute commands from a remote server ("goodnfortunes[.]com"), allowing it to collect directory and task lists, directory information from Desktop, Documents, and Downloads, installed antivirus product data, and mounted drives.
The harvested reconnaissance information is saved as "abc.pdf" and exfiltrated back to the C2 server via a curl command, after which the staged file is deleted from the host.
A second version of the script has been found to retrieve a file called "talk.log" from "techtalkhelp[.]com." The payload contains a Base64-encoded script to obtain additional instructions from the same server and execute them as PowerShell commands.
"This staging model gives the attacker operational flexibility, while the commands are updated server-side without pushing a new binary, avoiding PE drops and process injection that some security appliances could easily detect," Fortinet said.
The PapRAT malware delivered via the MSI installer in the second attack chain is designed for remote control. It supports eight commands -
- MSG, for remote shell
- FDD, for directory listing
- DEL, for file deletion
- RUN, for arbitrary file execution
- GDR, for drive enumeration
- SS1, for screenshot capture
- UPP, for uploading local files to the C2 server ("rivingtonclarks[.]com")
- DWW, for downloading files from the C2 server
A Rust version of the malware incorporates three more commands -
- MS2, for PowerShell command execution
- SLP, for sleeping and polling resumption
- BYE, for process termination
A notable aspect of the third attack chain is that it combines the salient aspects of the first two sequences by using a script to download an MSI installer via curl. Like before, the MSI installer serves as a conduit for PapRAT, which then proceeds to drop WmRAT, a malware previously identified as used by Bitter.
The findings indicate that the threat actor continues to refine its custom arsenal to establish and maintain access to targeted systems.
"These changes underscore the importance of monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Fortinet said. "Organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages."

articles.title: ‘It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas’: Governor-elect promises to protect Texans from AI firms’ data center expansions
articles.text:
‘I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas’: Incoming Texas Governor warns AI firms that the data center free-for-all is over
Pumping the brakes on data centers
- Texas Governor-elect wants more protections against AI expansion
- Gina Hinojosa says AI firms are ‘taking advantage of Texas’
- Communities must ‘have a seat at the table’ in AI discussions, Hinojosa says
Texas has long been one of the most data center-friendly locations in the US, with new facilities springing up at a tremendous rate of knots over the last few years. But with mounting public opposition and a so-called “blue tsunami” in the US mid-term elections, that could be about to change, with the state’s incoming Governor-elect warning that there will be a new game in town for the massive AI firms that have outsourced operations to Texas.
Speaking during an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said that any work with AI companies “has to be a partnership that benefits Texans. And right now, what has happened is that data centers have moved into mostly rural communities and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans. And Texans are being taken advantage of.”
Hinojosa promised to introduce laws to reverse that situation in the state’s dealings with AI outfits, adding that “we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections.” One of those changes, Hinojosa suggested, was to ensure that “communities have a seat at the table to decide if and how these data centers come into their communities.”
“We need to make sure they are partners in this effort,” she continued. “ It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas, and that stops when I’m Governor.”
Data center free-for-all
Hinojosa campaigned on the promise of a temporary data center moratorium in Texas. Her stance seems popular with residents of the Lone Star State, with a CNN poll showing that 75% of respondents in Texas opposed building data centers near where they lived.
Hinojosa is far from alone in her opposition to the expansion of data centers throughout the US, and many Democratic candidates who were victorious in the US mid-term elections campaigned on similar opposition to the facilities — as did some Republicans.
This could raise questions about AI companies’ future plans, with several of the biggest names previously planning to build data centers that could face stiff opposition from elected officials. For example, Anthropic noted in its recent IPO filings that the supply chain for its data center infrastructure is highly complex and any “delays or failures” along the way could significantly impact the company.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It’s not entirely clear what shape Hinojosa’s new approach to data centers could take. But from her statements so far, it looks like the expansion free-for-all that has affected Texas — and many other communities across the US — could be coming to an end.

articles.title: Cómo compartir el internet en un piso de estudiantes para que no se sature
articles.text:
Compartir internet en un piso de estudiantes sin que la conexión colapse exige algo más que contratar muchos megas. El problema no suele ser solo de velocidad: también influyen la cantidad de dispositivos conectados a la vez, la ubicación del router y las horas en las que coincide todo el piso navegando, estudiando o jugando online.
La solución pasa por tres frentes combinados: un plan de internet con suficiente capacidad para el número de personas que viven juntas, una configuración del router pensada para priorizar lo urgente y unas normas básicas de convivencia sobre cuándo realizar descargas pesadas.
Ninguno de los tres puntos funciona solo: una fibra potente con un router mal colocado sigue dejando habitaciones sin cobertura, y una red bien configurada con una tarifa insuficiente también se queda corta en las horas de mayor tráfico.
Qué velocidad de fibra necesita un piso compartido de varios estudiantes
Para una vivienda de cuatro a seis personas con uso intensivo, lo más cómodo suele ser una fibra simétrica de 1 Gbps, porque la velocidad de subida importa tanto como la de bajada cuando varios compañeros hacen videollamadas de clase o suben archivos a la vez.
Con un presupuesto más ajustado, un paquete de unos 600 Mbps simétricos puede bastar para seis personas con un uso razonable, aunque conviene revisar las ofertas vigentes en el momento de contratar, ya que los precios y condiciones de las operadoras cambian con frecuencia.
Contratar más megas no soluciona, sin embargo, un router mal situado o una banda de 2,4 GHz saturada por los vecinos. La tarifa es solo una parte del problema. En pisos con mucho gaming online, donde la estabilidad pesa casi tanto como la velocidad bruta, conviene también comparar la latencia que ofrece cada operadora antes de firmar.
Cómo configurar el router Wi-Fi para evitar la saturación de la red
El router debe colocarse en una posición central de la vivienda, como el salón o el pasillo, elevado y alejado de microondas, espejos o paredes gruesas que debiliten la señal.
La banda de 5 GHz, o de 6 GHz en equipos Wi-Fi 6, conviene reservarla para ordenadores, consolas y móviles, ya que ofrece más velocidad y sufre menos interferencias que la de 2,4 GHz. Esta última queda mejor para dispositivos de domótica o aparatos alejados del router.
En edificios con muchas redes vecinas compitiendo por el mismo espacio, entrar en el panel del router y ajustar los canales de forma manual puede evitar solapamientos que frenan la velocidad real en las habitaciones del fondo. Actualizar el firmware y cambiar la contraseña de administración por defecto son dos ajustes sencillos que muchos pisos de estudiantes nunca llegan a hacer.
Activar la calidad de servicio, conocida como QoS, es uno de los cambios con más impacto práctico: permite priorizar el tráfico de voz y video frente a otras tareas menos urgentes, de modo que una videollamada de clase no se corte porque alguien esté descargando un archivo pesado en otra habitación.
Cuándo y por qué se satura más la conexión en un piso de estudiantes
Conviene distinguir dos problemas distintos quenque explican por qué un piso compartido nota cortes en la red: la saturación del ancho de banda contratado, que colapsa la entrada de datos quencuando se supera el límite de la tarifa, y la saturación del propio Wi-Fi, provocada por interferencias o un router mal situado.
Si el fallo afecta solo a una habitación, suele ser de cobertura; si afecta a todo el piso a la vez, el cuello de botella está en la tarifa o en la configuración del router.
Las franjas horarias de mayor tráfico suelen coincidir entre semana por las noches, los fines de semana completos y las semanas previas a exámenes o entregas de trabajos, cuando buena parte del piso está conectada a la vez. Por las mañanas, con la mayoría fuera de casa o en clase, la red suele funcionar sin problemas.
El contraste se nota especialmente entre semana por la tarde-noche, cuando coinciden clases grabadas, partidas online y entregas de última hora. Los domingos por la tarde, con el repaso de apuntes y varias coladas pendientes, son otro momento típico de saturación, aunque suele pasar más desapercibido que un viernes de partidas online.
Qué actividades consumen más datos y cómo organizarlas entre compañeros de piso
No todas las actividades exigen lo mismo de la red. Las videollamadas de clase y los trabajos en grupo necesitan sobre todo una subida estable, mientras que el streaming en 4K, las descargas de juegos de consola y las actualizaciones de Windows consumen la bajada sin que nadie lo note hasta que el resto siente el frenazo.
Un solo compañero descargando un juego de varias decenas de gigas puede dejar sin margen de subida al resto del piso justo durante una videollamada de clase.
Las copias de seguridad automáticas en la nube y la sincronización de carpetas compartidas son otro clásico que suele pasar inadvertido: si se lanzan a media tarde, pueden monopolizar el ancho de banda durante horas.
Programar esas copias para que se ejecuten de madrugada, cuando casi nadie está conectado, es uno de los ajustes menos conocidos entre quienes comparten piso. Revisar de vez en cuando qué aplicaciones tienen la sincronización activada de fondo evita sorpresas justo antes de un examen, cuando la red debería estar más despejada.
Para organizar el uso entre varios estudiantes, puede establecerse una escala sencilla de prioridades: clases online, trabajo y videollamadas en el nivel más alto; streaming y eventos deportivos en un nivel intermedio; y descargas de archivos grandes en el nivel más bajo, reservado para las horas de menor actividad conjunta.
Router de la operadora, mesh o punto de acceso: qué conviene en cada piso
La elección del equipo depende de los metros cuadrados de la vivienda y de cómo esté distribuida. En un piso compacto de planta cuadrada, el router de la operadora suele bastar si se activan la QoS, se limita el ancho de banda de las descargas P2P y se crea una red de invitados separada para que los móviles de las visitas no compitan con los dispositivos de quienes viven allí.
Si el piso es alargado o tiene muchas paredes de carga, el equipo de la operadora se queda corto en las habitaciones del fondo, por buena que sea la tarifa contratada.
Un sistema mesh con dos o tres nodos reparte la señal de forma más uniforme por toda la casa, mientras que un punto de acceso conectado por cable Ethernet al router principal suele dar el mejor rendimiento por menos dinero, aunque exige pasar cable por la vivienda, algo que no siempre es viable en un alquiler.
Antes de invertir en un kit mesh completo, conviene comprobar con el móvil en qué habitaciones cae realmente la señal: a veces basta con reposicionar el router o añadir un único nodo para resolver el problema, sin necesidad de cambiar de operadora ni de tarifa.

articles.title: China plans an LED sphere a third bigger than the Las Vegas original, but for now it only exists on paper
articles.text:
China plans an LED sphere a third bigger than the Las Vegas original, but for now it only exists on paper
But nobody has been hired to build it yet
- A Hong Kong-led venture plans a 168m, 20,000-seat LED sphere in Hangzhou for ¥8 billion (~$1.2 billion)
- Its 72,000m² exterior screen would be a third larger than the Las Vegas Exosphere, the biggest of its kind, at least on paper
- The project is still at the planning stage, with no construction dates, screen vendor or display specs announced
A developer in eastern China has unveiled plans for a spherical entertainment venue that looks to beat the Las Vegas Sphere on every headline measurement, for less than half the price.
The catch is that, so far, the project amounts to a signing ceremony, a rendering and a set of very ambitious forecasts.
The project, dubbed the Eye of the World in English, was reported by AV Magazine after its public debut on October 30 2026 at a services-sector conference in Hangzhou's Qiantang District.
A bigger sphere on paper
According to City Express, the plan calls for a sphere roughly 168 meters across and 122 meters tall, skinned in about 72,000 square meters of exterior LED, with a 270-degree wraparound screen and 20,000 seats inside.
It would occupy a 56,000-square-meter plot on the Qiantang River in the Jinshazui New Town area, with around 160,000 square meters of neighboring land earmarked for supporting development.
On the spec sheet, the comparison is flattering when one compares it to the Las Vegas Sphere. AV Magazine puts the Las Vegas venue at 157 meters in diameter and 112 meters tall, with a 54,000-square-meter Exosphere and 17,600 seats, which makes the Hangzhou design about 7% wider and 9% taller, with a third, more exterior screen. The seating gap, however, is narrower than it looks, as Las Vegas reaches around 20,000 when its floor is set up for standing crowds.
The headline budget is ¥8 billion (~$1.2 billion), against the $2.3 billion Las Vegas eventually cost, and the project's forecast annual revenue is ¥2.6 billion, or $400 million. At the (relatively harsher) exchange rate implied elsewhere in Chinese coverage, the two figures come closer to $1.1 billion and $360 million.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The venture pairs Hong Kong-based Xinshi International Investment Co. with Vision Eye (Hangzhou) Digital Entertainment Technology Co., and Invidis reports that it is led by Huang Junhao, investment president of the former and general manager of the latter. He says the domestically designed project will show that Chinese applied technology and cultural innovation have reached "world-leading levels," and at the launch he described it as "a spectacle of unimaginable size and unimaginable form."
Interestingly, for an LED project, the most telling detail is what's missing: The invidis report also notes that no vendor or installer has been appointed for either the exterior screen or the interior wraparound display, that design, zoning and infrastructure arrangements are still in progress, and that no construction start or completion date has been given.
Nobody has published a resolution, pixel pitch or playback architecture either, and that matters, because the systems behind a screen like this are as demanding as the panels themselves.
In Las Vegas, TechRadar Pro reported that 150 Nvidia RTX A6000 GPUs drive nearly 750,000 square feet of LED with three layers of 16K video at 60 frames per second, fed by a Hitachi Vantara system of 27 nodes and 4PB of flash storage delivering 400GB/s.
The structure won't be simple either: One analysis notes that Las Vegas used parametric modeling to optimize its geodesic lattice shell and cast-steel nodes, cutting weight by around 40%, and warns that a larger sphere demands even tighter tolerances, where millimeter-level errors could show up as visible seams or patches of uneven brightness. Any claim to be the world's largest, it concludes, depends on the engineering meeting the paper specifications.
An analysis on a Chinese publication, The Paper's government affairs channel, argues the cost gap with Las Vegas rests on China's domestic LED sphere supply chain, which now has a track record of delivery, and that the real difficulty is keeping brightness, color, and seams consistent across tens of thousands of square meters of curved outdoor LED through direct sunlight and temperature swings.
The launch coverage on Sohu flags acoustics as another headache: a concave sphere focuses sound unevenly, and any absorptive treatment has to sit inside the lattice shell without breaking up the screen.
A bloated forecast with questionable demand in tow?
The commercial forecasts look even bolder than the project at hand: The developer expects 9 million to 13 million visitors a year. Spread evenly, that is roughly 24,700 to 35,600 people every day, so even the low end exceeds a sellout of the 20,000-seat bowl 365 days a year.
The Paper's analysis supplies useful context. In 2025, Hangzhou's entire performing arts sector drew about 10.25 million attendees across 19,194 shows and took ¥3.12 billion at the box office.
One venue is forecasting roughly the whole city's 2025 audience and revenue, totaling about 83% of that box office total, though the projected figure presumably also includes advertising, sponsorship, and food and drink. The same analysis also describes The Eye of the World as "still just a drawing, with construction yet to begin."
The owner of the original isn't standing still. Sphere Abu Dhabi, on Yas Island, carries a $1.7 billion construction budget and will match Las Vegas with a capacity of up to 20,000, depending on configuration, a 16K-by-16K interior screen, and 167,000 speakers, with completion due by the end of 2029. A 6,000-seat venue at National Harbor in Maryland is targeting 2030.
Sphere is also lining up the technology behind its screens. Announcing a multi-year partnership with media server specialist Disguise in September, Sphere executive vice president Ryan Dolan tied the deal to "offering these experiences to audiences in new Sphere venues around the world."
TechRadar Pro's June 2026 coverage of China's first Sphere-style domes analyzed a completely different story about going smaller and cheaper: Qianjiang's Tiangong Nova, with 7,500 square meters of exterior LED, and Shanghai's West Bund Starry Sky, budgeted at ¥1.2 billion for around 3,000 visitors at a time.
Hangzhou keeps prices low and scales up, but not everyone thinks the world needs it. Discussing China's smaller domes on an AVNation panel, AVIXA's Jennifer Weaver asked: "Massive replicas of the Vegas sphere all over the place? Probably not." Hangzhou is betting they are wrong; for now, though, it has a rendering, a riverside plot, and a set of forecasts, while the original, by all accounts, remains busy every day of the year as a revenue-generating juggernaut, bolstered, at least in part by a much more affluent audience to boot.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Rahim Amir is a UAE-based tech writer who enjoys building PCs as much as he enjoys writing about them. He has been professionally writing about PC hardware since 2023, focusing on buyer’s guides, hardware reviews, and sponsored content and features related to tech.
Having built hundreds of gaming PCs and being an avid gamer in his spare time, Rahim tends to have stronger opinions about hardware than most. This is particularly on display when he gets his way with powerful, but minimalistic RGB builds even as Small Form Factor (SFF) PCs come a close second.
