articles.title: Votre mairie protège-t-elle bien vos données ? La CNIL inflige dix amendes à des collectivités
articles.text:
Votre mairie conserve votre état civil et, parfois, les coordonnées bancaires que vous lui avez données pour payer la cantine de vos enfants. La CNIL a infligé dix amendes, de 3 000 à 20 000 euros, à des collectivités et à un établissement public, pour des failles dans la protection de vos informations.
L'an dernier, la CNIL a fait de la cybersécurité des collectivités l’une de ses priorités de contrôle, après la multiplication des cyberattaques contre les services publics. Ses agents ont inspecté des collectivités, mais aussi leurs prestataires informatiques, pour vérifier comment ils protègent les données des usagers. Au bout de ces vérifications, l’autorité a prononcé dix sanctions contre des collectivités et un établissement public. Plusieurs de ces collectivités avaient subi une ou plusieurs fuites de données, et selon la CNIL, des mesures adaptées auraient permis de les éviter.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Les failles de sécurité relevées par la CNIL dans les collectivités
Dans plusieurs collectivités, les administrateurs informatiques se connectaient à distance, notamment en télétravail, sans double authentification. Il suffit alors d’un mot de passe volé pour qu’un pirate prenne la main sur les comptes les plus puissants du réseau. La CNIL a aussi constaté que des éditeurs de logiciels gardaient un accès permanent au réseau de la collectivité, sans autorisation au cas par cas, ou se connectaient avec un compte partagé entre plusieurs salariés. En piratant Atexo, un éditeur de logiciels pour les administrations, des pirates ont ainsi pu accéder aux données d’usagers de la Région Hauts-de-France, RIB compris.
Les agents de la CNIL ont aussi trouvé des journaux de connexion incomplets, ou que personne ne consultait en temps réel. Sans ces traces, une collectivité peut laisser un intrus fouiller ses fichiers sans rien voir. Et sans cloisonnement entre les différentes parties du réseau, un pirate entré par un seul poste peut accéder à tous les serveurs. Certaines collectivités utilisaient encore des systèmes d’exploitation abandonnés par leur éditeur, donc privés de correctifs de sécurité. D’autres envoyaient en clair aux usagers leurs mots de passe, ou avaient mis en service des systèmes d’information sans l’homologation de sécurité exigée des administrations.
Si vous dirigez une PME, vous pouvez vérifier dès aujourd’hui les deux premiers points chez vous. Quels prestataires gardent un accès permanent à votre réseau, et vos administrateurs se connectent-ils avec une double authentification ? À Saint-Étienne, la CNIL a infligé à l’Hôpital privé de la Loire 500 000 euros d’amende, notamment pour ces deux failles, après le vol des données de plus de 500 000 patients.
La CNIL a fixé chaque amende selon les données en jeu
Avec la procédure de sanction simplifiée, la CNIL règle plus vite les dossiers sans grande complexité juridique, mais ne peut pas dépasser 20 000 euros par amende. « Ces montants tiennent notamment compte du nombre de manquements relevés et de leur gravité, des catégories de données traitées (données de mineurs, coordonnées bancaires, etc.), du budget de chacune des collectivités et du nombre de personnes concernées », souligne la CNIL.
Le RGPD impose une analyse d’impact avant tout traitement de données à risque élevé pour la vie privée. Plusieurs collectivités ont ouvert sans cette étude des portails d’inscription aux activités scolaires et périscolaires, où vous enregistrez les informations de vos enfants et vos coordonnées bancaires. D’autres ont installé des caméras de vidéoprotection sur la voie publique, alors que le règlement exige cette analyse pour toute « surveillance systématique à grande échelle d’une zone accessible au public ».
Si votre commune vous prévient d’une fuite de données, méfiez-vous des messages qui reprennent vos informations pour réclamer un paiement ou un code de confirmation.
En 2026, la CNIL consacre la moitié de ses contrôles et de ses sanctions à la sécurité des données. Comme l’expliquait Victor Nicolle, directeur des contrôles et des sanctions de la CNIL, quand l’autorité a annoncé renforcer ses contrôles, « de nombreuses procédures sont en cours, notamment auprès des collectivités territoriales, concernant des fichiers de l’État et des entreprises détenant un grand nombre de données ». L’autorité instruit d’autres dossiers, et elle pourra prononcer de nouvelles amendes ou des mises en demeure.

articles.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: SSHole Exploited, APT Root RCE, Robot Takeovers, 15K Hacked Sites, and More
articles.text:
A system doesn't always need a complicated bug to let someone in. Sometimes, a blank password is enough. That's one of the bigger stories this week. And it gets worse when the tools meant to keep systems updated or running safely become part of the attack.
Elsewhere, attackers are hiding inside normal web traffic, stealing credentials from network devices, and finding new uses for exposed systems. AI is helping some of them move faster, but old mistakes are doing plenty of the work too. Even forgotten settings and small changes made months ago are coming back to cause trouble.
There's a lot packed into this week's news, including some strange research findings, fresh attacks, and a few warnings worth taking seriously. Here's the full recap.
⚡ Threat of the Week
OpenSSH Flaw Sees Exploitation Attempts — Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration. As of November 9, 2026, a total of 20 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 13 unique IP addresses from Denmark, Iran, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Singapore, Sweden, Switzerland, and the U.S.
Harden Your CI/CD Pipelines With Drop-in Replacements for 1,000+ GitHub Actions
SHA pinning guarantees immutability, not security. If a pinned action is vulnerable or compromised, it still runs in your pipeline with access to your secrets. Chainguard Actions provides 1,000+ continuously hardened, drop-in replacements for standard GitHub Actions. Try it free for 30 days.
Try Chainguard Actions ➝
🔔 Top News
- Trojanized CWP Web Server Used to Deliver CWPdoor — A new Linux malware called CWPdoor is being distributed via a trojanized version of cwpsrv, the built-in daemon and web server that powers the Control Web Panel. According to XLab, a shell script named "cwpsrv_update.sh" is used to download "cwpsrv" from a remote server ("136.0.141[.]71") and replace the legitimate file on the system. "The downloaded cwpsrv is a passive backdoor that can be triggered by specific headers in HTTP/HTTPS traffic to remotely execute commands specified by the attacker," XLab said. "Its backdoor logic is triggered only when it receives a specially crafted request from the attacker. At the same time, it suppresses logging for that request, leaving no trace of the interaction in the access logs. This combination of directly replacing the legitimate cwpsrv binary, passive triggering, and log suppression makes CWPdoor exceptionally stealthy."
- Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Allows Code Execution as Root — A vulnerability in the APT package manager (CVE-2026-109518, CVSS score: 7.7) can be exploited to install a package under certain conditions and achieve code execution with elevated privileges. The issue affects Ubuntu and Debian operating systems. "Under specific conditions, when APT is configured to use HTTP package sources with retry settings enabled, a third-party with a network position between the host and the package mirror can cause APT to install a package that did not pass verification," Amazon said in an advisory. "Maintainer scripts within that package then run with elevated privileges."
- CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks Targeting Financial Organizations — The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country. Calling it a "significant escalation" in attacks, the threat actor is said to be re-targeting entities that were originally targeted last month after incomplete remediation, adding that the intrusions "have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response."
- Zyxel Fixes 0-Day exploited to Hack About 1,000 Network Switches — Zyxel has fixed a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that threat actors exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write flaw that could "allow a LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker to exploit the flaw and potentially execute OS commands via a crafted HTTP request." The activity has been attributed to a Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala (aka Red Heron). The attacker has been found to weaponize the flaw to deploy the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT, a ring 3 rootkit.
- cPGuard Update Mechanism Hijacked to Deliver Backdoor — Unknown threat actors compromised the update infrastructure for the cPGuard web security suite to distribute a backdoor and a data-stealing script. "On 2 November 2026 at 02:06 UTC, an unidentified attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to OPSSHIELD's update distribution infrastructure (CDN)," OPSSHIELD said. "The attacker used this access to distribute a malicious script through the cPGuard update channel." The attacker is said to have gotten in through its billing application at manage.opsshield[.]com and logged in to a customer account they had registered.
- mSecure Urges Customers to Change their Passwords — Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company said. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." However, the company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. The lack of specifics has understandably riled up customers, with one user on Reddit stating "their silence on this is mind-bending." In December 2025, Germany's cyber agency BSI found that mSecure's maker could, in theory, access the data users store in it.
️🔥 Trending CVEs
Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.
Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-16305, CVE-2026-16306 (INFINITT PACS), CVE-2026-13684, CVE-2026-13639, CVE-2026-13673, CVE-2026-6205 (Synology DSM), CVE-2026-58868, CVE-2026-58882 (Google Android), GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (Ruby on Rails), CVE-2026-102703, CVE-2026-102704 (Xen), CVE-2026-109518 (Debian apt), CVE-2026-98432, CVE-2026-121639, CVE-2026-121638, CVE-2026-121640 (WatchGuard), CVE-2026-76506 (Cisco), CVE-2026-119741 (rsync), CVE-2026-121156, CVE-2026-121229, CVE-2026-121246, CVE-2026-121035, CVE-2026-121247, CVE-2026-121203, CVE-2026-121126 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-98432 (Veeam), CVE-2026-83844 (Microsoft Paint), CVE-2026-19868 (SonicWall SonicOS), CVE-2026-123158 (OpenSSH), and multiple vulnerabilities in the BaseChat Android app version 9.8.1.
🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars
- Your SOC Has an Identity Blind Spot — Here's How Attackers Exploit It and How to Close It → Your SOC may be tracking threats, but is it missing the identities behind them? As attackers increasingly exploit human, machine, and AI identities, traditional security tools often lack the context needed to detect and contain threats quickly. Join this free webinar to learn how connecting identity security with SOC operations can expose hidden risks, reveal attack blast radius, and accelerate incident response.
- Your GitHub Actions May Still Be Vulnerable — Even With SHA Pinning. Here's Why → Think your GitHub Actions are secure because you use SHA pinning? Think again. Attackers can exploit hidden weaknesses in CI/CD workflows, even when standard security measures are in place. Join this expert-led webinar to discover how these attacks work, why SHA pinning alone isn't enough, and what you can do to protect your software supply chain.
📰 Around the Cyber World
- The Russian-speaking ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation known as Qilin (aka Agenda) has recorded 179 publicly reported attacks in 2024, and more than 1,000 claimed victims in 2025. This year alone, it has claimed more than 900 victims, making it one of the most active ransomware groups. "Affiliates commonly gain access through phishing, stolen credentials, vulnerable internet-facing systems and remote-management tools," Acronis said. "Qilin uses a flexible ransomware platform that allows affiliates to tailor attacks to the victim environment, including the encryption of local files, network shares and virtual machine infrastructure." One notable Qilin affiliate is Securotrop, which continues to operate within the Qilin affiliate network, while maintaining an independent channel for publishing stolen victim data.
- Exposed Dixell/Copeland XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers are being turned into abuse infrastructure, according to SecurityScorecard, which uncovered a suspected SMTP botnet that includes confirmed refrigeration controllers. Attackers are said to be using compromised Dixell/Copeland XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers as proxy exits and spam senders. "The SMTP cluster consists of nine IP addresses, three of them confirmed XWEB controllers," Security Scorecard said. "Of 1,041 targets, 508 were contacted by at least two nodes. The three most active nodes had approximately 47% of their target lists in common, the report’s strongest signal of coordination."
- A targeted Browser-in-the-Middle (BitM) phishing operation dubbed PhantomDOM is using custom DOM-mirroring to hijack Microsoft 365 sessions. "The attack began with a SharePoint-themed PDF distributed from an apparently legitimate sender and progressed through redirects and browser checks before presenting Microsoft authentication inside an attacker-controlled remote browser," ZeroBEC said. "The victim saw a familiar sign-in experience. The attacker controlled the browser in which that experience actually ran." According to the email security company, PhantomDOM goes beyond cloned login pages and conventional reverse-proxy phishing. "Its client reconstructs the remote DOM, forwards keyboard and clipboard interactions over WebSocket, survives connection interruptions and supports live operator control," it added.
- According to a report from the non-profit AI Alignment Foundation, AI agents assigned a sandboxed coding task to fix a broken pricing service "shared a private token and ran untrusted code in exchange for help from an agent forum." In an experiment tested against nine models, GPT-6.1-Sol refused every swarm request in 50 of 50 trials, while Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5 trials were cut short by their providers' content filters.
- A zero-day vulnerability has been disclosed in CPython that could enable bad actors to breach AI hosting platforms. "A memory-safety flaw in the CPython interpreter allows attackers to escape a code sandbox and execute code hidden in a specially crafted model," RunSybil said. "By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests. They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads." The findings build upon a previous out-of-bounds read in CPython that could result in a sandbox escape. The issue has been fixed and backported to 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches.
- The U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has issued an order effectively cutting off MEXC Global's access to the U.S. financial system under Operation Economic Outcast. "MEXC Global is a convertible virtual currency exchanger that has facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions connected to Iranian, North Korean, and Russian sanctions evasion, as well as cybercrime, including by transacting directly with sanctioned actors," FinCEN said. In response to FinCEN's ban order, MEXC said that its legal and compliance teams have launched a review of its sanctions and anti-money laundering (AML) controls. "MEXC is operating normally, and user assets remain secure," MEXC said. "We take the concerns raised seriously and intend to engage constructively with FinCEN, as well as other relevant regulators and competent authorities worldwide. We have also begun an independent review of our AML and sanctions controls."
- A new study of 25,964 U.S. government-related domains has found 43 whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. In one case, a misspelled domain's SPF configuration ("amzonses[.]com" instead of "amazonses[.]com") authorized at least 32,066 unique IP addresses to send email on behalf of a U.S. county. "These external dependencies authorize third-party senders, route incoming mail, provide DNS delegation, and receive security telemetry," SH Consulting said. "The government domains themselves can remain registered and be considered protected, because there are no signs to suggest anything is wrong." SH Consulting said it defensively registered 17 of these dangling DNS dependencies to prevent abuse.
- Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland and a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023 and has agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months. "He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict," said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.
- Huntress has warned of a "couple waves of activity across multiple organizations involving GeoVision camera software," pointing to broad exploitation of the platform to deliver malware. The activity originates from the IP addresses 45.32.117[.]34 and 156.246.94[.]183.
- A single AI-augmented threat actor (AAT) has been observed using a mesh of 12 AI agents called BOSSAI to conduct persistent campaigns in several countries. The mesh consists of combining HexStrike AI, Hermes, CyberStrikeAI, and HalberdStrike, alongside Grok, OpenClaw, and Claude Code, with some acting as infrastructure builders and maintainers, while others scan for vulnerabilities and attack. The findings once again show how a lone actor can mount offensive operations at scale. "Using the BOSSAI mesh, the operator targeted hundreds of organizations spanning government emergency services, banks and lenders, universities, military systems, phone directories, e-commerce platforms, and gambling sites in eleven countries," Acronis said. "It's unclear if the attacker has any specific affiliation or goal beyond compromising as many organizations as possible, presumably to monetize the activity." The threat actor is believed to be a single individual based in Hualien City, Taiwan.
- Truffle Security has launched the Secrets Revocation Program, a free initiative that helps API key issuers revoke 1.4 million secrets that have been confirmed to be live and leaked on GitHub, Docker Hub, npm, Hugging Face, and others.
- Gnosis Pay said it detected unauthorized access to the system powering its Gnosis Pay-branded cards on November 3, 2026, leading to the exposure of customer information. "The data breach was limited to the system powering Gnosis Pay-branded cards, which was already scheduled for retirement on 20 December 2026," it said. "We have increased our monitoring of card activity and wallets to detect fraud or attempts to access user funds. We have also implemented an extra verification step (3D Secure) and made it mandatory for all online card payments. These measures will stay in place until the B2C system is fully retired as planned on 20 December 2026." The company said it directly notified users about what information was accessed from their account, but did not reveal the number of customers impacted.
- The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned four individuals and 41 entities that are tied to scam compounds in Cambodia, Madagascar, and other countries across Southeast Asia and Africa. The sanctioned parties are said to have supported the business network of Prince Group. "Cyber scam syndicates continue to steal billions of dollars from American victims while relying on sophisticated international business networks to launder their illicit proceeds," said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. "The newly designated individuals and entities have helped sustain Prince Group TCO’s illicit global operations after the October 2025 and June 2026 designations by managing offshore corporate structures, concealing beneficial ownership, facilitating commercial activities, and providing administrative and financial services to senior Prince Group TCO executives."
- The U.S. Treasury also sanctioned Chui Kok Wa for his role as the leader of a scam compound in Madagascar that was dismantled earlier this year. Late last month, Wa was charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, as the leader of the NFT investment scam. "In the scheme, scammers posed as beautiful women who met victims on dating websites, eventually enlisting them to connect their cryptocurrency wallets to fraudulent websites associated with the NFT investments," the Justice Department said. "Once connected, the scammers willed the victims to continue to fund their cryptocurrency wallets, and then surreptitiously pulled money from the victims’ wallets without their knowledge." Wa's phones also allegedly contained employment contracts, detailing overnight work schedules in Madagascar and providing employees with bonus payments tied to money stolen, as well as scripts or guides for what scammers should say to victims and a roster containing employees' names, passport information, salary, hours, disciplinary actions taken against them, along with a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the employees.
- Vercel has launched Security Review, a new capability in Vercel Agent that scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories. "Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI," Vercel said. "With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings." In tandem, Vercel said it's starting the rollout of Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) for vercel[.]com to make it harder for stealer malware to siphon session cookies from a device. Google rolled out DBSC support in Chrome earlier this April.
- Fortra has revealed that attackers are creating convincing travel-booking pages that imitate trusted rental platforms. "The fake sites use familiar branding, realistic property listings, reservation details, and urgent messages to persuade travelers to provide sensitive data such as credit card information, usernames and passwords, and more," Fortra said.
- Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, has pleaded guilty today to wire fraud and money laundering related to using his access as an FBI agent to steal cryptocurrency. "From 2017 through early 2025, Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, worked at the FBI Boston Division on an investigative squad focused on an adversarial nation-state," the Justice Department said. "From February 2025 to July 31, 2026, Yaroch worked in the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, with access to FBI systems that contained cryptocurrency credentials that the FBI had collected as part of its investigations. Beginning no later than December 2024, Yaroch used his position to steal cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by the subjects of various other investigations or by adversarial nation-state actors, and from at least one wallet the FBI created to use in an operation. Throughout his wire fraud scheme, Yaroch conducted approximately 100 fraudulent transfers using credentials related to 35 separate FBI investigations. He illicitly gained approximately $2,474,380.66 in fraudulent proceeds." The stolen funds were used to pay off his debts and finance a new life abroad, even asking ChatGPT how to maximize profit from investments and where to live in the European Union. Yaroch will be sentenced in March 2027.
- DigiCert said it identified an event involving unauthorized access to one of its business systems, leading to exposure of names and email addresses. In some cases, driver's licenses, passports, utility bills, and other documents containing a name and address that its customers provided as proof were also compromised. The incident has been traced back to a February 2025 change that moved the internal business system to a different network segment, causing it to be opened to the public internet for more than 16 months. Unknown attackers abused a self-registration feature in the system's account manager to create a read-only account that had access to archived data between June 27 and July 2, 2026. Although DigiCert blocked the unauthorized account on July 2, it subsequently determined in October that the account was used to access archived customer contact information, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.
- OpenAI announced 2 that it is increasing payouts in its Security Bug Bounty program. The objective is to get the broader research community hunting for flaws that its own testing may have missed. "A critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000," OpenAI said. "Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses."
- Three people accused of using AI to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to plunder about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies and attorneys at major law firms in order to trick employees into sending large payments to bank accounts under their control between 2024 and 2026, according to the Justice Department. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain in June and August 2026, respectively, while Sheetrit was arrested in the U.K. in September 2026.
- A fake download campaign is targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers hosted on bogus sites to distribute multiple payloads. "We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device [WorldProxyPool], enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform [CharityEngine and BOINC], or installing additional utility-style software [AW Manager or Windows Manager], often without users' informed knowledge or consent," Microsoft said. "These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks."
- A Chinese-language exploitation framework called Greeter has targeted Flowise honeypots with thousands of chat messages reading only "hello" while weaponizing an old code injection flaw (CVE-2024-58351) to execute malicious instructions. The framework conducted system discovery, extracted environment variables, probed cloud metadata services, searched for SSH keys and other credentials, tried to set up persistence, and ran quick checks to determine whether the host could run payloads from memory. Era Security said it counted 4,372 Flowise instances exposed online, out of which 703 (21.5%) had no authentication enabled. "It reveals a new exploitation framework designed to turn exposed AI applications into entry points for code execution, credential discovery, and potentially broader cloud compromise," Era Security said. "The framework’s most consequential feature was its ephemeral, per-request execution model. Attack instructions were supplied through overrideConfig.javascriptFunction, while stored user messages contained only 'hello.' The malicious function could change with each request without altering the saved chatflow, leaving an incomplete picture for defenders inspecting workflow definitions or chat history alone."
- A threat actor has been abusing fake "suspended account" notices to hide phishing content from users revisiting its lookalike pages masquerading as business banking and treasury logins. The campaign, active since May 2026, has been relying on more than 300 fake domains, including 248 impersonating 189 U.S. financial institutions. The first domains were registered in late 2025, but most of them appeared between July and September 2026. "What ties them together is one mechanism: the kit remembers every visitor’s IP address, so the first visit gets a bank login page, and any return visit gets what looks like a closed hosting account. We call this cluster the 'Suspended' infrastructure," KELA said. "Most domains follow the same recipe, [keyword]-[bank].com, with keywords such as secure, disable, protect and cancel, which makes the cluster findable in newly registered domain feeds."
- Meta said it paid nearly $1.2 million in bug bounties to researchers who found and responsibly disclosed issues in its Muse AI assistant. The bug bounty program went public in September 2026. "The largest single award was paid out four months before launch for a bug that allowed a researcher to get access to conversations and tokens in pre-release VMs used by employees and engineers testing the product," Meta said. "An authentication check treated a header added by a local HTTPS proxy as proof that a request came from a trusted source. During a system migration, the environment gained a second proxy layer. That meant requests from outside could carry the trusted header too. A researcher found this and demonstrated the exploit." Meta paid a $300,000 bounty for this report.
- Chinese nation-state threat activity declined by 41.4% in the six months from April to September 2026, according to a new study by Trellix. The change is "a shift in operational focus, we assess, rather than reduced intent, and one that warrants vigilance rather than reassurance," it added.
- QNAP is urging users to update Plex Media Server on their NAS instances to the latest version available in the QNAP App Center following reports of active exploitation of a set of vulnerabilities known as Plex2Shell. "QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through these vulnerabilities," it said. "The QNAP Technical Support team is assisting affected users and has confirmed that no data loss has occurred."
- MetaMask has disclosed that the security incident it identified on September 28, 2026, resulted in unauthorized access to part of its infrastructure, and that it took steps to contain the incident and secure affected systems. "We have identified no indication that MetaMask wallets or our wallet infrastructure were compromised as a result of this incident," it said. "We have not identified evidence that the incident enabled unauthorized access to or withdrawal of customers' staked principal. However, a limited amount of execution-layer staking rewards was diverted during the incident." The attacker is said to have briefly altered the addresses used to receive execution-layer staking rewards for certain validators, diverting approximately 0.385 ETH in rewards. "These rewards are separate from customers' staked ETH," MetaMask added. "We have found no evidence that customers’ staked principal or withdrawal keys were compromised, and the affected systems have been secured."
- Infected security-themed GitHub projects are being used to target cybersecurity professionals to deliver backdoors and infostealer malware. According to Doctor Web, more than 2,000 PCs have been affected. The malicious code is embedded in Visual Studio project files, Python scripts, and Go source files. Once launched, the malware establishes persistence on the infected host, escalates privileges, disables security and recovery features, and deploys additional payloads, including AsyncRAT, a clipper malware, and an information stealer. The malware also attempts to remove ESET, McAfee, and Malwarebytes antivirus tools from the host and interferes with Windows backups. "The attackers behind these compromised development projects target blockchain game enthusiasts and (most intriguingly) information security professionals," the Russian cybersecurity company said. "The first infected repositories emerged two years ago. The early uploads targeted crypto wallet users – back then attackers used repositories containing Visual Studio projects related to blockchain games, game bots and cheating."
- Security researcher Scott Helme has revealed that about 15,579 websites are currently infected with malicious JavaScript delivering credit card skimmers, ClickFix lures, iOS exploitation kits like Coruna and DarkSword, and malicious redirects. These websites receive more than 135 million visits every month.
- A new report from Layer3 Intel has found that residential proxy traffic has exited through the White House network (AS2650) 236 times over a 30-day period between October 5 and November 3, 2026, with 28 separate residential proxy services able to route traffic through six of its addresses. "Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning," Layer3 Intel said. "That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them." In a post shared on X, Synthient said "several White House staffers are running a Windows 11 machine with InfaticaSDK installed," adding it found "a number of Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices beaconing to known proxy providers like Geonode, Infatica, and Mellowtel." The root cause is believed to be Rave[.]io, a shared streaming app that bundles 12 proxy SDKs into the platform. Rave allows users to watch content from YouTube, Netflix, and Disney+ with friends and runs on Mac, iPhone, Android, and Windows.
- A set of five vulnerabilities has been disclosed in Reachy Mini, an open-source, expressive companion robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face, that, when chained together, can allow an attacker to "execute attacker code, escalate to a persistent root via the robot’s passwordless sudo, and ultimately gain control of the device's motor," JFrog said. "A second variant of the attack works through the browser, where the operator visits a malicious web page, which silently compromises the robot."
- A phishing campaign built around fake registration pages for OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic events is luring marketing employees with rewards like "3 months of ChatGPT Pro" or "3 months of Grok Heavy" to get them to sign in with their work accounts. "This campaign uses them in email-delivered invitations that lead to AitM and device code phishing, expanding the use of AI-themed lures across various payload types," Push Security said. "Employees want access to the latest AI tools, making them excellent bait for attacks." The Microsoft option launches a device code phishing flow run through the Kali365 phishing-as-a-service platform, while clicking "Continue with Google" opens a VoidProxy reverse proxy of Google's sign-in page. It is unclear how the attackers initially distribute the phishing links. The kits used to build and deploy the fake event invite lure pages as ZoomMock and MSDRoot. Similar campaigns have been reported by ANY.RUN and Cofense in recent months.
- A U.S. school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group as part of a hybrid human-AI operation, according to Bitdefender. The exact initial access vector used is unknown, but the first recorded activity started on September 10, 2026. "Some parts show a human operator at the keyboard while others behave like an agentic loop, a language model reading each result and retrying with different commands," Bitdefender said. "With the exception of the encryptor itself, the whole operation was built on legitimate, built-in tools, which is standard for ransomware operations. What is different is how the attacker behaved, and several things point to an agentic loop, a program that feeds each result back to a model and runs what comes back. The retries behave like a loop too."
Conclusion
The strange part is how many of these attacks start with something small. A setting nobody checked, an update nobody questioned, or a system left online longer than it should have been. Add a little patience from the attackers, and suddenly a minor mistake becomes a much bigger problem. Not every attack needs a clever trick.
That's it for this week's roundup. Some of these stories will fade, while others may get worse as more details come out. Either way, there's enough here to keep security teams busy. Check what applies to your systems, fix what you can, and we'll be back next week with whatever turns up next.

articles.title: El CEO de Apple exigiría al jefe de software una estrategia más ambiciosa para que Siri sea un agente autónomo
articles.text:
John Ternus, director ejecutivo de Apple, exige a Craig Federighi, jefe de software de la compañía, una estrategia más ambiciosa de inteligencia artificial que permita transformar a Siri en un agente capaz de actuar de forma autónoma para los usuarios, según reveló Mark Gurman en el boletín Power On de Bloomberg.
El periodista detalla que, detrás del discurso público optimista, Ternus mantiene una postura interna mucho más crítica: sabe que Apple sigue atrás de sus competidores en la carrera de la inteligencia artificial.
Qué estrategia de IA exige Ternus a Federighi en Apple
Según el relato de Gurman, Ternus celebró en las últimas semanas una reunión a puerta cerrada con Federighi, quien asumió el rol de responsable de la IA en Apple tras el despido del anterior encargado del área el año pasado.
En ese encuentro, Ternus presionó a Federighi para acelerar la hoja de ruta de la compañía y avanzar más allá de las mejoras básicas que ya recibió Siri. El objetivo final es que el asistente deje de limitarse a responder órdenes puntuales y se convierta en un agente proactivo, con capacidad de ejecutar tareas completas sin supervisión constante del usuario.
Siri, en su versión actual, puede responder preguntas, redactar correos y mensajes, fijar recordatorios, extraer datos de internet y ejecutar acciones simples dentro de aplicaciones, como crear eventos en el calendario o tomar una fotografía.
Sin embargo, estas funciones están lejos de equipararse a los agentes autónomos que ya ofrecen rivales como OpenAI, Meta, Google o Anthropic.
Un asistente de inteligencia artificial autónomo es aquel capaz de ejecutar tareas completas por su cuenta, sin que el usuario deba supervisar cada paso: puede recordar proyectos, monitorear cambios en distintas fuentes y decidir cuándo retomar un trabajo pendiente. Esa es, precisamente, la meta que persigue Apple con la evolución de Siri.
Ternus insinuó estas ambiciones durante la última llamada de ganancias de Apple con Wall Street. “Hoy en día se basa principalmente en la solicitud, pero como hablamos en la WWDC, se basa en una arquitectura moderna impulsada por orquestadores que nos da un espacio real para ampliar sus capacidades con el tiempo”, afirmó el directivo, de acuerdo con la transcripción recogida por Gurman.
El ejecutivo agregó: “En cuanto a las capacidades de agente, creemos que estas son herramientas prometedoras para los usuarios. Solo queremos asegurarnos de que los usuarios estén al tanto de a qué están dando acceso. Queremos asegurarnos de que esto se haga de una manera que proteja la seguridad y la privacidad”.
Las tensiones internas entre Ternus y Federighi por el rumbo de la IA
Gurman describe a Federighi como un ejecutivo con reputación de escepticismo frente a la inteligencia artificial, marcada por preocupaciones sobre privacidad, seguridad y las implicaciones sociales y laborales de la tecnología.
Ese perfil contrasta con la urgencia que, según el periodista, reclama Ternus ante el avance de competidores como OpenAI y Meta Platforms Inc. El mundo cambió alrededor de Federighi y de la propia Apple, que ya no cuenta con el margen que antes tenía para mantenerse al margen de la revolución de la inteligencia artificial.
La situación expone, además, tensiones estructurales dentro de la organización de software de la empresa. Federighi es reconocido por un estilo de gestión práctico en reuniones y decisiones clave, que según algunos empleados citados por Gurman deja poco espacio para que ideas alternativas ganen tracción.
Su capacidad para debatir con dominio técnico le permite contrarrestar propuestas con las que no coincide, lo que en ocasiones generó frustración entre equipos de ingeniería y diseño.
Otro punto de fricción señalado por el periodista es el horizonte de planificación: Federighi prefiere ciclos de entre 12 y 18 meses, frente a las hojas de ruta plurianuales que favorece la división de hardware de Apple. Esa diferencia complicó en el pasado el desarrollo conjunto de productos y derivó en retrasos o lanzamientos menos ambiciosos.
Pese a las críticas, Gurman reconoce la capacidad de ejecución de Federighi. El año pasado, cuando quedó claro que el entonces jefe de IA, John Giannandrea, no podía cumplir con las ambiciones de Siri, Federighi tomó el control del proyecto y logró llevar al mercado una versión funcional del asistente en un plazo relativamente corto, un esfuerzo que internamente se consideró casi hercúleo.
Qué funciones nuevas incorpora Siri con iOS 27 y qué falta para igualar a sus rivales
El boletín de Bloomberg detalla que el mayor avance de Siri este año es su capacidad para extraer contexto tanto de lo que aparece en la pantalla del usuario como de información privada almacenada en el dispositivo, incluidos correos electrónicos y mensajes de texto.
Para lograrlo, Federighi, Mike Rockwell y el equipo de Siri reconstruyeron por completo el motor del asistente, con nuevos modelos basados en tecnología que Apple licencia de Google. Estas funciones se habían mostrado originalmente en la conferencia de desarrolladores de 2024 para iOS 18, pero recién llegaron, con retraso, como parte de iOS 27.
Según Gurman, la versión inicial de iOS 27 careció de una tercera capacidad clave anunciada en 2024: las acciones avanzadas dentro de aplicaciones. Esa función recién comenzó a mencionarse de nuevo con la primera beta de iOS 27.3, y permitirá que Siri interactúe con mayor precisión tanto con aplicaciones propias de Apple como de terceros.
El periodista ejemplifica que OpenTable podría habilitar reservas avanzadas de restaurantes a través de Siri, mientras que Uber Eats permitiría completar pedidos complejos por voz.
Dentro del ecosistema de Apple, la beta ya permite usar Siri para organizar pestañas en Safari, ordenar carpetas en Archivos, cancelar el envío de un iMessage o editar texto con precisión, además de ejecutar comandos de varios pasos en Fotos, como rotar, mejorar y compartir una imagen.
De acuerdo con el lenguaje de los anuncios de Apple, el soporte para aplicaciones propias podría llegar en diciembre, con la versión pública de iOS 27.3. El soporte para aplicaciones de terceros, en cambio, no llegaría hasta la primavera, vinculado a los lanzamientos de iOS 27.5 o 27.6, antes de la conferencia de desarrolladores de junio.
Gurman remarca que estas mejoras siguen sin acercarse a lo que ofrecen Dots de ChatGPT, Muse de Meta o Grok de Elon Musk, sistemas capaces de mantener responsabilidades continuas entre conversaciones, recordar proyectos y preferencias en el tiempo y actuar sin que el usuario inicie cada paso.
Los cambios de liderazgo que podrían reconfigurar el área de software de Apple
El informe de Bloomberg también señala movimientos de personal que podrían alterar el organigrama de la división. Mike Rockwell, creador de los auriculares Vision Pro y líder del desarrollo de Siri AI, continúa evaluando seriamente su salida de la empresa, lo que podría concretarse el próximo año.
Si Rockwell deja su cargo, la responsabilidad recaería probablemente en Amar Subramanya, veterano de Google contratado el año pasado para reforzar los esfuerzos de inteligencia artificial de Apple, y en Sebastien Marineau, actual diputado de Federighi. Marineau dirige hoy los equipos encargados de integrar la IA en iOS y es visto por algunos dentro de la compañía como un posible sucesor de Federighi al frente del software.
Gurman aclara, sin embargo, que cualquier proceso de sucesión real sigue siendo una perspectiva lejana. Federighi mantiene un control firme sobre la organización de ingeniería de software y no ha priorizado una planificación de relevo, lo que limita las oportunidades de los posibles herederos para posicionarse.

- Certaines fonctions réservées aux appareils Galaxy compatibles.

articles.title: Default 'admin:admin' Server Password Helps Researchers Hack Two Automakers, Unlock and Start Cars
articles.text:
The login systems behind two car brands' mobile apps could be taken over completely, two security researchers found, allowing them to access any customer's account and, for an owner with a connected car, unlock the doors and start the engine.
Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity, and on those servers the researchers reached an administrator console that still used its default password.
They tested the full attack only on their own and consenting owners' cars in the United States, in February 2026, and both systems were fixed about two hours after they reported the problem.
Shubham Shah and Sam Curry published their work late last week. They had started with the apps: both brands signed customers in through the same platform, which runs in two parts: one for login and one, called OpenIDM, that holds customer records.
OpenIDM comes with a built-in administrator console powered by the Apache Felix tool. ForgeRock's own hardening guide tells operators to remove this console or protect it before going live because it stores its own password separately from the rest of the system. On these servers, it was still there and still used the documented default: the word admin for both the username and the password.
The console was blocked from the open internet, but the edge that guards the site and the Java software behind it read the same web address differently. By adding encoded slashes and extra characters, the researchers made the edge treat the request as a harmless static file while the server treated it as the path to the console, and the default password did the rest. The full method is in their technical analysis.
Inside the console, the researchers used a built-in scheduler to run small scripts that execute their own code on the identity server. That gave them a command prompt on the machine that holds the customer records for both brands' logins.
The records sat behind the same block as the console, but the researchers' code reached them from inside the server. They changed a target account's email address and password, signed in as that customer through the normal app, and received the same access tokens the real app uses.
Those tokens were the keys to the car. Using the account's own vehicle commands, the researchers unlocked the doors and started the engine of a test car, with the owner standing next to it, then stopped the engine and locked it again.
The researchers were careful about what they had shown. They reported being able to open a session for any customer account on the affected servers, but they ran the vehicle commands only on cars they owned or were allowed to use. They said they "tested the complete chain only with US accounts and vehicles."
Shubham Shah published a second attack on the Australian systems behind the same brands. There, the way in was different: admin credentials for the identity server had been left in the app's code, intended for a test setup. He set out the full Australia chain in a separate post.
With both attacks together, the researchers said, they could send unlock and engine-start commands to the brands' cars in Australia, the United States, and Canada. That second post does not give a date for when the Australian systems were fixed.
The attack left little for an owner to notice. Changing the email and password did not log the owner out of their app, and the researchers could direct the account's alerts to their own phone, keeping them off the owner's phone.
The researchers put the real email address back after the test. Neither write-up says whether anyone else found or used the path before it was closed.
What Identity Teams Should Check
The brands' mistake was in how they ran ForgeRock, not a new bug in the product, so there is no CVE, the public ID that tracks a flaw, and no vendor advisory to follow. The console and its default password have been documented for years, and the maker's production hardening guide already tells operators to remove the console or change its password before going live.
For teams running the same identity software, now sold as PingIDM, two checks matter:
- Look for the Apache Felix console at /system/console, and remove it or change its default password.
- Do not count on edge or WAF path rules to hide an admin page. A path the edge and the server read differently can slip past the rules, as it did here.
The two researchers have a long record of this kind of work, usually breaking into the web systems behind the apps rather than the cars themselves. They have shown remote access to vehicles from Honda, Kia, and Subaru, among others.
A Subaru flaw they reported exposed owners' accounts and their cars through that carmaker's connected-car service, and a broader 16-brand study in 2023 found the same kind of web weakness across much of the industry.

articles.title: Quién es quién y qué pasó cuándo: la guía para entender el escándalo que sacude a Nvidia
articles.text:
El CEO de Nvidia admitió el domingo que fue infiel a su esposa con una ejecutiva a la que la inteligencia de Estados Unidos considera una agente china. El directorio lo investiga. Lo esencial, en orden, según The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, el Financial Times y Wired.
Quién es quién
Jensen Huang, 63 años, fundador y CEO de Nvidia, la empresa de los chips con los que se entrena la inteligencia artificial.
Alice Huang, ciudadana china, ex ejecutiva de Megaspeed. Sin parentesco con el CEO. No fue acusada de ningún delito.
Megaspeed, empresa de centros de datos de Singapur, nacida de un grupo chino y gran compradora de chips de Nvidia.
Heller, la consultora de crisis que, según Wired, maneja la comunicación de Huang desde hace un año.
Qué pasó cuándo
2023. Nace Megaspeed, escindida del grupo chino 7Road, meses después de que Estados Unidos restringiera la venta de chips avanzados a China.
Junio de 2024. Primera foto de Alice Huang y Jensen Huang juntos, en una fiesta tras una conferencia en Taipei.
Fines de 2024. El Departamento de Comercio investiga a Megaspeed por un posible desvío de chips a China.
Mayo de 2025. Segunda foto, en una cena privada en Taipei.
9 de octubre de 2025. The New York Times revela la investigación a Megaspeed y los vínculos entre los dos Huang. Según Wired, la nota irrita al CEO.
Fines de octubre de 2025. Nvidia ordena incluir a la consultora Heller en toda consulta de prensa sobre Huang, según Wired.
Octubre a diciembre de 2025. Huang pide a la Casa Blanca permiso para vender chips Blackwell en China. No lo consigue. En diciembre, Trump autoriza exportar el H200, menos potente, con el 25% de las ventas para el gobierno.
Primavera boreal de 2026. El secretario de Estado Marco Rubio supervisa un memo clasificado que advierte sobre la relación personal entre Huang y Alice Huang, según el Journal. El Departamento de Justicia ya lidera la investigación.
Mayo a octubre de 2026. Huang viaja con Trump a China, recibe su llamado en vivo en el podcast All-In y, el 8 de octubre, la Medalla Nacional de Ciencia.
29 de octubre de 2026. El Times y el Journal publican que la inteligencia estadounidense cree que Alice Huang es una agente china y que tiene una relación cercana con Huang. Nvidia responde que reunirse con clientes es parte del trabajo de un CEO.
6 de noviembre de 2026. El Financial Times informa que el gobierno cree que el vínculo era sentimental.
8 de noviembre de 2026. Huang escribe a los empleados: “Fui infiel a mi esposa. No hay excusa para lo que hice.” El directorio abre una investigación independiente y lo mantiene como CEO mientras dure. Trump, consultado, dice que debería seguir: “es un tipo honorable”.
9 de noviembre de 2026. La acción cae 5%, según CNBC. El Times publica que no hay sucesor evidente. Wired revela la contratación de Heller un año antes de la confesión. El 17 de noviembre, Huang presenta resultados con la investigación abierta.
Lo que está probado y lo que no
No está probado que Alice Huang haya sido reclutada por Beijing, que haya obtenido información de Nvidia ni que Huang supiera algo. China calificó la denuncia de infundada. Lo admitido es la relación. Lo abierto es la investigación.

articles.title: Chatbots, jouets connectés : Emmanuel Macron veut « interdire » l'IA partout où elle représente un risque pour les enfants
articles.text:
« S’il y a un risque pour les enfants avec certains usages de l’IA, alors il faut l’interdire », affirme Emmanuel Macron dans un entretien aux Échos. Un comité d’experts lui remet ses recommandations ce mardi, jour où OpenAI et Anthropic doivent s’engager dans une charte au Forum de Paris sur la Paix.
« Ce n’est pas parce que c’est de l’IA que ce doit être le Far West », lance le chef de l’État, pour qui le système actuel « n’est pas tenable ». Il veut le changer, « jusqu’à l’interdire s’il est mauvais », et parle de protéger la santé mentale des enfants et « leur cerveau ». Les entreprises de la charte accepteront, selon lui, « le principe d’un pré-audit et d’une pré-certification » de leurs modèles avant de les mettre entre les mains des plus jeunes. Mais dans cet entretien, Emmanuel Macron parle de « certains usages » sans en nommer un seul, et les laboratoires s’engageront dans sa charte de leur plein gré.
Emmanuel Macron s’inquiète des chatbots et des jouets dotés d’IA
En février, lors d’une interview à Brut, le président avait chargé deux professeurs de psychiatrie, Raphaël Gaillard et Amine Benyamina, de vérifier si les agents conversationnels « font naître des troubles, des dépendances, de la souffrance en termes de santé mentale chez les jeunes ». Il s’en prenait aussi aux jeux vidéo violents, auxquels certains adolescents jouent cinq ou six heures par jour, avant d’assurer quelques jours plus tard qu’il n’avait jamais été question de les interdire.
Les deux psychiatres font partie du comité qui lui remet ses recommandations ce mardi, avec Serena Villata, directrice de recherche au CNRS. Selon l’Élysée, les trois experts ont travaillé sur la santé mentale des enfants et sur leur risque de dépendance. La présidence veut aussi ouvrir une réflexion sur les jouets équipés d’IA, sans donner plus de détails.
Chez Energize Lab, le robot Eiliko laissait en accès libre les conversations de ses utilisateurs, enfants compris, et un chercheur a réussi à modifier sa personnalité à distance. L’an dernier, le fabricant de l’ourson Kumma, animé par GPT-4o, a retiré sa peluche de la vente après des tests où elle proposait des jeux de rôle sexuels et indiquait où trouver des couteaux dans la maison. Comme l’explique l’Élysée, « nous ne voulons pas d’une IA qui aille dans les mains des enfants » sans évaluation ni contrôle.
Emmanuel Macron veut passer par une régulation européenne
Une interdiction de ce genre existe dans le droit européen. Depuis février 2025, l’Union européenne interdit, avec l’AI Act, de mettre sur le marché une IA capable d’exploiter la vulnérabilité d’une personne en raison de son âge, si elle altère alors son comportement au point de lui causer, ou de risquer de lui causer, un préjudice important. L’entreprise en infraction s’expose à une amende de 35 millions d’euros ou de 7 % de son chiffre d’affaires mondial.
Une loi française devrait d’abord passer par Bruxelles, car chaque État membre doit notifier à la Commission européenne ses projets de règles sur les services en ligne. Pour les réseaux sociaux, la Commission a demandé aux États d’attendre au moins un an avant d’appliquer leurs interdictions nationales, le temps de faire adopter ses règles communes. Avec ce projet, l’EU Kids Act, elle imposerait la sécurité dès la conception aux réseaux sociaux, aux jeux en ligne et aux chatbots, pour tous les mineurs jusqu’à 18 ans. Le défilement infini et les badges pensés pour faire revenir votre enfant disparaîtraient. En France, le Conseil constitutionnel a censuré en août l’interdiction des réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans, une atteinte disproportionnée à la liberté d’expression des mineurs selon les Sages.
« Nous allons porter une régulation européenne et pousser pour que les Américains, les Canadiens, et les autres, fassent comme nous », souligne Emmanuel Macron. Il a réuni en visioconférence une cinquantaine de chefs d’État et de gouvernement, ainsi que Sam Altman, Dario Amodei et Arthur Mensch, les patrons d’OpenAI, d’Anthropic et de Mistral. Tous se sont engagés à faire évaluer de façon indépendante et publique les risques des modèles les plus avancés, et à mieux partager leurs alertes en cas d’incident grave. Le président quittera l’Élysée au printemps 2027, et pour les réseaux sociaux, une interdiction européenne ne s’appliquerait pas avant 2028, une échéance que le porte-parole de la Commission n’a pas contestée.

articles.title: Web3Auth Flaw Exploited to Steal Keplr Crypto, Provider Empties Other Wallets for Safety
articles.text:
Some people who set up a Keplr crypto wallet with their Google or Apple account have had money stolen by an attacker.
Keplr uses a company called Web3Auth to run that Google and Apple sign-in. The attacker used a security flaw at that company to reach the wallets, both companies said late last week.
Web3Auth then used the attacker's own route to empty other at-risk wallets before the attacker got to them, it said. It moved that money, with help from the wallet maker, into recovery wallets for safekeeping. So an empty balance may mean the money was rescued, not stolen.
Wallets made with a recovery phrase (a backup list of 12 or 24 words) or a hardware wallet are not affected, the wallet maker said. It has paused Google and Apple sign-in while it investigates.
What Affected Users Should Do
The wallet maker has given this user guidance for accounts created with Google or Apple login:
- Do not send new funds to the account.
- Do not re-import the account or recreate it anywhere.
- Move any funds that are not staked or locked to an account that uses a recovery phrase or a hardware wallet.
- Trust updates only from the official accounts of the wallet maker and the login provider, and ignore direct messages or links that offer "recovery."
Staked and locked assets are taking longer to secure. The wallet maker is also working with the login provider on a way for users to check whether their account was affected.
In the meantime, the login provider has published a recovery address list, which it says lets people tell its own transfers apart from possibly malicious ones.
It has also warned users not to assume that an unfamiliar destination address is linked to the attacker.
What Went Wrong
In an incident update, Web3Auth said a security issue in its own infrastructure affected certain wallets it provides inside the Keplr app.
Keplr went further, saying the flaw led to a "private key breach" for some users who signed in with Google or Apple. A private key is the secret code that approves payments from a wallet, so whoever holds it can move the money.
Neither company has said how the flaw worked, when the attacker first used it, or whether that route is now closed.
Where the Money Went
No dollar figure for the theft has come from either company. Josh Lee, a Keplr co-founder, gave an early estimate in his initial findings: about 20% of Google and Apple login accounts were affected, and only a fraction of those appeared to have been exploited.
GoPlus, a Web3 security company, said in a security alert that at least about $1 million had been stolen. It did not explain how it reached that figure.
The rescued money went into what the login provider calls secure recovery wallets, on 11 blockchains in the Cosmos family and eight Ethereum-style chains.
Bitquery, a blockchain data firm, counted at least $6.01 million moving from more than 44,000 wallets into the recovery wallets by late last week. The firm first reported the transfers as theft. It has since issued a corrected analysis that treats them as the rescue, though it says it cannot check who controls the recovery wallets.
The first of these transfers came 21 minutes before the login provider's first public notice, the firm's data shows. Most of the wallets, 86%, were emptied after the wallet maker warned users.
The moved funds are safe, the login provider said in its recovery thread, and it is working with the wallet maker to return them to users. It has not said how or when.
Beyond Keplr
The login provider said the issue affects its services used by some other companies, but Keplr is the only one it has named. It paused its embedded wallet service, which other apps use to build wallets for their users. Its status page still shows its login service as down today.
Consensys, the company behind the MetaMask wallet, bought the login provider in June 2025. Its acquisition announcement said the deal would let MetaMask users create and recover wallets with social logins. The provider said its initial investigation found "no evidence that MetaMask users are impacted."
