articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair amid Chinese spying allegations; board launches probe
articles.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair amid Chinese spying allegations; board launches probe
The AI chipmaker says it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised, even as US lawmakers seek answers over potential national security risks.
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into reports that its founder and CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation, following his admission of an extramarital affair with a business executive whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspect of passing information to Beijing.
The development has raised questions about corporate security and the potential exposure of sensitive information at the world's most valuable company, whose advanced chips are central to the global artificial intelligence race.
In a letter to employees obtained by multiple news organisations, Huang, 63, acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. He said he took full responsibility for his actions. "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility."
Nvidia's board announced on Sunday that it would examine reports suggesting Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The investigation will be overseen by a committee of independent directors, assisted by external legal counsel. The board said it had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia's confidential information had been compromised. However, it said the inquiry would review all available information.
Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation and will continue serving as CEO. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement, adding that Huang remained committed to leading the company without interruption.
Who is Alice Huang?
The investigation follows a report by The New York Times in October that US intelligence agencies had identified a close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and business executive who allegedly supplied information to Beijing. The two are not related. Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, subsequently became a senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, a major purchaser of Nvidia's AI chips.
According to The New York Times, Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years. US authorities have also scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped China obtain advanced AI processors subject to American export restrictions. The allegations involving Alice Huang have not been established by Nvidia's investigation, and the company has not reported evidence that its confidential information was compromised.
US lawmakers seek answers
The controversy has drawn attention from senior lawmakers in Washington, with three Republican congressional committee chairs seeking a closed-door briefing from Huang. In a letter dated November 4, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar and House Intelligence Committee Chairman Eric Crawford asked Huang to provide a briefing on November 18, according to Reuters.
The lawmakers raised concerns about whether the alleged intelligence operation could have exposed sensitive American technology or information to China. Nvidia previously said Huang interacts with thousands of customer executives annually and that its cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or information connected to US national security. The company also said it acts on information received from US authorities about parties or organisations of concern.
Trump backs Huang
US President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday, praising his leadership and indicating that the controversy would not necessarily affect their working relationship. Speaking to reporters before returning to the White House, Trump said Huang had done an exceptional job and indicated he remained open to taking the Nvidia chief on an upcoming trip to Asia. Huang serves on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, declined to comment on the allegations, citing the nature of the matter and Nvidia's internal investigation.
Why the investigation matters
The controversy comes at a sensitive time for Nvidia, which has become one of the most influential companies in the global AI industry. Its graphics processing units power the infrastructure used to develop and deploy advanced AI models. The company's dominance has also placed it at the centre of US-China technology tensions, particularly as Washington restricts exports of advanced chips to China.
The investigation presents Nvidia with questions extending beyond Huang's personal conduct, including the adequacy of corporate safeguards and whether intelligence concerns warrant changes to how senior executives engage with customers and business partners. For now, Nvidia's board has expressed confidence in Huang's continued leadership. Whether the investigation identifies any security lapses, and whether those findings lead to further corporate action, remains to be seen.

articles.title: Tesla ha jubilado los tres coches que la hacían deseable. Los dos que quedan tienen otro trabajo: pagar el robotaxi
articles.text:
En enero, Elon Musk avisó de que quien quisiera un Model S o un Model X tenía que pedirlo ya. En abril se acabaron los pedidos. Ahora ha anunciado el principio del fin del Cybertruck. La producción bajará a mediados de 2027 y su sitio en Texas será para el Cybercab.
Por separado, cada retirada tiene su explicación. El S y el X ya tenían sus años y no se vendían demasiado en comparación con 3 e Y. Por otro lado, el Cybertruck ha fracasado comercialmente. Juntas apuntan a algo más.
Por qué es importante. Eran los tres coches que hacían deseable a Tesla.
- El S demostró que un eléctrico podía ser un coche de lujo.
- El X, con sus puertas de ala de halcón, que podía ser un capricho.
- El Cybertruck se ha convertido en un icono, para lo bueno y para lo malo.
Quedan el Model 3 y el Model Y. Son buenos coches y se venden mucho, pero nadie se gira por la calle para mirarlos. Son funcionales, no aspiracionales.
Entre líneas. Lo que entra en esas fábricas cuenta más que lo que sale.
- En Fremont, la línea del S y el X fabrica ahora Optimus, el robot humanoide.
- En Texas, el hueco del Cybertruck lo ocupará el Cybercab, sin volante ni pedales, que Tesla ya prueba en Austin.
Ningún particular va a comprar ninguno de los dos para conducirlo.
Sí, pero. La lectura simple es la de un Musk que mata lo viejo para dejar paso a lo nuevo. Pero eso no encaja con el Cybertruck, porque tiene tres años. Musk llegó a hablar de 250.000 unidades al año y, según Electrek, andaba en torno a una décima parte.
Además, lo nuevo tampoco es un coche. Según The Information, un análisis interno recomendaba dar prioridad al Tesla asequible por delante del robotaxi. Musk lo desautorizó. Lo que ha salido son versiones recortadas del 3 y del Y.
El rastro del dinero. Al 3 y al Y les queda un solo trabajo: pagar las apuestas de verdad.
- En el tercer trimestre han sumado 478.237 de las 486.532 entregas, más del 98%.
- La venta de coches ha aportado 20.600 de los 28.050 millones de dólares de ingresos, un 3% menos que hace un año.
Dicho de otro modo: el negocio que financia el robot humanoide y el robotaxi no está recibiendo ningún producto nuevo, solo versiones más baratas de los dos modelos que van a seguir a la venta. El más antiguo de los dos es de 2017.
Y ahora qué. Tesla ha cambiado de cliente:
- Antes era alguien que quería un coche y quería que se notara. S, X y Cybertruck, cada uno a su manera, compartían presencia, notabilidad.
- Ahora es una flota que compra kilómetros o una fábrica que compra horas de robot. Eso es lo que paga la bolsa.
El riesgo son los tiempos. El robotaxi y Optimus tienen que escalar antes de que el 3 y el Y envejezcan. Mientras tanto, fabricantes chinos y europeos, especialmente los primeros, se van quedando con el hueco de los eléctricos asequibles.
Tesla consiguió como nadie hasta entonces que la gente deseara un coche eléctrico. Ahora está apostando casi todo a que no necesites uno.

articles.title: Le burn-in n’est pas le seul problème des TV OLED, avec le « edge rot » certains écrans s’abîment aussi sur les bords
articles.text:
Sur 16 téléviseurs WOLED soumis à son précédent test d’endurance, RTINGS en a vu 14 se dégrader sur leur pourtour. Les LG C1 et Sony A80J figurent parmi les cas sévères.
Pixels morts, amas noirs ou délamination, c’est-à-dire décollement de couches de la dalle : RTINGS regroupe ces dégradations des bordures sous le nom d’« edge rot ». Son analyse mise à jour le 5 novembre les distingue du burn-in.
Ces résultats ne constituent pas un taux de panne chez les particuliers. Comme nous l’avions expliqué dans notre bilan du précédent test d’endurance, les appareils ont subi près de trois ans de fonctionnement intensif, avec environ 18 000 heures d’utilisation et la diffusion répétée de CNN. L’objectif était de rechercher leurs points de rupture.
Des dalles LG Display, des dégâts variables
Les téléviseurs OLED examinés ont un point commun : leurs dalles proviennent de chez LG Display, y compris celles des modèles Sony comme l’A80J. Les dégâts varient cependant beaucoup d’un appareil à l’autre. Le LG OLED C2 ne présente que quelques pixels morts, tandis que le G3 ne montre aucune dégradation des bordures. Les trois téléviseurs QD-OLED du test sont également épargnés. Les observations dépassent toutefois le laboratoire. RTINGS présente aussi les défauts apparus sur deux téléviseurs utilisés chez ses salariés, un LG GX et un C1.
Pour rappel, le burn-in correspond à une usure inégale des matériaux lumineux : un logo ou un bandeau régulièrement affiché au même endroit peut finir par laisser une trace, comme nous l’expliquons dans notre dossier consacré au marquage OLED. Les protections logicielles cherchent notamment à limiter cette sollicitation inégale.
Pour les bordures abîmées, RTINGS envisage plutôt une contamination à la fabrication ou une encapsulation défectueuse. Interrogé par RTINGS, LG évoque des environnements sévères et juge le phénomène inattendu en usage normal.
L’encapsulation est l’enveloppe qui protège les matériaux OLED. Des recherches expérimentales sur ces barrières montrent que la pénétration de l’humidité et de l’oxygène peut dégrader les couches sensibles et provoquer des taches sombres. Ce mécanisme explique la piste étudiée, mais ne suffit pas à identifier la cause des défauts de chaque téléviseur. 
Quels recours pour les propriétaires qui seraient impactés ?
Photographiez les défauts et retrouvez votre facture pour vérifier les garanties encore applicables, notamment une éventuelle extension. Contactez ensuite votre vendeur ou le SAV du fabricant, en transmettant les photos et la référence du téléviseur, pour demander quelles possibilités de prise en charge existent.
La garantie des vices cachés peut constituer une autre voie : l’action doit être engagée dans les deux ans suivant la découverte du défaut, dans la limite de vingt ans après la vente. L’acheteur doit toutefois prouver un défaut caché, antérieur à l’achat et suffisamment grave pour rendre l’appareil inutilisable ou en diminuer fortement l’usage. L’enquête de RTINGS ne démontre pas, à elle seule, ces conditions pour chaque téléviseur. 
Quant aux cinq ans de garantie de dalle LG, il faut consulter l’offre correspondant au modèle et au pays d’achat. L’annonce de 2021 concernait les G1 et Z1, sans inclure le C1. Pour 2022, les conditions françaises publiées par LG désignaient certaines références G2 et Z2 : le C2 n’en bénéficiait pas. Ces conditions prévoyaient également une main-d’œuvre facturée de la deuxième à la cinquième année au titre de l’offre commerciale, sans réduire les garanties légales.
Chez RTINGS, le nouveau protocole Longevity 3.0 permettra de suivre les générations récentes. Cette enquête rappelle surtout qu’un téléviseur peut encore fonctionner tout en ayant perdu une partie de sa qualité d’image. C’est aussi cela qu’il faut mesurer quand on parle de durée de vie.

articles.title: Jordi Cruz, sobre la actitud de los trabajadores: “Hay un cambio generacional. Hemos pasado de ser espartanos y meterle catorce horas a hacer ocho y entenderlo de una forma distinta”
articles.text:
Es la época de las 14 horas versus las 8. Jordi Cruz habla de ese cambio de mentalidad en el sector hostelero. “Hay un cambio generacional”, afirma el cocinero en el pódcast Se me Antoja. Así explica en esta conversación cómo ha cambiado la mentalidad y las dificultades que tiene él para adaptarse.
El chef empezó a trabajar en cocina profesional con 14 años. Es uno de los rostros de la restauración (conocido por su restaurante ABaC y sus estrellas Michelin). También es jurado de MasterChef.
En su opinión, en 5 años ha cambiado la mentalidad. Antes era bonito y sacrificado. “Hemos pasado de ser espartanos, de meterle 14 horas”, afirma. Ahora hay que buscar un equilibrio y “hacer solo ocho horas”.
Esto tiene que ver con el cambio de mentalidad respecto al oficio. Se trata de buscar un equilibrio con la vida personal. Por otro lado, el cocinero admite que tiene dificultades para adaptarse.
Adaptarse a otra forma de entender el oficio
Se considera un “purista del oficio”. Por eso le cuesta. Tiene que hacer funcionar el restaurante. Pero además tiene los compromisos de la televisión, posee varios locales y tiene que hacerlos funcionar bien. Y encima tiene la presión de su mujer, que quiere que él también esté ahí…
Cruz también reconoce que se ha sentido solo al intentar adaptarse. Describe esa sensación como estar dando tumbos en un momento que considera complicado. Pero entiende el deseo de disponer de más tiempo fuera del trabajo: él mismo admite que le “gustaría conciliar un poquito más” y disfrutar de su vida, después de haber dedicado tanto tiempo a los demás.
Al hablar de sus empleados, explica que un buen sueldo ya no basta para responder a sus expectativas. En su opinión, hay trabajadores que prefieren cobrar menos y tener más tiempo libre. El cambio que describe afecta, por tanto, a lo que esperan recibir de la empresa por su trabajo y al peso que dan al salario frente al tiempo disponible.
El cocinero asegura que intenta atender esas demandas y que quiere que sus empleados estén satisfechos: “Yo quiero que tengan un buen sueldo y sean felices, porque la gente feliz sirve y cocina bien”. Aun así, dice que echa en falta un mayor vínculo con la empresa. Tampoco asegura tener una explicación para ello y reconoce que no sabe si se trata de falta de vocación.

articles.title: Assassin's Creed Hexe Reportedly Delayed Internally to 2028
articles.text:
Monday, November 9th 2026
Assassin's Creed Hexe Reportedly Delayed Internally to 2028
Assassin's Creed Hexe probably won't be out before 2028. Insider Gaming's Tom Henderson says sources told him as recently as October that the game had run into issues and was pushed back internally by another year. The claim was tucked into a larger report about two unannounced Assassin's Creed projects, including the Ancient Rome game codenamed Mars, though the Hexe bit is arguably the bigger news for anyone who has been waiting since Ubisoft first announced the game back in 2022. Henderson didn't say what the issues are. Up until now, 2027 looked like the target. A leaker pointed to June 2027 earlier this year, and NateTheHate later said Hexe wouldn't launch before the second half of 2027 at the earliest. 
Development hasn't exactly been smooth either. Ubisoft Montreal was reportedly reworking the combat deep into production in February, and around 50 developers were reportedly moved off the project a few months later. Ubisoft's latest official word came in its Fall 2026 franchise update at the end of October. The company said Hexe is making steady progress, though there is "still work ahead of us," and promised the next major update in 2027. That isn't a confirmation of anything, though it does leave room for a 2028 launch. Ubisoft hasn't given Hexe any official release window so far, so readers are advised to treat 2028 as an internal target that could still move.

articles.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
articles.text:
Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.
The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.
Attackers conducting “mature intrusions”
Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions” into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.
Greynoise said that GT10 is also installing the Python3 release on machines that don’t already have it because the package is required to run the hacker’s backdoor, which is tracked under the name TAC Agent. TAC Agent supports a wide range of functions, including shell commands, system reconnaissance, and persistence. OpenSSH has released a fix that prevents attacks from working.

articles.title: Google advances agentic AI custom silicon expanding TPU family with 8tx and 8i Max - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Google advances agentic AI custom silicon expanding TPU family with 8tx and 8i Max
Google LLC today introduced two new specialized silicon chips for artificial intelligence to its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit architecture family, aimed at higher compute density and secure inference.
At Google Cloud Next 2026 in April, Google introduced two specialized TPUs in the same generation, 8t for large-scale training and 8i designed for real-time reasoning. At the time, the company said it released the chips to handle demanding AI workloads across two primary tasks: building the models and running them.
Today’s expansion includes two new specialized chips across additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest possible compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx designed for secure and confidential inference.
TPU 8i Max, when memory is the bottleneck
Google said TPU 8i Max aims to scale compute and memory, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the high-bandwidth memory of TPU 8i. This gives processors as much memory as possible to handle data without swapping it out.
Additionally, the company added that 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the same rack footprint, lowering the floor space it takes per square foot and per watt in data centers.
This allows the new eighth-generation TPUs to provide customers with a purpose-built accelerator for larger models and the industry’s current push toward ultra-large context windows.
A context window acts as an AI model’s working space: how much data it can consider while answering a question. A larger window lets it work across a longer document, conversation history, audio file, video or collection of code. But expanding it comes at a cost. Processing and repeatedly consulting more information puts greater demands on chips to swap data in and out, requiring more on-chip memory and stronger connections that move data between processors.
Adding more on-chip memory reduces the need to move data between processors, lowering latency and reducing the power an AI model needs to “think” about information.
Google said it developed 8i Max alongside pushing massive context windows for its Gemini frontier model, which supports the 1 million-token industry standard. That represents roughly 750,000 words or 1,500 pages of text. Although flagship models tackle 1 million tokens, smaller models often support narrower window sizes between 128,000 and 256,000 tokens.
TPU 8tx, for confidentiality
Google said it optimized TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference, designing the chip for regulated enterprises and governments that want to run frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside the most sensitive data.
Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but when an AI model processes that same information, it must be decoded. Built on the same architecture as the TPU 8t, with custom AMD central processing unit hosts, the 8tx builds in a secure enclave directly into the hardware layer that keeps sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated.
The company said the architecture pairs training-grade compute with fast inference, meaning organizations can run and customize models on a single confidential system. The combination allows regulated services and industries to fine-tune models using private data, distill large models into smaller ones and train agents through reinforcement learning.
All of this can be done without migrating data between separate clusters, which could expose sensitive information to leaks.

articles.title: Apple pushing to get more agentic Siri ASAP: report
articles.text:
Apple is reportedly racing to get a more agentic version of Siri out to market.
According to Bloomberg Apple reporter Mark Gurman, Apple is working quickly to address the fact that its virtual assistant is behind others on the market. In particular, Gurman notes that agents like Meta’s Muse and SpaceX’s Grok can be used to handle various tasks for people, including goal tracking and decision-making without the user’s constant input.
Siri, however, currently lacks such functionality, and so Gurman says Apple “ultimately wants to go in this direction.” In fact, he says Apple is working to “make Siri more like an agent as early as next year.”
To help with this and other iOS development, Gurman says Apple is now giving engineers more time for coding and integration, which was seemingly made possible by advances in agentic coding tools. Time will tell how these improved pipelines will help Apple deliver on its hopes for Siri’s expanded agentic functionality.
All of this comes shortly Apple debuted a new version of Siri that it rebuilt using AI. On the hardware side, meanwhile, Apple just debuted its long-awaited foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, alongside its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro.

articles.title: Lawyer builds private AI server with eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs — up to 215 tokens per second to keep legal files offline, costing about $2,400 per four-GPU board
articles.text:
Lawyer builds private AI server with eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs — up to 215 tokens per second to keep legal files offline, costing about $2,400 per four-GPU board
The builder estimates 50% to 60% of their AI work can now skip frontier models, running on two office circuits.
A lawyer posted on Reddit about their private AI server built from eight used 2018-era Nvidia Tesla V100 data center GPUs so case files never have to leave the office. With two 4-card SXM2 NVLink boards, four PEX switches, and SlimSAS cables everywhere — plus one burnt power connector — the builder now runs the open DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model with every expert in GPU memory, at up to 215 tokens per second. The four-GPU boards cost about $2,400 apiece when the builder bought them.
The eight Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB cards, each with 32GB of HBM2 at 900 GB/s, plug into SXM2, Nvidia’s mezzanine socket for data center GPUs, rather than PCIe slots, and are split across two baseboards. Inside each board, all four cards are NVLinked — NVLink is Nvidia’s direct GPU-to-GPU link — for 128GB per board, but the two boards only communicate over PCIe. Each board connects to the host through two PEX (PLX) switch cards over SlimSAS cables, four switches in all, with each switch handling two GPUs at PCIe 3.0 x8 speeds over its own x16 uplink.
The given prices are already in the past, though: used V100 SXM2 32GB cards are now listed on eBay for about $900, more than double the roughly $400 apiece from the post, and listings suggest prices are still climbing. The system also already has some other necessary components: a Gigabyte Threadripper Pro motherboard with a 12-core 3945WX CPU to match, 8x 32GB DDR4 RDIMM, one NUMA node, and two PSUs, 2,800 W in total, are on separate regular office circuits. This is a real-world case for used data center hardware as a cheap route to getting lots of fast VRAM together in one place.
The server is currently in daily use for first-pass work on case files: it reads a folder of records, pulls out facts, dates, and numbers, summarizes them, and takes a first swing at routine drafting. “Nothing goes out the door without a real review,” which is a good human-in-the-loop policy in general. It also helps ensure privacy for cases where client files can’t be sent to a cloud or frontier model. RAG databases and tool calls are wired in; the operator can drive the system through a Discord-style interface over SSH, in this case from a Windows PC. For now, it handles only one request at a time.
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is compressed to mostly 2 bits here, and its weights still total 248.8GB. The model’s “experts,” the parts that do most of the work for each word, live entirely in GPU memory, while about 110GB of lookup tables, called Engram tables, stay in the system’s regular RAM. Fetching from RAM costs about 0.12 milliseconds per step, which the builder says barely affects the speed numbers.
The first half of the model’s layers (0–19) runs on the first SXM2 board and the second half (20–39) on the second. Each board handles its heavy traffic over its own NVLink, so only one hand-off per step has to cross the slower PCIe link between the boards. In an earlier post, the builder found that splitting every layer across all eight cards made speeds “fall off a cliff” because of that PCIe hop.
Performance is surprisingly good for a model this size. Code comes out fastest, at up to 215 tokens per second, because a small draft model built into DeepSeek guesses five tokens ahead, and code is easy to guess. Legal writing, which is what the server is for, runs at up to 118 tokens per second.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Long documents take longer to get going: the model reads prompts at about 2,200 tokens per second, so at 128K tokens, the first token arrives after about a minute. It can accept up to 524K tokens of context. Three days before the post, the same model on four of these cards managed just 36–38 tokens per second. The jump came with the second board, which could presumably double performance under ideal circumstances, and the builder credits custom kernels and prefill work for the rest. See the table for the full breakdown.
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on eight Tesla V100s, by prompt length |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Prompt length | Wait for first token | Code (tokens/s) | Legal writing (tokens/s) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 1K tokens | 1.2 seconds | 215 | 118 | 
| 32K tokens | 17.2 seconds | 200 | 117 | 
| 128K tokens | 59.2 seconds | 183 | 111 | 
| 256K tokens | 118.7 seconds | 160 | 103 | 
Builder’s measurements, Nov. 5; greedy decoding, 1,024 tokens out, mean of two runs.
It wasn’t as simple as hooking everything up and turning on the power. The host reset itself twice with a fatal PCIe error on the link to one GPU board, both times with a higher power limit and uncapped GPU clocks. In this state, the cards drew 192–232 W, past the 180 W limit. The best guess, although “not proven,” is that a board stops responding during load spikes.
The resets stopped after the builder capped the clocks and removed one board whose power connector had a burn mark; “Check your connectors, people.” Each card is now capped at 150 W, half of its 300 W rating, with the graphics clock capped at 1522 MHz. A 200 W cap brought no appreciable performance gains, according to tests.
The system memory hit uncorrected ECC errors, too, which went away after the builder dropped the RAM from DDR4-3200 to DDR4-2666. One GPU was connected at x4 instead of x8 at last check, and the builder plans to reseat it; one commenter traced the same kind of problem on their own V100 to a bad cable.
The pain was worth the payoff as an estimated 50–60% of the lawyer’s existing LLM workflows can now run on the box instead of frontier models. Helping bridge the gap is a second DeepSeek server on two DGX Sparks, where the two systems hand work off to each other. The setup does appear to save money, at least when compared to API pricing, although the builder says it’s not really faster. However, it will protect client data “once it is self contained, which is the goal.”
The builder added that the V100 box might also get a 240 V circuit. Beyond power, the system is also on borrowed time with the Nvidia R580 driver branch, which is the last to support Volta. For now, the lawyer admits that it’s mostly a hobby, but in the future it may be a business idea. The next step is to handle two or three requests at once, something built and checked on a test system but not yet on the server.

articles.title: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO's ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.
In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

articles.title: Meet Eric. He plays CDs, he's cheap, and he has loads of cool features
articles.text:
Gadhouse's new cheap portable CD player packs way more features than you'd expect for the price, and you can buy it now
Meet my mate Eric
- Gadhouse unveils Eric (a new CD player, not a robot)
- It's about a third of the price of other portable options we've seen
- Bluetooth, multiple headphone jacks, an FM radio receiver and a screen
I write one piece of audio news every day of the week for TechRadar's audio editor, and it's been ages since I covered any new earbuds or headphones for her. Why? Because so many new CD players, turntables and cassette players are launching. It's like I'm working in the 80s.
Taking the spotlight today is Eric. Not any old Eric; the Gadhouse Eric, with unconfirmed reports (which I've only just made up) saying that it was named after a man down the pub. Gadhouse is apparently turning into a madhouse for the physical media revival, after showing us the Gadhouse Miko cassette player earlier this year — and let's not forget last year's Gadhouse Duke & Roy powered speakers and turntable combo for vinyl lovers.
The Gadhouse Eric is set to cost just $84.50 / £59.99 (about AU$120), so it's a lot cheaper than the likes of the Shanling EC Player or FiiO DM13; they're both about three times the price.
At that money, this could be the budget portable CD player to beat. It's on sale right now, though Gadhouse says that it'll be launching new color options through 2027.
A range of extra features and tools
You want a CD player to do one thing: play CDs. Eric does that, sorted. Wait, it does more?
That's right, Gadhouse has slapped an FM radio receiver into the Eric, so you can skip the doomsday prepping with a hand-cranked option and use this if you'd prefer. This is presumably arranged via its little display, and the slider you can see in the picture.
What else does it do? Well, it lets you connect wirelessly using Bluetooth, which I bet your grandad's CD player doesn't do. It also has not one, but two 3.5mm audio jacks; you can connected to two headphones at once to share music, or connected to a hi-fi system if you'd prefer.

If there's any potential problem I foresee, it's that the battery life is only 4 hours long, so you're going to struggle taking this travelling. It can be recharged via a USB-C port in the back.

articles.title: Amateurfunker bringen einen Satelliten dazu, Doom zu spielen: Was das Experiment zeigen soll
articles.text:
Amateurfunker bringen einen Satelliten dazu, Doom zu spielen: Was das Experiment zeigen soll
Der OPS-SAT „Pretty“ befindet sich seit 2023 im Weltall und schwebt um die Erde herum. Der Satellit der Europäischen Weltraumorganisation Esa hat ein passives Reflektometer an Bord, um Signale von Galileo- und GPS-Satelliten zu empfangen, die von der Erde zurückgeworfen werden. Doch tatsächlich hat der Satellit noch mehr auf dem Kasten.
Ein sprachaktivierter Satellit spielt Doom
Wie Space berichtet, wurde der Satellit der Esa jetzt für ein besonderes Experiment genutzt. Auf der Cubesat-Hardware sollte der Ego-Shooter Doom gespielt werden. Dieses Vorhaben an sich, ist nicht neu. Schon auf dem vorherigen OPS-SAT der Esa hatte der Entwickler Ólafur Waage das Projekt „OPS-SAT Doom Media Coverage“ realisiert. Der Satellit kann dadurch eine rudimentäre Version des Shooters spielen und am Ende eines Levels zurückmelden, wie viele Abschüsse stattgefunden haben und ob Items und Geheimnisse gefunden wurden.
Das neue Projekt ging jetzt einen Schritt weiter. Denn dieses Mal wurde der Befehl, Doom abzuspielen, per Sprachbefehl von der Erde ausgelöst. Dazu wurden Amateurfunker:innen aus mehreren Ländern angehalten, dem Satelliten Nachrichten zu schicken, um den Befehl auszulösen. Zunächst gab es viele gescheiterte Versuche von Teams in Polen und Norwegen im Zeitraum zwischen April und Juli 2026.
Die „Norwegian Radio Relay League“ hatte schließlich mit ihrem Signal Erfolg. Sie schreiben dazu: „Wir sind Funkamateure mit der Betonung auf Amateure. Satellitenarbeit war nie etwas, was unser Klub verfolgt hat, und wir hatten kein Budget dafür. Aber wir haben uns ein Zitat zu Eigen gemacht, das fälschlicherweise Pippi Langstrumpf zugeschrieben wird: ‚Das habe ich noch nie vorher versucht, also bin ich völlig sicher, dass ich es schaffe!'“
Die Norweger:innen haben insgesamt 59 Tage damit verbracht, den Satelliten namens Pretty anzufunken. Dafür haben sie umgerechnet knapp 700 Euro ausgegeben, wobei laut eigener Aussage die Kosten für Pizzabestellungen schon einberechnet wurden. Der erfolgreiche Funkspruch wurde schließlich von einem Dach in Oslo abgesetzt: „Pretty, spiele Doom, Doom, Doom“.
Was soll das Experiment zeigen?
Bevor es dazu kommen konnte, mussten die Verantwortlichen bei der Esa noch einige Änderungen an der Spracherkennung von Pretty vornehmen. So war der Empfängerkanal etwa zu breit eingestellt. Dadurch wurden zwar Signale empfangen, aber sie waren unverständlich. Erst als der Kanal eingegrenzt wurde, konnte Pretty die Worte dahinter auch verstehen und umsetzen.
Künftig könnte die Spracherkennung von Satelliten in Notfällen genutzt werden. Funker:innen in abgelegenen Gebieten könnten die Satelliten kontaktieren, um einen Notruf auszulösen. Die Spracherkennung würde dann in Kombination mit einer KI die Koordinaten sowie wichtige Informationen an Rettungskräfte weitergeben. Denkbar wäre aber auch, dass Satelliten so Radiofrequenzen aus der Tiefe des Alls selbstständig analysieren und an die Erde oder Raumschiffe weiterfunken könnten.

articles.title: Powering AI Data Centers: Rethinking Energy Infrastructure for the Next Wave of AI Growth - EE Times
articles.text:
As AI drives unprecedented growth in data center capacity and power density, securing reliable, scalable energy infrastructure has become one of the industry’s most pressing challenges. With AI workloads pushing power demands to new heights and utility infrastructure struggling to keep pace, operators are rethinking how electricity is sourced, distributed, and managed to support the next generation of AI computing.
In this partner edition, Nitin Dahad interviews Nick Baileys, director of energy infrastructure solutions at Delta Electronics (Americas), at Delta’s booth during the OCP Global Summit. Their conversation explores the engineering challenges of powering AI data centers and the growing role of microgrids, on-site energy resources, and intelligent power management in addressing grid constraints and accelerating time to power.
The discussion examines the obstacles data center operators face when securing sufficient electricity for new AI capacity. As utility interconnection timelines, infrastructure limitations, and increasingly concentrated power demands complicate expansion plans, operators are evaluating more flexible approaches to energy infrastructure. Microgrids and on-site generation can offer additional options for improving energy resilience, supporting phased deployments, and complementing traditional utility connections.
Beyond securing power, the conversation explores how the increasingly dynamic nature of AI workloads is reshaping energy management requirements. Rapid fluctuations in computing demand create new challenges for maintaining stable and efficient operations. Energy storage systems, advanced power electronics, and intelligent controls can help manage load variations, coordinate multiple energy sources, and improve the responsiveness of data center power infrastructure.
The interview also tackles a critical question: Can microgrids keep pace as AI rack power requirements continue to climb? As computing architectures evolve toward higher power densities, operators must consider how on-site energy systems can scale alongside expanding facilities while maintaining reliability, efficiency, and operational flexibility. The discussion highlights the importance of designing adaptable power infrastructure that can respond to both immediate capacity needs and long-term growth.
Looking ahead, the conversation considers how the relationship between utility grids, on-site energy resources, and data centers may evolve. Rather than viewing grid power and on-site infrastructure as separate solutions, future AI data centers may increasingly rely on coordinated energy ecosystems that integrate utility connections, distributed generation, energy storage, and intelligent control systems.
As AI continues to transform the scale and complexity of data center operations, this discussion offers insights into the power strategies and infrastructure considerations that could help operators overcome energy constraints, accelerate deployment, and build more resilient and adaptable facilities for the AI era.
Why would ANY business put themselves at the mercy of (any) supplier?
Data Centers must have electricity to run operations and generate (yes, pun) cash from their services. Self contained power generation (choose a method) is the only way to heavy electricity users to choose. At least this aspect of their business is solely under their control rather than outside regulators or consumers.
Same for water: set up a self contained/enclosed recirculating cooling system (ala a car's radiator) where the consumption of 'new' water is minimal.
The next issue could be noise from the power generation.
Traffic should be a non-issue UNLESS you are talking about bandwidth in/out of the center. Car traffic is a non-event except during construction.

articles.title: Still Looking for Diamonds - EE Times
articles.text:
Last week, at an investment forum in Sofia, Bulgaria, I got a close look at silicon carbide, from its accidental past to its potential future.
Two men looking for diamonds
In 1891, Edward Acheson, a former assistant of Thomas Edison, heated clay and carbon with an electric arc in an attempt to make artificial diamonds. What he got instead was a batch of small, hard, blue-black crystals that he named carborundum. Two years later, the French chemist Henri Moissan was looking for diamonds in fragments of a meteorite in Arizona and found the same material in nature. The mineral was eventually named moissanite in his honor.
I referred to that story to close my remarks last week at the Green Semiconductors Investment Forum in Sofia, observing that more than 130 years later we had a room full of entrepreneurs and investors who were still trying to turn silicon carbide into diamonds. The forum, held under the patronage of the Bulgarian government and the British Embassy, centered on the initiative to establish Green Silicon Carbide Manufacturing (GSCM), a SiC fab in the country designed as an integrated device manufacturer. I sat on the investors’ panel, representing the startup ecosystem.
Silicon carbide has had a remarkable journey in the meantime. Thanks to its near-diamond hardness, it was an industrial abrasive for most of the 20th century, then an early radio detector, the crystal in which electroluminescence was first observed in 1907, a synthetic gemstone in the late 1990s (grown by Cree, the company later renamed Wolfspeed), and finally made it to power devices inside electric cars.
What follows are my notes from what I learned at the forum, plus some numbers I put together afterward, about the European and global scene for this special compound material.
The market perspective
The demand story is solid. Yole Group’s Poshun Chiu, who presented in Sofia, expects wide-bandgap power devices (SiC and GaN together) to pass $14 billion by 2031, growing at around 22% a year. Three drivers stand out: Electric cars are moving to 800V architectures, which use more SiC, and Yole expects their share of battery electric vehicles to grow from about 12% in 2025 to about half by 2031. Renewables, storage, and wind keep growing. And AI data centers are redesigning their power chain around 800V DC, with SiC moving upstream toward the grid connection (power shelves and, later, solid-state transformers fed at 10 to 20 kV), while GaN takes the stages closer to the processors.
But there is also intense competition: Chinese producers have pushed six-inch SiC substrate prices from around $1,500 to $500 or less, according to TrendForce.
Wolfspeed, the long-time market leader, filed for Chapter 11 in June 2025, reportedly with about $6.7 billion of debt, much of it raised to build new fabs ahead of demand. It re-emerged with 70% less debt and is clearly recovering, but slowly. In its latest quarter, to September 2026, it still reported a negative gross margin of about 13% (non-GAAP). Management called underutilization the main drag on margins and said that running the new Mohawk Valley fab at around 25 to 30% of capacity would be enough to reach gross-margin breakeven, which suggests it currently runs below that level (earnings call). It expects to approach gross margin breakeven this quarter, helped by AI data center demand, its fastest-growing market, and in October it secured a conditional $1.5 billion loan commitment from the U.S. Department of War, a sign of how strategic SiC has become.
Europe’s paradox
Here is the part I found most striking: According to Yole, European companies (ST, Infineon, Bosch, and others) hold roughly half of the global SiC device market. Granted, they are much weaker upstream, with only about 10% of the substrate market, and Europe itself is a small market for SiC in cars, around 12% of global demand against about 63% for China.
Yole also showed a map of more than $30 billion in announced SiC investment as of mid-2026. I re-sorted it by the headquarters of the investing company rather than by location of the target investment. By my rough tally, about half of the money comes from European companies, but only around 40% of that money is actually being invested in Europe, mostly in ST’s campus in Catania. The largest projects of European champions are elsewhere: Infineon’s fab in Kulim, Malaysia, Bosch in Roseville, California, X-FAB in Lubbock, Texas, and ST’s stake in its joint venture with Sanan in China. Chinese and Japanese companies, by contrast, invest almost entirely at home, and U.S. companies mostly do. One exception is Vishay, which bought the Newport Wafer Fab in Wales in 2024 to set up SiC production there.
The reasons are understandable. Companies follow demand, and most SiC car demand is in China. They also follow subsidies, and the U.S. CHIPS Act made American sites attractive. Finally, they follow energy prices, which matter a lot for a material whose crystal growth is extremely energy-intensive. Yole goes further and sees Southeast Asia becoming the next power SiC hub, thanks to Malaysia’s established back-end ecosystem, lower costs, government support, and geopolitical neutrality, with Infineon’s Kulim fab as the anchor. So Europe ends up with sovereignty by ownership, but much less sovereignty by location, which is what counts if supply chains break.
The European Commission’s presentation in Sofia added another angle. It listed 19 first-of-a-kind production projects approved for state aid under the Chips Act since 2023, worth more than €34 billion in total. Eleven of them are in Germany, and most of the rest are in Italy, France, and Austria, while almost none is in Europe’s peripheral countries. (The single exception on the list was onsemi’s SiC expansion in Rožnov, Czech Republic. However, just three days after the forum, onsemi and the Czech government announced that it will not go ahead, citing changes in the SiC market and in the project’s economics.)
The same slide noted that before the Act, state aid for fabs was limited to assisted regions, so the old rule was a relative advantage for places like Bulgaria, and opening aid to the wealthier core moved the money there. I would summarize it this way: Europe has become quite good at financing upgrades by incumbents, and much less good at financing new entrants.
This is consistent with how the European Investment Bank describes its own role. As EE Times reported earlier this year, the EIB is a lender that screens for cash flow, debt capacity, and execution risk, and strategic importance comes on top of bankability, never instead of it. Chips Act 2.0 is the obvious place to revisit the balance between the two, and I hope cohesion becomes part of that discussion.
IDMs vs pure play foundries
In silicon, the separation between design and manufacturing has been the norm for decades, with Nvidia and TSMC as the best-known example of how this relationship works. In SiC, almost all of the business, maybe even 90%, sits inside integrated device manufacturers. Here, the process largely is the product: Device performance and reliability depend on process details that are hard to separate from the design. Jen Walls, CEO of Clas-SiC, a boutique SiC foundry in Scotland, made a related point in her talk: Capital can buy the cleanroom, the tools, and the wafers, but it cannot buy the learning curve of yield, reliability history, and customer qualification, which builds up batch after batch.
Wolfspeed shows how unforgiving this is. It had technology leadership and an anchor customer, Renesas, which prepaid about $2 billion for wafer supply. It still went bankrupt because it built capacity on debt ahead of demand in a cyclical market while prices fell.
The consequence is that open SiC capacity for existing and potential fabless companies is scarce. As far as I know, neither TSMC, GlobalFoundries, nor Tower offers SiC. The main open options are X-FAB in Lubbock, a few Taiwanese players announcing 8-inch SiC lines, research lines such as Fraunhofer IISB, and Clas-SiC, which recently announced a £12 million (~$16 million) expansion. Yole’s map of the European supply chain makes the same point visually: strong IDMs, very few foundries, few packaging and power module players, and little direct engagement from end-system makers.
The view from a fabless ecosystem
Who would use open SiC capacity if it existed? Startups, first of all: niche high-voltage devices, radiation-hardened parts for space, sensors for harsh environments. Around them, a layer of independent businesses would grow, from gate drivers and power modules to test, reliability, and design kits, as happened in silicon. And possibly some very large customers. Tesla already designs its own SiC power modules and buys the chips, and in 2023 it announced it would cut its SiC use by 75% through design changes (CNBC), a reminder of how much leverage a system company has. If a hyperscaler or a carmaker eventually decides to design its own SiC devices, as many did with digital chips, I think they will look for a neutral foundry rather than an IDM that competes with them.
What an emerging location can do
To be honest, I was initially surprised by the Bulgarian initiative, promoted by Bulgarian-born Prof. Asen Asenov, who has spent the past three decades at the University of Glasgow. But the country starts from a better place than I expected: GlobalFoundries has a fairly large Sofia team, primarily of PDK engineers. Belgium’s Melexis has around 700 employees in Sofia. Milara, a Bulgarian-American company with engineering and manufacturing in Plovdiv, builds wafer-handling robots that go into semiconductor equipment worldwide. And the planned GSCM fab has assembled an impressive portfolio of partners that include the above-mentioned Clas-SiC for the SiC technology license, Synopsys and SemiWise for PDK development, and Milara for process automation.
IMHO, three things would make such a project more investable. The first is phasing: building capacity in steps as customers sign, as Infineon is doing in Villach, rather than all at once. The second is securing a customer base beyond European cars, which are a small market, toward wind, grid, storage, and data center power, where higher-voltage devices face less of the price war. The third is leaving the door open to fabless companies’ innovations.
Know who pays and for what
This is also the advice I gave startups on the panel: Before anything else, know which customer is going to pay for the technology you are developing.
I think the same applies to fabs, and to regions. Silicon carbide has surprised us several times in 135 years, and its next uses may surprise us again. A recent review by researchers at Singapore’s A*STAR Institute of Microelectronics describes SiC as a promising platform for photonic and quantum chips, largely because it can be processed in standard CMOS fabs, although the field is still at an early research stage. But investors do not finance surprises, especially not for a fab. They finance a customer today, while research for the next reinvention goes on in parallel and, if possible, separately.
Acheson never made his diamond. The material he found instead turned out to be worth much more, but it took more than a century and several false starts to find out how.

articles.title: Bornes d’arcade paralysées au Japon : une cyberattaque contre Sega prive les joueurs de plusieurs jeux
articles.text:
Les salles d’arcade japonaises tournent au ralenti depuis le 1er novembre 2026. De nombreuses bornes sont inutilisables ou privées de leurs fonctions en ligne dans tout le pays. Sega Fave, la filiale de Sega chargée des bornes d’arcade et des jouets, a en effet été victime d’un « accès non autorisé par un tiers ». Certains des serveurs du groupe ont été visités par des hackers.
A lire aussi : Vague de cyberattaques contre les supermarchés – l’Europe veut des plans d’urgence face à des menaces « profondément préoccupantes »
Deux services clés de Sega à l’arrêt
Les serveurs compromis font tourner deux services essentiels de Sega, à savoir ALL.Net, le réseau qui relie les bornes de Sega à Internet, et Aime, le système de cartes de joueur maison. Grâce à ces cartes, les joueurs retrouvent leurs scores, leurs classements et leurs objets d’une borne à l’autre. Par précaution, Sega Fave a coupé ces deux services. Sur X, le compte officiel d’ALL.Net a publié un message d’excuses à destination des joueurs.
 【重要】当社サーバーへの不正アクセスに関するお詫びとお知らせhttps://t.co/r0SOAZvf0A
— ALL.Netサービス情報 (@allnet_info) November 2, 2026
À la suite de la désactivation des serveurs, il est impossible de jouer en ligne sur les bornes, d’utiliser sa carte Aime ou de créer un nouveau compte SEGA ID. Les sites qui recensent les salles équipées de bornes connectées sont aussi hors service. Les jeux de Sega, comme Initial D The Arcade, maimai ou CHUNITHM, sont touchés. Étant donné qu’ALL.Net est aussi exploité par d’autres éditeurs, des titres de Bandai Namco sont également concernés, dont Mario Kart Arcade GP DX, Taiko no Tatsujin ou Mobile Suit Gundam Extreme Vs. Pour certains jeux, les parties hors ligne sont également devenues impossibles.
 【ALL. Netの各種サービス停止に伴うゲーム機の一時停止について】
ALL. Netの各種サービス停止に伴い、ゲームプレイが順次、一時的にご利用いただけない状態となります。オフラインでのプレイもできませんので、ご了承ください。
サービスの再開状況については、あらためてご案内いたします。… https://t.co/2TFylVOIK9
— 【公式】太鼓の達人 ゲームセンター版 (@taiko_team) November 2, 2026
Sur les réseaux sociaux, des photos de bornes hors service ont circulé tout le week-end. Les salles d’arcade ont aussi partagé l’état de leurs machines. La Taito Station de Machida, près de Tokyo, a ainsi publié la liste de ses jeux à l’arrêt, dont Mario Kart. De son côté, la salle WGC a dû couper ses bornes de Taiko no Tatsujin, faute de pouvoir les faire fonctionner hors ligne plus longtemps.
 太鼓の達人の稼働を停止となります。復旧まで暫くお待ち下さい pic.twitter.com/iqBOIzX4Fs
— WGC / WGC APPEND / CLUB EXA / WGC UPPER 情報アカウント (@wgc_tencho) November 4, 2026
Des tournois, comme la Double Ace Cup d’Initial D, ont même été annulés. Bonne nouvelle, les données des joueurs sont en revanche à l’abri. Selon les premières investigations réalisées par Sega Fave, aucune information sur les clients ou les partenaires n’a fuité. Les données de paiement, comme les numéros de carte bancaire, sont stockées sur d’autres serveurs et n’ont pas été touchées par les cybercriminels.
Près d’une semaine après l’attaque, Sega n’avait toujours pas communiqué de calendrier de reprise. Le 6 novembre, l’entreprise affirmait travailler « à rétablir les services », mais n’avoir « pas encore déterminé de date de reprise ». Depuis le 8 novembre, huit jeux de Bandai Namco, dont Mario Kart Arcade Grand Prix Deluxe, ont néanmoins progressivement repris du service.Les jeux de Sega restent quant à eux hors ligne.
Le Japon face à une vague de cyberattaques
Depuis la rentrée, le Japon est submergé par une vague de cyberattaques d’une ampleur inédite. Selon l’éditeur Trend Micro, plus de 600 intrusions ont été recensées à l’encontre d’entreprises et des collectivités japonaises entre janvier et septembre 2026, plus que sur toute l’année 2025.
Parmi les victimes, on trouve la chaîne de supérettes Lawson, le service de covoiturage Times Car , ou encore l’’éditeur de jeux vidéo Capcom. Les données de 11,7 millions de comptes Capcom ont été subtilisées. Le groupe GMO Internet a même reçu une demande de rançon de 50 millions de dollars à la suite d’une offensive. Selon la branche cybersécurité de GMO Internet, Artex, un outil chinois de test de sécurité basé sur l’IA, a été utilisé dans plusieurs piratages au Japon.
« La situation est grave »
Face à la menace grandissante, le gouvernement japonais s’est engagé à agir. Sanae Takaichi, la première ministre du Japon, a indiqué que « la situation est grave, l’inquiétude grandit quant (…) à l’utilisation abusive des informations divulguées, d’où la nécessité de renforcer rapidement les contre-mesures ». Le gouvernement vient d’ailleurs d’adopter un plan d’urgence cybersécurité pour endiguer la vague d’attaques.
Le plan prévoit notamment de mettre sur pied une équipe de secours, alliant des entités publiques et privées, pour épauler les entreprises à la moindre attaque. Sanae Takaichi s’est dite prête à exploiter « toute la force du gouvernement pour améliorer la capacité de réaction globale du Japon ». Les autorités japonaises demandent aux entreprises de corriger rapidement leurs failles, d’imposer l’authentification à deux facteurs et de mieux contrôler leurs sous-traitants, qui sont bien les maillons faibles exploités par les pirates.

articles.title: Windows Update: Las computadoras obsoletas dejarán de recibir actualizaciones en junio de 2027
articles.text:
Microsoft ha lanzado un aviso para aquellos que todavía utilizan versiones antiguas de Windows, ya que algunos PC podrían perder el acceso a Windows Update durante 2027. La compañía tiene previsto renovar sus certificados de seguridad que caducarán el 17 de mayo y el 19 de junio, y los equipos que no tengan los nuevos certificados instalados dejarán de recibir actualizaciones a través de este servicio.
Según explica Microsoft en su blog oficial, estos certificados sirven para comprobar que los dispositivos se conectan a servidores legítimos de Windows Update. El problema es que tienen fecha de caducidad y se deben sustituir cada cierto tiempo, pero la mayoría de usuarios que tengan una versión compatible de Windows y mantengan su ordenador actualizado no tendrán que hacer absolutamente nada.
No todos los ordenadores con Windows tendrán que hacer lo mismo
La situación cambia dependiendo de la versión instalada. Por ejemplo, quienes utilicen Windows 11 25H2 o una posterior pueden olvidarse del asunto, mientras que los equipos con Windows 11 24H2 necesitan tener instalada, como mínimo, la actualización de seguridad de septiembre de 2025. En otros sistemas compatibles, como Windows Server 2022 o las versiones de Windows 10 que todavía cuentan con soporte, Microsoft exige una actualización de julio de 2026 o posterior.
También existen casos con menos margen. Los dispositivos con Windows 10 Enterprise 2019 LTSC, Windows Server 2019 y Windows Server 2016 tendrán que instalar las actualizaciones correspondientes antes del 17 de mayo de 2027, en lugar del 19 de junio. Y si hablamos de versiones que ya no reciben soporte, la recomendación de Microsoft es actualizar a un sistema compatible.
Pero ojo, esto no significa que todos los ordenadores antiguos vayan a dejar de funcionar de golpe. Lo que perderán los equipos afectados es la conexión con Windows Update y, por tanto, la posibilidad de recibir actualizaciones mediante ese servicio. Además, Microsoft aclara que el cambio no afecta a los dispositivos que utilizan Windows Server Update Services (WSUS), una herramienta empleada para distribuir actualizaciones en redes empresariales.
Por su parte, Windows 11 26H2 ya está disponible para los dispositivos compatibles con las versiones 24H2 y 25H2. Microsoft también recomienda a los administradores informáticos revisar qué equipos siguen utilizando sistemas antiguos y preparar su actualización antes de que caduquen los certificados.

articles.title: De unos 320 millones de viajes y pedidos de Uber en la semana de Halloween, solo cuatro viajes y 500 pedidos de Uber Eats vinieron de agentes de IA
articles.text:
Halloween es una de las semanas más movidas del año para Uber, tanto por el número de desplazamientos que se registran como por el por número de pedidos de comida a domicilio que se registran en esas fechas. Solo unos días después de este pico de trabajo extra, la empresa contó a sus inversores cuánto de ese ajetreo había pasado por la tecnología de moda: los agentes de IA.
La tecnología que se vende como la próxima forma de comprar casi cualquier cosa, demostró en Halloween que tiene más truco que trato.
Cuatro viajes y 500 pedidos. En la presentación de resultados del tercer trimestre ante los accionistas, Balaji Krishnamurthy, director financiero de Uber, detalló que la compañía movió unos 320 millones de operaciones durante el pasado Halloween. Esta cifra engloba los viajes de Uber y los pedidos de Uber Eats. De ellos, unos 500 pedidos de comida llegaron a través de agentes de IA que encargaron la comida en nombre de sus usuarios. Sin embargo, esa cifra se hundió a la hora de pedir un transporte para volver a casa, en el que los agentes solo reservaron cuatro viajes.
Según contaba The Verge, es la primera vez que Uber desglosa la cifra de pedidos que procede de agentes de IA, y lo hace en un trimestre especialmente bueno en el que el volumen de viajes y pedidos ha generado 4.100 millones de viajes y 59.800 millones de dólares en reservas brutas. Una semana antes, Tony Xu, CEO de la empresa de reparto DoorDash, admitió que los agentes de terceros habían generado unos cientos de pedidos en total, pero no por semana, sino desde que existen.
Mucho ruido y pocas nueces. Muse, el agente personal de Meta, se presentó el 8 de septiembre. En solo una semana ya era la app gratuita más descargada de la App Store en EEUU. Meta asegura que supera los 10 millones de usuarios y que muchos lo usan para comprar.
Instinct, otra startup de agentes personales, cerró su última ronda con una valoración de 10.000 millones de dólares. Frente a ese entusiasmo que vende a estos agentes como los asistentes de compras definitivos, los registros de Uber y DoorDash cuentan otra historia muy distinta: todos esos millones de usuarios, de momento, no se atreven a dejar sus compras en manos de estos agentes y, por tanto, no se convierten en pedidos.
Pedir la cena ya es fácil. El consejero delegado de Uber, Dara Khosrowshahi, dio una pista de por qué sucede esto. Un usuario tarda una media de 50 segundos en reservar un viaje en la app de Uber. Lo mismo sucede cuando repites un pedido favorito en Uber Eats. En ese caso se tarda unos 90 segundos. Con esos tiempos, dejar en un agente de IA lo haga por ti apenas ahorra tiempo o, de hecho, puedes tardar más explicárselo al agente que en hacerlo directamente.
Otra cosa son los trámites que nadie quiere hacer. Dar de baja una suscripción o pelear con una gestión administrativa sí te puede ahorrar horas, y ahí un agente tendría más sentido. También, por ejemplo, en para encontrar ofertas en un determinado producto o en compararlos.
Un gigante dormido. Que por el momento el uso de los agentes de Ia sean algo casi anecdótico en los balances de las grandes plataformas de venta no implica que los agentes vayan a quedarse en esa situación para siempre. Uber se muestra abierto a colaborar con las empresas de IA, pero su gran baza continúa siendo conseguir una experiencia de uso tan sencilla en su app, que simplemente no compense pedírselo a un agente.
El otro frente son las puertas cerradas. Amazon bloqueó a Muse alegando seguridad, y un agente no ve anuncios, ofertas ni productos "gancho" que arrastran a compras compulsivas, y eso pesa en los beneficios de la compañía.

articles.title: La Unión Europea demandó a tres empresas por los retrasos de su nuevo control digital fronterizo
articles.text:
La agencia de la Unión Europea que gestiona los grandes sistemas informáticos de las fronteras, eu-LISA, demandó a IBM, a la francesa Atos y a la italiana Leonardo por los retrasos en el desarrollo del nuevo sistema digital de control fronterizo, informó el Financial Times este lunes 9 de noviembre, citando comunicaciones internas.
El Sistema de Entradas y Salidas (EES, por sus siglas en inglés) registra de forma electrónica el paso de los ciudadanos de países ajenos a la Unión Europea por las fronteras exteriores de los 29 países del espacio Schengen, la zona de libre circulación europea. Reemplazó el sellado manual de los pasaportes y busca detectar a quienes se quedan más tiempo del permitido.
Un juicio presentado en Estonia en diciembre de 2025
Según el resumen del informe del Financial Times , eu-LISA presentó la demanda civil en Estonia, donde tiene su sede. Un portavoz del tribunal del condado de Harju confirmó que aceptó el caso, pero no hay audiencias celebradas ni fijadas. La agencia reconoció el litigio en su informe financiero anual, difundido en julio, y precisó que inició la acción en diciembre de 2025.
En ese documento, citado por el diario, la agencia dijo haber iniciado “los recursos disponibles” para proteger sus intereses financieros ante los retrasos reiterados del consorcio. Eu-LISA y la Comisión Europea aseguraron que el juicio trata de las demoras durante el desarrollo y no del funcionamiento actual del sistema.
El proceso “no tiene impacto” en el funcionamiento del EES, declaró eu-LISA al Financial Times. Una portavoz de la agencia añadió que la disputa no guarda relación con la forma en que opera hoy el sistema.
La agencia adjudicó en 2019 el contrato central del EES a un consorcio con IBM Bélgica, Atos Bélgica y Leonardo. El acuerdo, de seis años, abarcaba la construcción y el mantenimiento del sistema central. Según el diario, su valor subió de 142 millones de euros a 212 millones en 2021.
Cartas de 2021 y 2022 muestran años de disputa
El Financial Times revisó cartas entre las partes. En octubre de 2021, Atos Bélgica e IBM Bélgica cuestionaron “tanto el principio como el cálculo” de una multa impuesta por la agencia: sostuvieron que los atrasos se debieron a factores externos, como la pandemia de covid-19.
Pocos meses después, en febrero de 2022, las tres empresas rechazaron los nuevos plazos fijados por eu-LISA. También criticaron la gobernanza del programa. En marzo de 2022, un representante de IBM aceptó que la agencia retuviera parte de los pagos hasta resolver la cuestión de los daños, según el diario.
El contrato original venció el año pasado y un nuevo consorcio asumió la implementación. Atos, Leonardo e IBM siguieron trabajando en el sistema hasta agosto de este año, según eu-LISA.
El sistema debía funcionar en 2022, según el Financial Times. Comenzó a desplegarse en octubre de 2025 y quedó activo en todos los países de Schengen el 10 de abril de 2026, según eu-LISA. Tras ese día, las asociaciones de aerolíneas Airlines for Europe y de aeropuertos ACI Europe informaron esperas de entre dos y tres horas en los controles fronterizos.
En septiembre, la Unión Europea permitió a al menos nueve países, entre ellos Francia, Alemania e Italia, suspender la toma de datos biométricos si las filas se volvían excesivas, informó Biometric Update. Hasta abril, el sistema había registrado más de 52 millones de entradas y salidas, según un informe del Parlamento Europeo.

articles.title: Il fait tourner une IA avec 2 800 milliards de paramètres sans GPU, mais sa RAM surchauffe
articles.text:
Faire tourner un modèle d'IA en local sans carte graphique, c'est faisable ? Pour un utilisateur qui s'est lancé ce défi, c'est oui. Cependant, pas à n'importe quel prix.
Un utilisateur a publié sur Reddit les caractéristiques de sa machine capable d'exécuter Kimi K3, un modèle d'IA avec 2 800 milliards de paramètres développé par Moonshot AI, uniquement avec un processeur. Il utilise un Xeon Scalable de 3ᵉ génération doté de 40 cœurs et de la mémoire Optane PMem 200, une gamme aujourd'hui abandonnée. Le tout, sans carte graphique.
Une configuration professionnelle
Ce modèle n'est pas conçu pour un usage à domicile. Moonshot AI recommande des moteurs d'inférence adaptés aux datacenters, et même la plus petite quantification produite par la communauté demande au moins 610 Go de RAM. La mémoire Optane d'occasion est l'un des rares moyens d'atteindre une telle capacité sur une machine à domicile. Les prix de la DRAM ayant fortement augmenté, la mémoire Optane coûte selon l'utilisateur « une fraction » du prix d'une quantité équivalente de DRAM.
Intel a lancé la gamme Optane Persistent Memory 200 en 2020, pour ses Xeon Scalable de 3ᵉ génération, en capacités de 128, 256 et 512 Go. Sur les plateformes à deux sockets, elle fonctionne à une fréquence plus élevée que la première génération et peut offrir en moyenne jusqu'à 32 % de bande passante en plus.
La mémoire Optane peut fonctionner en Memory Mode ou en App Direct Mode. En Memory Mode, l'Optane sert de mémoire système et la DRAM de cache.
Moins de 1 token par seconde
Mais voilà, les performances sont nettement inférieures à celles d'une configuration avec de la DRAM classique. Le montage monte à 0,85 token par seconde avec une quantification en 1 bit, et 0,75 avec une quantification en 3 bits. Sur Reddit, un commentaire indique qu'il juge ce débit très faible, selon lui, à ce rythme-là, une tâche de 50 000 tokens prendrait environ 13 heures.
Une autre configuration atteignait environ 4 tokens par seconde, mais la comparaison est difficile à faire. La configuration en question était dotée d'une RTX 3060, utilisant le Memory Mode et une quantification en 2 bits, en faisant tourner Kimi K2.5, un modèle plus petit et plus ancien, avec « seulement » 1 000 milliards de paramètres.
Attention, ça chauffe !
L'auteur d'un autre montage a également dû gérer la chaleur. Lors de tâches prolongées, les barrettes Optane deviennent « extrêmement chaudes » selon lui, ce qui pourrait mettre en danger la DRAM voisine. Un refroidissement actif des barrettes semble alors obligatoire. Afin de ramener la température à un niveau acceptable, il a dirigé deux ventilateurs de 12 watts vers ses barrettes.
- Chat dans différentes langues, dont le français
- Générer, traduire et obtenir un résumé de texte
- Générer, optimiser et corriger du code
- Excellente compréhension des consignes complexes
- Très bon niveau en rédaction
- Analyse de longs documents efficace
Intel prévoit en effet un flux d'air forcé pour cette mémoire, à entre 2,4 et 2,7 mètres par seconde, soit ce que l'on trouve dans un datacenter, mais pas dans un PC personnel.
Chaque module de RAM consomme entre 12 et 15 W, selon les conditions d'utilisation. Cela représenterait avec quatre barrettes, jusqu'à 60 W de chaleur à proximité immédiate de la mémoire du système. À 83 °C, le throttling (limitation de fréquence) se démarre, et à 85 °C, la mise en sécurité arrête les modules pour surchauffe. À titre de comparaison, la mémoire serveur DDR4 classique s'arrête à 95 °C.
Source : Tom's Hardware

articles.title: Néo-rétro : pourquoi les marques ressuscitent la 2CV et la 4L en électrique — Frandroid
articles.text:
Lors du Mondial de l’Automobile 2026, qui s’est tenu en octobre dernier, un constat très clair s’est imposé sur les stands des constructeurs : le design automobile opère un grand retour en arrière. Pour convaincre les automobilistes de passer à la voiture électrique, les marques ont décidé de réveiller leurs modèles les plus légendaires, misant sur l’émotion plutôt que sur de simples promesses d’autonomie.
Le grand hold-up nostalgique de Renault
Renault s’est clairement imposé comme le chef de file de ce mouvement. Après le succès de la nouvelle R5 électrique, la marque au losange multiplie les clins d’œil avec des concepts surprenants. On retient notamment la réinterprétation de la 4L JP4 des années 1980, sorte de buggy de plage sans portes arrière, mais aussi le concept Espace qui ressuscite le profil typique du monospace des années 1990. On y croise aussi le concept Gordini, qui reprend les bandes blanches de la fameuse R8, ou encore une sculpture annonçant la future Alpine A110 électrique, épaulée par le concept A310 Vision.
Face à des véhicules parfois jugés trop lisses ou froids, le design d’autrefois apporte une identité forte. Même Peugeot s’est prêté au jeu avec son i16 Concept, évocation musclée de la mythique 205 Turbo 16 du Groupe B, affichant une fiche technique folle de 816 chevaux pour un 0 à 100 km/h abattu en 1,6 seconde. D’un autre côté, cette débauche de puissance sert surtout à faire parler : sous cette robe se cache en réalité la base technique de la future 208 électrique de série.
Citroën capitule et ressuscite la 2CV
Longtemps réticente à l’idée de recycler des design d’époque, la marque aux chevrons a fini par céder face au carton commercial de son rival historique. Citroën a ainsi dévoilé un concept de 2CV électrique particulièrement fidèle au modèle d’origine de 1948, avec ses phares ronds, sa capote en toile et sa silhouette si caractéristique. La marque prévoit même une version fourgonnette pour les professionnels d’ici 2028, avec un prix cible sous la barre des 15 000 euros.
Même Fiat s’engouffre dans la brèche en osant ressusciter le Multipla sous la forme du concept Multiplay. Ce modèle hybride entre le SUV et le pickup tente de faire oublier la réputation esthétique compliquée du monospace original tout en conservant son habitabilité légendaire. Reste à savoir si cette vague nostalgique suffira à convaincre les acheteurs sur le long terme, une fois l’effet de surprise passé.

articles.title: Startup ecosystem sees sharp rise VC inflow;Building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand
articles.text:
Startup ecosystem sees sharp rise VC inflow; Building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand
Industry watchers expect that a post-US midterm slowdown in AI funding could work in favor of Indian startups.
Happy Diwali,
Financial services firm Angel One has climbed to the position of India’s second-largest stockbroker by active client count, according to the latest National Stock Exchange (NSE) data.
By the end of October, the brokerage reported 69.98 lakh active investors, commanding a 14.97% share of the exchange's total 4.67 crore active client base.
Meanwhile, benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty edged lower during Sunday’s special Muhurat trading session as profit-taking halted a seven-day rally, snapping an eight-year Diwali winning streak.
The BSE Sensex dipped 28.62 points, or 0.04%, to settle at 80,999.40, with 16 of its constituents ending higher and 14 lower. During the special session on Diwali, it hit a high of 81,442.11, surging 414.09 points, or 0.51%, PTI reported.
In the world of technology, a new cybercrime ‘gold rush’ is emerging as more and more people use the internet. Per a BBC Future article, around two billion people are expected to come online for the first time by 2030, but this digital leap comes with serious risks. Rather than entering a simple web, these newcomers are stepping straight into sophisticated cybercrime traps powered by AI, automated scams, and localised fraud.
As CrowdStrike’s Zeki Turedi notes, while the internet unlocks life-changing opportunities, today's digital landscape is far more complex and dangerous for first-time users than the one earlier generations navigated.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Startup ecosystem sees sharp rise VC inflow
- Building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand
Here’s your trivia for today: What iconic consumer luggage company was founded in 1971 by Dilip Piramal, named after a Roman goddess of victory? (Scroll down for answer)
Venture capital
Startup ecosystem sees sharp rise VC inflow
November began on a positive note for the Indian startup ecosystem with venture capital inflow seeing a sharp rise. In total, the amount was $263 million across 23 deals against $115 million raised a week ago.
This week marked two notable milestones for the Indian startup ecosystem. Total weekly funding comfortably crossed the $200 million mark—rebounding after a four-week slump below that threshold. Simultaneously, jewellery brand GIVA snapped the ecosystem’s month-long megadeal drought with a $100 million round.
Key takeaways:
- Industry watchers expect that a post-US midterm slowdown in AI funding could work in favor of Indian startups.
- Consumer AI startup EloElo Group raised $80 million from Hornbill Capital, NBCUniversal, MIT Investment Co, Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners.
- Peppermint Robotics raised Rs 100 crore (~$10.5 million) from pi Ventures, Crane Venture Partners and Asiana Fund.
Social impact
Building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand
While pursuing a master’s in Social Entrepreneurship at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Pavitra Joshi decided to return to the mountains, determined to tackle regional challenges through enterprise.
What began as a classroom project soon evolved into KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand. In 2021, Joshi turned the initiative into a full-time venture alongside his mother, Sangeeta, and Anuj Sharma, founder and CEO of impact incubator Alsisar Impact.
Key takeaways:
- KumaonKhand’s product range is largely focused on hemp seed and hemp fibre. From hemp seed, they process hemp seed oil, which is in high demand in the skincare and pharmaceutical industries.
- The company uses hemp in its own skincare range: lip balms, face creams, moisturisers, and handmade, sulphate-free soaps. It also makes hemp protein powder that has 44 grams of protein per 100 grams, making it one of the best sources of vegan protein.
- Built using hemp-based materials, KumaonKhand’s factory incorporates hemp plaster and leftover hemp stalks as construction material. The material, known as hempcrete, is also being developed into a pre-mix plaster combining hemp and lime.
News & updates
- Binance hack: Days after Binance saw a massive heist of $6.3 billion, the cryptocurrency exchange said that its finance chief Kaiser Ng is leaving the company to pursue another venture. Justin Yek, a longtime finance executive who was most recently vice-president of finance at Airwallex, is taking over as CFO.
- Infra push: Adani Enterprises Ltd plans an annual capital expenditure of Rs 35,000 crore to Rs 40,000 crore over the next few years, positioning airports, data centres, and a planned PVC complex as its primary growth drivers amid a broader infrastructure push.
What you should watch out for
