articles.title: Nerding out about 40 years of Zelda with Canada's Maitreyi Ramakrishnan
articles.text:
Maitreyi Ramakrishnan is in her element.
As we get ready for our interview, the Canadian actress marvels at Nintendo’s new store-within-a-store at Toronto’s flagship EB Games on Yonge St. “That’s a big Mimikyu!” the Never Have I Ever star says excitedly, referring to a plushie of the ragdoll Pokémon that resembles Pikachu. “I fear I need that. There’s a lot right now!”
It’s her first time seeing the store following a press tour for Best of the Best, her new Netflix comedy about collegiate Bollywood dance. With that having wrapped, the Mississauga native’s focus is now all on Nintendo — or, more specifically, the company’s highly-anticipated Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. It launched Thursday, the morning of our chat, and she’s clearly riding the high.
“I’m blessed. I get to be Nintendo’s favourite child,” she says. Indeed, her love of Nintendo has been well-documented over the years, from repeated posts about visiting New York’s Nintendo Store to appearing in numerous Nintendo ads with her family.
And when we last spoke with Ramakrishnan at the 2023 midnight launch for Tears of the Kingdom, she mentioned that she has a fondness for Ocarina of Time, specifically, because she relates her “annoying younger sibling” relationship with her brother to the dynamic between Link and Navi. (She’s since even gotten a tattoo of the fairy.)
“With my brother, just getting to watch him play the game again and let him have fun is just great. I think for me personally, I am really excited to just hear the soundtrack again because I think some of the best Legend of Zelda songs in the whole franchise come from this game. I mean, ‘Song of Storms‘ is one of my favourite like Nintendo pieces of music, so getting to hear that again is really cool,” she says.
“Because my brother and I both like music, the feature where you can play an instrument and let your Switch hear the song — I’m excited to try that out with my brother because he plays guitar, I play piano. So I think that’ll be really cool.”
As we chat, she picks up a Pro Controller to play through the opening of the game in Kokiri Forest on a big demo station. While Nintendo let her try out the game earlier this year, she’s still in awe at the experience.
“Objectively, this is gorgeous, and as a cosplayer, the ideas are flowing in my head. They really did an insane job when it comes to the graphics and the visual effects. One of my favourite details is actually the water — every body of water being a distinct shade of green-slash-blue, depending on where you are,” she says. “And the fact that his tunic is so detailed, and you can see it get wet after. Those details matter to me — little things that make a big difference.”
Notably, all of this comes during Nintendo’s Zelda 40th anniversary celebrations. For Ramakrishnan, that longevity comes down to the series’ timeless storytelling.
“I just think it’s really cool that certain franchises like The Legend of Zelda have existed for so long and have been such a core staple of like pop-culture, especially in the video game world. It’s really cool to me that lines like ‘it’s dangerous to go alone!’ still remain so iconic today to young kiddos that can’t fathom the concept of 40 years yet, but they will in time. It’s truly a testament to good storytelling,” she says.
“And with all the Legend of Zelda games, there’s such an immersive world for people to dive into, and that’s what makes me excited about this remake. This remake helps push, for another however many years, the love for The Legend of Zelda franchise, for Nintendo as a whole, for the gamers that really want a good hero’s journey. When I tell people what this game is about, it’s a typical hero’s journey. ‘Young boy wants to leave his town to go fight the big bad, save everyone, save this princess, and also figure out why he’s different than everybody else in his little town.’ Hero’s journey! Who doesn’t love that?”
View this post on Instagram
All of this talk reminds me of a Pokémon 30th anniversary video that Ramakrishnan took part in earlier this year alongside the likes of Lady Gaga, Jisoo and Trevor Noah. In it, the celebrities named their favourite Pokémon, with Ramakrishnan shouting out the Gen IV Electric Type Luxray.
Since we’re now celebrating a different Nintendo anniversary, I had to ask: who is Ramakrishnan’s favourite Zelda character?
“No one’s asked me this yet!” she admits. “I feel like I’m supposed to say Navi because of my tattoo. So Navi, yes, but also, of course, my baddie Midna [from Twilight Princess]. Midna, the GOAT. So I have to give it to her, too. And Lady Riju, but specifically Tears of the Kingdom Lady Riju.”
Given Nintendo’s push into film adaptations with the likes of Illumination’s Mario series and next year’s live-action Zelda, as well Ramakrishnan’s role in next month’s The Angry Birds Movie 3, the actress even throws her hat into playing Riju. “I do think I’d be a really cool Lady Riju. I think I’d be really, really sick,” she says. “That’s honestly just one of my dream cosplays. So, hey, one day we’ll see it on my Instagram!”
But she admits that she’d be happy for Nintendo to put her into anything. “I just said earlier today that I will be a Goomba that gets stomped on, and if that’s my credit, I’m okay with that. I will take the crumbs that they give me, and I’m okay with that. I’m happy to be a part of any video game adaptation that honestly respects the IP and understands the fanbase.”
Clearly, she’s good at manifesting things. In a recent interview with Polygon, she joked that Nintendo remastered Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door, one of her favourite games, just for her. Since we’re here talking about this brand-new version of Ocarina of Time and Nintendo has teased that more remakes are on the way, I ask what other classic games Ramakrishnan would next like to see.
“Give me some Nintendogs. Nintendogs, bring it back! Or Cooking Mama, because I can’t cook. But in Cooking Mama, call me Gordon Ramsay, I’m up there!” she says. “Tell me that wouldn’t be awesome! I want that comfort whimsy right now. I think that would be really great.”
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is now available exclusively on Nintendo Switch 2.
Best of the Best is now streaming on Netflix. The Angry Birds Movie 3 flies into theatres on Dec. 23.

articles.title: Smartphones Galaxy : Samsung teste un abonnement payant pour ses outils IA
articles.text:
Depuis le lancement des Galaxy S24, le géant coréen propose ses fonctionnalités d’intelligence artificielle gratuitement sur ses smartphones compatibles, même si l’entreprise a toujours laissé un flou sur la question. Mais on commence à y voir plus clair, puisque Samsung teste en ce moment une formule payante de son IA dans le cadre d’un programme d’accès anticipé. Certains utilisateurs peuvent en effet s’inscrire pour tester ce service payant, sachant que les dépenses réalisées durant cette phase de test leur seront remboursées à la fin du programme.
Une version gratuite limitée et des fonctionnalités inédites pour les abonnés payants
Source : SammyGuru
La formule gratuite continuerait de donner accès aux fonctions standard de Galaxy AI, mais ces dernières pourraient bientôt être soumises à des limites d’utilisation. Une fois les quotas épuisés, il faudra acheter des packs de crédits pour continuer à en profiter. Les utilisateurs gratuits retrouvent ainsi les fonctionnalités suivantes :
- Assistance à la navigation
- Now Brief (résumé instantané)
- Creative Studio
- Capture intelligente
- Clavier Samsung
- Assistant photo
- Agent personnel
L’abonnement payant « Max » offrirait des quotas quatre fois plus élevés et débloquerait également d’autres fonctionnalités :
- Génération de vidéo
- Bixby Action
- Briefing quotidien
Source : SammyGuru
Des prix (en dollars) ont également pu être dénichés en fouillant dans le code de l’application : 4,99 dollars par mois ou 47,99 dollars par an, même si ces tarifs restent pour l’instant indicatifs.
Les Galaxy S27 servis en premier ?
Le code de l’application montre que les fonctionnalités évoquées plus haut seraient prévues pour 2027, ce qui suggère que les nouveautés pourraient être lancées avec les Galaxy S27 en début d’année prochaine. On ne sait pas encore dans quelles régions du monde cet abonnement serait disponible. À minima en Corée du Sud et aux États-Unis, mais on connaît les difficultés qu’ont les géants de la tech à adapter leurs fonctionnalités aux réglementations européennes.
À lire : Quels smartphones Samsung vont recevoir les nouveautés Galaxy IA de One UI 9 ?
Le nouveau service de Samsung étant encore en accès anticipé, on imagine qu’il finira par arriver sur d’autres appareils de la marque. Pour Samsung, les abonnements sont un moyen de diversifier ses revenus à l’heure où la crise des composants vient réduire ses marges sur certains de ses produits. Reste maintenant à voir comment les utilisateurs de smartphones Samsung répondront à une telle offre.

articles.title: Apple lanzará HomeView por 299 dólares, pero instalarlo en casa cuesta al menos 358 dólares
articles.text:
Apple pondrá a la venta el 13 de noviembre HomeView, su primera pantalla para el hogar, a USD 299 en sus dos versiones, de mesa y de pared. El modelo de pared no incluye soporte ni fuente de alimentación, por lo que el costo mínimo sube a USD 358, según el cálculo de Tom’s Guide.
HomeView tiene una pantalla cuadrada de 7 pulgadas, el chip A18 y una cámara de 12 megapíxeles con encuadre automático. Reconoce el rostro de hasta seis personas y muestra a cada una sus mensajes, calendario y recordatorios, siempre que su iPhone o iPad esté cerca y desbloqueado, según la ficha que compiló MacRumors.
Funciona con Siri AI, la versión del asistente de Apple que responde de forma conversacional y llegó con iOS 27. Controla dispositivos del hogar, hace llamadas de FaceTime, reproduce música y guía recetas con temporizadores. Puede reemplazar a un HomePod, pero no a un iPhone, porque varias funciones dependen de uno cercano.
Un precio que cambia según la instalación
El soporte con alimentación USB-C para la versión de pared cuesta USD 59, según Tom’s Guide. Otra opción, para dejar la instalación sin cables a la vista, vale USD 79 y requiere un electricista, que Apple recomienda contratar a través de un acuerdo con la empresa de seguridad ADT.
El HomePod mini, que también incorpora Siri AI pero no tiene pantalla, cuesta USD 149, la mitad que HomeView, según MacRumors.
La pantalla se venderá en Estados Unidos, el Reino Unido, Canadá, Nueva Zelanda, Australia, la India y Singapur, según MacRumors. No llegará a la Unión Europea porque Siri AI todavía no está disponible allí en iPhone, iPad ni Apple Watch. Apple dice que trabaja con el bloque para encontrar una vía.
Qué se probó y qué falta
Las primeras impresiones de The Verge, Wired y otros medios salieron de demostraciones en el evento del 13 de octubre. Según un resumen del sitio AppDook sobre siete notas, ningún periodista pudo probar por su cuenta el reconocimiento de rostro ni de voz: un portavoz de Apple lo mostró en equipos ya vinculados.
Wired escribió que todo depende de si Siri cumple y recordó que el asistente no tiene el mejor historial. Según The Mac Observer, la letra chica de Apple indica que las funciones que corren en sus servidores, entre ellas Siri AI, tienen límites diarios y que el acceso ampliado “estará disponible por una tarifa en el futuro”.
El código de iOS 27.3 apunta a chatbots
La versión de prueba de iOS 27.3 incluye una categoría llamada “Apps conversacionales” para HomeView, según el investigador de código conocido como pdfu. The Verge planteó que podrían sumarse chatbots como ChatGPT o Claude, aunque el código no indica qué aplicaciones ni cuándo.
La misma versión agrega audio bidireccional y gestión de sesiones, que según pdfu todavía no están conectados del todo. También suma una protección contra suplantación: tras tres intentos fallidos, la pantalla pedirá autenticarse con un iPhone, y habrá bloqueos de espera creciente, desde una hora en el segundo hasta ocho en el cuarto.
Apple no anunció ninguna de estas funciones ni dio fechas, según The Verge. HomeView llegará a las tiendas el viernes 13 de noviembre.
Apple excluye a HomeView del mercado europeo por falta de Siri AI
Apple confirmó que HomeView, su nuevo hub para el hogar inteligente de 299 dólares, no llegará a la Unión Europea. La razón: el dispositivo depende de Siri AI, el asistente conversacional que aún no opera en los iPhone de esa región.
Sin esa inteligencia artificial, HomeView pierde funciones clave como el control por voz y la búsqueda de contenido. Apple afirmó que negocia con la UE, sin precisar plazos ni el origen exacto del obstáculo. El equipo saldrá a la venta el 13 de noviembre en ocho países, ninguno europeo.

articles.title: Dejé de escribir a ChatGPT, Claude y Gemini durante una semana y descubrí una mejor forma de usar la IA
articles.text:
Escribir instrucciones para ChatGPT, Claude o Gemini se ha convertido en una costumbre para los que usan herramientas cada día, pero la cosa se complica cuando tenemos que explicar algo un poco difuso. Por eso, la periodista Mahnoor Faisal decidió probar durante una semana una alternativa bastante sencilla: dejar de escribir sus peticiones y empezar a hablar de manera natural con la IA.
Según cuenta en XDA Developers, el experimento le permitió descubrir que podía proporcionar más información a los chatbots sin dedicar tanto tiempo a preparar sus instrucciones. Para ello, utilizó dos funciones que conviene diferenciar: el dictado y el modo de voz. Sí, las dos permiten olvidarse del teclado, pero no sirven exactamente para lo mismo.
Hablar con la IA le permitió explicar mejor sus ideas, pero también descubrir otras nuevas
El dictado fue especialmente útil cuando necesitaba dar instrucciones largas. Faisal explica que, aunque escribe bastante rápido, muchas veces sus pensamientos van por delante de sus dedos y termina omitiendo detalles por no tener que escribirlos. Al hablar podía contar todo lo que necesitaba, incluidos los intentos anteriores o los requisitos de una tarea, algo que le vino especialmente bien al utilizar Claude Code para programar.
También recurrió a Wispr Flow, una herramienta que va más allá de transcribir palabras porque elimina muletillas y organiza el texto automáticamente. Sin embargo, para preparar artículos, estudiar o ensayar entrevistas encontró más interesante el modo de voz, que permite mantener una conversación con el chatbot, interrumpir sus respuestas y plantear nuevas preguntas sobre la marcha.
De hecho, una de las aplicaciones que destaca es Gemini Notebook, antes NotebookLM, donde utiliza sus apuntes universitarios para consultar dudas en voz alta. En lugar de limitarse a pedir una explicación, puede detenerla cuando algo no le queda claro y pedir que se lo cuenten de otra manera, mientras que para preparar entrevistas utiliza la IA como interlocutor y practica con preguntas que quizás no habría previsto.
La periodista reconoce que ninguna de estas funciones mejora por sí misma los modelos de inteligencia artificial. La diferencia está en cómo los utiliza: el dictado le permite aportar más contexto y las conversaciones de voz le ayudan a desarrollar ideas que todavía no tiene del todo claras, sin depender de encontrar las palabras perfectas antes de empezar.

articles.title: N-able takes cloud platform offline after 30+ "zero-days" published
articles.text:
N-able has taken its hosted N-central environments offline and urged on-premises customers to shut down their servers after a security researcher publicly disclosed more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities, including exploits that could let attackers take over vulnerable systems.
Security researcher Sean Bales disclosed the vulnerabilities late Sunday, November 8, and published a GitHub repository called Able2Shell containing proof-of-concept exploits for the flaws.
N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely.
The researcher says the vulnerabilities were tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release version of the software, and believes most, if not all, flaws also affect earlier versions.
Bales also confirmed to BleepingComputer that the discovery of the vulnerabilities was AI-assisted.
The disclosed vulnerabilities include authentication bypasses, credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws.
One of the most critical exploit chains abuses an unauthenticated XXE vulnerability in N-central's service-import functionality to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands on the server as the nable user.
The same exploit can also create an enabled Default Administrator account with attacker-controlled credentials, providing rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface.
Bales shared a video demonstration of this exploit, showing terminal output reporting successful administrator account creation, login authentication, access to protected administrative functionality, and remote command execution as the nable user.
Other disclosed exploits include a stored XSS that can execute commands as root when an administrator views malicious patch metadata, and a privilege-escalation flaw that allows code running under the nable account to execute commands as root.
Bales confirmed to BleepingComputer that the unauthenticated XXE-to-RCE exploit was the most critical of the disclosed vulnerabilities.
N-able takes servers offline worldwide
After the disclosure, N-able announced a critical security incident and took its hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific regions.
While BleepingComputer has not independently verified all the reported vulnerabilities, N-able confirmed it is developing a hotfix to address the security issues, lending credence to the researcher's claims that at least some of the flaws are legitimate zero-days.
"N-able is actively responding to non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central late Sunday night, November 8, found by an independent researcher," N-able told BleepingComputer.
"As a precautionary measure, we took our Hosted N-central environment offline today, November 9, and provided guidance to customers operating on-premises N-central servers to temporarily take their servers offline until further notice."
"Our Security, Engineering, and Operations teams are actively working to implement the necessary remediation. At this time, we have not observed active exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Protecting our customers and their environments remains our highest priority, and we will provide additional updates as they become available."
In a subsequent status update, N-able said it was continuing to develop and validate a hotfix and had found no evidence of active exploitation or unauthorized data access.
While the N-central classic environment is unavailable, N-able said Ecoverse services accessed through N-able Login remain operational.
N-able has not provided an estimate of when N-central will come back online but says it plans to publish updates every four hours, or sooner if new information becomes available.
Researcher claims previous vulnerability reports ignored
Bales told BleepingComputer that he deliberately released the N-central vulnerabilities without notifying N-able beforehand because the company allegedly failed to address vulnerabilities he had previously reported in a different N-able product.
According to Bales, he disclosed two unrelated remote code execution vulnerabilities and a privilege-escalation flaw approximately five to six months ago, but those vulnerabilities remain unpatched.
"I disclosed 2 unrelated RCEs for a different N-able product, along with a priv esc vulnerability 5 or 6 months ago. These have yet to be patched. I did not disclose any of the 0-days I posted last night," Bales told BleepingComputer.
He also claims to have sent follow-up emails over the past four to six weeks without a response.
Bales says his previous experience with N-able's vulnerability disclosure process and that "they don't take disclosure seriously" led him to publish the N-central zero-day exploits.
However, he said these exploits target a different N-able product than the ones he previously disclosed.
The researcher also claimed that he received no payment through N-able's bug bounty platform for his earlier reports.
Bales confirmed that N-able executives, including the company's CEO and CTO, contacted him following the disclosure and asked him to remove the GitHub repository and work with the company.
"They did not threaten me or anything though. Only asked to take down the repo, work with them, etc."
BleepingComputer asked N-able about Bales' allegations concerning the previously disclosed vulnerabilities, their patching status, and the alleged lack of responses to his follow-up emails.
However, the company did not address those questions, providing only the statement concerning the N-central security incident and the precautionary shutdown.
The previously reported vulnerabilities are not included in the publicly released Able2Shell repository and allegedly remain unpatched.

articles.title: L'audace, c'est ça : ce PC portable chinois mise sur un Intel Core i3... lancé il y a 8 ans
articles.text:
Propre sur lui, le nouveau BMAX MaxBook X15S Pro est un ordinateur portable chinois comme on en voit émerger des dizaines. Orienté bureautique et équipé de 12 Go de RAM, cet appareil fort commun aurait pu passer inaperçu. C’était sans compter sur son choix en matière de processeur.
Voilà un PC portable pas tout à fait comme les autres… Non pas grâce à son design, son écran ou une fonctionnalité particulière, mais parce qu’il s’appuie sur un processeur mobile que l’on ne s’attendait clairement plus à voir sur le marché en cette fin d’année 2026 : le Core i3 8109U. Oui, vous avez bien lu, nous parlons d’une puce Intel « Coffee Lake », lancée en 2018. Une éternité dans le monde informatique.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Quand Coffee Lake refait surface… Après sa mise au rebut
Lancé plus précisément au second trimestre 2018, l’Intel Core i3 8109U a pour particularité d’être complètement abandonné par Intel, qui l’a retiré de son catalogue il y a déjà bien longtemps. Pire, la firme a arrêté de déployer des mises à jour pour cette référence en juin 2025. Dans ce contexte, il est très surprenant de voir cette vieille puce « Coffee Lake » faire un come-back, encore plus dans un appareil flambant neuf. Nul doute que BMAX a trouvé un vieux stock qui traînait à prix cassé.
Pour rappel, le Core i3 8109U se limite à une toute petite configuration dual-core. On y retrouve donc deux cœurs et 4 threads cadencés entre 3,0 et 3,6 GHz et 4 Mo de cache L3. Gravé en 14 nm (une finesse de gravure utilisée par Intel entre 2014 et 2021, avec un arrêt définitif des livraisons début 2024), ce processeur intègre une partie graphique Iris Plus Graphics 655 et affiche un TDP de 28 W. À tout point de vue (performances, iGPU, consommation, I/O…) le Core i3 8109U est donc dépassé face aux standards actuels.
Un petit bout de 2018 en 2026
Quoi qu’il en soit, cette puce de 2018 se loge dans un PC de 2026. Enfin là aussi c’est vite dit. Car le BMAX MaxBook X15S Pro affiche également un certain retard technique. Équipé d’un écran LCD IPS Full HD (1920 par 1080 pixels) et 60 Hz de 15,6 pouces, au format 16:9, l’appareil intègre 12 Go de mémoire vive (DDR4 ou LPDDR3 puisque le Core i3 8109U n’est pas compatible DDR5) et 256 ou 512 Go de SSD (PCIe Gen 3 selon toute logique).
On y retrouve pour le reste trois ports USB-A 3.0, un port USB-C, une sortie HDMI, une prise d’alimentation, un lecteur de cartes micro-SD et une prise casque. La connectivité est assurée par un antique modem Wi-Fi 5 / Bluetooth 5.0 et BMAX nous promet jusqu’à 7 heures de lecture vidéo en local via une batterie de 51,3 Wh.
Une fiche technique flétrie… mais un prix étonnamment élevé : comptez 469,99 euros en promotion pour ce modèle normalement vendu 539,99 euros au catalogue européen du constructeur chinois. Aucun intérêt, donc, sauf si vous mourez d'envie de renouer avec les contraintes techniques que nous connaissions sur l’entrée de gamme il y a 8 ans.
Source : VideoCardz / BMAX

articles.title: Pour le pré Black Friday Darty fait -240 € sur un ultraportable Asus OLED 14" avec Core Ultra 5 pour travailler sans se prendre la tête — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’Asus Vivobook S14 est un PC portable à la fois léger et puissant, pensé pour travailler au quotidien et être facile à transporter, avec comme atout principal un écran OLED et un processeur Intel Core Ultra 5 qui suffit largement pour la bureautique. Il coche pas mal de cases pour plaire au plus grand nombre. Il lui manque quelques options, mais la promotion de 23 % chez Darty pendant le pré-Black Friday permet de fermer plus facilement les yeux sur ces quelques petits manquements.
Les atouts de l’Asus Vivobook S14 OLED
- Son écran OLED de 14 pouces au format 16:10
- Son processeur Intel Core Ultra 5, avec 16 Go de RAM et 512 Go de stockage
- Son poids plume de 1,3 kg qui facilite son transport
Chez Darty, le prix classique de l’Asus Vivobook S14 OLED est de 1 019,99 euros, mais avec le Black Friday qui s’invite en avance, vous pouvez le commander pour 779,99 euros jusqu’au 30 novembre.
Une puce Intel Core Ultra 5 efficace pour travailler
L’Asus Vivobook S14 OLED ne cherche pas à jouer dans la catégorie des stations de travail, mais sa configuration fait qu’il peut convenir à une grande majorité des utilisateurs. Il embarque un Intel Core Ultra 5 226V de génération Lunar Lake, avec 8 cœurs et une fréquence maximale de 4,5 GHz. Le processeur est accompagné de 16 Go de RAM LPDDR5X et d’un SSD NVMe de 512 Go. C’est une combinaison réactive pour lancer des applications, naviguer sur Internet, travailler sur de gros documents et jongler entre plusieurs logiciels.
La partie graphique est confiée à l’Intel Arc 130V, intégrée au processeur, qui peut gérer l’affichage, la lecture de vidéos en haute définition et même quelques jeux peu gourmands. N’en attendez pas pour autant les performances d’un PC gamer. En revanche, le NPU intégré au processeur lui permet d’obtenir la certification Copilot+ PC. Bref, c’est une machine pensée pour la productivité. Mais il faut faire attention à la mémoire vive de ce PC qui est soudée, ce qui limite l’évolutivité de l’appareil.
Un écran OLED et un format léger qui séduisent
Le principal atout de cet Asus Vivobook S14 reste son écran OLED de 14 pouces qui affiche une définition WUXGA de 1 920 x 1 200 pixels au format 16:10 avec un taux de rafraîchissement classique de 60 Hz. La dalle couvre un large espace colorimétrique (DCI-P3), ce qui est un atout pour regarder des films et des séries dans de bonnes conditions, sans oublier son but premier : travailler ou encore faire des retouches photo occasionnelles. Sa luminosité annoncée à 300 cd/m² reste classique et peut montrer ses limites dans les environnements très lumineux. L’écran est aussi brillant et non tactile, mieux vaut le savoir avant de passer commande.
Côté format, ce Vivobook S14 mérite bien son étiquette d’ultraportable, avec un châssis en aluminium. Avec seulement 1,3 kg sur la balance et une épaisseur de 15,9 mm, vous comprenez à quel point il est facile de l’emmener dans un sac. La connectique est aussi un bon point avec deux ports USB-A, deux ports USB-C Thunderbolt 4, une sortie HDMI 2.1, le tout accompagné du Wi-Fi 7 et du Bluetooth 5.4. Il propose une webcam infrarouge compatible avec la reconnaissance faciale Windows Hello. Mais il a aussi ses petits défauts avec un clavier qui n’est pas rétroéclairé et un chargeur absent dans la boîte. Il vous faudra donc prévoir un adaptateur USB-C Power Delivery avec une puissance comprise entre 45 et 65 watts.

articles.title: Ce que la fusée géante Starship va tenter dans les airs minute par minute, si tout se passe bien
articles.text:
C’est reparti pour un tour. Sauf coup de théâtre, SpaceX tentera en fin de semaine la capture de l’étage supérieur (Ship) avec les bras de sa tour de lancement. Un succès marquerait un jalon important dans le développement du Starship, et serait par ailleurs l’étape ultime pour la mise au point d’un lanceur intégralement réutilisable.
Le vol s’annonce intense : le vaisseau bouclera 14 tours de la Terre à 275 km d’altitude pendant plus de 22 heures, le temps d’aligner son orbite avec la base texane de Starbase.
Dans l’espace, il déploiera 26 satellites Starlink V3, dont trois dotés de caméras pour inspecter son bouclier thermique. Les images aideront SpaceX à valider l’état du vaisseau lors de trois points de contrôle (près d’Hawaï et au large du Chili) ; au moindre doute, SpaceX pourra écourter la mission et faire amerrir le Ship dans des zones dégagées du Pacifique.
Si tout roule, le vaisseau quittera son orbite pour entamer un retour inédit au-dessus de la terre ferme. Après sa rentrée dans l’atmosphère, il survolera le nord du Mexique et le sud du Texas, puis rallumera ses moteurs pour se redresser à la verticale et se glisser entre les bras mécaniques de la tour, 22 heures et 32 minutes après son décollage.
Rendez-vous dans la nuit du vendredi 13 au samedi 14 novembre pour le décollage, et dans la soirée du 14 pour voir le retour du Ship.

articles.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
articles.text:
The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.
It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.
But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.
Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.
One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.
Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.
Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.
Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.
Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).
Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?
Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.
But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.
So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.
But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title: What could China get from Jensen Huang?
articles.text:
It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump.
What could China get from Jensen Huang?
The Nvidia CEO has been in a unique position to to influence AI export controls.
What could China get from Jensen Huang?
The Nvidia CEO has been in a unique position to to influence AI export controls.
This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry.
Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls.
Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry
US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. Alibaba is reportedly one of Megaspeed’s top customers.
“It’s not entirely surprising that the CEO of arguably one of the most important, if not the most important, AI chip companies is the target of some sort of intelligence-gathering from countries like China,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at CSET, said in an interview with The Verge, adding that an alleged spy would potentially be interested in “better understanding what the US government is thinking on export controls,” as well as gathering information on Huang’s conversations with the Trump administration, attempting to influence policy, and gathering information on trade secrets like “who’s buying Nvidia’s chips, who’s getting them first, what’s coming next in terms of AI chips.”
Megaspeed’s sister company, headquartered in Malaysia, spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, the Times reported, citing trade records from trade platform ImportGenius. The transaction sizes were outside the norm for a small company, particularly when Nvidia chips are so difficult to get.
”Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job”
Nvidia spokespeople had said Huang’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was strictly business. Their interactions were described as “not unusual or unexpected” in statements to the press. Nvidia’s line was, “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.”
But at some point, their relationship became personal. In June 2024, just before Megaspeed became an Nvidia customer, photos show the two with other AI executives at a bar in Taipei after a local trade show; the following year, they reportedly had a business dinner in Taipei with others as well. But in private, according to US officials cited by the Times, the two’s relationship raised alarm bells for the US government — they had reportedly been surveilling the Megaspeed executive for months, if not longer, and that’s how it came out that she was in close contact with Huang.
The revelation is particularly concerning because of Huang’s lobbying role. He’d been trying to convince the Trump administration and Congress to loosen export controls for sending advanced semiconductors to China, ostensibly so that Nvidia could sell more chips. We now know this was happening around the same time that Huang was spotted at the Taiwan dinner with Alice Huang in May 2025, according to Culper Research, which shorted Nvidia’s stock earlier this year. That dinner occurred shortly after Nvidia had shared the Trump administration’s new restrictions on its China-specific H20 chips in April.
Just a couple months after the Taiwan dinner, Huang reportedly met with Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to plead his case for loosening export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. Days later, the company announced that the administration had blessed sales of its H20 chips to China. Huang had argued that spreading American chips to China would help establish US technology as the standard, rather than allowing for Chinese chips to grow, according to The New York Times. After setbacks earlier in the second Trump term in export policy to China, Huang began speaking with then-White House AI czar David Sacks in 2025, who became the key advocate for Nvidia’s view that selling American chips to China would be beneficial, the Times reported.
By October 2025, Huang was lobbying Trump to allow Nvidia to sell more advanced chips to China, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, per the Times; but after Trump considered the proposal, he ultimately decided not to move forward. (That same month, Huang hired an external PR firm known for handling sex scandals, Wired reported.)
Months later, in December 2025, Trump changed course slightly, allowing Nvidia to sell H20 chips to a greenlit list of “approved customers” in China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut of those sales. The same rules would apply to other US chipmakers, he wrote on Truth Social at the time.
“It is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions”
CSET’s Dohmen said that during the past two years, the US has seen a light loosening of AI export control regulations under the Trump administration, driven partly by Huang’s own lobbying. But it’s important to note, she said, that “even without any kind of intelligence operations from the Chinese side, it is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions.” Any restrictions by definition stifle Nvidia’s business expansion and cut off potential sales to help it grow its already stunning market cap — which is currently about $4.25 trillion, second only to Apple.
Huang’s relationship with Trump is also particularly relevant here. The president lavished praise on Huang during a speech last year, saying that until recently, he hadn’t even heard of Nvidia, and then he wanted to break it up. But after meeting Huang, he said, he understood why it would be difficult to re-create the company he’d built. More recently, Huang put Trump on speakerphone when the president called him during an appearance onstage at the All-In Summit, publicly displaying his close access to the Oval Office.
This past spring, a classified memo — the writing of which was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, per the Times — circulated among Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, warning of the Megaspeed executive’s alleged involvement in surveillance on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security. Her reported goal was to learn about advanced AI chips in the US and try to influence them being made available to China on a large scale. Asked if he had known about the memo reviewed by Rubio at a press briefing on Monday, Trump said, “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Earlier in the briefing, he said he was unaware of the alleged spy connection ahead of his trip to China.
Huang was initially left off the list of executives joining Trump on the trip, but the president later asked him to join. Trump had been briefed about a year ago that US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive to be a China intelligence operative, according to the Times, and that she had a close relationship with a US citizen who turned out to be Nvidia’s CEO. At the time, he reportedly chose not to take action.
So far, the allegations haven’t affected Huang’s future at Nvidia. He’ll continue to lead the company during the investigation. Trump has also stood by him since news broke of the affair, telling reporters this past weekend, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”
Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised”
On Sunday, Huang wrote an internal memo to Nvidia employees — some of which are his own family members — writing, “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He then addressed Nvidia’s board, partners, and shareholders, adding that he is “fully committed” to leading the company and “will work to earn back your confidence.” This weekend, Nvidia’s board of directors launched an independent investigation into the national security allegations. Huang will not have control over the participants in the investigation, and Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”
Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note on Monday that Morningstar “can’t rule out the investigation fading away and Nvidia returning to business as usual,” particularly since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” There’s also the fact that Huang’s Nvidia struck deals in August with six large financial institutions to provide more than $500 billion in financing for the buildout of AI data centers and other infrastructure, and as the US-China AI race intensifies, those are high-stakes agreements.
“It’s unclear to us what these partnerships and financing deals would look like with a different Nvidia CEO,” Colello wrote. “Costs of capital may rise for future investments if perhaps the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals.” Morningstar still maintained a very high uncertainty rating for the company, with Colello writing that it’s possible US approval of Nvidia to sell H20 chips to China will be revoked and that the company could ostensibly be sanctioned as well.
Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO of Nvidia and that he would “certainly take him” on his next trip to China. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump told reporters. “He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.”

articles.title: 👨🏿🚀TechCabal Daily – ‘Too much Access’ - TechCabal
articles.text:
Good morning. ☀️️
The biggest news in global tech is not about artificial intelligence (sorry, Anthropic, your IPO plans are exciting), but a very human affair. And, as it turns out, a possible intelligence operation. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an affair after reports linked him to a former chip distributor executive whom US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. NVIDIA’s board is now investigating whether Huang was targeted in a foreign espionage operation.
The $4.28 trillion NVIDIA makes the chips powering much of the global AI boom, and the US has spent years restricting China’s access to its most advanced technology. The company said it has no reason to believe its secrets were compromised, but the affair has raised questions about the security of one of the world’s most valuable companies.
Let’s get into today’s dispatch.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Banking
Access Holdings may sell a foreign subsidiary in rethink of its African expansion strategy
Building a banking empire across Africa sounds good until some branches start costing more than they bring in. Access Holdings, the parent company of Access Bank and one of Nigeria’s largest banking groups, has found itself at that point. After years of expanding into new markets through acquisitions and new subsidiaries, it’s considering selling at least one overseas.
What happened? Access Holdings chairman Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede disclosed that the group is considering exiting at least one foreign market after identifying an underperforming subsidiary. Speaking to Bloomberg on the sidelines of the African Financial Industry Summit (AFIS) in Luanda, Angola, he said the group would be prepared to sell businesses that fail to meet their cost of capital or strategic objectives.
Explain like I’m new here: Under Section 19(8)(c) of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020, Nigerian banks cannot invest more than 10% of their shareholders’ funds in foreign banking subsidiaries. The provision is intended to prevent banks from committing too much capital to overseas operations at the expense of their financial strength at home.
Access was making moves: Access has spent years growing beyond Nigeria through acquisitions and new banking subsidiaries. It now operates across 16 African markets, including Tanzania, Kenya, Angola and Sierra Leone. In May, the bank’s exposure stood at 19.4%, almost twice the regulatory limit.
Access is considering either recalling excess capital from subsidiaries, selling minority stakes, or restructuring businesses. It has completed one capital repatriation exercise involving six subsidiaries and is engaging regulators in five countries to facilitate further capital returns. The group has not disclosed which five countries are involved.
Who could be leaving? Access has not named the subsidiary it is considering selling. However, the group’s international operations have not all performed equally. Its South African operation has recorded persistent losses, while its Kenyan business reported a loss in H1 2026. Mozambique, which previously struggled after an acquisition, returned to profitability in 2025.
In 2014, the tier-1 bank sold its loss-making Ivory Coast subsidiary after an earlier CBN directive restricted Nigerian banks from using parent-bank capital to support foreign operations. In July, it sold a 7.44% stake in its Ghanaian subsidiary. The current exercise could follow a similar route.

Banking
Kenya’s banks have two bosses arguing over their capital
Kenya’s banks have been given two different timelines to raise capital, and the regulatorsare now trying to agree on which one counts. The Treasury (the Finance Ministry) wants to give lenders until 2032 to reach KES 10 billion ($46 million) in core capital, but the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) wants them to do it by 2029.
What’s happening? John Mbadi, Kenya’s Treasury Cabinet Secretary, and CBK Governor Kamau Thugge are in talks to settle the disagreement, which became public after Mbadi announced an extension in his 2026 Budget speech, in June.
Mbadi’s proposal would scrap the CBK’s annual capital targets and give banks three extra years. The regulator wasn’t having it. It told lenders to stick to the original schedule and ordered banks with less than KES 5 billion ($38 million) in core capital to explain how they would meet the December 2026 target.
Under the CBK’s plan, banks must hold $38 million by December 2026, KES 6 billion ($46 million) in 2027, KES 8 billion ($62 million) in 2028, and KES 10 billion ($77 million) in 2029.
Why it matters: Smaller banks have warned that meeting the higher capital requirements could force them to cut lending to businesses and households, putting them at odds with the government’s push to increase private-sector credit.
As of June 2026, 14 banks had less than the KES 5 billion ($46 million) required by December. Seven had already missed the previous year’s KES 3 billion ($23 million) target. For these lenders, the extra three years Mbadi is proposing could make a big difference.
The bigger question: The CBK wants banks with larger capital buffers, but parliament wants to avoid a process that drives smaller lenders out of the market or limits access to credit. Both have a point. But until Mbadi and Thugge agree on a timeline, banks are left planning for two different deadlines.
Telecoms
MTN and Cell C disagree over network deal
In South Africa, MTN helps keep Cell C’s customers connected. Cell C helps banks and retailers become mobile operators without building their own networks. Now MTN wants more of that business for itself.
What’s happening? In a trading update published on Monday, MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, said it failed to agree with Cell C, the South African mobile network operator, on certain terms of their longstanding commercial relationship. MTN didn’t disclose what the disagreements were, but said both companies would work to resolve them under their existing agreement. Cell C confirmed that the deal runs until 2032 and that existing terms remain unchanged, according to local publication TechCentral.
Explain like I’m new here. Unlike MTN and Vodacom, Cell C no longer operates its own radio network. Instead, it relies on infrastructure-sharing agreements with both companies to provide nationwide coverage. Under its arrangement with MTN, Cell C gets access to network infrastructure, while MTN gets access to some of Cell C’s licensed spectrum, the radio frequencies used to carry mobile signals.
Here’s where it gets interesting: Cell C has built a growing business serving mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs), companies such as Capitec Connect that sell mobile services without operating their own networks. In its FY2026 results, Cell C estimated that it hosts 80–85% of South Africa’s MVNO market. Its wholesale revenue grew 20% to R1.76 billion ($107.2 million) in the year to May, supporting 5.71 million MVNO lines.
But MTN wants a bigger slice of that market. It wants to become South Africa’s leading MVNO wholesaler and is introducing new wholesale pricing arrangements to compete for customers.
Between the lines: MTN is both Cell C’s infrastructure partner and a direct competitor for wholesale customers. That creates an uncomfortable relationship between the two operators. Cell C needs access to MTN’s infrastructure to serve its customers, while MTN earns revenue from that arrangement even as it competes for the same business.
Neither company has disclosed the exact reason for the disagreement.
Zoom out: Cell C’s strategy of relying on other operators’ networks has reduced infrastructure development and maintenance costs, letting it focus on acquiring customers and growing its wholesale business. But the model also makes the terms of its network agreements critical to its profitability.
For now, both companies say customers won’t experience service disruptions. But Cell C has to answer questions about how it can protect its fast-growing wholesale business as the company supplying its network competes more aggressively for the customers it serves.
Funding
South Africa’s Yoco secures $100 million credit facility
Yoco, a South African fintech, has secured a $100 million credit facility from US investment firm Victory Park Capital to expand Yoco Capital, its merchant cash advance business. The facility gives the company greater control over how it finances merchants, including pricing advances and managing the associated risks.
Here’s what Yoco does: Yoco Capital uses payment data to assess merchants for financing. Eligible merchants receive offers through the Yoco app based on their sales history. Advances range from R2,000 ($121.8) to R1.5 million ($91,360), with no collateral required. Repayments are automatically deducted from daily sales,
Explain like I’m new here: South Africa’s small-business financing gap is estimated at R350 billion ($21.3 billion), according to the 2025 Finfind and African Bank MSME Access to Finance Report. SMEs receive just 13% of national bank lending, compared with 51% for large corporations. Yoco is betting that its existing relationship with merchants gives it an advantage in serving some of that unmet demand.
Yoco wants to do more: Since launching Yoco Capital in 2018, the company has advanced more than R6.5 billion ($395 million) to over 40,000 merchants. It now wants to extend the service to more of the 200,000-plus businesses on its platform. It has expanded its point-of-sale software, acquired Dyner AI, a software business, in May, and is developing an AI-powered platform for small businesses. With the new facility, Yoco is betting that the payment data it has collected over the years can become a bigger business than processing transactions alone.

articles.title: New PlayStation Portal Player Gets Built-In Storage in Japan and Korea, Purpose Still Unknown
articles.text:
Monday, November 9th 2026
New PlayStation Portal Player Gets Built-In Storage in Japan and Korea, Purpose Still Unknown
Sony is adding built-in storage to a new PlayStation Portal model for Japan and South Korea, though it hasn't said how much storage it has or what it will be used for. The PlayStation Portal Player Midnight Black goes on sale December 10 for ¥39,980 in Japan and ₩378,000 in South Korea, the same price the current model sells for after this year's price hikes. Preorders open November 13, and each unit ships with one month of PlayStation Plus Premium. Like the Japan-only Midnight Black PS5, both versions are locked to the local language and only work with PlayStation accounts registered in that country. Sony's Japanese post only says the storage is there for future features, with details to follow once those are decided.
Interestingly, the Korean post calls it expanded internal storage instead of new storage, which makes sense since the Portal needs some flash just to run its OS. The "Remote" part of the name is also gone, so the device is now simply the PlayStation Portal Player, as it can stream games from the cloud without a PS5 these days. Everything else carries over, including the 8-inch 1080p 60 FPS LCD, haptic feedback, adaptive triggers, and 3D Audio. That also means no OLED panel, which leaker KeplerL2 claimed back in January would come with a refreshed Portal sometime in 2026. Offline play or local downloads would be the obvious guess for the storage, though Sony hasn't confirmed anything along those lines. There's also no word on a wider release, so buyers elsewhere shouldn't hold out for this model just yet.
