articles.title: Distributed LLM Inference on Kubernetes with llm-d, Wasm, & TornadoVM
articles.text:
In this episode, Edoardo Vacchi discusses the evolving landscape of WebAssembly on the backend, running Java workloads on GPUs using TornadoVM, and optimizing distributed AI inference using llm-d and vLLM on Kubernetes. Edoardo explains how llm-d manages cache locality (KV and prefix caches), request routing, and batch inference across Kubernetes clusters to maximize expensive GPU utilization.
Key Takeaways
- Wasm has matured into a backend runtime for sandboxing, cross-language compilation, and workload migration between browsers and end-user devices.
- TornadoVM allows developers to compile and run Java code directly on GPU backends, enabling projects like GPU-accelerated Llama 3 written entirely in Java.
- While vLLM optimizes high-throughput inference on a single instance via PagedAttention, llm-d extends this across Kubernetes clusters to manage multi-node distributed inference.
- Traditional Kubernetes load balancers break LLM efficiency; llm-d balances staying with the same instance to leverage cached conversational context while preventing node overload.
- llm-d introduces batch inference during idle cluster periods and semantic classification to route prompts to right-sized, cost-effective models without sacrificing privacy.
Subscribe on:
Transcript
Olimpiu Pop: Hello everybody, I'm Olimpiu Pop an InfoQ editor, and I have in front of me today, Edoardo Vacchi, one of the two Italians that usually talk about boxes inside of boxes. The other one is Andrea Peruffo. Eduardo worked for a long period of time in the WebAssembly ecosystem, he did some spotting around other types of VMs, and today he's back at Red Hat and he's trying to make things easier in terms of Kubernetes and inference. Is that correct?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. I mean, on my team. It's a few people working on this, and I'm just one of them, but fair description. We're working on distributed inference on Kubernetes specifically, and that's called llm-d, and it's part of the VLLM family of projects. So, yes, it's super exciting to be back at Red Hat and work on the bleeding edge.
State of WebAssembly on the Backend [01:35]
Olimpiu Pop: Yes, that sounds nice. But before we go there, because that's the gist of your current work, tell us what happens currently in the WebAssembly space. And I'm asking you because, besides working on the Java side of WebAssembly, you had exposure to Wazero, if I remember correctly.
Edoardo Vacchi: That's right.
Olimpiu Pop: So, maybe just have a short refresher. I know that the WebAssembly space is moving fast, so maybe if you can just provide a short summary where it is, what changed, and what's to be expected in the upcoming period.
Edoardo Vacchi: Right. So, for the benefit of our audience, I don't know how much all of them are familiar with it, but you will know that Wasm was born for web browsers, but more recently, and by recently now it means a few years, people were also interested in running it outside the browser, and for the backend specifically. So, running software on Wasm. And in that sense, it could be seen as a sort of a similar thing to the JVM in spirit. And that's why I guess some of us that were working on the JVM were interested in working on Wasm as well. So, Wasm has changed fast in some senses, it evolved quickly in some senses, it evolved just slowly in others. So, there's been a lot of discussion around the component model, which is this new modular system that's built around WebAssembly. That is probably where a lot of the development happens these days, I'd say.
But I'd say that the space for WebAssembly on the backend has changed a lot in the last few years. I think that all of our development landscape has changed. So, things have shifted a little bit. I think it's very meaningful and relevant today, even more possibly than it was when there was much more hype, because it has a lot to do with sandboxing. And as you know, sandboxing is all the rage these days.
Olimpiu Pop: One good scoring point for WebAssembly was earlier this year I was talking to the local first community, and what was interesting was that they were mentioning that one of the libraries they built, the name is eluding me now, but what they said is that rather than just thinking about providing implementation in different programming languages, they built it in Rust, and that meant that they can just compile it to WebAssembly and then use it via WebAssembly to different programming languages. And that was the nice part from their side, and they were quite happy with the result. And I think that's where the power of WebAssembly comes. Or I think the previous year I spoke to a couple of guys that used to work on infrastructure and they spoke about Firecracker. And what was nice, is that they said that most often than not, the harder that you have in the server acts is idle.
So, what they did on top of those idle space, they just had very small WebAssembly machines... Well, containers, I think it's a better wording for that. That was doing very small things that were quite useful for other people. So, I feel that there are all those different scenarios where people are using WebAssembly.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. I think one interesting aspect that connects to what you were saying right now is even migrating workloads somehow, like running stuff in the browser, but then you also have these WebAssembly run times that can run, even on devices or in general outside the browser, and you have the same workload that runs on your browser, and we have demos of things that are migrated, even live migrated, from the browser to an end user device without breakage. That's really fascinating. And I think these days when we talk about agentic workloads, that's an interesting space. That's where I think Wasm is still relevant. I mean, Wasm is still relevant, especially for browser related work, and many other, but these scenarios for the word that's changing a lot these days for developers, those are the use cases with really good shine.
Olimpiu Pop: Yes. As you mentioned, isolation is important and is getting more and more important these days. So, I think that's quite useful. What is bugging me for at least one week now, and probably I'll try it the following week, let's see what you are going to say to that, I'm just thinking to run a small language model inside the WebAssembly in a browser, is that feasible? Is not feasible?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, I mean it is feasible, there are examples of that. The thing is, I've been on the receiving end of this question a few times now, so it depends is the short answer.
Olimpiu Pop: Perfect.
Edoardo Vacchi: WebAssembly is meant to run on the CPU first. And as we know, we can do inference on the CPU, but generally it works much better. And for the way LLMs, modern LLMs, I mean, the modern architectures for LLMs are designed, they are meant to be run with highly parallel architectures. And the CPU is parallel, but not as parallel as a GPU. So, long story short, smaller models, which basically make sense to run in a browser, for instance, do make sense to run in WebAssembly, much bigger workloads... Well, those in general, we probably want to run on a GPU anyway. However, there are experiments that I'm aware of to translate WebAssembly into GPU kernels.
So, yes, possibly. But the short version of it is for all those workloads that are meaningful to run on a CPU, so relatively small language models, Wasm can be used, and there are many versions of these workloads that exist. I think that Hugging Face for some of the smallest models will run them on your browser, I think. And there are a few examples, on the Wasm I/O conference, there were quite a few talks of people showing this, running these workloads in the browser especially to do inference. So, yes, it does work, it depends on your workload.
TornadoVM: Translating Java Code to GPU Kernels [08:26]
Olimpiu Pop: Yes. Well, I'm going to say it anyway, it's simple, it's more about just trying and seeing how things evolved, and fingers crossed that something will happen and not just smoke. But in order to work and consolidate the point that I stated about an expert into putting boxes into boxes, you had the posts, I think last year or the previous year, about TornadoVM. I know that you just had a small exposure to it, so maybe just have a short summary what's TornadoVM and when should we use it?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. So, TornadoVM is, we could say a flavor of the JVM or an add-on, a plug into the JVM, depends on how you see it. TornadoVM allows you to run Java code essentially on the GPU. This is the bottom line, the selling point, the very short version of it. It's a little bit more nuanced than that. But yes, basically you can, speaking of boxes inside boxes, yes. It's called the VM because it allows you to translate on the fly your Java code, and compile it on the fly into GPU-specific kernels. So, PTX for NVIDIA, SPEAR-V, whatever. And it handles for you this translation. So, you can basically write Java code and then it will translate for GPU backend. Now, the code that you write there, it is Java code, but you have to write the code in a specific way. You might have to use some libraries that TornadoVM provides you.
You cannot run basically any code... You won't be able to run Spring on TornadoVM. I mean, yes, but it will run in Java mode. You won't run Spring on the GPU, that's the point. But yes, you can write GPU kernels using Java, and that's the beauty of it. And the blog post you were referring to, I think it was last year's, I'm walking through the reader... One of the examples in the code, I think there is an example of writing a simple kernel and running on the GPU, that's one thing that we show in the blog. But then we run GPU Llama 3, which is an implementation of the Llama 3 model that runs on GPU. And this implementation is completely written in Java. So, that's fascinating. The blog post walks you through how this works.
In the latest DevOps Belgium, if people want to catch up a little bit, they had demonstrated, I think there was definitely a talk about TornadoVM, there were talks from the GraalVM team of the similar projects to run Llama and other language models using GraalVM that will do the acceleration for you, and then there was also former GraalVM team member that spun off his own startup. I think his name is Alfonso Alfonso, I remember it because his nickname is Alfonso Squared. And he started his own startup branching off some work that he did originally in GraalVM, again to run Java code, I think, on the GPU and LLM.
So, yes, fascinating stuff. And so, bottom line, the reason why I started to look into this is fan of boxes inside boxes, fan of languages and compilers, so it felt like a natural evolution of the things that I did in the past, including compilation to WebAssembly to learn about compilation to the GPU.
vLLM vs llm-d [12:11]
Olimpiu Pop: That sounds quite interesting, and it definitely makes sense these days. For instance, I saw that a lot of the big companies are just using Java for inference, and that makes perfect sense to just have this closing the loop. Today, you are part of the team at Red Hat, back again at Red Hat, that is working on llm-d. And in my understanding, what llm-d is, taking a step back, if VLLM is making sure that everything runs perfectly on one box, llm-d is trying to make sure that everything is efficient if you have a Kubernetes cluster. Is that a correct affirmation or did I understand wrong?
Edoardo Vacchi: No, no, it is correct on a high level. More specifically, so VLLM is our inference engine. So, you can think of it, if you will, as the JVM of language models. So, it has support for several language models, there's an interesting aside here, it is a platform to run LLMs. The interesting aside here is you would expect that this is a general sort of VM, and the LLMs are sort of software that you load on top of it. But unfortunately every LLM architecture is slightly different. So, VLLM has to basically include the implementation of every LLM that gets released. So, when people release LLMs, they do not release the software to run them, they release the weights. So, all of these inference engines, such as VLLM, what they do is implementing basically the software, the kernels, the components that actually load the weights and then actually do the inference.
So, VLLM is our platform to run the core and effectively VLLM is able to serve, it's a server... I mean, it's an inference engine, it's also server that exposes endpoints that you can call to do inference, and it does so efficiently. It was originally VLLM, I think the V in VLLM originally stands for virtual, as in virtual memory allocation. Because it was the first engine to implement page detention, basically a mechanism inspired by good old systems programming to do paging of memory, memory pages, but for memory that gets allocated on GPU, this is in a very high level way. So, VLLM is able to do high throughput inference. So, you can do several requests at once and VLLM will pack them and try to serve them together, and do inference in one pass for several requests at one time, this is called continuous batching. But this gets you to a point.
Essentially, at some point you have your GPUs on your machine, and your inference engine and that's it. You will not be able to scale further than the resources that you have on that machine. So, how do you scale further? Well, you can scale by having more VLLM instances, right? So, you have several VLLM instances and you want to serve your inference requests using these few VLLM, these few VLLM instances that you have. Now, you have another problem. How do you route requests across your VLLM instances? So, if you are on Kubernetes, what you will do... And most people are on Kubernetes these days, it's the standard for platforms for serving services in an efficient way. So, you can scale your VLLM instances and have several VLLM instances that serve the possible the same request... I mean that gets selected by the scheduler, by the VLLM scheduler.
If you do it the traditional way and let the Kubernetes normal router to pick across the VLLM instances that you have replicated, you won't get necessarily good performance. The reason is inference does not behave like a traditional service, a traditional HTP service. Basically, if you send a request to one specific VLLM instance, especially if you are doing conversation, if you're doing a chat and if you're doing agentic coding, it's still a chat basically. There's a lot of exchanges back and forth between you and your server, between your agent and your server. You want to stick for as much time as possible to the same VLLM instance. This might be counterintuitive in a way because for microservices, we know we don't want to hammer the same service on and on because otherwise it will get overloaded. We want to do sort of round robbing or random robbing across the replicas.
But the thing is microservices or service in general, these are usually in a way stateless. The state is usually stored somewhere else and it's not part of your request. I mean, the request can be served independently by any instance. Unfortunately for LLMs, in order for LLMs to do their inference in an efficient way, you want to stick for as much time as possible to the same instance. But at the same time, you cannot stick forever to the same instance because at some point you will reach some limit. You are not the only user of that VLLM instance. You want to serve and distribute the load across your VLLM instances. So there's a balance that you have to strike between staying with the same instance and benefit of the caches, the KV caches, the prefix caches that are in place, the systems that allow you to do inference in an efficient way and lower costs.
But at the same time, you don't want to overload the same instance too much. So you also have to keep this into account. This is not the job for a traditional Kubernetes schedule. And that's where llm-d comes into place. That's what llm-d does. llm-d is not just a router or a scheduler. It's actually a family of projects and they are all meant to give you a set of tools to do distributed inference so that you can leverage all of the GPUs that you have and use it at their maximum as much as possible so you get the best value, the best bang for your bucks because these hardware is expensive whether you loan it or you own it. So you want to use it 100% as much as possible. And that's why we provide scheduler. We have something that we're going to release. I mean, in the open source ecosystem, it's already been released.
We're going to release also as part of product of Red Hat. This is called batch inference. Batch inference is using your cluster even when it's under load. So you can schedule request to do batch processing in the background when your cluster is underused because basically this hardware is so expensive that you want to keep it at 100% all the time. So even when there is no live inference going on, you can schedule batch processing to run when you're sleeping when there's less work to be done live. So that's what llm-d does. It uses your hardware as much as possible so that the money you spend gets you the best value and you do it on your own hardware so you can do inference without leaking data to a third party, which is important these days.
Olimpiu Pop: So, what you're saying is that we will be able to use our previous Kubernetes clusters. So, what we still have from the cloud native era, because everything was native these days, and just make sure that we can rebuild it to build our privacy also for the AI native era.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. It allows you to make cloud native inference and evolve your infrastructure in such a way that you can do AI on-premises, in a similar way as you did cloud native development before AI.
Olimpiu Pop: Well, that was always an issue, but now it feels that we are discussing in the cloud-native; most of the times we spoke about stateless. Whenever you call something, you didn't always ring on the same doorbell because that was one issue. Another issue was in the Kubernetes space, it was the part with I/O, well, most particularly persistent data, like database and stuff like that. Whenever you spoke to infrastructure guys, they told you, "Well, we can have everything in Kubernetes except for databases because then those things become more complex." But let's take them one by one. How do you bring in a stateless ecosystem like Kubernetes, worked a lot in Bing, something that theoretically should be stateful?
Because if I have a conversation, I would like to continue my conversation about, I don't know, whatever stupid thing I speak to Gemini or Cloud or OpenGPT or whatever stuff, I don't want to have my responses coming for what Eduardo was speaking to his LLM.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, it's a complex problem for sure. As I said, one part of the story is that... Well, I mean, if people that are hearing that the audience know how LLM generally work, essentially the stateful nature of the LLM in a way is fake, in that they are really stateless. The way they do inference is that we send them the entire history of a conversation every single time. So, maybe I jumped at-
Olimpiu Pop: At the conclusion.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, to the conclusion earlier. And I said a lot about prefix caches and KV caches, but yes. So, essentially the way an LLM works is that essentially you always send the entirety of the conversation to the LLM. And what really happens is the LLM completes the conversation. I don't know if people recall how OpenAI and the GPT Lab playground worked a few years ago. Basically, it was the completion API. You wrote a sentence and then the LLM wrote the continuation of that. And the cool thing was that someone discovered if you wrote that prompt as a conversation, as a dialogue with quotes, user says da, da, da, computer says... The LLM will continue the conversation. And that's how ChatGPT basically was born. People notice this, and notice this pattern.
Now, LLMs are being trained with this pattern, but that's how basically originally it work. So, if you think of it this way, every conversation really is a very long prompt to the continuation of that conversation. The way LLM works, you send the history of the conversation and then they continue with the next answer, and then you get back the answer, and then you continue with your answer, and so on, so forth, so on and so forth. If you are using LLMs, you will know that pricing for these things, depending if you're using token-based spend or a subscription... Well, if you're using a subscription, that doesn't really matter. But if you're using token-based pricing, you will know that there's a difference between cached responses and responses.
The reason is, if you don't do a cached response, then you are sending the entire history of your conversation to the LLM. The LLM does not have that conversation in cache, so it will have to do inference on the entire prompt, and that's why that will be particularly expensive. But if you've been going back and forth for a while without long pauses and the cache on the server has not been evicted, then you've been reusing stored cache estate to continue the conversation. That does not mean necessarily that you haven't sent the entire history to the LLM, it just means that even though you are sending the entire history, the history is recognized as part of a prefix of a cache, and so the LLM can compute only the continuation instead of the entire prompt.
So, we have these mechanism for caching in place so that basically LLMs, if the cache exists, can only infer the last few tokens that continue the conversation instead of have to re-compute the entire state from the prompt. llm-d does that for you. So, it maintains this cache both in the form of a KV cache, with one going to the deals how that works, and a prefix cache. And both these caching mechanism allow you to persist the state across the exchanges in your conversation, persist as in volatile memory because these are caches... Usually they're not persistent for a long time. And that's the reason also why you want to stick usually to the same VLLM instance, even though llm-d also gives you ways to move around across instances. It's a lot, we cannot explain how all that works. But in general, llm-d allows you to do this, allows you to have an efficient use and even for stateful conversation of your hardware.
Olimpiu Pop: Okay. So, llm-d, it's also donated, if I remember correctly, to the CNCF Foundation, right?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. It recently reached 1.0 a few days ago. Yes.
Olimpiu Pop: Okay, congratulations. So, we are right in time. In what state is it? Is it production ready? Should we wait for it?
Edoardo Vacchi: Oh no, it's definitely production-ready, there's a number of companies that are already using it. At Red Hat, we're actually partners with NVIDIA for a bunch of things. We have a lot of success stories already, people using it in production. And yes, you should definitely take a look at it. In fact, sometimes I go to conferences and I realize people are already using it, or maybe they're using VLLM on their infrastructure and they're not aware of llm-d. So, VLLM allows you to do inference up to a degree in a very high performance, high quality way, and the llm-d and VLLM projects are sister projects in a way. I mean, there's a lot of exchanges across the stack, so we are part of the same team in a way. But yes, llm-d gives you that edge. For instance, VLLM does not do automatic flow control, even if you are only running a one VLLM instance, llm-d gives you control over quality of service and prioritization of HTTP requests.
So, that is something that VLLM, at least until a few days ago, I don't know if things have changed recently, could not do. So, you can get benefit from llm-d even if you're not necessarily running in a very highly distributed situation.
Olimpiu Pop: So, what does that mean? Even if you don't have a cluster, use llm-d?
Edoardo Vacchi: Even if you don't have a lot of GPUs, even if you don't have to distribute the load across different GPUs, llm-d might still be useful. And yes, you can also run it bare metal. So, you might want to evaluate llm-d even if you're not using Kubernetes. I mean, Kubernetes is the first target, but it is supported also on bare metal.
Olimpiu Pop: Okay. So, it's focusing on inference, even if you don't have already existing infrastructure. So, it just tries to provide the best usage of your resources, even if you have or you don't have an infrastructure already existing. It seems that at the point when we are recording this, it's end of October, and it seems that llm-d started at the end of October in 2024.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes.
Olimpiu Pop: So, it's a good moment to have the first major version out in this period. So, congratulations.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes.
Observability and Hardware Heterogeneity in AI Clusters [29:34]
Olimpiu Pop: But staying in the Kubernetes space, one of the reasons why people prefer to use things that they are already familiar, Kubernetes is not that old of a solution comparing to other types of solution that were out there, but it's still one of the most mature in the cloud native space. And one of the things that are very important these days, or they always were important, but now they are more than ever, it's observability. What should we expect from that perspective in terms of observability when we're discussing about llm-d? I mean, as you mentioned, everything related to LLMs is more complex than everything else, how can we make that complexity easier to digest through the observability solution already existing?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, so I mean, it depends. It's a very wide question. So, the way llm-d actually works, it leverages a lot of signals that are metrics-based. So, there's a lot of insights that are being exposed by VLLM, metrics and data that explains essentially what's going on inside the inference engine. And llm-d uses this information to actually do what I explained earlier, that is this inform the routing across instances. What this means is essentially when you use llm-d and VLLM, you don't just have a system to do efficient inference, you also are getting for free, if you will, a rich system to get insight on what's going on, not just on your cluster, but in your inference engines. You can see how many tokens are being produced, how many failures you're getting, what's the throughput, you can get alert on situation where you might want to intervene.
For instance, you have control over the saturation of your cluster, which means saturation means essentially you have so many requests that you are struggling to serve them. And then at that point you can add more machines, you can throttle the incoming requests. So, you have a lot of knobs that you can work on. The observability story for llm-d is pretty interesting as well, and you have all the tools to get insights of what's going on in your cluster from a GPU and inference perspective as well.
Olimpiu Pop: Well, you already mentioned that it was complicated to get it right, but which thing was the hardest?
Edoardo Vacchi: Ah.
Olimpiu Pop: Everything.
Edoardo Vacchi: That's an interesting question. Yes, everything. Well, one thing that is interesting in this ecosystem is that everything is very new. I would say one of the things that are challenging, maybe not the hardest is that, well, NVIDIA is probably the biggest, most important vendor, but there's also AMD, there's Intel, there's Google's GPUs, and there are more. There are also a lot of startups that are building their own hardware. And while for the PC, we benefit for a lot of time now of a standardized set of hardware components, with a very well-defined instruction set, for these accelerators and GPUs, the languages are very different. So, one of the challenging part for VLLM itself and inference in general is that, and the reason why we need a framework on top of that, is that you can't write the kernel for a GPU computation once and target every single accelerator there is because everything is different.
It's like having Intel, but also ARM, but also RISC-V, but also Power PC, and you have to use all of them depending on your vendors, and you have to support all of them. I mean, in our case, you want to support as many as possible. So, that's probably one of the most challenging things that happen in this case. The other thing that is also possibly challenging from a hardware perspective is that there's a lot of data that has to be transferred. LLMs are large language models, and we hear about trillions of weights of parameters, these translates in gigabytes, terabytes, petabytes of data. And this data have to be moved across machines. You don't just have expensive GPUs, but you also have to have expensive connection between just GPUs. We're talking about RDMA. So, you have to connect this hardware with very expensive type of connection that allow you to have very fast data transfer.
So, I would say in general, from another perspective, these are things that are very challenging. And at the same time, it makes this space very fascinating and interesting.
On-Premises AI and Semantic Routing to Right-Sized Models [34:35]
Olimpiu Pop: Yes, that's for sure. But one, you did mention that the beach of possibilities is quite wide when we're discussing about GPUs, which were intended for something else, but now people, like usual, they adapted and they used it in a different perspective. But now we can see that there are companies that they started building their own hardware, we're discussing about DPUs. How will that change the game?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, that's an interesting question. I don't know. Hopefully it might make things more affordable. I mean, competition is always good. The one side is that this makes things challenging for people that are building infrastructure and software on top of these things, it makes things challenging for people that want to source this hardware because it's still very expensive. But at the same time, if there is more competition, hopefully prices eventually will go down. I think one thing that is very important, and I think this is also the message that we want to bring across with llm-d, VLLM, we're getting to a point where first of all, you don't really need extremely expensive hardware to do inference to a certain degree of quality.
Obviously, frontier models will always be more capable than older models, but open models are getting better and better, even relatively small models that can run on consumer hardware. I have a relatively beefy Mac myself, with 48 gigabytes of RAM, this is a company Mac, so I didn't pay for it, and it was probably bought before the price rises, so it was a good time. But it's a relatively small amount of shared memory because it's shared across CPU and GPU, that's the point. And I can run 27B, I think, 27 billion. Which is not huge, but it's pretty capable. And people have talked recently about Qwen 3.8-27B, this does not run very well on my laptop, but it runs on laptops still, and it runs on a laptop even though it's not super fast.
So, if you get a server that is only slightly bigger than my laptop, you will be able to serve a lot of requests in a very efficient way. And this model has been compared to Opus 4.6. And Opus 4.6 is only one year old. And we were super excited and impressed by Opus 4.6 last year. So, let's not get too carried away by all the announcements we read on social media about how all of these models are super capable, and the old models are no longer useful.
The old model are still useful, and they're even more useful if you can run them on your hardware because this is very important, you don't have to share your data with a company that you don't know you can really trust after all. And this is, I think, the message we want to bring across. You can own your own AI, you can own your own token inference on hardware that now it's relatively... Relatively is the word here?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, affordable. And this is especially true for companies. I'm not talking about consumer, this is true for consumer to some extent, but it's very true for companies. They can source the sort of hardware, they can do inference for these models, that are not as big as the frontier, but they're definitely quite something, and they can solve a lot of interesting problems already.
Olimpiu Pop: Yes. What I think it's important for people to understand is that do we actually need frontier models for everything.
Edoardo Vacchi: Exactly.
Olimpiu Pop: Because in the end, as you mentioned, it's becoming tangible that you can run them on even laptops.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes.
Olimpiu Pop: I was mentioning it's something quite basic. It's ordering, I don't know, something. And then you don't actually need anything else but details in terms of human understanding. And then a very small model, it's more than enough, but it's very niched. And then that's the thing is that yes, we do need a perspective where we do that stuff, and we need, I don't know, the Argons, the Opuses and all the other frontier models out there, but now a lot of people are doing experimentation.
And at the point where you're getting into the production space, you have to do the refining, you have to do the efficiency part, and then definitely get on the right spot. And I saw something similar even on the edge side, where they had very tailored models that were just being focused on a very thin, narrow use case, and that's it. But now a lot of us are exploring, and we're measuring stuff that actually don't matter.
Edoardo Vacchi: For sure. I think another interesting aspect, this is another project that we are incubating in llm-d, it's called llm-d Semantic Classifier. It deals with routing, not just efficiently, but to the right model for some definition of right. So, right might be cost-based or it might be topic-based. And so, this system, there's another sister project that's called the VLLM Semantic Router. If you're interested, llm-d semantic classifier is sort of a sibling, if you will, with different targets. But the goal is the same. You have a prompt, you have a conversation going, and you want to route this conversation to the right model, which might mean right sized. And that's exactly what you were saying. So, it doesn't really matter, sometimes you have a very large model that is able to answer every possible question, it might be useful in many situation, of course, but you have also to bring to the table the cost efficiency.
So, you might have specialized models that are trained or fine-tuned on specific domains, and I think that's where we should go where the next thing should be. Because that really brings LLM inference, AI in general, agentic stuff to the people, it allows you to run this stuff on your hardware, with things that are attainable, goals that are attainable, not just super expensive hardware that nobody can afford.
Olimpiu Pop: I think we are adept, let's say teenage years, of what LLMs and AI will mean for the future because everybody's priding themselves on how much horsepowers do our models have. But actually we are stuck in traffic hours and it doesn't actually matter if it's there or not.
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. Teenage years is a good metaphor, I'd say.
llm-d Roadmap [41:36]
Olimpiu Pop: Maybe just to close up with what's on your roadmap. So, version one is out, what's in the next period? So, upcoming months, upcoming years, what's the target for llm-d?
Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, I mentioned a few already actually. So, llm-d itself is able to run because on this hardware, you have to use it efficiently, it's able to run very large models, mixer expert models by sharing them across machines. But things that we are experimenting and we are getting more and more refined are this batch inference concepts so you can leverage your hardware more efficiently and use those dead moments in your traffic to serve and do inference, even scheduled inference, without the live interaction, so you can 100% reuse that hardware that you have.
And the other is obviously, as I just mentioned, semantic classification so that you can not just use the right machines, but also use the right model at the right time. For instance, let's say you have a very big model that is expensive to run, and smaller models that are more efficient to run and you can run on hardware that is much cheaper. Depending on the conversation that you're having on the prompt that you're sending, you might want to use the larger model in some situations or the smaller model in some situation. So, these are the things that we are working on currently, there are more, and I cannot even list all of them. But it's an exciting space and I think you're going to see a lot of interesting stuff in the next coming months.
Olimpiu Pop: Okay, thank you for your time.
Edoardo Vacchi: Thank you.

articles.title: Nova tendência? Jovi pode seguir Huawei e apostar em celular mais largo • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nova tendência? Jovi pode seguir Huawei e apostar em celular mais largo
Fabricante estaria desenvolvendo smartphone convencional com proporções próximas às telas externas de novos dobráveis.
Durante anos vimos celulares cada vez mais altos e estreitos, mas algumas fabricantes parecem testar o caminho contrário. A Vivo Mobile — dona da Jovi, no Brasil — é a mais recente delas: a empresa estaria desenvolvendo um smartphone com tela mais larga e pode lançá-lo já em 2027.
A informação vem do informante Digital Chat Station, conhecido por vazar dados da cadeia de produção de aparelhos na China. Ele descreve o aparelho no formato “barra de chocolate”, sem tela dobrável. Ainda não há detalhes sobre especificações ou qual linha receberia o dispositivo.
A especulação é de que o celular chegue com uma tela com menos de 6,5 polegadas, assim como a tela externa dos dobráveis nesse formato, como o iPhone Duo (5,4 polegadas) e o Galaxy Z Fold 8 (5,5 polegadas). Caso acompanhe o valor praticado pela Huawei, o celular chegaria por volta de 6.999 yuans, algo em torno de R$ 5.777 em conversão direta.
A experimentação do formato ocorre após o lançamento do Huawei Pura X View, um smartphone convencional com tela mais larga do que a encontrada na maior parte dos aparelhos atuais. O aparelho tem uma tela OLED de 6,39 polegadas e especificações de topo de linha, incluindo o chip proprietário Kirin 9030s.
O modelo se aproxima das proporções adotadas pelos dobráveis em formato passaporte quando fechados, mas sem tela adicional. Até então, parece ter dado certo: segundo o mesmo leaker, o Huawei Pura X View chamou a atenção do público no país asiático e se tornou o aparelho mais vendido na semana de lançamento, em setembro, com 280 mil unidades vendidas em apenas cinco dias.
Desde então, outras fabricantes começaram a aparecer em rumores de aparelhos semelhantes. Xiaomi, Oppo e Honor também estariam estudando smartphones mais largos, de acordo com o GSMArena.
A movimentação das chinesas parte dos próprios dobráveis, que começam a aparecer em opções menores após investir nas telas gigantes nas primeiras gerações. Modelos mais recentes passaram a adotar painéis mais largos quando fechados, como o iPhone Duo e o Galaxy Z Fold 8.
Vale lembrar, porém, que a própria Huawei deu o ponta-pé inicial no formato mais largo e menor de dobráveis, com o Huawei Pura X Max, após rumores de que o aparelho da Apple seguiria essa ideia. A própria Jovi, no entanto, ainda não se aventurou com dobráveis nessa proporção.
Essa popularização dos dobráveis largos pode estar atraindo o interesse no sentido contrário: smartphones menores, mas que mantém o aproveitamento de tela para conteúdos de mídia, como vídeos e jogos.
Não há expectativa de que o Pura X View chegue no Brasil e nem informações de que os prováveis celulares das outras chinesas sejam lançados fora da China. Ainda assim, caso o formato realmente se popularize, isso pode ocorrer. Além da Huawei, a Xiaomi, Honor e a Vivo Mobile, através da Jovi, têm presença oficial no país e costumam trazer alguns de seus principais modelos — e até mesmo alguns modelos caríssimos e nichados, como o Jovi X300 Ultra.

articles.title: New Democratic Congress will likely strip the gilding from Trump's Golden Dome
articles.text:
Israeli air defense systems are activated to intercept Iranian missiles over Tel Aviv amid a barrage of Iranian rockets on June 16, 2025. The name of the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense shield is a nod to Israel's Iron Dome, but the US version would include Space-Based Interceptors and must protect a much larger geographic area.
Credit:
Menahem Kahana/AFP via Getty Images
Israeli air defense systems are activated to intercept Iranian missiles over Tel Aviv amid a barrage of Iranian rockets on June 16, 2025. The name of the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense shield is a nod to Israel's Iron Dome, but the US version would include Space-Based Interceptors and must protect a much larger geographic area.
Credit:
Menahem Kahana/AFP via Getty Images
Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon’s Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump’s signature second-term defense initiative.
The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch.
The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon’s budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome’s most controversial component and give the program a new name.
That’s the opinion of a half-dozen current and former officials in industry and government. Ars spoke with sources before and after last week’s congressional elections to get a sense of how a new Democratic Congress might make its imprint on missile defense.
It’s important to know that much of what the Trump administration calls “Golden Dome” was already in development (or in some cases, operational) when Trump signed the executive order outlining the initiative 22 months ago. Trump’s order created a new program to consolidate the Pentagon’s existing missile defense efforts, accelerate work already underway on new Ground-Based Interceptors (GBIs), and deploy a new layer of orbiting sensors and Space-Based Interceptors (SBIs) to defend the US homeland against both traditional ballistic missiles and new emerging threats like drones and hypersonic weapons.
Ramming it through
The Golden Dome was immediately politicized. The first tranche of its funding—approximately $24 billion—was part of Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” along with some of the White House’s other contentious policy priorities. The bill passed Congress on a party-line vote. This meant the budget for Golden Dome was not part of the normal military budgeting process in Congress, which usually involves both parties. Instead, it passed Congress through a controversial shortcut known as reconciliation.
Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said in a September hearing that the White House’s decision to link Golden Dome’s first tranche of funding to a partisan reconciliation bill was unnecessary. “This should have been on a bipartisan basis,” Rounds said. Indeed, Capitol Hill Republicans refused the Trump administration’s effort to add $350 billion to the Pentagon’s budget this year through a similar reconciliation mechanism.
Lawmakers also formed an all-Republican “Golden Dome Caucus” soon after the unveiling of Golden Dome. Seven House members of the caucus either lost their reelection bids or did not run for reelection at all in the 2026 midterms. These include the caucus’s co-chair, Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.), and the chair of the House subcommittee overseeing Golden Dome, Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.). Both are among the Golden Dome’s biggest cheerleaders in Congress.
The Democratic ranking member of the House Subcommittee on Strategic Forces, Rep. Scott Moulton (D-Mass.), is retiring from Congress. That leaves Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) as the next-senior Democrat on the subcommittee, with a path to becoming chairman when the new Congress convenes in January. In remarks earlier this year, he called Golden Dome a “massive, extraordinarily expensive, and ultimately inadequate defensive system.”
John Plumb, then-assistant secretary of defense for space policy, testifies before a subcommittee of the House Armed Services Committee on March 30, 2023.
Credit:
Alex Wong/Getty Images
John Plumb, then-assistant secretary of defense for space policy, testifies before a subcommittee of the House Armed Services Committee on March 30, 2023.
Credit:
Alex Wong/Getty Images
“When you use the words Golden Dome, now it’s political, and when you politicize national security, you get a political response, so it is damaging,” said John Plumb, who supervised military space policy for the Biden administration, in a panel discussion at the CyberSat conference this week.
The Trump administration projects Golden Dome will cost $185 billion over the next 10 years, a figure that’s hard to verify with the scarce information military officials have released about how the system will work.
Other cost estimates are significantly higher. The Congressional Budget Office concluded that a national missile defense system meeting the requirements set out in Trump’s executive order would cost about $1.2 trillion. The American Enterprise Institute released a report last year with a menu of potential Golden Dome architectures, ranging from a quarter-trillion dollars (without SBIs) to $3.6 trillion at the high end.
Pentagon officials chafe at these numbers, claiming they do not take into account the military’s assumptions for low-cost launches and mass-produced satellite networks.
The shiny new thing
The military envisions at least hundreds, and perhaps thousands, of Space-Based Interceptors in the uppermost layer of Golden Dome. These interceptors would loiter in orbit to wait for a missile attack. SBIs have never been placed into orbit before, despite decades of research and development. The idea has been around at least since the 1980s, when former President Ronald Reagan pushed the Strategic Defense Initiative, or “Star Wars,” weapons program.
“The most ambitious element of Golden Dome is the Space-Based Interceptor layer, and that is going to face significant technical challenges,” said Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), in a congressional hearing earlier this year.
“The cost, the physics, the likely reliability, in my view, do not support a full-scale space-based intercept architecture,” said Kelly, a former Navy combat pilot and astronaut. “This means that we could spend more than a trillion dollars and end up with a system that’s not going to work, and it’s not going to meaningfully improve our security.”
Some critics call out Golden Dome’s potential negative impact on global stability, fearing it could spark an arms race driving the world’s other nuclear powers to expand their arsenals. “It motivates the other side to just build more missiles because the easiest way to overcome a defense like that is just to buy more,” said Frank Kendall, who served as secretary of the Air Force in the Biden administration.
Others point to the risks of weaponizing space—a similar argument used against the Reagan-era Star Wars program. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink lifted that taboo in September with the first public disclosure that the US Space Force already has weapons in orbit.
A ground-based Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor is launched from the Reagan Test Site, Kwajalein Atoll in the Republic of the Marshall Islands, on a flight test on August 30, 2019. THAAD interceptors are currently operational, but they’re expensive, estimated to cost about $13 million per shot.
Credit:
Missile Defense Agency
A ground-based Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor is launched from the Reagan Test Site, Kwajalein Atoll in the Republic of the Marshall Islands, on a flight test on August 30, 2019. THAAD interceptors are currently operational, but they’re expensive, estimated to cost about $13 million per shot.
Credit:
Missile Defense Agency
But there’s more to the story than SBIs. The satellites and radars that detect and track missile launches are either in use today or were already in development during previous administrations. The same goes for Ground-Based Interceptors, which have been deployed for decades to take out missiles as they approach their targets. Under President Biden, the Pentagon’s Missile Defense Agency awarded Lockheed Martin a $17 billion contract to develop a next-generation Ground-Based Interceptor to defend against more sophisticated missile threats.
Optimism meets skepticism
The $24 billion Congress approved for Golden Dome last year was a one-time allocation for fiscal year 2026, which ended on October 1. The program’s funding dried up last month because the government is currently operating under a continuing resolution—an extension of last year’s regular military budget, which, of course, did not include the $24 billion Golden Dome infusion routed through reconciliation. The preliminary funding bills in the House and Senate for fiscal year 2027, if passed as-is, would provide only a fraction of the more than $17 billion the Trump administration requested for Golden Dome in this budget cycle.
That’s because the Trump administration again separated a significant part of its record $1.5 trillion topline military budget request into a reconciliation package outside of the normal congressional appropriations process. The supplemental $350 billion funding request—which included funds for Golden Dome—went nowhere in the Republican-controlled Congress. And it won’t happen when Democrats take the gavels next year, either.
It’s impossible to judge the realism of the Pentagon’s aim to get a first draft of Golden Dome up and running by the end 0f 2028, before the end of Trump’s presidency, because so much of the system is classified—but skepticism is the safer bet. Military officials have said little about Golden Dome’s design, architecture, or concept of operations, citing a national security imperative for secrecy.
One thing we do know is that a homeland defense shield like Golden Dome will need international partners to host radar sensors, ground stations, and missile batteries. Canada is an obvious target for such a partnership, and a fully deployed Golden Dome would notionally provide protection over all of North America.
However, this part of the program is off to a slow start. Michael Guetlein, the four-star Space Force general in charge of Golden Dome development, said earlier this year that tariffs—a core Trump administration policy—were limiting his interactions with foreign governments.
Gen. Michael Guetlein, direct report program manager for Golden Dome for America in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, appears before the House Armed Services Strategic Forces subcommittee on April 15, 2026, in Washington, DC.
Credit:
Luke Johnson/Getty Images
Gen. Michael Guetlein, direct report program manager for Golden Dome for America in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, appears before the House Armed Services Strategic Forces subcommittee on April 15, 2026, in Washington, DC.
Credit:
Luke Johnson/Getty Images
The hardest problem
So what can we expect when the next Congress convenes with Democratic majorities in January? The consensus among the experts Ars interviewed is that military leaders will still push for new options in missile defense, a need they say is underscored by their experience during the US war with Iran and Russia’s persistent missile strikes on Ukraine.
Modern missiles and drones can easily dodge existing defense systems. The stark expense of existing Western interceptors compared to the cost of Iranian missiles and drones can make defenders think twice about whether to shoot or keep their powder dry for a future attack.
“I feel like the entire effort would benefit from a better problem statement,” one former military space official told Ars. “Why do we think we need something that we don’t currently have? What’s changed? What’s different? What is it?”
This official offered some answers to these questions: “We are not in the 1970s or 1980s anymore, where it was us and the Soviet Union. The vast share of strategic threats to us were strategic ballistic missiles that we could see coming. That’s how things used to be.”
“Today’s environment is different,” he continued. “You have a host of strategic threats that are making classic ballistic missiles shrink in share. You’ve got hypersonic weapons. You’ve got endo-atmospheric hypersonic vehicles. You have increasingly accurate and harder to detect cruise missiles. It’s no longer just Russia. It’s China now, and to a lesser extent, North Korea and Iran.”
These new missile threats and the ubiquity of one-way attack drones make US and allied bases more susceptible to attack, the official said.
“What do we do about it? Do we just build more Mutually Assured Destruction platforms, or is there something else we can do? I think that’s what gets you to maybe we should look at ways to at least interfere with a potential attack against us.”
But some parts of Golden Dome, if followed to the letter of Trump’s executive order, simply may not work, at least at the scale required for global coverage, the official told Ars. One of them is a requirement to develop SBIs that can destroy enemy missiles during their boost phase soon after launch. This is in contrast to midcourse intercept in space or terminal intercept as the missile homes in on its target.
“The boost-phase intercept is a much bigger challenge,” the former military official said. “I’m probably going to have to have an interceptor that can survive reentry, track through reentry, and hit something while it’s still in the atmosphere. Hitting something in midcourse, as it’s left the atmosphere and is in space is just an easier problem… The original executive order talked about boost-phase intercept, and I was always skeptical about that one.”
An SBI aimed at a boost-phase ballistic missile would have to look down toward the Earth, not up toward space. The interceptor would have to distinguish the missile it’s tracking against the background of Earth, with clouds, cities, land, and water. It’s much easier to do that against the cold blackness of space. There are some benefits to a boost-phase intercept. For example, the ballistic missile is traveling slower soon after launch, and you might have another shot to intercept it if you miss.
The window for intercepting a missile in boost phase is also exceptionally narrow. The time from a launch detection to a shoot-down decision might be less than a minute, and a commander charged with making a “kill decision” would likely want more time to understand what’s happening before pulling the trigger on an interceptor.
“When does the person who has the authority for weapons engagement release the weapon? If your answer is it’s all automated, that’s interesting, but it’s also a little scary,” the former military official said. “Now I’m going to explain to the president why you just killed three taikonauts (Chinese astronauts) coming off a launch pad because no human was there. If you do need a human to say, ‘OK, I authorize release of the weapon,’ then that’s a time gap.”
Guetlein, the man in charge of Golden Dome, has acknowledged this challenge.
“I do believe that the technology exists to get after that threat today, and we believe we can solve it, but… can I do it at scale, and can I do it affordably? That’s going to be the huge challenge for boost-phase intercept,” Guetlein told lawmakers in an April hearing. “I will tell you, because we are so focused on affordability, if we cannot do it affordably, we will not go into production.”
This infographic produced by the German Institute for International and Security Affairs illustrates the elements of a space-based missile defense system.
Credit:
German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), 2025/CC BY 4.0
This infographic produced by the German Institute for International and Security Affairs illustrates the elements of a space-based missile defense system.
Credit:
German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), 2025/CC BY 4.0
There are other ways to take down missiles if engineers can’t close the case for boost-phase intercept, Guetlein said. “If boost-phase intercept from space is not affordable and [doesn’t] scale well, we will not produce it because we have other options to get after it.”
If proven feasible, directed-energy weapons using microwave or laser beams would provide US forces near-endless “magazine depth” in responding to massive salvos of missiles and drones, eschewing the need for “kinetic” SBIs for missile defense. Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a hearing earlier this year that the Space Force should spend more on directed-energy research than on space-based kinetic kill vehicles.
Plumb, the former Biden military space policy chief, pointed to bipartisan support for the Pentagon’s existing missile defense programs, along with new initiatives to improve tracking hypersonic missiles. “I think any administration, Republican or Democrat, is going to continue to improve missile defenses for the US, 100 percent,” he said, adding that it is “probably unlikely” that SBIs survive the coming cull.
So what do the people actually building Golden Dome think? Their answer is similar. Some missile defense priorities will survive, but maybe with a new name.
The name Golden Dome is a “brand,” said Dylan Taylor, chairman and CEO of Voyager Technologies, which works with Anduril on SBIs. “It’s a proxy for layers of a protective onion, if you will, and there are elements of what is being called Golden Dome, where the technology is very advanced, and it works. The systems work. They’re more functional than I think people have reported on or have indicated.”
“Golden Dome is a lot more than SBIs,” said another executive at a space company working on the project. “It’s one layer and element. We believe that there’s bipartisan support for this capability because it is a required capability for national security. The question is whether it can be achieved at a price that makes it executable and palatable. The technical aspect of this closes, and there’s just a question about scalability and cost.”
The executive told Ars that newer, smaller space companies can do the job for less money than the Pentagon’s legacy contractors. Many companies are spending private capital on Golden Dome-related research and development with the promise of future Pentagon business. Military leaders have added stops on Wall Street and with venture capital firms to their usual tours of bases, command centers, and test ranges.
“There’s real hardware being built by all the players,” the official said, suggesting optimism about fielding a working preliminary version of Golden Dome by 2028. “From us, on our execution to date, we’ve conducted engine tests and thermal tests and communications tests.
“My fiduciary responsibility is to turn our investment into these critical technologies into future value, and I wouldn’t have made that call had I not been comfortable with the survivability of the program, assuming we can achieve the technical and financial targets, which we’ve convinced ourselves we can,” the official said.
Rocket Lab is another company with business ties to Golden Dome. The company’s founder and CEO, Peter Beck, told Ars he was convinced missile defense will remain a priority no matter who controls Congress or the White House.
“Is it a national security imperative that we go to the Moon? Probably not. Is it a national security imperative that we can protect the nation from incoming missile threats? Yes,” Beck said. “With these sorts of things, I’d say it’s what shape and scale they are, not whether they survive.”
“There are elements of Golden Dome that I don’t think are going to be politically vulnerable, and there will be other parts of Golden Dome that, of course, will be,” Taylor said. “The point I want to emphasize is people who say, ‘Well, Golden Dome is dead; the whole thing is dead,’ they don’t necessarily understand that there are four or five or six layers to the system, and some are vulnerable and some are not.”
Voyager’s expertise for missile defense is in advanced propulsion, and Taylor said those technologies are relevant for a range of systems, not just Golden Dome.
“There’s no doubt that whatever it’s going to be called, it won’t be called Golden Dome, and there will definitely be machinations in the system, but it won’t be a ‘throw the baby out with the bath water’ approach,” Taylor said. “Given the risk profile, I don’t see that happening.”
President Donald Trump speaks alongside Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in the Oval Office at the White House on May 20, 2025, in Washington, DC.
Credit:
Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
President Donald Trump speaks alongside Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in the Oval Office at the White House on May 20, 2025, in Washington, DC.
Credit:
Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
In a Senate hearing in September, Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, proposed the idea of a name change as one option to “depoliticize” the missile defense issue.
“It is no secret that the ‘Golden Dome’ moniker has contributed to political polarization around the effort,” Karako said in his testimony. “Several options exist to depolarize and depoliticize the effort. It belongs to Congress to name or rename executive departments—witness the pending proposal to rename the Department of Defense as the Department of War. Congress likewise has legislative power to rename the Golden Dome initiative in a future national defense authorization act.”
“There are things in the program that make sense,” said Sen. Kelly, who serves on the Senate Subcommittee for Strategic Forces. These include new capabilities for “detecting launches,” he said. “The Space-Based Interceptor part is really, really hard, and the physics clearly favors the offense,” Kelly said. “We could go down this road, spend hundreds of billions of dollars, and not get any return on that investment, and missile defense is too important to pursue this just based on aspiration alone.”
Kathy Warden, the CEO of Northrop Grumman, acknowledged last year that with SBIs, “more invention is required than other parts of the [Golden Dome] architecture.”
The most recent trends in warfare, as seen in the Middle East and Ukraine, highlight the need for cheaper, mass-produced countermeasures to use against massive drone and missile attacks. In other words, it requires magazine depth, as some military commanders like to say. Democrats seem likely to conclude that the path to magazine depth does not include SBIs.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: Microsoft is making Windows keyboard accessibility features less annoying
articles.text:
Something to look forward to: Windows is finally changing how users interact with two of the operating system's most prominent accessibility features. Sticky Keys and Filter Keys, first introduced in Windows 95, will soon be easier to disable permanently. As a result, users who don't have trouble interacting with a keyboard should experience fewer interruptions during critical tasks – or, perhaps more importantly, leisure activities.
Sticky Keys is a classic accessibility feature available across all major computer operating systems. System 6 reportedly introduced the feature on Mac systems in 1988. The option provides a way to "serialize" keystrokes, allowing them to press and release a modifier key – Shift, Ctrl, Alt, or Win – just once when using a standard keyboard shortcut, rather than holding it down while pressing another key.
Filter Keys, meanwhile, is a Windows-specific accessibility option designed to ignore brief or repeated keystrokes. People affected by hand tremors or other physical conditions can benefit greatly from this feature, which helps prevent typing and other input errors.
Both features are designed to improve accessibility in Windows, but they can also become a nuisance if you don't need them. Traditionally, these options can be activated by simply pressing the Shift key five times or holding it down for an extended period. The operating system might interrupt gaming sessions, or other immersive experiences, with an annoying "Turn Sticky Keys on?" pop-up.
Starting with Windows 11 Insider Beta Preview Build 26320.9876, the system interface will offer a new option to permanently dismiss these pop-ups. Microsoft said users who don't need Sticky Keys or Filter Keys should have an easier time dealing with the features, reducing interruptions caused by the surprisingly persistent notifications.
I've lost count of how many times the Sticky Keys pop-up has interrupted my daily computing tasks across multiple Windows versions. Most likely, the new dismissal option is targeting exactly the kind of user I am. However, Microsoft will still have a hard time convincing me to abandon Windows 10's almost rock-solid experience and upgrade to Windows 11.
Currently in beta, this change to Windows' accessibility interface should soon become part of the Windows 11 26H2 experience. Before this new Insider beta release, users had to navigate Windows Settings or the intricacies of Control Panel to disable Sticky Keys or Filter Keys.

articles.title: Meta lanza Muse Ember: una IA ultrabarata para programar y automatizar tareas con agentes
articles.text:
Meta ha presentado Muse Ember, su modelo de IA más pequeño y eficiente hasta ahora. El nuevo modelo está pensado para ejecutar procesos complejos como los que realizan los agentes en segundo plano. Ember se une a Spark, Glimmer, Wonder y otros integrantes de la familia Muse, desarrollada por el equipo de superinteligencia de Meta.
A diferencia de los grandes modelos como Claude Sonnet, GPT-6 Sol o el mismo Wonder, Muse Ember se enfoca en tareas repetitivas. De acuerdo con Meta, actividades como analizar documentos, extraer información, enrutar solicitudes o ejecutar subtareas de programación son las que consumen la mayor parte de los recursos cuando un agente de IA trabaja de forma autónoma.
Muse Ember admite hasta un millón de tokens de entrada y puede generar hasta 512.000 tokens de salida. Esto le permite procesar bases de código completas o colecciones de documentos en una sola solicitud. En términos de desempeño, Meta afirma que su modelo iguala a Claude Haiku 5.5 en algunos benchmarks y supera a GPT-6 Luna en otras pruebas, todas con un coste menor por tarea.
El nuevo modelo de Meta también tiene capacidades multimodales, las que le permiten comprender texto, imágenes, audio y video de forma nativa. Esto habilita a los agentes para que puedan analizar capturas de pantalla, diagramas, documentos escaneados, grabaciones de voz o vídeo sin necesidad de usar un modelo adicional. En la prueba OSWorld, que mide la capacidad de un agente para controlar el ordenador de forma autónoma, Muse Ember supera a GPT-6 Luna y Claude Haiki 5.5, todos con el razonamiento al máximo.
Muse Ember supera a Claude y ChatGPT en varias pruebas de programación y agentes
Según Meta, Muse Ember está diseñado para subtareas de programación, como leer archivos, ejecutar pruebas y hacer correcciones específicas. Los ingenieros optimizaron el modelo para tareas concretas que suelen ejecutarse cientos de veces durante una sesión de desarrollo. Meta añade que las tareas más avanzadas, como planificar estrategias generales, pueden realizarse con Muse Wonder, mientras que Ember se encargará del trabajo operativo.
En Terminal Bench 4.0, la prueba que mide si un agente puede llevar a cabo tareas reales de ingeniería, Muse Ember obtiene una calificación de más del doble de GPT-6 Sol. La parte alta de la tabla está reservada para los modelos de Anthropic (Opus, Astra y Sonnet), mientras que la parte media se la disputan otros modelos grandes de código abierto y Ember.
De acuerdo con una publicación en el blog de Meta, Muse Spark se mantiene por debajo de los umbrales de alto riesgo. El modelo cuenta con las mismas medidas de seguridad en el entrenamiento y ejecución que tienen otros integrantes de la familia Muse. Esto significa que no tiene capacidades para hackear y llevar a cabo otras tareas prohibidas, aunque siempre valdrá la pena tener cuidado con los permisos que habilitas para que la IA trabaje con tus archivos.
Muse Ember ya está disponible a partir de hoy a través de Meta Model API y Muse Code. EL modelo tiene un coste de 0,10 dólares por millón de tokens de entrada y 0,50 dólares por millón de tokens de salida.

articles.title: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users.
Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price.
Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system, long a sticking point for many enterprise clients.
It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR, which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain.
Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”
Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card.
“Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.”
Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.”
Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question.

articles.title: Apple passt die Entwicklungsphasen für iOS an: Wofür Entwickler künftig mehr Zeit haben sollen
articles.text:
Mehr Raum für Kreativität: Apple stellt Entwicklungsprozesse von iOS 28 um
Apple hat die Entwicklungsphasen für sein neues Betriebssystem iOS 28 angepasst. Dadurch sollen Entwickler:innen mehr Zeit haben, um neue Funktionen zu entwickeln und auszuprobieren, wie der Bloomberg-Reporter Mark Gurman in seinem Newsletter berichtet. Der gesamte Arbeitsablauf verschiebt sich, wodurch mehr Raum für Kreativität geschaffen wird.
Das soll sich jetzt bei Apple ändern
iOS 27 ist erst seit dem 14. September verfügbar. Trotzdem steht schon fest, dass es mit dem Nachfolgesystem etwas anders laufen könnte. Bisher war die Entwicklung in drei Phasen unterteilt, die auch als M1, M2 und M3 bezeichnet werden. Normalerweise dauerte jede Phase acht Wochen. Vier flossen in die Programmierung und weitere vier in die Konvergenz.
In der Konvergenz werden die neu entwickelten Funktionen in die Betriebssysteme integriert. Apple soll diese Phasen jetzt zugunsten einer intensiveren Programmierphase in M1 verschoben haben. Künftig haben Entwickler:innen sechs Wochen für die Programmierung und Funktionsentwicklung Zeit. Die übrigen zwei Wochen sind für die Konvergenz reserviert. Die Änderungen sollen für iOS 28, iPadOS 28 und macOS 28 gelten.
Laut Bloomberg stoße die Änderung intern weitgehend auf Zuspruch. Sie schaffe vor allem mehr Raum für Kreativität und senke den Integrationsdruck. Durch den stärkeren Fokus auf die M1-Phase haben Entwickler:innen mehr Zeit, vielversprechende Ansätze zu verfolgen, bevor sie diese ins Betriebssystem integrieren müssen. Am üblichen Veröffentlichungszeitplan soll sich dadurch aber nichts ändern.
Laut Gurman bestehe die Hoffnung darin, dass die zusätzliche Zeit die Gesamtqualität der Funktionen optimiert. Anstelle kleiner, schrittweiser Verbesserungen könnte Apple so grundlegendere Neuerungen entwickeln. Welche konkreten Funktionen das für iOS 28 bedeutet, steht aber noch nicht fest.
Gibt Apple dem Druck des Marktes nach?
Laut Gurman sei es denkbar, dass Apple im Rahmen der Neuerung auch auf den steigenden Druck reagiere, bei der KI-Entwicklung aufzuholen. Ein zentrales Ziel bestehe darin, Siri zu einem agentischen System weiterzuentwickeln, das komplexe Aufgaben übernimmt und Drittanbieter-Apps bedient. „Wie mir berichtet wurde, möchte Apple langfristig in diese Richtung gehen”, so der Bloomberg-Reporter. „Ich glaube, dass das Unternehmen Siri schon im nächsten Jahr stärker zu einem Agenten machen könnte – nicht, dass es angesichts der aktuellen Verbraucher- und Marktanforderungen eine große Wahl hätte.“
Diese Einschätzung widerspricht in Teilen den Aussagen des neuen Apple-CEOs John Ternus. Im Interview mit Wired erklärte er kürzlich, er betrachte den vermeintlichen KI-Rückstand mit Gelassenheit. „Mir gefällt unsere derzeitige Position sehr gut“, so Ternus.
Er sehe in der Technologie keinen Selbstzweck. Sie solle nur dort zum Einsatz kommen, wo sie einen Mehrwert liefern kann. Deshalb werde die Entscheidung über Produktneuheiten beim Menschen bleiben. Dennoch könnte Apple durch die rasante KI-Entwicklung in einer Zwickmühle stecken, wie es auch Gurman beschreibt. Auf der einen Seite steht der eigene Anspruch – auf der anderen der Druck des Marktes.

articles.title: 6 000 km de détour pour battre Boeing : l'Airbus A350-1000ULR s'approprie un record vieux de 21 ans
articles.text:
C’était un vol qui avait passionné les amateurs d’aviation pendant l’été. Les 27 et 28 juillet 2026, un Airbus A350-1000ULR a relié Melbourne à Toulouse sans escale en 24 heures et 24 minutes. Une journée complète en vol, et même un peu plus. Au passage, il est devenu l’un des vols les plus suivis de l’histoire de Flightradar24, le site qui affiche en temps réel la position des avions.
Depuis le 9 novembre, il a désormais son record officiel : Airbus annonce que le fameux Guinness World Records l’a reconnu comme le plus long vol en distance jamais réalisé par un avion de ligne, avec 23 155 kilomètres parcourus. L’avionneur européen efface ainsi un record de Boeing établi 21 ans plus tôt, jour pour jour.
Les 9 et 10 novembre 2005, un Boeing 777-200LR avait parcouru 21 601 kilomètres entre Hong Kong et Londres en 22 heures et 42 minutes. Lui aussi avait pris le chemin le plus long, vers l’est, en survolant le Pacifique, l’Amérique du Nord puis l’Atlantique.
Pourquoi 23 155 kilomètres pour relier Melbourne à Toulouse ?
À vol d’oiseau, les deux villes ne sont séparées que de 16 888 kilomètres. Or, la campagne d’essais exigeait un vol de 23 heures, du départ du parking à l’arrivée, pour simuler les plus longs vols commerciaux prévus. L’avion a donc pris le chemin le plus long, vers l’est. Il a survolé Sydney, traversé le Pacifique en direction de Los Angeles, puis l’Amérique du Nord et l’Atlantique, avant de survoler Londres et de rejoindre Toulouse.
En somme, un détour de plus de 6 000 kilomètres (plus qu’un Paris-New York, environ 5 800 kilomètres) pour prouver l’endurance de l’appareil. À bord, Airbus avait réuni trois de ses pilotes d’essai, deux pilotes de Qantas, sept ingénieurs et un représentant de la Fédération aéronautique internationale, qui a validé les données du vol avec Flightradar24.
Un avion conçu pour relier Sydney à Londres sans escale
Ce vol de très grande endurance n’était pas là que pour la frime. Il figurait dans la campagne d’essais de l’A350-1000ULR (pour Ultra Long Range, très long rayon d’action). Cette version de l’A350-1000 a été développée pour le Project Sunrise de Qantas, qui doit relier sans escale Sydney à Londres et à New York.
Ces trajets représentent près de 10 000 milles nautiques (environ 18 500 kilomètres) et jusqu’à 22 heures de vol. Aujourd’hui, il faut au moins une escale pour relier ces villes. La compagnie australienne a commandé douze appareils, et les premières liaisons sont attendues en 2027.
