articles.title: Anthropic, l’IA "responsable" ? L’entreprise dépense 3,4 milliards pour des générateurs à gaz
articles.text:
L’intelligence artificielle (IA) offre un second souffle à l’exploitation de gaz en s’imposant comme une solution privilégiée pour alimenter les data centers. Et Anthropic a visiblement opté pour cette solution qui pose très clairement question.
Depuis sa fondation en 2021, Anthropic a bâti sa réputation sur la sécurité et la responsabilité, en opposition à sa grande rivale OpenAI. Mais ses principes se heurtent évidemment à la réalité du marché. À l’approche de sa très attendue entrée en Bourse, l’entreprise a toujours plus besoin de puissance de calcul, au risque de reléguer ses beaux principes au second plan.
Un montage peu commun
Car d’après le Financial Times, Anthropic a passé, fin septembre, un accord à hauteur de 3,4 milliards de dollars avec OnePWR Solutions, un fournisseur basé au Texas, portant sur 1,7 gigawatt de générateurs à gaz de forte puissance. Il s’agirait du plus gros achat de ce type jamais connu pour un laboratoire d’IA.
D’autant que le montage du deal est très particulier. Il y a deux ans, OnePWR a commandé des générateurs au constructeur Caterpillar, mais avait besoin de financements pour mener l’opération à son terme. Anthropic, plutôt que de devenir cliente, a finalement préféré reprendre directement ces commandes à son compte. L’accord inclut, en outre, les compétences d’ingénierie et de construction nécessaires pour installer les dispositifs.
L’ambition de la société est claire : alors que l’accès à l’électricité est devenu un enjeu crucial pour l’IA, la demande de turbines et de générateurs explose. Leurs délais de fabrication se comptent désormais en années. Posséder sa propre infrastructure permet de contourner ces obstacles.
- Excellente compréhension des consignes complexes
- Très bon niveau en rédaction
- Analyse de longs documents efficace
Les géants de la tech foncent sur le gaz
Même son de cloche du côté de SpaceXAI a acheté plus tôt cette année des turbines mobiles à gaz pour 2 milliards de dollars. De son côté, Alphabet a mis la main, fin 2025, sur le fournisseur Intersect. Qu’il s’agisse de nucléaire ou de gaz, toutes cherchent à sécuriser leur propre électricité, et à aller vite, quitte à mettre au placard leurs objectifs environnementaux.
Car le recours au gaz est loin d’être anodin. Son principal composant, le méthane, a un pouvoir de réchauffement supérieur à celui du CO2 sur 20 ans. Selon l’Agence internationale de l’énergie, ce gaz à effet de serre est responsable d’environ 30 % du réchauffement depuis la révolution industrielle.
À cela s’ajoutent des polluants comme les oxydes d’azote et les particules fines, qui peuvent pénétrer profondément dans les poumons. À Memphis, les turbines à gaz de SpaceXAI font d’ailleurs l’objet d’une plainte menée par plusieurs ONG, qui l’accusent de dégrader la qualité de l’air.

articles.title: MENA startup funding plunges 96% to $40 million in October 2026 as megadeals dry up
articles.text:
MENA startup funding plunges 96% to $40 million in October 2026 as megadeals dry up
Startup investment across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) plunged in October 2026, with 32 startups raising just $40 million, as the absence of large funding rounds brought September’s short-lived rebound to an abrupt halt.
The total represents a 96% month-on-month decline from the $1.1 billion raised in September and a 95% drop from the $784.9 million recorded in October 2025, making October one of the weakest months for regional startup funding this year.
The sharp reversal underscores the volatility of MENA’s investment landscape, where a handful of outsized transactions can dramatically reshape monthly funding figures. September’s performance was heavily driven by three Saudi fintech deals worth a combined $762.5 million, accounting for nearly 70% of the month’s total.
October offered a starkly different picture. With no megadeals or later-stage rounds to lift the headline figure, funding remained concentrated in smaller, early-stage transactions, reflecting a more cautious investment environment amid persistent geopolitical and economic uncertainty.
Yet the slowdown was not uniform. Saudi Arabia maintained its lead, fintech continued to attract investor activity, and business-to-business (B2B) startups secured the overwhelming majority of available capital.
Saudi Arabia retains the lead despite funding slump
Saudi Arabia remained MENA’s most-funded startup ecosystem in October, with nine startups raising a combined $18.8 million, accounting for 47% of all capital deployed during the month.
The kingdom’s performance was largely driven by Autobia’s $12 million Series A round, which alone represented nearly 64% of Saudi Arabia’s total funding.
The UAE followed in second place, with 10 startups securing $12.9 million. Although the country recorded more transactions than Saudi Arabia, its overall funding remained lower, highlighting the difference between investment activity and deal value.
Qatar climbed to third place with a single $5 million transaction, overtaking Egypt, which slipped to fourth despite recording six deals worth a combined $1.7 million.
Egypt’s performance marked a sharp retreat from September, when seven startups raised $49.2 million, largely supported by Paymob’s $35 million funding round. The October figures point to continued difficulty in attracting sizable investment commitments to one of the region’s largest startup ecosystems.
Further down the rankings, Kuwait secured $650,000 across two deals, followed by Jordan with $560,000 from a single transaction. Syria rounded out the list, with three startups raising a combined $365,000.
The regional distribution highlights a familiar pattern: Saudi Arabia and the UAE continued to dominate funding, attracting nearly 80% of October’s total, while smaller ecosystems accounted for a limited share of investment.
Autobia propels autotech to the top
Autotech emerged as October’s most-funded sector, driven entirely by Saudi startup Autobia’s $12 million Series A round.
Fintech ranked second by funding value but remained the most active sector by deal count, with five startups raising nearly $10 million.
The result suggests that investor interest in financial technology has not disappeared, even as the sector moved away from the exceptionally large financing rounds that dominated September.
Adtech came third, attracting $5 million through a single transaction secured by UAE-based JustAd.
Together, the three leading sectors accounted for roughly two-thirds of October’s funding, leaving the remaining capital spread across a broader range of industries.
Megadeals disappear as early-stage funding dominates
October saw a complete absence of megadeals and later-stage funding rounds, marking a sharp departure from September, when several established startups secured substantial financing.
Instead, early-stage startups dominated both funding value and deal volume, raising $33.7 million across 24 transactions.
That represents more than 84% of all capital deployed during the month and 75% of the total number of deals.
Debt financing played a limited role, accounting for approximately $550,000 through a single transaction, equivalent to just 1.4% of total funding.
Another seven startups raised a combined $5.7 million without disclosing their funding stages.
The shift toward early-stage investment offers a more nuanced view of the slowdown. While larger funding commitments largely disappeared, investors continued to back younger companies, albeit with considerably smaller amounts of capital.
B2B startups capture the majority of funding
Business-to-business startups maintained their dominance in October, raising $34.3 million across 21 transactions, equivalent to nearly 86% of all capital deployed.
Business-to-consumer (B2C) companies followed at a considerable distance, securing just $2.4 million through four deals.
Startups operating hybrid business models, serving both businesses and consumers, attracted $3.3 million across seven transactions.
The figures reinforce a recurring trend in MENA’s investment landscape, where B2B startups continue to secure the largest share of capital.
Female-founded startups receive just 0.5% of funding
The gender funding gap widened further in October, with male-founded startups capturing 99.5% of all investment, equivalent to approximately $39.8 million across 30 transactions.
Only two funded startups had female founders or mixed-gender founding teams, collectively raising just $200,000.
The disparity is particularly striking given the already limited amount of capital deployed during the month.
Even as investors continued to fund early-stage businesses, female-founded and mixed-gender startups remained largely excluded from the region’s investment activity.
The imbalance extends a persistent trend across MENA. In the third quarter of 2026, male-led startups attracted more than 98% of total funding, while female-led companies secured less than 1%.
A sharp correction, but not the full picture
October’s collapse in startup funding marks a difficult start to the final quarter of 2026, reinforcing concerns about the sustainability of the region’s investment recovery.
The decline comes against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty, regional conflict and volatile economic conditions that continue to complicate investment decisions and business planning.
But the magnitude of the month-on-month drop also requires context.
September’s $1.1 billion total was inflated by a handful of unusually large transactions, including substantial debt financing. October’s lack of comparable deals therefore magnified the apparent contraction, making the headline decline more dramatic than the change in deal activity alone might suggest.
Indeed, while total funding fell by approximately 96%, the number of transactions declined by 56%, from 73 in September to 32 in October.
That distinction matters. The region did not experience a complete withdrawal of startup investment. Rather, capital continued to flow into early-stage businesses, while large funding commitments were largely absent.
The more concerning signal is the limited breadth of that activity. Funding remained heavily concentrated in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, a single transaction accounted for 30% of regional investment, and female-founded startups continued to receive a negligible share of capital.
Despite these challenges, MENA startups have attracted approximately $3.4 billion in funding during the first 10 months of 2026, demonstrating that significant capital has continued to reach the ecosystem through a year marked by geopolitical and economic disruption.
The remaining two months will test whether investors regain the confidence to back larger transactions or continue to favour smaller, more selective commitments.
October’s sharp decline may not signal a sustained downturn, but it exposes the fragility of MENA’s funding recovery, which remains heavily reliant on a handful of large transactions rather than broad-based investment activity.
For MENA’s startup ecosystem, the challenge is no longer simply attracting capital. It is building a funding market that can sustain investment beyond the occasional megadeal.
These monthly reports are a collaboration between Wamda and Digital Digest.

articles.title: Yoco taps $100 million credit facility to scale merchant cash advances
articles.text:
Yoco, a South African fintech, has secured a $100 million credit facility from US investment firm Victory Park Capital to expand its small-business cash advances operation and take greater control of the financing offered through its payments platform.
The deal marks a new phase for Yoco Capital, which has advanced more than R6.5 billion ($395 million) to over 40,000 merchants since 2018, working with specialist credit providers. The new facility is expected to give Yoco greater control over the pricing and risk of its merchant loans as it scales the business.
The bigger bet is that transaction data generated by merchants using Yoco’s card machines and online payment tools can help the company assess businesses that traditional lenders may struggle to evaluate. If that data advantage holds, Yoco could turn its payments relationship with more than 200,000 businesses into a larger cash advance operation, while testing whether its model can remain profitable as it scales.
Yoco Capital, a data-driven funding for small businesses, provides working capital advances to merchants already using the platform. Rather than requiring an application, eligible offers appear in its app after merchants are assessed using live sales data from in-person and online payments. Advances range from R2,000 ($122) to R1.5 million ($91,185), with no collateral required.
Yoco automatically deducts repayments from a merchant’s daily takings rather than requiring fixed monthly instalments. The model is designed to make repayments move with sales, although it raises questions about how merchants fare when revenue falls, or trading becomes unpredictable.
“We have spent a decade building an operating system that runs a merchant’s whole business, payments, point of sale, and now the decisions in between. Financing was the one layer we didn’t fully control. This facility changes that,” Carsten Holtkemeyer, Yoco’s chief executive officer (CEO), said in a statement on Monday.
Yoco describes it as one of Africa’s largest dedicated merchant cash advance facilities, giving it direct control over the financing layer at scale for the first time. The company says it has not recorded an unprofitable lending cohort since it began advancing capital in 2018, including during the Covid-19 pandemic. But it did not provide cohort-level performance figures, default rates, or write-offs with the announcement.
The model relies on a different view of a small business’s finances. A bank statement or credit bureau report offers a snapshot, while payment records can show sales patterns in real time. Yoco says that information can help it tailor funding to a merchant’s trading history and business needs.
Merchants typically use advances to buy stock ahead of busy periods, hire staff, upgrade equipment or open branches, according to Yoco. The company plans to extend Yoco Capital to more of its 200,000-plus merchants across retail, hospitality and services in South Africa.
Access to finance remains a constraint for smaller businesses. The 2025 Finfind and African Bank SA MSME Access to Finance Report puts South Africa’s small-business financing gap at about R350 billion ($21.3 billion). It estimates that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) receive 13% of national bank lending, compared with 51% for large corporations.
Victory Park Capital brings experience in private credit and asset-backed finance to the arrangement. The firm says it has invested more than $12 billion across 260 investments since 2007. Its senior partner, Jason Brown, said Yoco had demonstrated a track record of supporting small and independent businesses.
“We’re supportive of Yoco’s mission to expand access to flexible financing solutions for South African entrepreneurs,” Brown said.
Yoco believes the facility fits a broader effort to become an operating system for independent businesses, combining payments, point-of-sale software and financing. The company has expanded its product offering, acquired software business Dyner, and said it is developing an AI-powered platform. It also says it has reduced merchant fees by R250 million ($15.20 million) a year.
Yoco’s next test is whether it can scale cash advances without compromising the discipline behind its model. For merchants, the real measure will be simple: whether the funding arrives when they need it most, helping them keep the doors open and the tills ringing.
Editor’s note: This story has been updated to clarify that Yoco’s $100 million credit facility will support its merchant cash advances operation, rather than merchant lending more broadly.

articles.title: Frigos piratés : le FBI alerte sur des « systèmes ciblés dans le monde entier »
articles.text:
Le piratage des frigos ne se cantonne plus à l’Europe. Ce jeudi 5 novembre 2026, l’agence américaine de cybersécurité (CISA) et le FBI ont publié une alerte conjointe au sujet des cyberattaques à l’encontre des systèmes de réfrigération. Les ministères américains de la Santé, de l’Agriculture et des Transports se sont associés à cette mise en garde. Brett Leatherman, directeur des opérations de la division cyber du FBI, révèle que les systèmes de réfrigération sont « ciblés dans les secteurs d’infrastructures critiques du monde entier ».
« Les systèmes de réfrigération industrielle et de surveillance de la chaîne du froid protègent les aliments, les médicaments et d’autres produits sensibles à la température, ce qui en fait des cibles attrayantes pour les acteurs malveillants », explique Brett Leatherman dans un communiqué de presse.
À lire aussi : Après les supermarchés, les hackers ciblent les frigos des hôpitaux « pour les vaccins ou les poches de sang »
« Partir du principe qu’elle pourrait être une cible »
Selon les autorités américaines, les pirates s’attaquent aux régulateurs de température et aux contrôleurs de frigos des supermarchés et des entrepôts réfrigérés. Pour arriver à leurs fins et prendre le contrôle de systèmes, ils exploitent les failles d’appareils obsolètes, bien souvent accessibles depuis Internet par n’importe qui. Une fois aux commandes, ils peuvent forcer les frigos à chauffer ou à lancer une opération de dégivrage, ce qui va faire surchauffer le contenu.
Outre les stocks perdus, les autorités américaines évoquent l’usure prématurée des équipements, un risque d’incendie et un danger sanitaire pour les consommateurs. Si des produits surchauffés passent inaperçus, les acheteurs risquent évidemment une intoxication alimentaire. Les pirates peuvent d’ailleurs aussi empêcher les administrateurs de voir la température réelle de leurs installations, ouvrant la porte à la vente de produits avariés.
« Toute organisation qui dépend de systèmes de réfrigération et de surveillance doit partir du principe qu’elle pourrait être une cible », prévient Chris Butera, directeur adjoint par intérim pour la cybersécurité de la CISA.
L’alerte survient peu après qu’une vague de cyberattaques ait déferlé sur les frigos des supermarchés européens, et surtout français. Le mois dernier, des centaines de supermarchés français ont vu leurs frigos grimper jusqu’à 50 °C en pleine nuit. Quelques semaines plus tard, des attaques analogues ont touché plusieurs pays européens, ainsi que les chambres froides de l’Établissement français du sang. Comme le montre l’alerte émise par les autorités américaines, la menace ne se limite pas à l’Europe. Aux États-Unis, le Pentagone enquête sur des pannes de congélateurs suspectes dans des bases militaires, indique Reuters.
Les autorités américaines recommandent d’agir « immédiatement », de couper tous les équipements d’Internet, de changer les mots de passe par défaut, d’appliquer les mises à jour, et de remplacer systématiquement les vieux appareils que le fabricant ne prend plus en charge.
Moins de contrôleurs accessibles sur Internet
Dans ce contexte, les entreprises ont d’ailleurs commencé à réagir pour se protéger. Les équipements Danfoss, l’une des entreprises dont les contrôleurs ont été piratés durant l’offensive nationale sur la France, ont été massivement retirés d’Internet. Selon les chercheurs de la société Censys, le nombre de contrôleurs Danfoss exposés sur Internet est passé de 3 004 à 708 entre le 9 octobre et le 5 novembre. C’est un progrès, mais des milliers de contrôleurs restent accessibles. On en trouve encore plus de 700 chez Danfoss, et encore 2 420 chez Dixell, une autre marque visée par des intrusions.

articles.title: Corea del Sur multó con USD 467 millones a aplicaciones de delivery por presionar a los restaurantes con los precios
articles.text:
El 9 de noviembre, el organismo antimonopolio de Corea del Sur anunció multas provisionales por 631.900 millones de wones (USD 467 millones) a Baemin y Coupang Eats, las dos principales aplicaciones de reparto de comida del país, por abusar de su posición dominante frente a los restaurantes.
La Comisión de Comercio Justo fijó 331.100 millones de wones (USD 243 millones, según la agencia Yonhap) para Woowa Brothers, la operadora de Baemin, y 300.800 millones (USD 220,59 millones, según Reuters) para Coupang, que gestiona Coupang Eats. Según The Korea Herald, es la mayor sanción impuesta a apps de delivery en el país.
El regulador sostiene que ambas empresas obligaron a los restaurantes a ofrecer condiciones al menos tan favorables como las de las plataformas rivales. En el caso de Coupang, fueron seis: precios del menú, pedido mínimo, descuentos y costos de envío para el cliente, entre otras. La práctica duró de julio de 2023 a enero de 2026.
Quien no cumplía perdía el estatus de local “Wow”, que permite a los suscriptores de la membresía de Coupang recibir descuentos y envío gratis. Según la Comisión, el porcentaje de restaurantes que aceptaron las exigencias pasó del 13% en julio de 2023 a casi el 94% en octubre de 2025.
Baemin aplicó requisitos parecidos entre mayo de 2024 y octubre de 2025. Limitó los descuentos de envío de los suscriptores de Baemin Club a los pedidos hechos en locales que cumplieran sus condiciones.
Los locales excluidos vendieron menos de la mitad
Los restaurantes tenían poco margen para resistirse, según el organismo, porque quedar fuera de los programas de membresía reducía sus ventas de forma notable. En Coupang, las ventas diarias promedio de los locales excluidos bajaron de 220.000 a 90.000 wones (USD 162 a USD 66). En Baemin, de 110.000 a 30.000 wones (USD 81 a USD 22).
Baemin tenía el 58,45% de los pedidos del mercado coreano de reparto en 2025, medido por valor, y Coupang Eats el 34,44%. Juntas suman 92,89%. La Comisión, según recogió The Korea Herald, afirmó que imponer las mismas exigencias a la vez restringió la competencia de un modo similar a una colusión, es decir, a un pacto entre rivales.
El organismo también vinculó la práctica con los precios. Según su investigación, el 75% de los restaurantes que cedieron ante Coupang empeoró sus condiciones en Baemin en lugar de mejorarlas en la plataforma rival. En agosto de 2024, Baemin subió la comisión de su reparto propio del 6,8% al 9,8%, igual a la de Coupang Eats.
Baemin empujó su reparto propio
La Comisión sancionó a Baemin por otra conducta: forzar a los restaurantes a pasar del servicio en que ellos organizan el envío al servicio en que la plataforma reparte. Los ingresos de Baemin equivalían al 28% del valor de cada pedido con reparto propio en 2024, frente al 7,8% en el otro modelo.
Para ampliar ese reparto, según el regulador, la app redujo o bloqueó la visibilidad del servicio alternativo y mostró tiempos de entrega que lo hacían parecer más lento. Los envíos organizados por los restaurantes tardaban en promedio 1,4 minutos menos, pero la app los presentaba como 13 minutos más lentos, indicó The Korea Times.
Las mayores comisiones llevaron a los restaurantes a subir los pedidos mínimos y los precios del menú para proteger sus márgenes, indicó el organismo. Con las medidas correctivas, la Comisión espera que los locales fijen precios y mínimos con libertad en cada plataforma y que nuevos competidores puedan entrar.
Coupang calificó la multa de excesiva: dijo que equivale a más de 600 veces la sanción de un caso comparable de 2020. Aseguró que la Comisión incluyó ingresos ajenos a la conducta investigada y que la impugnará en la justicia. Woowa Brothers lamentó que sus argumentos no hayan sido aceptados y dijo que revisará la decisión.
Coupang defendió el programa Wow como una forma de ofrecer precios razonables y envío gratis a los consumidores y de ayudar a vender más a los restaurantes. La Comisión ordenó además a la empresa modificar en 60 días las cláusulas que le permiten calcular comisiones sobre precios previos al descuento, incluso cuando el local financia esa rebaja.

articles.title: York University breach exposed personal information dating to 2007
articles.text:
York University in Toronto has confirmed that a threat actor breached its systems and accessed personal information submitted through online forms.
The unauthorized access was discovered on October 25 and affected forms submitted on 14 university websites between 2007 and 2026.
York University is a major university based in Toronto, Canada, with more than 55,700 students across 200 undergraduate and graduate degree programs, and an administrative staff of 7,000.
“York was recently subject to a cybersecurity incident involving an unauthorized actor accessing limited online forms used by University departments,” the university stated on Friday.
“While York acted quickly to contain the incident following discovery, we regret to confirm the theft of personal information from some departmental forms.”
The announcement lists the exposed data in detail, by category. Across the affected forms, the attacker accessed the following:
- Email address
- Phone number
- Date of birth
- York identification number
- Government ID information
- Third-party contact information
- Health information
- Academic history
- Employment history
- Financial status
- Criminal background
- Demographic details
- Photos and other images
The exact data types exposed vary by person, and most stolen records contained basic contact information and York ID numbers, the university said.
Exposing contact information alongside other sensitive data significantly increases the risk of phishing and social engineering attacks for affected individuals.
The announcement says the website forms are now secure and safe to use. York University said it will directly notify individuals whose government ID or financial account information was exposed and offer two years of credit monitoring and identity theft protection coverage.
Individuals who did not receive a notification may contact the university directly to learn what specific types of data were exposed in their case.
At this time, the educational institution has not specified how many individuals have been impacted by the cybersecurity incident.
No details have been provided about the perpetrators. At the time of writing, BleepingComputer did not find any ransomware group claiming the attack.

articles.title: Hundieron 2 millones de neumáticos en el océano para crear un arrecife: 50 años después, el problema continúa
articles.text:
A comienzos de los años 70 se empezaron a tirar neumáticos usados junto al condado de Broward (Florida). Se trataba de un arrecife artificial. En total se lanzaron entre uno y dos millones de neumáticos. Se pretendía conseguir así un mayor hábitat para peces y disponer de un sitio para estos residuos. Más de medio siglo después todavía están en pleno proceso de retiro.
Se trata del Osborne Tire Reef. Se lanzaron en una zona de arena entre dos arrecifes naturales. Cercano hay otro arrecife artificial (Osborne Reef) de estructuras de hormigón. En el informe de Florida se diferencian los dos.
En el mismo momento de su vertido comenzaron los problemas de inestabilidad. Algunas de las cintas que mantenían unidos los grupos se rompieron en la propia descarga. Además, los cierres metálicos se corroían y las cintas se iban soltando. También las corrientes y el oleaje de las tormentas han provocado que se hayan ido arrastrando hacia los arrecifes próximos.
En el plan de restauración (con los estudios de 2019 y 2024) se estimaron unos 521.000 neumáticos superficiales (no enterrados) en las zonas analizadas. Esto no incluye los que están totalmente enterrados o escondidos bajo otros organismos. Tampoco tiene en cuenta los que están fuera de estas zonas. Es decir, corresponde a estas campañas de estudio. Posteriormente, pueden haber cambiado en su número.
De ellos, 429.000 están en hábitats arenosos. Hasta 92.000 han entrado en contacto con hábitats de arrecife coralino. De esta manera hay que diferenciar los lugares donde se trabaja. Para los neumáticos que están sobre el arrecife se prevén métodos y permisos concretos.
Cómo se retiran los neumáticos
En cuanto a la búsqueda de los residuos, se han utilizado técnicas de sonar y cartografía submarina. En la documentación oficial se habla de la extracción con buzos. Se hacen grupos de neumáticos que se izan a la embarcación con una grúa o cabrestante.
En el informe de 2023 se habla de ir a Port Everglades cuando se completa la carga (unos 300 neumáticos). Allí se descargan en un remolque y se llevan a una planta de tratamiento de este tipo de residuos. Conforme van quedando menos neumáticos, es más difícil y lleva más tiempo encontrarlos y juntarlos para llenar cada carga.
Además hay que tener en cuenta que en algunos casos sobre las ruedas se han desarrollado formas de vida. En el plan de restauración se habla de mover los corales antes de retirar los neumáticos de la arena. En algunos puntos del arrecife se plantea dejar algunas ruedas si al retirarlas se producen importantes daños adicionales.

articles.title: Samsung prépare un Galaxy AI payant pour les Galaxy S27, malgré sa promesse d’IA gratuite — Frandroid
articles.text:
Quand une entreprise promet que l’essentiel restera gratuit, il faut toujours lire sa définition de « l’essentiel ». Samsung en fait la démonstration avec Galaxy AI : une application de test repérée par le média spécialisé SammyGuru décrit une offre baptisée Galaxy AI Premium, avec des fonctions gratuites mais plafonnées, des recharges de crédits et une formule Max payante.
L’application invite à rejoindre un programme d’accès anticipé, sur inscription, et précise que les sommes dépensées pendant le test seront remboursées à la fin. Dans son code, la formule Max apparaît à 4,99 dollars par mois ou 47,99 dollars par an (prix américains hors taxes, soit environ 4,45 et 43 euros), soit 20 % de remise sur l’annuel par rapport à douze mensualités. Elle offrirait quatre fois plus d’utilisations que la version gratuite, nommée Standard, et trois exclusivités : Gen Video, qui transforme des photos en vidéos générées par IA, Bixby Action, censé automatiser des tâches entre plusieurs applications, et Daily Briefing, livré sans la moindre description.
Rien n’indique encore si la France aura droit à cette offre. SammyGuru n’a trouvé aucune liste de pays exclus dans l’application. La disponibilité dépendrait du compte Samsung, et le site s’attend au minimum à un lancement en Corée du Sud et aux États-Unis.
Côté gratuit, l’application liste sept outils déjà présents sur les Galaxy, dont Browsing Assist, qui résume les pages web, et Photo Assist, qui efface ou ajoute des éléments dans une image.
Personne ne sait encore ce que vaut un crédit. Sur les captures publiées par SammyGuru, la formule Max mensuelle affiche 40 000 crédits et un pack ponctuel 3 000 crédits, avec des prix encore provisoires. Aucune fuite ne dit combien de crédits consomme une requête, ni combien coûtera une recharge.
Gratuit, mais avec un compteur
SamMobile, autre site consacré à Samsung, a trouvé dans la même application une autre grille, avec trois paliers baptisés Starter, Plus et Pro, dotés de 10 000, 20 000 et 50 000 crédits, ces unités décomptées à chaque requête.
Selon Josh Skinner, l’auteur de l’article de SammyGuru, ces noms sont inscrits dans l’application, tandis que les formules Starter et Max arrivent des serveurs de Samsung, signe que la grille tarifaire bouge encore. Plus embêtant, SamMobile affirme dans un fil sur X que toutes les fonctions Galaxy AI actuelles resteront gratuites, sans évoquer de plafond. Les deux fuites ne racontent donc pas tout à fait la même histoire.
Samsung, de son côté, n’annonce rien mais ne dément rien. Dans une déclaration transmise à la presse, la marque assure que les fonctions « de base » de Galaxy AI resteront gratuites, tout en prévenant que certaines capacités avancées ou nouveaux services pourraient devenir payants.
En 2024, une note de bas de page limitait la gratuité à fin 2025, puis Samsung a promis en 2025 que les fonctions présentes « par défaut » sur le téléphone ne seraient jamais facturées.
Un outil gratuit mais plafonné resterait techniquement conforme à cette promesse, ce qui consolera peu de monde le jour où le compteur tombera à zéro.
Google applique déjà ce modèle à Gemini. L’application reste gratuite avec des limites d’usage, et l’abonnement Google AI Plus, passé de 7,99 à 4,99 euros par mois en juin 2026, donne plus d’usage et 400 Go de stockage.
Le Galaxy S27 en éclaireur
L’application vérifie une « version d’IA » fixée à 2027, ce qui laisse penser que l’offre sera d’abord réservée à la gamme Galaxy S27, attendue début 2027.
Faire payer la vidéo générée par IA, très gourmande en serveurs, n’a rien de choquant, et 4,99 dollars par mois reste un tarif raisonnable. Plafonner des outils présentés depuis deux ans comme inclus dans des smartphones à plus de 1 000 euros poserait un tout autre problème. articles.title: World of Warcraft: Forever launched on 70,480 CPU cores and 251,136 GB of RAM
articles.text:
Take that, bean counters: World of Warcraft: Forever officially opened its doors on November 4, allowing a massive number of players to experience WoW's origins while introducing new content and storylines along the way. According to Blizzard's latest social media posts, WoW: Forever's massively multiplayer world is running on some seriously impressive hardware – the kind of infrastructure that very few game servers – or even data centers – can match.
Soon after launch, Blizzard revealed some of the most impressive details about the hardware powering the game. The new-old MMO is running on 3,924 virtual machines, 251,136 GB of memory, and 70,480 CPU cores. The "memory" figure is suspiciously precise, especially coming just a few days after Sam Altman shared his now-notorious opinion about "terrible" PC users wasting precious DRAM chips that would be better off inside one of OpenAI's data centers.
Either way, WoW: Forever's "wasteful" hardware infrastructure seems to have paid off handsomely, helping the game deliver a remarkably smooth launch. Blizzard executives have celebrated the positive reception, and some players have described the game as one of the smoothest they have ever experienced.
 – World of Warcraft (@Warcraft) November 5, 2026
Blizzard confirmed that WoW: Forever was already breaking the company's records for concurrent players. The game attracted more players than any previous WoW launch, bringing in the highest number of new players for a WoW release in 15 years. Needless to say, Forever also set a record for the number of returning players in the franchise's history.
Blizzard has not shared any specific figures detailing how many players are currently wandering through Forever's online world. However, the company seems happy enough with the game's popularity just days after its launch.
World of Warcraft: Forever is an alternate version of the WoW experience, based on the settings and gameplay mechanics players enjoyed in 2004. Blizzard said this alternate "universe" will evolve as a standalone branch of the original WoW, running alongside the game's modern version and World of Warcraft: Classic's "vanilla" edition.

articles.title: QNAP Releases 24-Bay Dual-Active Controller ES2486AFdc
articles.text:
Monday, November 9th 2026
QNAP Releases 24-Bay Dual-Active Controller ES2486AFdc
QNAP Systems, Inc., a leading innovator in storage, networking, and data protection solutions, today launched the ES2486AFdc, a high-availability (HA) NVMe all-flash storage array engineered for mission-critical applications. The ES2486AFdc is QNAP's first enterprise-class storage combining Active-Active dual controllers with a U.2/U.3 NVMe all-flash architecture. Addressing the market challenges of high costs and limited availability caused by a shrinking number of SAS SSD suppliers, it breaks the performance bottlenecks of traditional HA systems limited by SAS interfaces. Utilizing a PCIe Gen 4 architecture, it delivers exceptional low latency and high throughput. Powered by the ZFS-based QES operating system, it ensures zero data loss and serves as the perfect foundation for enterprise virtualization environments, VDI desktop deployments, and core databases, providing outstanding reliability to minimize downtime and prevent business interruptions.
With the high cost of enterprise-grade SAS SSDs today, the ES2486AFdc's active-active shared storage architecture enables dual controllers to share a single all-flash storage pool. This eliminates the heavy expense of building two separate storage systems, greatly maximizes hardware resource utilization, and significantly reduces the total cost of ownership (TCO) for enterprises.
Sean Teng, Product Manager of QNAP"The ES2486AFdc delivers outstanding performance and a reliable high-availability storage solution. The ZFS-based QES operating system ensures zero data loss and maximizes storage efficiency through advanced data reduction technologies. From critical database transactions and VDI Boot Storms to 4K/8K media inline editing, the ES2486AFdc provides uncompromising stability and extreme performance to our customers."
Key Features
High availability with Active-Active dual controllers: Two completely independent controllers process I/O requests simultaneously (Active-Active). In the event of a single controller failure, the other controller instantly takes over all NVMe SSDs and network IP via the high-speed PCIe non-transparent bridge (NTB) interconnection, ensuring seamless failover without interrupting front-end applications.
Data protection and storage efficiency with ZFS-based QES: QES (QNAP Enterprise Storage) operating system ensures end-to-end data integrity. Inline data deduplication and inline compression significantly reduce file sizes and the amount of data written, maximizing the cost-effectiveness of flash storage while extending SSD lifespans.
NVMe performance and low latency: Breaking the SAS bandwidth limits, every drive bay features a direct PCIe connection architecture. The NVMe protocol drastically reduces instruction queue waiting times, significantly boosting query and transaction speeds for latency-sensitive applications like SQL Server and Oracle Database.
Advanced disaster recovery (DR): Built-in BBU (Battery Backup Unit) with Copy-to-Flash technology ensures that in the event of an unexpected power outage, cache data in the DRAM is safely written to the M.2 SSD protection area to prevent data loss. It supports up to 65,536 snapshots and SnapSync, which transfers only block-level changed data for real-time remote backup, perfectly integrating with VMware Site Recovery Manager (SRM) for enterprise-class disaster recovery.
Optimized for virtualization and diverse applications: Supports VMware and Hyper-V virtualization environments, with VAAI and ODX offload capabilities. iSER (iSCSI Extensions for RDMA) support reduces CPU loads and latency, effortlessly handling VDI Boot Storms where hundreds of employees boot up simultaneously.
Petabyte-scale expansion: By installing optional QXP mini-SAS HD PCIe expansion cards for dual-path connections, up to seven QNAP expansion enclosures can be added, allowing the construction of petabyte-class logical storage capacity.
Key specifications
ES2486AFdc: Intel Xeon D 8-core processor (up to 3.0 GHz) and up to 512 GB DDR4 ECC memory per controller; 24x dual-port U.2 / U.3 NVMe PCIe slots. Each controller features four built-in 10GbE SFP+ network ports and two PCIe expansion slots for 25GbE or Fibre Channel expansion cards; redundant power supplies.
The ES2486AFdc Enterprise NVMe All-Flash Storage is available now.

articles.title: PCs com 32 GB e 64 GB de RAM recuam pela primeira vez • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
PCs com 32 GB e 64 GB de RAM recuam pela primeira vez
Dados do CPU-Z mostram queda nas configurações de maior capacidade em meio à alta dos preços da memória.
Configurações de PCs com 32 GB e 64 GB de memória RAM registraram queda inédita na comparação anual, conforme dados recentes do programa CPU-Z. Os recuos foram de 2,5% e 18%, respectivamente.
A mudança ocorre em meio à alta dos preços e à escassez global de memória, impulsionadas pela forte demanda de data centers de inteligência artificial. Com fabricantes direcionando parte da produção para atender ao mercado de servidores e aceleradores de IA, os módulos voltados ao consumidor ficaram mais caros e difíceis de encontrar.
Os números, porém, não representam as vendas globais de computadores. O CPU-Z reúne apenas informações de máquinas cujos usuários utilizam o programa. Portanto, os dados mostram mudanças na base monitorada pela ferramenta, mas não necessariamente uma redução na quantidade de memória instalada nos PCs em geral.
Apesar da queda, 32 GB continuam sendo a capacidade mais comum entre os computadores monitorados pelo CPU-Z, com participação de 37,2%. Os sistemas com 16 GB aparecem logo atrás, com 33%, após crescimento de 12,9% na comparação anual.
As configurações com 8 GB também avançaram 5,5%, chegando a 11% da base. Já os PCs com 64 GB representam 7,3%, enquanto máquinas com 24 GB correspondem a 2,3%. Essa última categoria teve crescimento de 19,7%, indicando maior procura por uma alternativa intermediária entre 16 GB e 32 GB.
O movimento indica que o encarecimento da memória está levando parte dos consumidores a reconsiderar configurações mais robustas. A tendência também acompanha a retração do mercado de computadores: as vendas globais de PCs caíram pela primeira vez em dois anos.
Outro dado que chama atenção é a recuperação da memória DDR4. A tecnologia mais antiga representa 54,5% das configurações identificadas pelo CPU-Z, com crescimento de 6% na comparação anual. Já o DDR5 aparece em 32,9% da base, após recuo de 2,9%.
A diferença de preços ajuda a explicar a mudança. Embora as duas tecnologias tenham ficado mais caras, o DDR4 continua sendo uma alternativa um pouco mais acessível para quem pretende montar ou atualizar um computador sem trocar toda a plataforma.
Processadores como os Ryzen 5000, da AMD, e modelos Intel Core de 13ª geração, por exemplo, permitem aproveitar placas-mãe compatíveis com DDR4. O levantamento também identificou crescimento na participação de chips como Ryzen 7 5700X, Ryzen 5 5600 e Ryzen 5 5500.

articles.title: Agentic AI Architecture: Current Challenges and Future Opportunities
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Agentic AI architectures are set to dominate the IT industry in not-so-distant future. Yet, this emerging software architecture is still in its infancy and requires significant investment from organizations interested in adopting it.
- The new architecture adds a significant degree of complexity atop dominant microservices and cloud-native architectures, forcing architects and engineers alike to learn new concepts, techniques, and technologies.
- Many well-established fields within predominant software architecture types require rethinking or substantial adaptation to meet the unique requirements of agentic AI systems.
- Agentic AI architecture will, for quite a while, co-exist with architectures we know today until they morph into a single unified paradigm.
- The adoption of agentic AI architectures will be greatly supported by homegrown or vendor platforms that simplify and scale the delivery of complex IT products.
| This article is part of the "Agentic AI Architecture" article series. In this series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream. | 
Most software engineers and architects are innately familiar with microservices and cloud-native architectures and have been involved in building systems based on these architectures for many years. Microservice-based systems tend to consist of tens or hundreds, and sometimes even thousands of services, responsible for different types of data processing, be it API endpoints, data pipelines, back-office workflows, and anything in between, but they do have one thing in common - they merely process data using a logic determined either by code or based on data retrieved from data stores. This doesn’t mean that such systems are simplistic - far from it. Still, despite their complexity, they can be reasoned about deterministically, which helps define and scope functionality, implement and test changes, and operate such systems, even in the face of infrastructure- or application-level failures.
All of this is about to change. Indeed, a good share of future software systems will still be deterministic and resemble what we are used to today. Still, quite soon, swathes of IT systems being designed and delivered will be leveraging AI-based solutions to power user-facing functionality. For most, if not all, architects and engineers, this will require significant adaptation to the new reality of the IT industry.
The adoption of AI in software architectures is driven primarily by the new capabilities that it offers, which are particularly useful for products used by knowledge workers. Historically, IT systems focused on storing, processing, and making data available via APIs and user interfaces. At the same time, humans were responsible for a good portion of data administration, utilizing business rules, procedures, office "tribal" knowledge, and their own judgment. It’s fair to point out that some, or even much, of this intelligence was built directly into IT systems to improve productivity, particularly when scaling business operations was critical. With AI-enabled capabilities, software systems can shift from operating on raw data to knowledge, thereby elevating IT's role from merely a data management and processing function to knowledge-level support for business operations and end-user functionality.
It’s difficult to gauge to what extent AI-based solutions will dominate next-generation software systems. Still, by all signs, the impact will be so substantial that we can speak about a new type of software architecture, one where AI powers large areas of functionality, making humans using products built on top of next-generation systems much more productive. Agentic AI Architecture is a software architecture in which agentic AI systems are leveraged on a substantial scale, geared towards making optimal use of generative AI (and other) models. This type of architecture builds on microservices and cloud-native architecture and adds agentic AI capabilities.
The Emergence of Agentic AI Systems
Agentic AI isn’t exactly new, but equally, it’s not yet well established either. Over the last couple of years, agentic AI systems have evolved from simple, single-agent solutions to chains, to graphs and multi-agent systems (MAS), where multiple agents collaborate, organized in various topologies. This area is still undergoing active development, and more elaborate use cases will inevitably emerge. It’s fair to say, though, that different collaboration strategies or topologies work best for specific use cases, so choosing a simpler solution can be advantageous in many cases.
Agents make the most of the large language models (LLMs) they interact with by providing the right context. Here again, after starting with predefined prompts, the solutions gradually shifted to a dynamic context based on output from other agents, context propagation, or data fetched from external sources via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
As the amount of context accumulated from different sources began to cause problems with diminished reasoning, engineers developed new ways of managing context, and context engineering emerged as a separate practice. The progressive context disclosure technique can further enhance the context preparation step by allowing the agent to selectively load detailed information into the context window based on the user’s prompt.
Since LLMs have effective limits on context size, the role of context engineering is to ensure that the context used maximizes the model's likelihood of producing the desired outcome, or at least minimizes the chance of hallucinations due to vague or inadequate context. Effective context engineering requires context management to store, optimize, and reuse context elements for subsequent agent invocations.
Lately, memory systems for AI agents have also emerged, enabling further enhancements to context editing. These systems organize different types of long-term memory (episodic, semantic, procedural) for storage and querying, thus allowing agents to supplement the context with past experiences/decisions, relevant facts/definitions, rules, or learned behaviors.
Context engineering has become a foundational architectural concern for agentic AI systems. It will undoubtedly continue to evolve as the needs and expectations for building and operating AI-based products grow.
Agentic AI has developed its own specialized set of communications protocols. This process was largely driven by challenges related to the complexity of agent development, the need for standardization, and the need for improved interoperability:
- Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) - designed for multi-agent systems, allows interoperability between AI agents
- Model Context Protocol (MCP) - focuses on communication between AI agents and external services (databases, tools, etc.).
From Agentic AI Systems To Agentic AI Architectures
For agentic AI systems to be valuable, they need to be integrated into a bigger enterprise architectures. In the enterprise setting, incorporating an agentic AI system can be done by:
- Embedding an agent into a microserive exposing an API (HTTP/GRPC)
- Using an agent as an MCP tool or with A2A protocol
- Having an agent microservice consumer messages from an asynchronous channel (queue/topic)
A large-scale enterprise-level architecture may comprise many specialized agentic AI systems. Since AI agents can use MCP to use database, services/APIs or any arbitrary data sources directly, it’s important to ensure that their interactions are constrainted within a bounded context, as defined by the domain-driven design (DDD). Limiting the reach of agentic AI systems within larger architectures reduces coupling between distant or unrelated components and data sources, allowing more cohesive areas to be maintained by engineering teams without excessive dependencies or large blast radius if changes are introduced.
Figure 1: Multiple Agentic AI Systems in Separate Bounded Contexts (Source: created by the author)
Figure 1 (above) depicts somewhat simplified architecture with two bounded context, each one embedding an agentic AI system with multiple agents (A), as well as other microservices (S). Agents only use local data sources and services for context expansion or as tools, hence limiting the coupling with other parts of the boarder software system.
Performance and Scalability of Agentic AI Systems
The scalability of cloud-based software architectures is well understood, as architects and engineers have been building and operating them for some time. The same can’t be said for agentic AI systems, where LLM call latencies are higher, and more complex multi-agent systems can further increase processing times. The performance of agentic AI systems can’t be measured solely by standard metrics such as throughput, latency, or error rates.
Researchers at Google and MIT published a paper introducing a framework for scaling multi-agent systems. The team behind the framework tested various multi-agent coordination strategies, each with several configuration parameters, including the number of LLM calls, agents, and interactions per agent. Scientists concluded that the best coordination strategy is task-dependent: financial reasoning does better with centralized orchestration, while web navigation benefits from a decentralized strategy.
The results shared by Google and MIT demonstrate that there is no one-size-fits-all approach when it comes to agentic AI, and teams building complex solutions have to experiment and empirically establish the agent coordination strategy that is best suited to the task.
Security Challenges of Agentic AI
Incorporating agentic AI into the distributed system architecture significantly alters the security model. Agentic AI contributes additional security threats, particularly around the agent runtime, tool servers (MCP or others), and the model provider. AI agents, for instance, can be susceptible to prompt injection, instruction confusion, or tool output poisoning, leading to unintended actions or leaking data they have access to. Additionally, using external LLM models introduces risks around data residency, retention, or usage.
Furthermore, present access-control models, honed over many decades, are ill-suited to cater to agents, which can’t really be treated as human users or backend services. Cameron Pavey, senior developer at Auth0, recently proposed a new permission model specifically targeting AI agents. He argues that regular (non-AI) backend services are generally more trusted because they are deterministic and auditable, while authentication sessions and user interfaces restrict users. Agents, on the other hand, can arbitrarily trigger multi-step workflows that involve other agents and tool calls without the user’s explicit knowledge or permission.
Pavey proposes using capability-scoped permissions and task-scoped credentials as key steps toward solving the problem of agent permissions and adopting fine-grained authorization systems for layered enforcement.
It’s worth pointing out that this is not the first time that the security landscape has experienced a marked expansion. When microservices and cloud-native architectures entered the scene, we observed a shift in this area as well, leading to a revision of the access control mechanism and protocol and the emergence of now-common technologies such as JWT and OAuth.
Observability
Considering the non-deterministic nature of agentic AI systems, observability is key to being able to effectively build, enhance, troubleshoot and operarate them.
Teams should aim at complete coverage across all pillars of modern observability platforms:
- Logging - use structured logs recording decisions with reasons and evidence; include correlation IDs; scrub personally identifiable information
- Metrics - measure quality, latency, spend, create SLO dashboards for performance and budgets
- Tracing - trace tasks/steps (plan, tool, validate); include correlation IDs
- Alerting - alert on performance degradation, latency spikes, anomalies
- Runbooks - maintain a suite of runbooks with regular reviews
Blending of Microservices, Cloud-Native, and Agentic AI Architectures
Despite the expected rise of agentic AI as the driving force behind future IT products and services, we cannot expect an instant switch. For many years, the distributed systems architectures we know today will coexist with the next-generation ones (which build on top of them), similar to how service-oriented architecture (SOA) was phased out in favor of microservices over a few years.
Additionally, given the relative infancy of agentic AI, this space will take time to mature and gain widespread adoption, allowing for a gradual transition and the emergence of new patterns, best practices, and technologies that will further drive adoption.
Finally, not all products or business processes need to leverage agentic AI, or the use of AI may not be immediately financially viable. It may be that certain industries or classes of products or systems will not benefit from AI at the same pace as others. In that sense, microservices and cloud-native architectures are here to stay in one way or another.
From Microservices and Cloud-Native to Agentic AI Platforms
With Agentic AI taking center stage and maturity and adoption within the industry growing, I expect many components and solutions, currently often custom-built, to be offered as features of more generic platforms that will support multi-agent system delivery and operations, as well as the integration of those into broader enterprise-level architectures.
In particular, foundational agentic AI building blocks, such as agent memory, asset registry, guardrails, and orchestration, as well as support for observability and operations, should all become built-in capabilities of agentic AI platforms, whether homegrown or offered by vendors or cloud providers.
There are several agentic AI platforms/frameworks that developers can use today, including LangChain (with LangGraph), CrewAI, Azure AI Foundry, Google Agent SDK (ADK), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.
This process will follow the same path as it did for microservice architectures, where growing needs from organizations adopting these new architectures have necessitated the creation of internal, self-operated solutions that externally hosted and managed products will gradually replace.
The Future of Agentic AI Architecture
The industry is on the verge of a major shift, and Agentic AI Architecture has a strong chance of becoming a dominant architecture for distributed systems over the coming years and decades. This doesn’t mean that microservices and cloud-native architectures will become obsolete; rather, they will form the basis of the next generation of systems, in which AI powers much of the user experience. What architects and engineers are familiar with today will form a foundation for delivering robust AI-powered products and services that combine data, knowledge, and compute-based reasoning.
The shift described here will increase productivity and improve ease of use for many knowledge workers across many sectors. It will greatly reshape not only the IT industry but our entire modern society.
While we are still in the early days, with a lot of innovation, moving goalposts, experimentation, and learning, we can certainly expect an exciting road ahead.

In this series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream. |

articles.title: Adiós a James Gunn: DC despide al arquitecto de su nuevo universo y lo reemplaza con un veterano de Marvel
articles.text:
James Gunn y Peter Safran abandonarán la dirección de DC Studios y serán reemplazados por un veterano de Marvel Studios. Tras cuatro años al frente de la división, Gunn y Safran dejarán su cargo como copresidentes del estudio. La responsabilidad de DC estará en manos de Jeremy Latcham, productor de películas clave como Guardianes de la Galaxia y el primer film de Iron Man con Robert Downey Jr.
De acuerdo con Variety, la dupla que dirigía DC Studios ya no continuará al mando. La noticia tomó por sorpresa a todos, ya que Gunn y Safran formaban parte del equipo directivo vinculado a la nueva etapa de Warner Bros. Discovery, luego de que Paramount cerrara la compra del estudio a inicios de octubre. Según el reporte, los ejecutivos volverán a un trabajo centrado en el desarrollo creativo de películas y series, aunque muchos sabemos que es el final para ambos.
Durante su gestión, James Gunn y Peter Safran intentaron reconstruir el universo cinematográfico de DC, que llevaba años de descalabros y polémicas. La apuesta principal fue reiniciar todo con Superman, una película que logró recaudar 618 millones de dólares en todo el mundo y convenció a la crítica y los fanáticos. El problema es que después vinieron proyectos de menor calibre y una película que terminó por matar cualquier intento por revitalizar el cine de superhéroes.
Supergirl fue uno de los fracasos más sonados del año. A pesar del carisma de la actriz, la película no consiguió aprovechar la esencia del cómic y tuvo una pésima adaptación. Con un presupuesto de producción de 170 millones de dólares y otros 120 millones para publicidad, Supergirl apenas consiguió recuperar 126 millones de dólares en la taquilla a nivel mundial.
Además del cine, la dupla amplió la presencia de DC con series como Peacemaker y Linternas para HBO Max. La primera consiguió conectar con la audiencia, pese a que se trataba de un personaje menor, pero Lanterns generó críticas por su enfoque de thriller terrenal y por la decisión de matar a Hal Jordan.
¿Quién es Jeremy Latcham, el reemplazo de James Gunn en el Universo DC?
En un comunicado, James Gunn y Peter Safran dijeron sentirse orgullosos de devolver a Superman al centro de la estrategia de DC. Los directivos aplaudieron el trabajo de actores, productores y todo el personal que colaboró con ellos en esta etapa. También le dieron el voto de confianza a Jeremy Latcham, quien tomará las riendas del Universo DC a partir de ahora.
Si el nombre no te suena, Latcham es uno de los productores más reconocidos de Marvel. El ahora jefe de DC Studios se unió a Marvel en 2004 y fue pieza clave en el desarrollo del Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel junto a Kevin Feige. Entre sus créditos figuran producciones como Iron Man, The Avengers, Guardians of the Galaxy, Avengers: Age of Ultron y Spider-Man: De regreso a casa.
Jeremy Latcham será el nuevo jefe de DC, supervisando películas, series y proyectos de animación, además de dirigir la estrategia creativa. El ejecutivo dijo que su objetivo será construir una nueva etapa capaz de satisfacer tanto a los fanáticos veteranos como a las nuevas generaciones. Gunn y Safran colaborarán en una transición a la nueva etapa de DC, que todavía tiene en puerta el estreno de Batman 2 y Superman: Man of Tomorrow.

articles.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
articles.text:
Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
Scott Wiener has made AI regulation a cornerstone of his political career. Now he’s headed to Congress.
As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.
I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.
“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”
Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”
Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.
Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.
“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”
Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.
He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he says.
And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”
Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”
He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.
“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”
Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.
But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

articles.title: New report highlights just how important video games are to Canadians
articles.text:
Canada is one of the biggest game development hubs in the world. With over 800 studios bringing in $5.1 billion to our GDP through popular games like Mass Effect, EA Sports FC, Assassin’s Creed, Warframe, and Dead by Daylight, our national game sector truly is a global powerhouse. Now, a new report is spotlighting the many ways in which gaming makes an impact on Canadian gamers themselves.
In its latest ‘Essential Facts’ survey, Canadian gaming industry lobbying group Video Games Canada (formerly the Entertainment Software Association of Canada) examined the role that gaming plays in Canadians’ lives. Most notably, 48 per cent of Canadian adults aged 18-64 report playing games on a regular basis, while 93 per cent of children and teens say they play weekly. Further, sixty per cent of them regularly play on mobile and consoles, with 44 per cent doing so on PC and 13 per cent on handhelds. Genre-wise, meanwhile, action-adventure is the most popular in Canada (44 per cent), following by puzzle games (40 per cent), strategy/simulation (37 per cent) and casual/social (35 per cent).
But for Paul Fogolin, VGC’s president and CEO, it’s the reasons why Canadians play games that really stand out.
“A couple things jumped out to me in this report, and one of them was the amount of Canadian players who talked about how they use games to unwind, to reset. The term I use is ‘self-care.’ So people talk about self-care. It’s an important aspect of modern life — we’re living in a stressful world,” he says. “I think there might have been a time where the idea of activities and hobbies that help relax and unwind would have been taken for granted. We can’t do that anymore. So, 91 per cent of players say that games help them relax and unwind.”
He adds that games can have deeper benefits, with 78 per cent of adults and 69 per cent of teens saying games make a positive impact on their mental wellness. Seventy per cent of respondents also said that games help them stay connected, while 63 per cent said games build community and encourage social connection.
“Those are resounding numbers. And again, we are living in interesting times where there’s a cost of living crisis. There are uncertainties in the world. Mental health challenges are, I think, more prevalent than ever,” he says. “So when you have Canadians saying, ‘Here is a hobby, here’s a pastime, here’s something that I can do to unwind, to relax, and, actually, I feel better, my mental health improves after I play, either if it’s a single-player experience where I’m delving into a world that I love, or something I’m doing with my friends and family online, or new friends that I meet — that is huge.”
Canadians made similar comments in VGC’s last iteration of Essential Facts in 2022, demonstrating gaming’s enduring positive impacts on well-being. But something this latest report dove into for the first time was Canadians’ sentiments towards Canadian-made games and the national gaming industry as a whole.
“We wanted to get a sense of: Do Canadians play Canadian-made games? Do Canadian players know they’re playing Canadian-made games? Is there a sense of pride in the industry? Is there a sense of patriotism around the industry? Is this an industry that Canadians think is worth investing in? Is this an industry Canadians think that we should spend more money investing in?” says Fogolin. “And the results were very positive in that regard.”
This line of questioning pertains to one of the other key findings that stood out to Fogolin: the number of Canadians interested in getting into the gaming industry. In particular, the report found that 54 per cent of teens, 52 per cent of Gen Z and 44 per cent of millennials are interested in pursuing games careers.
While that’s certainly good to see, it’s also important to not sugarcoat the state of the industry to aspiring game developers. After all, we’ve seen tens of thousands of layoffs since 2022 alongside studio closures, consolidations and numerous project cancellations.
“Here in Canada, we’re not insulated from the global pressures the industry has faced. More investment than ever was seen during the pandemic in the industry globally. Canada was a part of that,” says Fogolin. “A re-adjustment post-pandemic, not just with the end of the pandemic, but into new macroeconomic conditions, impacted the industry. Capital is tighter than ever when it comes to investment. Budgets are higher than ever when it comes to making games. And so the act of making games has never been so competitive.”
What does help counter those headwinds, he says, is Canada’s large pool of developer talent.
“Here in Canada, we are blessed with an advantage, a foundational advantage in the industry, in the level of talent we have — the infrastructure, the community, the knowledge, the studios, whether it’s larger global studios, our homegrown indie studios, and everything in between,” he says. “Because of that foundation, we have fared better than most jurisdictions during this time, and because of that foundation, we are poised to continue to be a global leader in game-making that punches above our weight.”
Fogolin also says he was heartened to see a rise in a national sense of pride for Canadian games in the 2026 Essential Facts report. In particular, 68 per cent of respondents say it’s important that video games created by Canadian developers are available to play, 61 per cent said they believe the gaming industry is important to Canada’s economy and 77 per cent said Canada should invest the same amount as, or more than, competing countries to bolster our national gaming industry.
But of course, that’s only part of the story.
Supporting Canada’s game developers
No real discussion about the Canadian games sector can be had without BioWare, the beloved Edmonton-based developer recently shuttered by Electronic Arts. People around the world have been mourning the prolific RPG maker, with many developers in Canada, especially, having been heavily influenced by the studio.“Anytime there’s a studio closure in the industry or any job loss, it’s incredibly difficult. That’s their livelihood. There’s families. There’s implications. It was hard to see a studio with such a rich history close — it’s like we’re going to a new chapter,” says Fogolin. “I try to focus on the incredible games that they’ve made, the creators themselves, the talent that grew up in Edmonton, in BioWare, and that talent remains. That talent is here in Canada. That talent can and should be able to continue to make games.”
On that note, there’s been a lot of discussion in the wake of BioWare’s closure about what, indeed, should be done in Canada to sustain game developers. Most notably, NDP leader Avi Lewis has argued that the federal government should help former BioWare workers reclaim the studio and the Mass Effect intellectual property (IP) from EA. To be clear, there’s no indication that either EA or the federal government would ever even entertain such a scenario, but the latest Essential Facts report clearly shows that many Canadians do want game makers to be supported.
That begs the question, then: outside of existing government funding opportunities like the Canada Media Fund (which just got a “historic” federal investment of $213.4 million), what else should be done to help Canadian game makers avoid BioWare’s fate?
“I want to separate a couple things. There’s individual studio decisions — every company has their own business model, large, medium, or small, that informs their business decisions and how they move forward with different studios, and so there’s no one or two factors that lead to a studio closure or downsizing or, similarly, expansion on the positive side,” says Fogolin. “So I would not draw a parallel between government incentives and one particular studio closure, or any other particular market condition. I think it’s a package. It’s a holistic package when you think about investment and you think about conditions that allow the businesses in this industry to succeed.”
That package, he says, includes everything from “capital availability” and “talent availability and mobility” to incentives that make each province “more attractive” to investors. It’s for that reason that he calls for a “national strategy” for Canada’s video game industry.
“Having a conversation, especially at the national level about coordinating policies and approaches to this industry, is where we need to be, and I think that there’ll be ideas coming from all across the industry and all the different players, at different levels, at different sizes, on how best to coordinate that,” he says.
“If you look at the [2026 federal] budget from [last week], there’s a section on strategies for different industries, and there’s AI, and there’s forestry, and there’s robotics, and there’s modular housing and things. To me, this industry belongs in that conversation to say, ‘Alright, what’s going on here? What’s working? What’s not working? What else is going on in the world in competitive jurisdictions? How are they trying to support the video game industry, and what can we do better to compete?’ And I think that would be an ideal place to be as we move forward.”
For now, he says he’s hopeful conversations will move in the right direction, based on something else he saw in Budget 2026.
“It lists ‘industries of the future,’ essentially growth industries of the future, where there’s the most opportunity for economic benefits for Canada. And it’s specifically those where we already have, according to the Government of Canada, an advantage, and games were on that list. And it was incredible to see. It’s ‘finally at the big kids’ table.’ There’s things like AI and automotive and robotics and cybersecurity, and games were right up there,” he says.
“So to me, that’s such a strong signal that our partners in government understand that we have an advantage, and they also understand that this is one of 10 to 15 industries with real growth potential, despite the challenges, and so that gives me some optimism for the future.”
The 2026 Essential Facts survey was conducted by Burson using the Leger Opinion online panel to survey 1,650 adults, 250 children (aged 6-12), and 250 teens (aged 13-17) between Oct. 1-16, 2026 in Canada. All respondents played video games within the past four weeks on a device they own.
The full survey can be found on VGC’s website.
