articles.title: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation. On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners.
This follows the company’s announcement in March of a $155 million Series B extension at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens at Founders Fund. That round was a “preemptive” deal — meaning an offer initiated by the investor, not the startup. Other investors in the company include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.
Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers. One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force.
Nominal CEO and co-founder Cameron McCord (pictured) is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer and an Anduril alum.

articles.title: AMD admits GPU driver bug is writing data continuously, wearing out SSDs — Radeon owner claims External Events Utility used up 1% of SSD health every month for over a year, company promises a fix soon
articles.text:
AMD admits GPU driver bug is writing data continuously, wearing out SSDs — Radeon owner claims External Events Utility used up 1% of SSD health every month for over a year, company promises a fix soon
Radeon drivers may be quietly racking up thousands of gigabytes in SSD writes
An SSD can spend most of its day doing very little, particularly when a PC is sitting idle. That may not be the case for some AMD Radeon systems, however, with reports suggesting that AMD’s External Events Utility (EEU), which is installed alongside Radeon drivers, may be writing data to the system driver continuously, even when the computer is barely being used. The issue drew attention again on November 8, when Reddit user ‘darklinkpower’ highlighted reports of the unusual drive activity.
One Radeon owner claimed the problem had been quietly eating into their drive's reported health for more than a year, writing: "I just found out that the driver eats up 1% of my SSD health every month for 16 months." Another user reported sustained writes of approximately 5MB/s while their PC was idle. Another one claimed their SSD health had dropped by about 1% every month for 16 months. AMD has acknowledged the problem. In an October 21 response on its community forum, a company representative confirmed that they were investigating. “Yes. We're looking into it with the aim to resolve it in a future driver release." He said. Another representative, AMAD Vik, subsequently offered a more encouraging update on Reddit, apologizing and saying, “This is hopefully fixed in the next one."
Notably, the EEU is not an entirely unfamiliar culprit. Last November, a similar issue involving AMD chipset drivers arose, with a Redditor claiming he had discovered that the software repeatedly updated a log file whenever on-screen elements were moved or resized. That incident also prompted questions about whether stopping the service would affect FreeSync. The latest reports are a different proposition, though, with some users now seeing writes that barely let up, even when their PCs are doing nothing.
The numbers are worth looking at. At 5 MB/s, an SSD would receive about 18GB of host writes per hour. Over a full day, that's 432GB, and a month of uninterrupted activity could push the figures close to 13TB. That, however, does not necessarily mean being written to the NAND flash itself. SSD controllers use caching and wear-leveling, and other techniques, to manage incoming data. How much of that reported activity thus translates into actual flash wear is still unknown. The user's claim of losing 1% of drive health each month also hasn't been independently confirmed.
Moreover, there doesn't appear to be clear patterns across Radeon driver versions. Reports include systems running Adrenalin 26.19.2, as well as older releases, suggesting the problem may not be limited to the latest update. AMD's October 30 release notes for Adrenalin 26.20.2 don't mention the issue either. For now, it's difficult to say which driver versions, hardware combinations, or system configurations are responsible.
That said, there are two reported workarounds. The first involves opening the Windows Services application by pressing Win + R, entering services.msc, and locating AMD EEU. Users can then stop the service or change its startup type to Disabled. That appears to stop excessive writeups, but isn’t necessarily a clean solution. The second workaround involves disabling Resizable Bar (ReBAR), which another user reported had stopped the disk activity without disabling the EEU. This, however, isn’t ideal either, as ReBAR can improve gaming performance by allowing the PC to access the GPU’S memory more efficiently.
For now, checking whether the problem actually exists on your PC is probably the most sensible first step. Open Windows Resource Monitor by pressing Win + R, typing resmon, and selecting the Disk tab. Sort by write activity and look for sustained writes from atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe. AMD has indicated that a fix is in the works, but hasn’t published a confirmed release date. Until then, Radeon owners may want to monitor their storage activity rather than immediately disabling driver services or changing BIOS settings.

articles.title: ChatGPT erreicht 20 Prozent von Googles Suchvolumen – und liefert Unternehmen jetzt endlich die passenden Klickzahlen
articles.text:
OpenAI: So findest du bald heraus, wie oft dein Unternehmen in ChatGPT auftaucht
OpenAI arbeitet an einem Analytics- und Unternehmensbereich, der an die Search Console von Google erinnert. Die bisher unveröffentlichte Betaversion des Tools lässt User die Eigentümerschaft von Unternehmen verifizieren. Anschließend können sie Analytics-Daten zur Unternehmensperformance auf ChatGPT einsehen, Unternehmensdaten und Produkte einpflegen und sogar selbst Kontexte für Antworten auf Fragen zum Unternehmen mit einem dedizierten Business-Agent festlegen.
ChatGPT Analytics womöglich vor dem Launch: Auch Kontrolle über Businessanfragen wird gestärkt
Bisher ist das neue ChatGPT-Tool nicht öffentlich verfügbar. Das gilt ebenso für die Betaversion. Diese konnten erste User allerdings schon vor einem geplanten Launch entdecken. Dazu gehört der Business-Entrepreneur Juozas Kaziukėnas. Auf Linkedin zeigt er einen Screenshot des geplanten Business-Hubs von ChatGPT, der an die Search Console erinnert.
Auf der Startseite lädt ChatGPT dazu ein: „Claim your business in ChatGPT“. Unternehmenseigentürmer:innen oder qualifizierte Admins können ein Unternehmen dann dort eintragen und verifizieren. Das kann vermutlich auch über die Verknüpfung mit dem verifizierten Unternehmensprofil aus dem Shopify-Profil geschehen.
Die verifizierten Unternehmen können dann drei zentrale Vorteile wahrnehmen, um im ChatGPT-Umfeld besser agieren zu können. Zum einen können sie Analytics-Daten einsehen. Als First-Party-Daten stehen Angaben zu Impressions und Klicks bereit. Die Angaben werden pro Tag wiedergegeben und in einem Graphen dargestellt.
Zum anderen können die Unternehmensverantwortlichen Angaben zum Unternehmen einpflegen, auch Produkte, Öffnungszeiten und Website-Informationen gehören dazu. Das erinnert an das Google-Business-Profile.
Schließlich gibt es noch eine Option zum Einsatz eines Business-Agents. Damit können die User selbst Details und Informationen vorgeben, auf deren Basis der Agent unternehmensspezifische Fragen beantwortet. Sie können also den Antwortkontext bei Businessanfragen selbst kontrollieren.
Unternehmen brauchen Third-Party-Daten für besseres Verständnis
Die Möglichkeit, Angaben zum eigenen Unternehmen integrieren und einen Business Agent einsetzen zu können, stärkt die Kontrolle über die sachgerechte und aktuelle Darstellung der eigenen Marke auf ChatGPT ungemein. Die Analytics-Daten wiederum dürften den Unternehmensverantwortlichen wertvolle Einblicke in ihre alltägliche Performance in diesem so wichtigen Umfeld geben – das immerhin 1,2 Milliarden User pro Woche zählt und nach eigenen Angaben 20 Prozent von Googles Suchvolumen erreicht hat. Allerdings sind diese Daten aus erster Hand ohne den Kontext einer Prompt-Analyse, eines Wettbewerbsvergleichs oder gar Rankings nur bedingt aussagekräftig. Für die Einschätzung der Performance im Kontext des Wettbewerbs und die Einordnung von etwaigen Schwankungen eignen sich dann Third-Party-Daten aus anderen Tools. Der SEO-Experte Matthäus Michalik schreibt dazu auf Linkedin seine persönliche Einordnung:
Meine Einschätzung: Prompt-Tracking wird dadurch nicht überflüssig, eher im Gegenteil. Ohne Prompts weiß niemand, woher die Impressions kommen. Erst beides zusammen zeigt, ob eine GEO-Strategie wirkt […].

articles.title: My pick of the deals on Nothing, JLab, Sennheiser and Soundcore headphones as an audio editor — why wait for Black Friday?
articles.text:
Huge deals on Nothing, Sennheiser and JLab headphones just landed — and as TechRadar's Audio Editor, I wouldn't wait for Black Friday
Top brands for buds and cans; new low prices
Black Friday is almost upon us, unofficially heralding the start of the festive season — and before you know it, all the gifts will have been wrapped and given, and another year will have flown by!
The good news is that, simply by being here, you're already ahead of the Black Friday deals curve, especially if you're looking for noise-cancelling headphones and earbuds (and why wouldn't you be? With prices starting at just £19, they're excellent stocking fillers).
This roundup isn't like the others. Why? Because, unlike other publications, I've linked a full, no-holds-barred TechRadar review of each pick in the product description box, along with a rating of the deal, and whether it's a new lowest-seen offer, a return to its lowest-ever price, or merely close to it.
So, you know exactly what you're getting, and you know about the price you're paying — that's why you stick with me.
I've reviewed over 180 audio products since becoming a full-time audio tech journalist in 2019, ranging from super-budget earbuds to elite turntables. Before joining TechRadar, I spent three years at our sister publication What Hi-Fi? testing everything the world of audio had to offer. Before that, I was a professional dancer. What I'm saying is, I'm someone with firsthand experience as a struggling artist, so I know about living on a tight budget but still needing music for a happy life…
Top of the pile for me? I adored the CMF Headphone Pro when I reviewed them, and now they're just £49 (was £79). However, if you really need to save that extra tenner, the slightly older but beautifully teardrop-shaped JLab JBuds Lux ANC have absolutely no business being £39 (was £79) and they'll look and sound so much pricier than that.
Came here for buds? Simple: JLab's Pop ANC are literally £19.99 (was £24.99) in one of the best colourways I've ever seen — or there's the Nothing Ear (3), Nothing's flagship buds that landed just over a year ago, not to be confused with the newer, in-call recording Ear (3a). I loved the 'Super Mic' function there and only knocked the audio quality for the money, although of course, that's not nearly so much of an issue now…
Want the newest of the new in this roundup? That would be the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro, launched on September 28, 2026 and reviewed by yours truly. This is also their first ever discount — to clarify, the also-featured Nothing Headphone (1) are the company's inaugural model, launched on July 15, 2025.

Which pair is the best of the two? Oh, the newer pair without a doubt — apart from the case, which sadly is bulky, plastic and more of a fashion statement. If taking care of your listening gear is of paramount importance, I might still pick the originals, which is why I've listed them here.
Want something from a trusted name in audio? You can't get much more tried and true than Sennheiser's Accentum True Wireless, although these are also the oldest earbuds pick in the roundup, having arrived in May 2024. That said, they're oh-so-tiny and stuffed with features. And if you want a cheap set of buds with a nifty dial for volume on the case, the CMF Buds 2 are a great shout for this money.
Lastly, don't sleep on the Anker Soundcore Space One, despite their 2023 release date. We called them a "bargain Beats alternative with ANC" under intense review, and at this new-low price, there's an awful lot there for £64 (was £89)…
The best early Black Friday headphones and earbuds deals
Becky became Audio Editor at TechRadar in 2024, but joined the team in 2022 as Senior Staff Writer, focusing on all things hi-fi. Before this, she spent three years at What Hi-Fi? testing and reviewing everything from wallet-friendly wireless earbuds to huge high-end sound systems. Prior to gaining her MA in Journalism in 2018, Becky freelanced as an arts critic alongside a 22-year career as a professional dancer and aerialist – any love of dance starts with a love of music. Becky has previously contributed to Stuff, FourFourTwo and The Stage. When not writing, she can still be found throwing shapes in a dance studio, these days with varying degrees of success.

articles.title: Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
articles.text:
President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang.
Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
In a White House press conference, President Trump was vague about when learned of Jensen Huang’s affair.
Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.
In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.
Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel.
When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time?
I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. I’ve known him a long time. It’s the largest, by value, the largest or one of the largest companies in the world. He did that with a chip. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. He’s an amazing guy.
I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem. I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement. And I believe he’s suffering greatly. Moreso because of his family. His wife who he loves and his family. But he is definitely suffering.
Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question.
Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago.
When is that?
We’ll look into it. I know the FBI’s looking into it in terms of something else. I think that he’ll be in good shape.
…
Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week?
No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. He built a great company. American company. I think he’s a very honorable guy. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.
Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then?
No, I didn’t hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question, did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said, I had no idea that she was a spy. And I really believe him.
…
I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang.
Oh, I’d have to check. But this has been going on…
But there are reports that Secretary Rubio put an intelligence memo out last year. Did you read that memo?
I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.

articles.title: A $60 billion fintech hired a 14-year-old. Its CEO explains why.
articles.text:
A $60 billion fintech hired a 14-year-old. Its CEO explains why.
Ramp hired a 14-year-old intern after discovering an app he had built for fun that attracted attention from roughly a million people on Twitter.
Co-CEO Eric Glyman discussed the hire during a November 5 interview with founder and editor of Upstairs Media, Alex Konrad, explaining how the $60 billion fintech company evaluates engineering talent beyond traditional qualifications, a recalibration playing out across the industry as AI redraws what a junior role even means.
A viral app, no assignment
“We had an intern who was 14 years old,” Glyman said. “Part of how we found him was he had built his own app for fun that was genuinely useful, and a million people saw it on Twitter and interacted with it. There was no one who was telling him, ‘Hey, go build this project.’ He just was interested in it.”
Glyman did not identify the teenager or specify when he worked at Ramp.
“Part of how we found him was he had built his own app for fun that was genuinely useful, and a million people saw it on Twitter…”
The Minecraft server test
Glyman says Ramp looks for developers who have pursued projects on their own, even when that experience doesn’t come from a conventional job, a premium on self-direction that grows sharper as AI erodes the entry-level tasks that once trained new engineers.
“A lot of what we’re looking for is strong evidence that someone has built something on their own, created something on their own, and shown their drive where it didn’t come from other people saying, ‘I need you to go do something’.”
“A lot of what we’re looking for is strong evidence that someone has built something on their own… and shown their drive where it didn’t come from other people saying, ‘I need you to go do something’.”
In a separate November 3 interview with Blackstone, Glyman said Ramp also looks for developers who got their start running Minecraft servers as teenagers.
Some teens built their own servers before high school, gaining practical programming experience long before entering the workforce.
Glyman acknowledged that the approach has limits, since talented candidates who haven’t had the time, resources, or opportunity to build something independently could be overlooked at precisely the moment the entry-level rungs of the industry are already thinning out.
A 28-year-old running engineering
In June, Ramp appointed Rahul Sengottuvelu as chief technology officer at 28, replacing co-founder Karim Atiyeh, who became co-CEO alongside Glyman.
Sengottuvelu joined Ramp through a 2023 acquisition and later led its applied AI team. He was already building AI products before ChatGPT became a household name.
In its leadership announcement, Ramp pointed to Sengottuvelu’s experience building AI products and his ability to make tough technical decisions. He took over as CTO as the company was putting AI to work in more of its products and day-to-day operations.
Small teams own the call
Glyman also described how Ramp organizes its engineers into small teams of five or six people, giving them responsibility for deciding how to complete their projects.
“If you look really deep into Ramp’s organizational design, it’s tons of small teams where we say, ‘Here’s the outcome we want you to drive, but it’s up to you.’ You can make the call on how you want to spend your time. Why hire someone who can surprise you with their creativity and then tell them, ‘Don’t make your own recipe’?”
“Why hire someone who can surprise you with their creativity and then tell them, ‘Don’t make your own recipe’?”
Glyman says adding more engineers doesn’t always mean getting work done faster since bigger teams often mean more people weighing in on decisions, which can add churn and slow workflow.
Ramp instead gives smaller groups ownership of specific projects, with leadership setting the goals rather than prescribing every step.
For Glyman, hiring people capable of making their own decisions only makes sense if they’re allowed to do so once they’re on the job.

articles.title: Okra Solar secures $7m debt facility from BII to scale mesh-grids in Nigeria - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian off-grid energy startup Okra Solar has secured a US$7 million debt facility from British International Investment (BII) to accelerate clean energy access.
Founded in 2016, Okra provides mesh-grid technology for off-grid communities, combining solar generation, battery storage and smart controls so that neighbouring homes and businesses can share electricity cost-efficiently. The model delivers more power than typical solar home systems while needing less infrastructure than conventional mini-grids.
Okra currently has more than 13,000 households connected and over 2.3MW of installed capacity. The US$7 million financing from BII, the UK’s development finance institution and impact investor, will allow it to procure equipment for roughly 150,000 new connections, a more than tenfold increase, with the potential to bring electricity to 750,000 people in rural Nigeria for the first time.
The facility tackles a key barrier to scaling distributed renewable energy – access to flexible working capital. By buying inputs upfront and in larger volumes, Okra expects to cut equipment costs and shorten delivery times to Nigeria from four months to about two.
“Every month a project is delayed is another month a community goes without power,” said Afnan Hannan, CEO of Okra Solar. “Until now we would only order components once a transaction had closed, in batches of a few thousand units. With BII’s facility we are procuring long lead time components, batteries, and solar PV equipment upfront and in volume, reducing costs and having stock ready when a developer signs.”
Faster delivery should also help Okra’s developer customers bring projects online sooner and access results-based grant payments earlier. Mesh-grids are eligible under Nigeria’s Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme, which is run by the Rural Electrification Agency with World Bank support.
“For innovative energy companies such as Okra, access to the right type of finance can be just as important as the technology itself,” said Geoffrey Manley, director and head of infrastructure and climate debt for Africa and South Asia at BII. “We believe this will help demonstrate the commercial viability of mesh-grids and establish the model as an increasingly important part of Africa’s distributed renewable energy market.”

articles.title: C'est officiel, Android Auto abandonne le support de millions de smartphones
articles.text:
Nous l’évoquions le mois dernier et c’est désormais officiel, Google indique désormais clairement qu’il est nécessaire d’avoir un appareil sous Android 11 minimum pour faire fonctionner Android Auto dans votre voiture. Après l’abandon d’Android 6 en 2022 et d’Android 8 en 2025, c’est au tour d’Android 9 et 10 de passer à la trappe.
Sortie de route pour Android 9 et 10
C’est la page de support d’Android Auto qui officialise ce changement de cap. Dès le mois d’octobre, des avertissements avaient commencé à s’afficher pour les utilisateurs d’Android 10, indiquant une interruption imminente d’Android Auto pour les appareils concernés. Des modèles emblématiques restés bloqués sur cette version, comme le Samsung Galaxy S9 et le Galaxy Note 9, sont directement concernés par ce changement.
Certains utilisateurs ont déjà constaté que leur appareil sous Android 9 ou 10 n’est plus en mesure de faire tourner Android Auto. C’est d’autant plus triste que le fait que les utilisateurs aient encore ces appareils montre qu’ils sont fonctionnels. Certains d’entre eux vont donc peut-être devoir remplacer un smartphone qui jusqu’alors leur convenait, simplement pour pouvoir encore profiter d’Android Auto dans leur véhicule.
Une mise à niveau forcée pour des millions d’automobilistes
Si vous avez un smartphone sous Android 9 ou 10, on vous conseille de vérifier si une mise à jour vers Android 11 est disponible. Si ce n’est pas le cas, vous allez devoir changer d’appareil pour continuer d’utiliser normalement Android Auto. Le couperet tombe donc officiellement pour environ 93 millions de smartphones sous Android 9 (3,1% du parc mondial) et 170 millions de téléphones sous Android 10 (5,7 % du parc mondial).
À lire : Six ans après, un smartphone sur dix est toujours sur Android 11
Ces dernières années, les smartphones Android profitent d’un support logiciel étendu, souvent autour des 6 ou 7 ans pour les smartphones Google Pixel ou Samsung. articles.title: France blames Iranian hackers for supermarket attacks that sparked fires
articles.text:
France has linked October cyberattacks that disrupted refrigeration systems at more than 700 supermarkets and other retail locations to Iranian state-backed hackers, saying the attacks caused food losses and sparked at least 15 fires.
In a statement issued Monday, France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs blamed the attacks on Shahid Kaveh, a cyber-offensive unit affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
"France condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran against its interests," reads the statement.
The attacks occurred overnight on October 11–12, when hackers compromised industrial refrigeration controllers and remotely changed defrost settings to high temperatures, disrupting systems used to preserve food.
As BleepingComputer reported, the attacks affected an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets, forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen products.
French authorities have now revealed that approximately 700 retail locations were targeted, with the cyberattacks causing at least 15 fires.
A technical report published by France's CERT-FR says Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché, along with smaller butcher shops, a slaughterhouse, and cooperative food-processing facilities, were affected by the attacks.
French authorities say the attacks caused tens of millions of euros in food losses and significant material damage.
French investigators also detected attacks against Schneider Electric industrial equipment at small hydroelectric installations during the same period, which they linked to the same campaign.
These incidents reportedly had moderate effects on the targeted equipment.
The October attacks were followed by a second wave of refrigeration system attacks reported in November, affecting more than 115 stores across six European countries.
France's national blood service also reported a similar incident that altered temperature and defrost settings at three facilities used to store blood products.
Last week, the FBI and CISA warned of ongoing cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide.
The French government says it will summon Iran's ambassador to condemn the attacks and propose new European Union sanctions against Iranian individuals and organizations involved in malicious cyber operations.
However, France has attributed only the October attacks against French supermarkets to Iranian hackers, not the later attacks.
Iran's Shahid Kaveh blamed for attacks
France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center (C4), which includes the country's cybersecurity agency ANSSI, military cyber command, and intelligence agencies, attributed the attacks to the Iranian Shahid Kaveh IRGC unit.
According to CERT-FR, Shahid Kaveh operates through several online hacktivist identities, including CyberAveng3rs, Soldiers of Solomon, Mr. Soul, and Cyber Isnaad Front.
"The cyberattack targeting refrigeration controllers was relayed on the propaganda outlet CyberbanNews, associated with the Shahid Kaveh unit, as early as October 13, 2026," the C4 says.
French investigators linked the refrigeration attacks to Shahid Kaveh through the following observations:
- The attacker's infrastructure was also used to conduct reconnaissance against Schneider Electric industrial systems, using techniques previously associated with the Iranian unit.
- The attackers used the FOFA internet-connected device search platform, which CERT-FR says the group commonly uses in its operations.
- CyberbanNews, which France says is linked to Shahid Kaveh, publicized the refrigeration attacks on October 13.
- Investigators discovered traces of Farsi-language used in the attacker's infrastructure.
CERT-FR says Shahid Kaveh claimed responsibility for a large-scale sabotage campaign targeting Israeli and U.S. interests in March and April 2026, including attacks on Israeli refrigeration equipment and other industrial control systems.
In April 2026, the unit was observed conducting large-scale reconnaissance of Schneider Electric industrial control systems, including systems in France.

articles.title: Quería quitar las aplicaciones que Android no me deja borrar. Así que le pedí a la IA mi propio desinstalador: en media hora lo tenía
articles.text:
Cada vez que compro un móvil, o analizo uno, este viene con un buen montón de aplicaciones que no necesito. La primera configuración suele ser larga, porque me dedico a iniciar sesiones, ordenar los escritorios y siempre quito app por app las que no necesito. El problema es que hay unas cuantas que no se dejan ni eliminar ni deshabilitar. Son las aplicaciones de sistema.
Android facilita la personalización en mayor medida que iOS. Esta brecha se ha ido reduciendo con el paso del tiempo, siempre hasta cierto punto, porque Google continúa permitiendo el acceso al sistema con cierta profundidad. Si en mis tiempos jóvenes usaba Titanium Backup para una limpieza completa con root, ahora me conformo con ADB. Una app que programé con IA me ayuda en la tarea.
Deshabilitando las apps de sistema en Android
Desde el gestor de aplicaciones resulta posible eliminar las aplicaciones del usuario y también algunas de sistema. Aparte, varias aplicaciones más también pueden deshabilitarse: no se desinstalan físicamente, pero sí dejan de funcionar en segundo plano. Hay otras que no se dejan quitar de ninguna de estas dos formas.
Dado que hace años que dejé de rootear mis móviles Android, siempre que quiero limpiar de manera profunda un teléfono acudía a Universal Android Debloater. Es una herramienta para PC que permite eliminar la instalación de casi cualquier app del teléfono, una acción que el gestor propio del teléfono no siempre permite. El Debloater usa ADB y sus comandos para obrar la magia, pero me hacía falta un PC.
Un día pensé: ¿por qué no tener en el móvil un desinstalador universal que funcionase internamente con ADB para así prescindir del ordenador? Me serviría para aquellas aplicaciones tozudas que no se dejan ni eliminar ni deshabilitar desde el teléfono. Y, como Shizuku ya gestiona por sí sola las peticiones ADB desde el propio teléfono, solo necesitaba unir mi app a dicho Shizuku para obtener un desinstalador universal.
Para la tarea usé Grok en modo Build. Le pedí que quería una aplicación tipo Universal Debloater, con acceso a ADB a través de Shizuku. Le especifiqué que debía crear el APK y, tras unas cuantas iteraciones, y algo más de media hora de trabajo, me entregó una versión suficientemente estable. Grok la llamó Brisa, le dejé ese nombre.
Un desinstalador local y en bloque
Android ya deja eliminar buena parte de las apps, aunque algunas de sistema se resisten. ADB puede meter mano casi hasta la cocina, siempre con cuidado: hay cierto riesgo de fastidiar el sistema si se toca según qué tecla. Brisa facilita el trabajo, incluye una papelera, restauración y un detalle que me parece importante: puede encadenar la desinstalación de múltiples aplicaciones. No solo de sistema.
Con la app que me hizo Grok puedo marcar lo que no quiero de una lista, tanto da que sea de sistema como de usuario. Tras el enlazado con Shizuku (esta se aprovecha de ADB inalámbrico), Brisa realiza un proceso automático para el que antes yo necesitaba un buen rato de dedicación. Y puede sacar de mi móvil el rastro de aplicaciones que desde Android no se dejan ni deshabilitar.
Aparte de quitar el bloatware, Brisa hace rápida la eliminación y mucho más sencilla. Puede rescatar las aplicaciones eliminadas y las deshabilitadas. Todo con una interfaz amigable y fácil de utilizar. Y como sé de qué manera está hecha, y me impliqué en todo el proceso, me aseguro la privacidad de todos los datos.
Cómo probar Brisa
Lo ideal es que te armes tú la app de desinstalación a tu manera. Si quieres probar la mía, la he dejado en este enlace. Necesitas Shizuku instalado en tu Android y activo: en Android 11 o superior basta con la depuración inalámbrica, sin cables ni ordenador.
Como dije antes, eliminar algunas aplicaciones es un riesgo: ve con mucho cuidado. Todos los cambios que hagas pueden deshacerse, pero si el sistema da error porque le falte algo es probable que ya no puedas arrancar correctamente el teléfono.

articles.title: Una química japonesa pagará USD 11.600 millones por JSR, que provee materiales clave para fabricar chips
articles.text:
La japonesa Mitsui Chemicals comprará JSR, una de las mayores fabricantes de materiales para producir chips, por 1,84 billones de yenes (USD 11.610 millones). Según el documento que la empresa presentó el 9 de noviembre, el banco estatal Development Bank of Japan (DBJ) también invertirá en la operación.
Reuters la describió como una de las mayores del sector. Es más que los USD 8.000 millones aproximados que pagó Showa Denko en 2020 por Hitachi Chemical. JSR produce fotorresistentes, las sustancias sensibles a la luz con las que se transfieren los circuitos a las obleas de silicio. Según Bloomberg, sus clientes incluyen a TSMC, Intel y Samsung Electronics. Mitsui Chemicals la ubica en el segundo puesto mundial en ese mercado.
Los vendedores son los fondos de JIC Capital, el brazo de inversión de Japan Investment Corp, un fondo respaldado por el Estado japonés. JIC compró JSR en 2024 por 900.000 millones de yenes, según Reuters, con el plan de usarla para consolidar la industria de materiales para chips.
Un precio que supera el valor de la compradora
El tamaño del pago preocupa a los inversores. La capitalización de mercado de Mitsui Chemicals era de 664.600 millones de yenes (USD 4.200 millones), según datos de LSEG citados por Reuters, menos de la mitad del precio de la operación.
Las acciones de la compradora caían cerca de 13% el lunes, hasta unos 1.500 yenes, después de haber bajado más de 10% la semana anterior, cuando Reuters informó que sería la compradora final.
El precio de 1,84 billones de yenes suma el valor de las acciones, 1,3921 billones de yenes, y 447.900 millones de yenes de deuda de JSR que Mitsui asumirá. Según la presentación de la empresa, equivale a 16 veces el EBITDA (las ganancias operativas antes de ciertos cargos contables) previsto para este año fiscal.
Un préstamo puente de USD 10.300 millones
Mitsui Chemicals financiará la compra con un préstamo puente, un crédito a corto plazo, de 1,64 billones de yenes (USD 10.360 millones). Lo refinanciará con varias fuentes y venderá acciones propias por hasta 150.000 millones de yenes. DBJ aportará 200.000 millones de yenes en acciones preferentes sin derecho a voto.
La compañía dijo que reducirá su deuda en tres años para conservar una calificación crediticia de rango A. Para ello planea vender la unidad de ciencias de la vida de JSR y otros negocios que no son centrales.
Mitsui Chemicals espera que JSR le sume 40.000 millones de yenes de ganancia anual. La empresa también fabrica películas que protegen las plantillas con los diseños de los circuitos, con las que podrá combinar los productos de JSR en el proceso de litografía.
El Gobierno japonés busca ganar competitividad en materiales para chips, un sector en el que el país es un proveedor mundial central. Según Reuters, la operación puede cambiar la cadena de suministro japonesa.
El cierre depende de las aprobaciones de las autoridades de competencia y de inversión extranjera. Mitsui Chemicals prevé completarlo en el segundo semestre del año fiscal que termina en marzo de 2028.

articles.title: Moins de 33€ pour le Philips OneBlade 360 Visage et ses deux lames : que vaut cette offre Black Friday ?
articles.text:
Les premières offres Black Friday d’Amazon touchent aussi la salle de bain, avec un rasoir hybride pensé pour entretenir une barbe courte. Le Philips OneBlade 360 Visage passe à 32,99 € au lieu de 54,99 €, un tarif proche des 29,99 € que nous avions relevés en juin, pour un pack livré sans accessoire pour le corps.
Le OneBlade 360 Visage occupe une place à part chez Philips : ni tondeuse classique, ni rasoir à grille, il réunit les deux usages dans un seul manche. Sa lame 360 pivote pour suivre la ligne de la mâchoire et du cou, là où une tête fixe oblige à multiplier les passages. Cette version QP2734/30 est livrée avec deux lames et un sabot réglable, de quoi tenir plusieurs mois avant le premier rachat de consommable.
Pour le Black Friday, le Philips OneBlade 360 Visage est affiché à 32,99 € sur Amazon, soit 40 % de moins que son prix de 54,99 €. L’offre s’adresse d’abord à ceux qui entretiennent une barbe courte au quotidien.
Le Philips OneBlade 360 Visage passe de 54,99 € à 32,99 € chez Amazon, avec ses deux lames 360 et son sabot réglable 5 en 1 dans la boîte.
Pourquoi choisir le Philips OneBlade 360 Visage ?
- Une lame qui suit le visage : La tête 360 pivote et épouse les courbes de la mâchoire, du menton et du cou. Vous travaillez les zones délicates sans tordre le poignet ni repasser sans cesse au même endroit.
- Cinq longueurs avec un seul sabot : Le sabot réglable couvre les longueurs de 1 à 5 mm. Une barbe de trois jours ou une barbe courte bien nette se règle sans chercher le bon peigne au fond d’un tiroir.
- Deux lames, donc du temps devant vous : Il faut compter un remplacement de lame tous les quatre mois environ. Avec la lame de rechange fournie, le premier achat de consommable est repoussé de plusieurs mois.
Une barbe courte à entretenir, sous la douche ou devant le miroir
Le principe du OneBlade est de faire deux gestes avec un seul outil : tondre la barbe à longueur égale avec le sabot, puis raser à blanc les zones à dégager. La conception étanche autorise un passage sous la douche, pratique si vous préférez vous raser sur une peau mouillée et rincer la lame à l’eau claire. Côté autonomie, comptez environ 45 minutes pour une charge de 8 heures. C’est assez pour plusieurs séances d’entretien rapides, mais la recharge demande un peu d’anticipation.
Ce modèle convient bien à une barbe courte à mi-longue que vous entretenez souvent, ou à une première expérience du rasage hybride sans investir dans un appareil plus cher. Il est moins adapté si votre barbe est très dense : un rasoir rotatif ou à grille obtient un rendu plus précis et plus net sur ce type de poil. Et si vous cherchez aussi à entretenir le corps, ce pack visage ne fournit aucun sabot dédié.
Entre la tondeuse basique et le OneBlade Pro 360
À ce prix, le OneBlade 360 Visage se place au-dessus des tondeuses mono-fonction d’entrée de gamme, qui coupent sans raser, et sous le OneBlade Pro 360, vendu habituellement autour de 80 €. Ce dernier se montre plus endurant et sa lame dure plus longtemps, deux arguments qui comptent si vous vous rasez tous les jours. Le modèle en promotion garde l’essentiel : la même lame pivotante et un réglage suffisant pour une barbe courte. Pour quelques séances par semaine, l’écart de prix pèse plus lourd que l’écart de fonctions.
✅ Les points forts
- Lame 360 pivotante qui épouse la mâchoire et le cou
- Sabot réglable 5 en 1, de 1 à 5 mm
- Conception étanche, utilisable sous la douche
- Deux lames dans la boîte, soit plusieurs mois d’usage
- Un seul appareil pour tondre et raser
❌ Les limites
- Autonomie d’environ 45 minutes pour 8 heures de charge
- Aucun sabot pour le corps dans ce pack visage
- Rendu moins précis qu’un rasoir rotatif ou à grille sur barbe épaisse
- Lames à racheter tous les quatre mois environ
Avant de valider, vérifiez sur Amazon que le prix de 32,99 € s’applique bien au pack visage QP2734/30, livré avec ses deux lames 360.
À 32,99 €, le Philips OneBlade 360 Visage redevient un achat raisonnable pour entretenir une barbe courte avec un seul appareil. La remise de 40 % est calculée sur le prix de 54,99 € affiché par Amazon, celui que nous relevions déjà comme son prix habituel en juin. Nous l’avions alors vu descendre à 29,99 €, juste avant le Prime Day : l’écart de 3 € ne change pas l’intérêt de l’offre, mais il rappelle que ce modèle a déjà été proposé plus bas.
Si vous taillez une barbe de quelques jours plusieurs fois par semaine, il fera le travail sous la douche comme devant le miroir. Le jeu GTA 6 a le droit à un lancement très particulier. Non seulement, le prochain titre de Rockstar Games est très attendu, mais il initie aussi une sortie en deux temps qui pourrait bien devenir la norme.
En effet, alors que la sortie de GTA 6 est attendue pour le jeudi 19 novembre, le préchargement de la version numérique ouvre dès ce mardi 10 novembre.
Jouez dans les meilleures conditions avec la TV TCL C79L : une expérience gaming fluide en 144 Hz et un son immersif signé Bang & Olufsen, actuellement en promotion !
Quant à la version physique du jeu, il s’agit d’un simple « Code in a Box », c’est-à-dire un code de téléchargement pour le PlayStation Store ou le Xbox Store, sans le disque du jeu dans la boîte. Impossible de le prêter ou de le revendre.
Cette version physique, souvent moins chère que la version numérique en France, va arriver dans les prochains jours.
Les premières expéditions
L’enseigne Leclerc, qui avait déjà communiqué avec ses clients sur le lancement de GTA 6, a commencé à expédier les premières précommandes. Certains clients ont ainsi leur numéro de suivi de colis. Les premières livraisons sont attendues autour du 12 novembre officiellement. De quoi laisser une semaine pour précharger le jeu sur PS5 et Xbox Series.
Leclerc n’est évidemment pas le seul à se préparer pour ce lancement. Micromania indique que les premières boîtes GTA 6 arriveront en magasin ce jeudi 12 novembre.
Pour rappel, GTA 6 est disponibles en précommandes à partir de 79,99 euros en version numérique, mais on peut le trouver à 60 euros en version physique.

articles.title: How Milsat built Nigeria’s digital address system
articles.text:
For years, finding an address across much of Nigeria has depended far less on a number than on a description. A visitor might be directed to a street, told to look for a distinctive building, instructed to turn at a familiar shop, or advised to keep walking until reaching a landmark tree. Delivery riders often know a neighbourhood intimately yet still struggle to identify the correct front gate. Across the country, the gap between arriving in a community and reaching a specific doorway remains considerable.
Nigeria’s new digital postcode system is designed to narrow that gap. Launched on October 1, 2026, it moves beyond the traditional postcode, which identifies a broad area, to assign codes at the level of individual buildings or delivery units. The ambition is to make it possible to identify a particular building with greater precision, whether it is in a busy city, a developing suburb or a rural community.
But the system is more than a new set of numbers and letters. Behind it is an attempt to build a national location-data infrastructure: a system that can collect information about buildings, verify it, update it as places change and make it useful to government agencies, businesses and ordinary Nigerians.
For Taslim Salaudeen, Milsat’s chief executive and co-founder, the project is about something bigger than giving building codes.
“The clear answer is that we are not another addressing company. We are a location-data infrastructure company,” he said. “Our job, or our holistic mission, is to unlock the location-data gap that exists in African developing countries like Nigeria.”
That distinction helps explain how the company became involved in a national postal project, why it spent years developing mapping technology and what it believes the new postcode system could eventually make possible.
From paper maps to usable data
Milsat’s involvement in the project grew out of its earlier work on mapping and data collection. The company’s central argument is that many African countries have information about their people, buildings and communities, but too often that information is collected in ways that make it difficult to reuse.
Data may be gathered manually, recorded on paper or stored in systems that cannot easily be updated or shared. A government agency might complete a mapping exercise for a particular purpose, only for the information to become difficult for another institution to access or apply.
Salaudeen said Milsat was established in 2017 to address that wider problem. Location data, he explained, can support far more than postal delivery. It can help governments map populations, plan public services and identify where children live in rural communities so vaccination programmes can reach them. It can also help businesses understand where customers are, organise deliveries and make decisions based on geography.
“Location address is just one type of location service,” he said, pointing to the company’s work in census mapping, mapping children in rural areas for vaccine delivery and postcode systems.
Before such technology became available, he said, many data-collection exercises were conducted “manually, on paper and pen, on paper maps”. The information could not easily be reused, distributed or accessed by other organisations.
The problem, in his view, was the absence of infrastructure designed around the realities of African geography and communities. Milsat wanted to build tools that would allow organisations to collect information, manage it and make it useful beyond the original project.
“So this is why we believe the first step to fixing data unavailability or data inaccessibility in Nigeria particularly is first to build the infrastructure that can allow Nigerians or Africans to collect data the way it is meant to be collected, operate it the way it is meant to be operated and distribute it towards people that really need it,” he said.
The postcode system is one of the most visible applications of that ambition.
Milsat’s relationship with NIPOST began towards the end of 2021, according to Salaudeen. The company had been recommended to the postal service after work it carried out with the National Population Commission (NPC) on mapping buildings and other features for census-related activities.
Salaudeen said Milsat’s technology supported the mapping of more than 65 million buildings, alongside roads and points of interest. That figure is his account of the earlier mapping work, not a count of buildings that have all received postcodes.
The recommendation brought Milsat into discussions with NIPOST, which had been trying to develop a national addressing system for years. Salaudeen said the postal service already had a policy framework and a concept for what the country’s postcode system should look like. The challenge was turning those plans into something that could function in the real world.
“Our job then was to see the theoretical component that they wrote, their wishes, and then, as a technical partner, transform that into a practical, functional system,” he said.
A system built before the national rollout
To demonstrate that the proposed system could work, Milsat participated in a pilot in one or two local government areas in Abuja. Salaudeen could not recall precisely which areas during the interview.
The pilot was a joint effort involving NIPOST and other agencies. Salaudeen said Milsat contributed technology, training and operational support, with some of the work carried out at its own expense. The company saw the exercise as an investment in a national infrastructure project it believed was important.
“We did a pilot to prove that we know what we are saying and we know what we are promising,” he said.
He described the exercise as a collective effort, with different agencies contributing to its success. Milsat took responsibility for the technology and training, while also covering some operational costs.
The pilot demonstrated that the government’s postcode concept could be translated into a working system. Users could query a postcode, retrieve it and associate it with a particular location.
“The pilot was proving that from theory to reality,” Salaudeen said.
The path from pilot to national launch was not immediate. There were changes in leadership and the usual complications of government projects. There was also the question of how to finance and organise the work at national scale.
Salaudeen said Milsat had developed much of the underlying technology before the national project was formally approved. That preparation, he argued, helped explain the speed of the eventual rollout. The company was not starting from scratch when the opportunity to deploy the system across Nigeria emerged.
He also offered an account of how the national project was organised. According to him, Milsat was not the company that directly secured the main project contract. He identified MEED Network as the company involved in securing the contract and said the two companies subsequently collaborated, with Milsat contributing its location-data technology and technical expertise.
Salaudeen was candid about the distinction between developing technology and navigating the process of securing a government contract. “We don’t really envy bidding; we envy delivery,” he said, explaining that Milsat preferred to concentrate on what it knew how to do.
He described the eventual arrangement as an example of organisations recognising their different strengths and working together. Once the partners aligned, they could build on technology that had already been tested.
“We were prepared even before anything was sealed,” he said. The partners were able to configure and deploy the system quickly because the technology had already been developed and tested at earlier stages.
What a postcode now identifies
The biggest change is the level of detail.
Nigeria’s older postcode system used numerical codes that generally pointed to an area or district. A postcode could identify a broad part of a city, but it did not necessarily tell a delivery service which building to visit.
The new system is designed to go further. Its structure moves through several geographical levels, from state to local government area, district and area, before identifying an individual building or delivery unit.
Salaudeen said the shift reflects a wider movement towards building-level addressing. While older systems in many countries identify regions or areas, the new approach is intended to take the code down to the individual unit.
“So it starts from state, LGA, district, area and unit, with unit being your home or your house or delivery unit,” he explained.
That final level is important. A code is no longer intended only to say that a parcel belongs somewhere in a neighbourhood. It is meant to identify the particular structure where the parcel should be delivered.
Adedamola Baderinwa, who also participated in the interview, explained part of the system’s geographical logic. An area can contain a maximum of 99 buildings, while a district can contain up to 400 areas. In places where buildings are spread out, and there are fewer than 99 within a defined space, the model also takes geographical coverage into account. Baderinwa said an area could be based on roughly two hectares where the building count is lower.
The aim is to make the system work in places with very different patterns of development. A densely built part of Lagos may contain many buildings close together. In a less densely populated part of the country, buildings may be separated by large stretches of land. A system based only on the number of buildings could treat those places unevenly.
The new model attempts to account for both.
It also defines a building in practical terms. For NIPOST, a unit is a place where a delivery can be made: a structure where a postal worker can arrive, knock on the door, and leave a parcel. If a compound contains three separate standing buildings, each can have its own unit code.
“A unit is a standing structure,” Salaudeen said. “So if you have three standing buildings in a compound, they have independent unit codes.”
That definition has consequences for what the system includes. A temporary kiosk, construction shelter, or movable structure may not qualify as an addressable building, even if someone is staying there. Salaudeen said NIPOST applies a standard definition of a delivery unit, rather than treating every temporary structure as a permanent address.
The distinction is important in a country where people live in a wide range of housing arrangements. It also points to one of the system’s limits: a postcode database built for postal delivery will not necessarily describe every place where people live or work.
Mapping Nigeria as it is
Building a national addressing system presents a challenge that is not solved by importing mapping technology developed elsewhere.
Nigeria’s geography and settlement patterns vary widely. In some places, buildings are arranged along planned streets. In others, they emerge gradually, with roads and houses developing in ways that do not follow a formal layout. Communities may be organised around waterways, informal paths or landmarks that residents know well but that are difficult to represent through conventional mapping systems.
Salaudeen said Milsat had to build its technology with these differences in mind. He described communities where people live in houses along rivers, in caves or in structures that might not fit a narrow Western definition of a conventional building.
“In the desert, you see white domes; in river areas, you see houses on the river; in the East, you see people in caves,” he said. “These are places where people reside and live and call their homes.”
The company’s earlier field experience, he said, helped it understand how housing and settlement patterns differ across the country. The challenge was to create one system that could recognise those differences while still operating according to consistent standards.
Baderinwa pointed to another example: household structures in parts of northern Nigeria. A family may be spread across several buildings, with members living in separate structures but sharing food from the same pot. A mapping system designed around the assumption that one household occupies one building could misunderstand that arrangement.
These details may appear small, but they matter when location data is used for planning, service delivery, or population-related work. A system that misreads how people live can produce information that looks precise on a map but does not accurately reflect life on the ground.
For Milsat, the answer was to build technology that could accommodate local realities without abandoning international standards.
“Our technology adapts to culture while maintaining global standards,” Salaudeen said. “We have global standards and a solution that works in our local culture.”
He said much of the technology used to operate the postcode system was developed locally. Satellite imagery is integrated into the company’s field-mapping application, helping teams compare what they see on the ground with geographical information and confirm whether the mapping model fits a particular location.
The technology also provides tools for validating information, checking data quality, and managing updates. Human fieldwork remains part of the process. Satellite imagery can help identify structures and geographical features, but it does not remove the need for people to confirm what exists in a community.
Salaudeen described the wider technology as an operating system for data, allowing organisations to collect, verify, distribute and govern information rather than leave it sitting unused in storage.
A postcode that must keep changing
A national postcode system cannot be treated as a project that ends when the software is launched. Buildings are constructed, demolished, divided and modified. New settlements emerge, and existing communities expand.
The system is designed to accept updates from different sources. A resident or property owner may submit a request or suggest a change. Government agencies may contribute information from their own records, including data generated through building-permit processes. NIPOST’s postcode department is responsible for reviewing submissions and approving changes.
Where there is uncertainty, officials can arrange for information to be checked on the ground, Salaudeen said.
He described the process as one in which different information pipelines feed into a central system, but submissions still pass through data-quality checks before they are approved.
This is particularly important because the existing mapping data is not complete or permanent. Salaudeen said the earlier census-related work provided a substantial starting point, but new buildings have appeared since that exercise. He estimated that almost 50 million buildings were already represented in the postcode database, while acknowledging that the number would continue to grow. The figure was provided by the company’s executives and was not independently verified in the interview.
Rather than beginning with an empty map, NIPOST is building on information that had already been collected. Residents whose buildings are missing can request a postcode, allowing the database to expand as new locations are identified.
Salaudeen stressed that the system should not be judged as though it were a one-time mapping exercise. “Postcode is not something where we say we have finished,” he said. “It is a continuous growth because people keep on building houses.”
For Milsat, the longer-term ambition is to make the database one of the richest sources of location information about Nigeria. Baderinwa said the company hoped it would reach that point within five years.
Reaching people beyond smartphones
A digital postcode system is only useful if people can access it. That raises a practical question in a country where not everyone owns a smartphone, has reliable internet access or is comfortable navigating a digital map.
Salaudeen said the partners viewed public access as a continuing process rather than something solved by launching a website or application. The system may allow a person to find a postcode online, but the company is also considering ways to make the information available through organisations and services that already collect people’s addresses.
Banks, hospitals, public health centres, utilities and other institutions could become points through which people discover their postcodes. A customer who has previously provided a home address to a bank or hospital might eventually be able to receive the corresponding postcode through that institution.
The company also discussed working with local representatives who could visit communities and help residents identify their codes. In some rural areas, printed lists or gazetted postcode information may be more practical than asking people to navigate a digital interface.
Salaudeen said the partners were exploring whether telecommunications networks could help people retrieve their postcodes through text messages or USSD, services that do not require a smartphone. These were possibilities under consideration, not capabilities he said were already fully available.
His position is that technology should not become a barrier to receiving the service.
“We are a diverse country. Every layer of development requires a different strategy in disseminating information,” he said. “We will meet you where your knowledge is, just to deliver the same result: knowing a precise postcode.”
What businesses can do with it
The system is also intended to become infrastructure for businesses that depend on accurate location information.
A logistics company, for example, could use building-level postcodes to organise deliveries more efficiently. A financial institution could improve the way it records customer addresses. Other businesses could use the information to plan services, identify customers or connect their own data to precise locations.
To encourage adoption, the partners have opened a route for businesses to integrate the postcode system into their own products. Baderinwa said companies could visit dashboard.postcode.gov.ng, create an account, complete a know-your-business verification process and request access to the application programming interface, or API. A sandbox environment allows developers to test how the system works before using it in their services.
He said about 700 companies had registered at the time of the interview, although that figure was not independently verified. Larger organisations with more complex requirements can seek additional integration support.
Salaudeen said Milsat’s role is not simply to deliver a database and walk away. It wants to help agencies and businesses keep their data operational, updated and useful over time.
He described this as turning data into an asset: information that can be maintained and used by different organisations rather than left unused after a project ends.
“Our business model is making a big enterprise or a government agency sustainable by operating their dataset,” he said. “We make data an asset for any agency or business. We make it operable, make it living, and connect it to the sectors or enterprises that can use it for their daily activities.”
The reported cost of the national project was below ₦8 billion, according to Salaudeen. He said the financing covered a range of requirements, including field equipment, software deployment and infrastructure for NIPOST. He did not provide a detailed breakdown of the spending or specify how much Milsat itself earned from the project.
For now, the more difficult test is whether the system can remain accurate, accessible, and useful as Nigeria changes. A postcode that points to a building that no longer exists, or fails to include a new settlement, will quickly lose value. A database that residents cannot access will struggle to become part of everyday life. And businesses will have little reason to integrate it if the information cannot be trusted.
The launch has provided Nigeria with a new way to identify buildings. Keeping that system alive will require continued fieldwork, reliable oversight, cooperation between public institutions and private companies, and participation from the people whose homes and businesses it is meant to locate.
Salaudeen’s larger argument is that the postcode is only the beginning. The infrastructure being built around it could support other forms of location-based services, from public planning to commercial delivery and data management.
That is a bigger ambition than giving every building a code. It is an effort to make the places where Nigerians live and work easier to identify, describe, and connect to the services that depend on knowing exactly where they are.
The real measure of the system, then, will not be how quickly it was launched. It will be whether it can keep finding Nigeria as Nigeria keeps building itself.

articles.title: Bill Gates advierte sobre la agitación económico-social durante 20 años debido a la IA
articles.text:
Bill Gates cree que tendremos un periodo de 20 años en el que se presentarán muchas transformaciones. Es decir, que habrá cambios económicos y sociales. Durante este periodo pueden surgir algunos problemas. Incluso en un escenario en el que se maneje bien la tecnología, hay que atravesar un duro proceso de transición.
“Mi gran preocupación es este periodo de transición de 20 años. Hay ganadores y perdedores. Es un periodo muy disruptivo”, explicaba el cofundador de Microsoft.
Es un periodo de más o menos 20 años, dependiendo de cómo avancen las tecnologías y si decidimos frenarlas o no, y según él, tampoco está garantizada la abundancia.
Lo que preocupa es cómo vamos a atravesar este periodo. Habrá tanto cosas buenas como malas, ganadores y perdedores. El problema es el periodo de transición a esta posible abundancia.
El trabajo que podríamos reservar a las personas
En nuestro futuro tendremos la combinación de inteligencia artificial y robots humanoides. De esta forma podemos automatizar muchos trabajos físicos. Por ejemplo, podemos construir casas o producir alimentos. También pueden realizar operaciones quirúrgicas. De esta forma podemos reducir las carencias de bienes y servicios.
Por ello es importante pensar en qué aspectos podemos reservar a las personas.
Gates ve beneficios en otros sectores como la salud o la agricultura. Sin embargo, cree que los gobiernos y la sociedad no están bien preparados. Es relevante que haya más supervisión pública y adoptar medidas técnicas de protección frente a ciberataques o amenazas biológicas. No puede dejarse todo en manos de las empresas de IA.
Hay que tener en cuenta que el desarrollo de la tecnología es rápido. Podríamos estar ante uno de los periodos más turbulentos de nuestra historia.

articles.title: Huawei says its new desktop PC is 100% Chinese-made, with a few asterisks
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Huawei says it has built the first desktop PC containing nothing but China-made components. While this claim does appear to be true, there are some caveats, including continued reliance on foreign technology used in the chipmaking process.
China has long been pushing to lessen its reliance on US tech. Huawei says with its Qinyun HM650 series desktop computers, the machines are 100% domestically made. They also use the company's own HarmonyOS operating system.
The PC's component list includes 16 GB of LPDDR5 memory from China's CXMT, a 256GB or 512GB SSD that's likely from YMTC, and the company's own Kirin X90 system-on-chip, used in its more recent MateBook products.
Designed by Huawei HiSilicon and manufactured by SMIC, the Armv8-based Kirin X90 features 10 custom Taishan CPU cores in a 4+4+2 configuration, supporting 20 threads through simultaneous multithreading. It also has an integrated Maleoon 916 GPU.
It's the use of this SoC that adds a caveat to the Qinyun HM650 being 100% domestically made. Before the Kirin X90's release, rumors suggested it would use SMIC's newer 5nm process. However, TechInsights confirmed that it uses the foundry's 7nm-class N+2 process, first seen in Huawei's Mate 60 Pro in 2023.
The custom Taishan cores also use technology originating from Britain's Arm design giant. Huawei's 2013 Armv8 architecture licensing agreement allows it to design its own cores, but those designs still rely on overseas intellectual property.
SMIC has relied on foreign chipmaking tools, with US Commerce Department documents detailing shipments of Applied Materials ion implantation equipment to the foundry.
Other components in the PC depend on the likes of equipment and materials from outside of China, and HarmonyOS comes with a similar caveat. Huawei develops the operating system, but its documentation confirms the use of international open-source software and tools. While the exact components in the Enterprise Edition remain unverified, the fact that HarmonyOS is developed in China doesn't necessarily mean every line of code was written in the country.
Software compatibility could also be an issue for customers. HarmonyOS can't run Windows .exe applications natively, so businesses may need alternative apps or virtual machines to use their existing software. Huawei offers guidance on third-party virtualization tools, but companies would still need to check whether their essential programs and peripherals work.
Back in August, China told some state-linked organizations to uninstall a customized edition of Windows 10 several months ahead of schedule. The country introduced government purchasing rules requiring "safe and reliable" processors and operating systems in 2023. The approved CPU list consisted entirely of Chinese products, while Intel and AMD chips, Windows, and foreign database software were being phased out.

articles.title: DapuStor Launches Enterprise NVMe M.2 Boot Drive for High-Performance Data Centers
articles.text:
Monday, November 9th 2026
DapuStor Launches Enterprise NVMe M.2 Boot Drive for High-Performance Data Centers
The DapuStor J5101, an enterprise NVMe M.2 boot drive, built with the PCIe Gen 4 interface and a compact M.2 form factor, delivers fast, reliable server boot with low power consumption and flexible capacity options. These capabilities improve operational efficiency and lower total cost of ownership (TCO) in virtualization, AI, HPC, and cloud environments.
As AI infrastructure and data centers scale, server configurations are becoming denser and more complex, with higher costs per node. M.2 boot drives have become a critical component in server reliability and cluster operating costs, with evolving requirements in three key areas:Reliable Boot
Growing server software stacks add complexity to AI node boot and recovery. As an alternative to traditional PXE network boot and SATA boot drives, NVMe M.2 boot drives provide dedicated local boot storage for reliable system startup and recovery.
High-Density Deployment
Internal space is increasingly constrained by highly integrated AI servers. The compact M.2 form factor preserves drive bays for primary data storage, supporting high-density deployments.
Cost Efficiency
Flexible capacity options allow customers to configure storage capacity to system requirements and manage per-server acquisition costs. Low power consumption helps reduce energy costs across large-scale deployments.
01 | Power Efficiency at Scale
Even modest power savings per drive can add up across thousands of servers. The DapuStor J5101 M.2 Boot Drive consumes just 2 W at idle and has an active power consumption as low as 4.5 W, helping reduce energy use and optimize total cost of ownership (TCO) in high-density data centers.02 | System Reliability and Data Protection
The J5101 incorporates 4K error correction and ASIC-accelerated machine learning capabilities, minimizing NAND retries and adapting to varying NAND operating conditions to enhance data processing efficiency and system stability.
The J5101 combines several features to support system reliability and data security:
- Power Loss Protection (PLP) and end-to-end data protection help reduce the risk of data loss.
- Secure Boot and firmware integrity checks help protect the boot process and firmware.
- Dedicated boot storage separates the operating system from application data drives.
03 | Compact Design for Better Space Utilization
With a compact M.2 2280 form factor, the J5101 fits compatible server platforms without occupying a front-accessible data drive bay, improving overall space utilization.
Available in 480 GB, 960 GB, and 1.92 TB capacities, it enables flexible configuration to match system boot requirements, avoiding unnecessary capacity costs and providing a more cost-competitive solution.

articles.title: Pinterest Replaces Journey Clustering with 4B Qwen3 LLM, Reports Improved Engagement
articles.text:
Pinterest has moved its user-journey inference system from a multi-stage clustering pipeline to a fine-tuned 4-billion-parameter language model, reporting a 1.1% improvement in email click-through and 1.3% higher push opens.
Rather than clustering keywords into interests, the model examines users' activity histories to identify longer-term goals and feeds those journeys into Pinterest's existing recommendation infrastructure.
Pinterest defines a "journey" as a goal that connects interests, intent, and context across multiple sessions. Someone renovating a kitchen, for example, might search for cabinet designs, save countertop ideas, and later explore backsplash tiles or lighting. These interactions collectively suggest a coherent project rather than several unrelated interests.
("User Journey" - Source: Pinterest)
The company's previous system extracted keywords from user activity, grouped them using embeddings and hierarchical clustering, named the resulting clusters, and ranked them with additional models and diversity heuristics.
Although effective compared with earlier interest-based notifications, the approach could fragment related activities into separate journeys, produce generic labels, or mistake incidental engagement for sustained intent.
The new system instead treats journey inference as a generation task. A fine-tuned LLM reads a chronological history of up to 150 user actions across a 360-day window, alongside a compact user profile, and generates a ranked set of journey names. Search and save actions carry more weight than incidental clicks, while the prompt instructs the model to consider repeated engagement, recency, and specificity.
("Journey Inference" - Source: Pinterest)
The consolidation moved much of the previous system's ranking and filtering behavior into the prompt. Instructions discourage unrelated interests from being merged, suppress one-off activity and noisy automatically generated tags, and allow an empty result where there is insufficient evidence of a meaningful journey. Pinterest treats changes to these instructions as production launches rather than simple prompt edits.
To build the system without an extensive human-labelled dataset, Pinterest used frontier models to generate synthetic training examples from its user activity histories. These examples were used to fine-tune smaller open-weight Qwen3 models through supervised fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation (LoRA).
The team tested models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, selecting the 4B model for its balance of inference quality and serving throughput.
Running the resulting model at Pinterest's scale presented a separate engineering challenge. The company deployed NVIDIA Dynamo in front of vLLM workers running on L40S GPUs, using continuous batching, PagedAttention, and prefix-cache-aware routing to improve inference efficiency.
(Journey Inference Architecture - Source: Pinterest)
However, one of the largest throughput improvements came from avoiding unnecessary inference altogether. The system tracks when each user's journeys were last generated and skips users processed within the preceding couple of days.
Pinterest evaluates journey quality through side-by-side comparisons, a separate LLM judge assessing relevance and support from user activity, and online experiments. Initial A/B testing in the US and Canada produced the reported 1.1% email click-through and 1.3% push-open improvements over the clustering-based system, alongside statistically significant engagement and retention gains.
The approach has parallels with Netflix's work on foundation models for personalised recommendations. Netflix has described learning from long sequences of member interactions to create representations that can be reused by downstream recommendation models.
While Netflix focuses on reusable preference representations and Pinterest generates explicit journey descriptions, both approaches use longer-term behavioural histories to enrich existing personalisation infrastructure rather than replace it entirely.

articles.title: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
articles.text:
The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
Plus: Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made
—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm
This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.
But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story.
Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.
The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. 
For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. 
—Matthew Ponsford
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss
Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. (NYT $)

2 Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech
