+ Here’s why the midterms sparked an AI stock selloff. (BBC)
3 The UN annual climate meeting starts today
It’s the first to be held after confirmation the planet will exceed 1.5 °C warming. (Nature)

4 Connecting fridges to the internet looks like a bad move now
We still don’t know who is behind recent hacks, or even if they’re connected. (The Atlantic $)
+ Experts say they should be a “wake up call” for the industry. (NPR)
+ Are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic? (The Guardian)
+ AI is already making online crimes easier. It could get much worse. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Tesla is axing the Cybertruck 
RIP, we hardly knew ye. (Wired $)
+ The Cybertruck was on our “worst tech flops of 2025” list. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Iran might attack subsea cables if the US escalates again
That’s the message it’s sending via several loitering tankers. (FT $)
7 Chinese AI labs are struggling to poach Silicon Valley workers
Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot have an uphill battle as they try to fill new US offices. (Rest of World)
+ China’s AI models have Trump’s AI world at war with itself. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Online piracy is back 🏴☠️
But this time, archivist zeal is at least as big a draw as accessing content for free. (The Verge) 
+ Inside the race to save our online lives from a digital dark age. (MIT Technology Review)
9 How do you land on a moon with almost no gravity?
It’s a huge challenge to land on Martian moon Phobos—here’s how Japan’s going to attempt it. (IEEE Spectrum)
10 Meet Philadelphia's delivery robot saboteur
Carolyn Marvin is going to court for blocking them, and it’s turning her into a local hero. (The Guardian)
Quote of the day
“Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility.”
—Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia employees for his affair with a suspected Chinese spy in a mass email sent yesterday, the Washington Post reports.
One more thing
AI is coming for music, too
AI models are marching into a creative field that is uniquely vulnerable to disruption: music.
AI-generated creative works—from orchestra performances to heavy metal—are poised to suffuse our lives more thoroughly than any other product of AI has done yet.
The songs are likely to blend into our streaming platforms, party and wedding playlists, soundtracks, and more, whether or not we notice who (or what) made them.
Here’s why AI is set to forever change how we make music.
—James O’Donnell
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

articles.title: Disney tiene un plan para que tus películas favoritas se hagan más rápido gracias a la IA
articles.text:
Disney ha firmado un acuerdo con Adobe para desarrollar herramientas de IA adaptadas a sus necesidades creativas. La alianza permitirá al estudio usar los modelos de Adobe en diversos proyectos que van desde la producción de contenido hasta el diseño de atracciones para sus parques temáticos. Esta sería la primera vez que Disney tiene un acercamiento con otra empresa que desarrolla IA, luego del fiasco que resultó el acuerdo con OpenAI.
De acuerdo con el comunicado de prensa, el objetivo es integrar las tecnologías de IA en los procesos internos de Disney sin depender de herramientas genéricas. Adobe se convertirá en socio de innovación del gigante de Hollywood y proporcionará acceso temprano a los modelos de Firefly y aplicaciones como Photoshop y Premiere. La alianza también permitirá a Disney obtener recursos de ingeniería e investigación para desarrollar soluciones personalizadas.
Según el reporte, Adobe creará modelos de IA entrenados específicamente para Disney. En lugar de usar los modelos convencionales, ambas empresas trabajarán en un sistema que pueda comprender las características de personajes, estilos, escenarios y otros elementos de las películas y series del universo Disney. El objetivo es que la IA pueda generar contenido que se pueda usar en un entorno de producción real, manteniendo las características de lo que exige Disney.
Si bien muchos de los modelos comerciales no tienen problemas para generar imágenes o vídeos de personajes de Disney, la compañía quiere hacerlo de forma legal. Si hacemos memoria, el estudio demandó a Midjourney a mediados de 2025 por infracción de derechos de autor. Esto obligó a que empresas como OpenAI y Anthropic implementaran filtros para evitar la generación de contenido que pudiera violar el copyright de Disney.
¿De qué va el acuerdo de IA entre Disney y Adobe?
Los primeros frutos de la asociación entre Disney y Adobe ya se están dando dentro de Walt Disney Imagineering, la división encargada de diseñar los parques temáticos. Según las compañías, los equipos de investigación y desarrollo están utilizando Firefly Foundry para acelerar la fase de conceptualización. Entre las herramientas se encuentra un sistema que puede transformar bocetos a mano en arte conceptual en 2D, así como otro capaz de generar activos visuales alineados con las marcas de Disney.
El acuerdo también se extenderá a StudioLAB, el laboratorio de innovación de Walt Disney Studios, y a ESPN Edge, una división que se dedica a experimentar con nuevas tecnologías para las transmisiones deportivas. En el caso de esta última, ESPN analizará cómo la IA puede mejorar la forma en la que se presentan historias y se aumenta la interacción con los aficionados.
Disney parece apostar por un modelo de IA más controlado y especializado que el que adoptan otras empresas del sector. En lugar de limitarse a usar herramientas externas, la compañía construirá sistemas entrenados con sus contenidos y adaptados a sus procesos creativos. Esto tendrá un impacto en la producción de sus nuevas películas o series animadas, donde los artistas y diseñadores tendrán que adaptarse para usar las nuevas herramientas.

articles.title: France blames Iran for mass-hacks targeting freezers in grocery stores and blood banks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The French government has formally blamed Iran for launching cyberattacks that targeted thousands of internet-connected industrial refrigerated and freezer units across the country and broader Europe.
This is the latest in a string of destructive cyberattacks attributed to Iran this year, following a spate of hacks targeting U.S. water providers and other online intrusions that caused mass-disruption to U.S. medical device maker Stryker and others.
The U.S. government linked the attacks to pro-Iranian hacktivists who are working for Tehran, likely in response to the U.S./Israel-led war against Iran which killed its supreme leader in February.
Two recent waves of cyberattacks throughout October and into November saw hackers remotely break into web-based controllers that manage fleets of industrial cold and chilling units at grocery stores and retail supermarkets, and raise the temperatures to spoil food and destroy goods. Medical blood banks were also hacked but the attacks were stopped before any blood was spoiled, according to the French Blood Establishment.
Security researchers have since warned that the web-based controllers are vulnerable to remote hacks, with some of the affected models made by Danish company Danfoss no longer receiving security fixes.
In a statement given to reporters in Paris on Monday, French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “I am able to confirm that responsibility for this act lies with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” referring to Iran’s military and hackers.
“This was an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression; it represents the first large-scale act of sabotage on our national territory and constitutes a major assault on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” said Barrot, adding that the hacks will “not go without consequences.”
The French government has summoned Iran’s ambassador. Reuters first reported France’s attribution to Iran, citing sources ahead of the foreign minister’s remarks. The French government said it would also issue European-wide sanctions against those who carried out the hacks. Barrot said that the matter was now in the hands of the French justice system.
A spokesperson for Iran’s consulate in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The U.S. government is also reportedly looking into whether freezer units on military bases were hacked, following reports of similar outages and disruption earlier this year. U.S. officials have reportedly also linked the freezer-related cyberattack to Iran, but the intelligence community has not yet made a formal or public attribution.

articles.title: Vor dem Black Friday: So locken Temu, Shein und Joybuy schon am Singles Day
articles.text:
Vor dem Black Friday: So locken Temu, Shein und Joybuy schon am Singles Day
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
In Deutschland – und hier vor allem im Westen und Süden der Republik – ist der 11. November immer noch vor allem mit dem Beginn der Session rund um Karneval und Fastnacht verbunden, eventuell noch mit dem Martinstag. In China sieht das gänzlich anders aus: Dort steht das Datum seit einigen Jahren für den Singles Day – hergeleitet aus der Symbolik 1 für Single.
Wann ist der Singles Day 2026?
Der Singles Day, auch „Double 11“ genannt, ist speziell in den letzten zehn Jahren zu einem der umsatzstärksten Tage im E-Commerce geworden. Der Singles Day fällt in diesem Jahr auf einen Dienstag, aber zu erwarten ist, dass schon im Vorfeld zahlreiche Sonderangebote online und in den Geschäften zu finden sind.
Allein in China wurden rund um den Singles’ Day am 11. November 2025 nach Berechnungen des Marktforschungsunternehmens Syntun Waren im Wert von umgerechnet rund 206 Milliarden Euro über Onlineplattformen verkauft – 17,5 Prozent mehr als im Vorjahr. Seit Jahren ist der Singles Day, der dort Double-Eleven heißt, vor allem in China ein multimediales Ereignis, das auch mit TV-Shows gefeiert wird und weit größeres Ausmaß in der Berichterstattung hat als etwa hierzulande der Black Friday. Übrigens ist der Begriff „Double 11“ in China zwar geschützt, in Deutschland hat das Patent- und Markenamt hier allerdings nicht mitgespielt, als Bonprix 2017 versuchte, sich einige Begriffe rund um diesen Schnäppchentag zu sichern.
Was steckt hinter dem Singles Day?
Die Idee dahinter ist so naheliegend wie schlüssig aus Sicht des Handels: Der Alleinstehende, der naturgemäß nicht für die eigene Familie sorgen muss, hat Geld übrig und kann und soll sich mal etwas gönnen. Und alle anderen dürfen und sollen natürlich mitfeiern und auch Geld ausgeben.
Zurück geht der Tag der Alleinstehenden (Guanggun Jie auf Chinesisch) wohl auf einige Studierende, die ihn erstmals im Jahr 1993 feierten. Als Shopping-Tag populär gemacht hat „Double 11“ dann Alibaba, die den Tag, ähnlich wie Amazon seinen Prime Day, seit 2009 mit immer umfangreicheren Sonderangebotsschlachten feiern. Man beschenkt sich gegenseitig – und findet im Zweifelsfall auch selbst das eine oder andere Sonderangebot, auf das man schon länger gespart hat. Ursprünglich sollte der Tag übrigens mal als willkommene Möglichkeit dienen, andere Singles vergleichsweise ungezwungen kennenzulernen oder wahlweise auch als Tag, an dem Singles ausgelassen feiern.
Singles Day: Wie wird der Tag in Deutschland gefeiert?
Inzwischen ist auch in den westlichen Märkten der Singles Day vor allem ein Konsumtag, der sich nahtlos ins beginnende Weihnachtsgeschäft einreiht. Denn ähnlich wie der Black Friday und der Cyber Monday rund um das erste Adventswochenende (und nach dem amerikanischen Thanksgiving) sorgt auch der Singles‘ Day nicht nur in China, sondern auch in Mitteleuropa für satte Umsätze.
Mehrere Händler:innen berichteten uns im vergangenen Jahr, dass der Tag zu den umsatzstärksten im November zählte – und das, obwohl sie keine höheren Rabatte gaben als in anderen Zeiträumen im November. Wie auch die Preissuchmaschine Idealo berichtet, sind gute Angebote nicht nur rund um die Tage Ende November zu machen, sondern eben auch schon den ganzen November über.
Übrigens sehen wir gerade in diesem Jahr auch zahlreiche Geschäfte im Präsenzhandel, die den Singles Day mitfeiern – und das nicht nur in den genussorientierten Handelssegmenten. Das hat auch damit zu tun, dass der Handel sich im aktuellen Jahr mehr denn je darum bemüht, möglichst frühzeitig die Kund:innen zum Kauf zu bewegen. Das hat mit der vergleichsweise großen Unsicherheit und der Kaufzurückhaltung breiter Teile der Verbraucherschaft zu tun. Zu erwarten ist außerdem, dass aufgrund des Wochentags zumindest im Onlinehandel das gesamte Wochenende zum Singles Day ausgebaut wird, sodass du auch am Sonntag noch von den Angeboten profitieren können wirst.
Besondere Angebote könnte es hierbei auch von den in Deutschland wachsenden Plattformen Temu und Shein geben. Beide blenden (kund:innenspezifisch unterschiedlich) schon einige Angebote und Vergünstigungen bei den Versandkosten ein. Hier ist damit zu rechnen, dass in den nächsten Tagen zahlreiche Angebote online und in der App kommen werden. Doch wie immer ist das Ganze eher individuell und in seiner Ausgestaltung undurchsichtig.
Verlängerte Rückgabefrist soll Umsatz ankurbeln
Hinzu kommt, dass immer mehr Händler:innen eine Art Preisgarantie auf die Black-Friday-Zeit bieten. Amazon beispielsweise hat ab November sämtliche Rücksendungen bis Ende Januar verlängert. Die Idee dahinter ist so klar wie vernünftig: Wenn der Kunde jetzt kauft und später ein günstigeres Angebot findet, könnte er, ohne groß zu diskutieren, die Ware noch im Rahmen der per Fernabsatzrecht zugebilligten Rückgabefrist zurückgeben und neu bestellen. Die Folge wäre eine teure Retoure – jede Retoure kostet einen Händler im Schnitt 20 Euro und unterm Strich nicht mehr Umsatz.
Doch Kund:innen sollten einen kühlen Kopf bewahren, weil erwartungsgemäß nicht jedes Sonderangebot auch ein Bestpreis ist oder signifikant unter den sonstigen Preisen liegt. Gerade bei Produkten, die derzeit ohnehin mehr gefragt sind als sonst, sehen wir bei den Angeboten noch Luft. Denn bereits jetzt und bis zum kommenden Dienstag, dem eigentlichen 11. November, werben Händler:innen auch in Deutschland mit dem Shopping-Tag.
Singles Day: Diese Händler in Deutschland könnten mitmachen
Welche Händler sich in diesem Jahr am Singles Day beteiligen werden, ist noch nicht bekannt, da die Ketten erst sehr kurzfristig davor die Werbetrommel rühren. Im vergangenen Jahr war aber beispielsweise der Versender Otto* mit elf Prozent auf zahlreiche Artikel der Unterhaltungselektronik und Mode dabei. Auch Saturn und Mediamarkt* sind wieder mit dabei und stellen erneut Sonderangebote bereit, die sich – ähnlich wie bei Amazon – einfach in die ohnehin vorhandenen Novemberangebote einfügen. Möglicherweise werden auch Ebay, Douglas, Hunkemöller, Cyberport und Thalia* den Singles Day wieder als Thema aufgreifen.
Amazon* feiert ohnehin schon den gesamten November mit Angeboten, bei denen sich durchaus auch jetzt schon attraktive Angebote finden lassen. Wahrscheinlich überlässt das Unternehmen aber bewusst den chinesischen Händlern das Feld beim Singles Day, da hier natürlich Alibaba und JD.com wieder weit vorne liegen werden. Aliexpress beispielsweise wirbt mit Rabatten und Coupons von bis zu 80 Prozent rund um den 11. November, wobei dieser hier nicht als Singles Day bezeichnet wird, sondern nur als 11 11. Auch Händler und Plattformen wie Shein oder Temu werben mit ähnlich ambitionierten Rabatten beim Singles Day. Auch die zu JD.com gehörende europäische Plattform Joybuy hat bereits eine Singles‘ Day-Landingpage. Hier wirbt das Unternehmen mit einer Vielzahl an Sonderangenboten aus allen Abteilungen, wobei nicht jeder Rabatt auch wirklich überzeugend ist. Genau vergleichen sollten Kund:innen also dennoch.
Über konkrete Angebote werden wir euch noch in den nächsten Tagen – insbesondere am Tag selbst – informieren.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 07.11.2024 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: 'This represents an important evolution in AI governance': Infosys lays out how your business can thrive with the new generation of autonomous AI agents
articles.text:
'This represents an important evolution in AI governance': Infosys lays out how your business can thrive with the new generation of autonomous AI agents
How your business can prepare for the age of autonomous AI agents
As organizations look to embrace a new generation of autonomous AI agents which can access enterprise systems, make decisions and interact with other AI agents, new questions are emerging around how these systems are governed and secured.
As the governance of agentic AI and non-human identities rapidly one of the most significant challenges organizations will facein the coming years, we spoke to Umashankar Lakshmipathy, EVP and Head of Cloud, Infrastructure, and Security Services, EMEA, Infosys, to find out more.
- As organisations move from AI assistants to autonomous AI agents, what new security and governance challenges are emerging?
The move towards autonomous AI agents creates new security and governance challenges because these systems can make decisions and take actions with limited human involvement. Unlike AI assistants that primarily generate information or recommendations, agents can access enterprise data, use applications and tools, communicate with other agents and act on behalf of people or business processes.
This greater autonomy increases the potential business impact of an error, manipulation, or security compromise. An agent may have a valid identity and legitimate system access but could still take action that falls outside its intended purpose. The risk becomes more significant when agents operate across several systems, as one incorrect decision can trigger a sequence of actions that are difficult to detect, explain or reverse.
Organisations must therefore govern more than the AI model. Every agent needs a defined business purpose, an accountable owner and clear limits on the data, systems, and actions available to it. Sensitive or high-impact activities require stronger safeguards, while organisations need sufficient visibility to trace an outcome back to the person or process that initiated it, the agent that acted and the tools it used.
This represents an important evolution in AI governance. Organisations must continue to manage the quality and safety of AI-generated content, but they must now also control the decisions and actions that autonomous agents can execute. Getting that balance right will be essential to achieving the productivity benefits of agentic AI without creating unacceptable operational, financial, or regulatory risks.
- As agentic AI adoption grows, why are “non-human identities” becoming such an important issue for enterprises? What are the risks and opportunities when AI agents begin communicating and making decisions with other AI agents?
Non-human identities are becoming an important enterprise issue because a growing proportion of digital activity is performed by applications, APIs, service accounts, automation and AI agents rather than by employees. AI agents increase the significance of these identities because they can interpret information, make decisions and initiate actions, rather than simply execute predefined instructions.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
This makes visibility, ownership, and access management essential. Organisations need an accurate inventory of the non-human identities operating across their environment, together with a clear understanding of their business purpose, accountable owner and access to systems and data. Without this foundation, excessive permissions, long-lived credentials, and identities that remain active after their original purpose has ended create material security exposure.
Communication between agents creates significant business opportunities. Specialised agents can work together to automate complex processes across customer service, operations, software engineering and cyber defense. A process that previously required several teams and systems could potentially be coordinated by a group of agents operating at much greater speed.
However, agent-to-agent collaboration also creates chains of dependency and trust. A compromised or poorly governed agent could pass inaccurate information through a workflow, influence another agent’s decisions or attempt to use a more privileged agent to perform an action that it could not execute directly. These risks can multiply when organisations cannot establish which agent initiated an action or under whose authority it was performed.
Organisations should therefore enable agent collaboration within defined business and security boundaries. The identity, authority and purpose of each agent should be evaluated independently rather than allowing trust or access rights to pass automatically from one agent to another. This approach allows enterprises to benefit from multi-agent automation while preserving control and accountability across the complete business process.
- How can organisations strike the right balance between giving AI agents autonomy and maintaining appropriate oversight and control?
The appropriate level of autonomy for an AI agent should be determined by the business impact of its activities, the sensitivity of the information involved and how easily its actions can be reversed. Applying the same level of oversight to every agent would either create unnecessary friction or leave higher-risk activities insufficiently controlled. For example, an agent that analyses public information or produces an internal summary can operate with relatively light oversight. An agent that accesses customer information, changes production infrastructure, makes regulatory decisions or initiates financial transactions requires much tighter boundaries.
However, organisations should introduce autonomy progressively. Some agents will remain assistive and provide recommendations for people to consider. Others may prepare actions that require human approval. More mature agents can operate independently within approved limits, escalating situations that fall outside their normal authority. Agents performing highly predictable and well-controlled activities may eventually be given broader autonomy, provided their actions remain visible, governed and capable of being stopped.
Human oversight remains important, but requiring approval for every action would undermine the efficiency that agentic AI is intended to deliver. It can also lead to approval fatigue, where reviews become routine and provide little meaningful protection. Human involvement is most valuable for actions that are financially significant, legally sensitive, difficult to reverse or outside the agent’s established operating boundaries.
The aim is not to give agents the maximum possible autonomy. It is to give each agent enough autonomy to deliver business value while keeping its decisions within an acceptable level of risk. Routine and reversible activities can be automated, while consequential decisions remain subject to stronger safeguards and clear organisational accountability.
- Are existing cybersecurity, identity and governance frameworks sufficient for the age of agentic AI, or do organisations need a new approach?
Existing cybersecurity, identity and governance frameworks provide a strong foundation for agentic AI, but they are not sufficient without further adaptation. Organisations do not need to replace established capabilities such as Zero Trust, identity governance, privileged access management and AI risk management. They do, however, need to apply these capabilities more dynamically to agents that can make decisions and take actions at machine speed.
Many traditional controls were designed around granting access to a person, application or service and reviewing that access periodically. Agentic AI introduces a more dynamic operating model. An agent may access several data sources, invoke multiple tools, interact with other agents and make numerous decisions during a single business process. Authentication alone cannot establish whether every subsequent action is appropriate.
Existing frameworks therefore need to be extended in several practical ways. Every agent should have a unique identity, an approved business purpose, an accountable owner and a managed lifecycle. Its authority should be limited to the task it is performing and should not remain active for longer than necessary. Stronger safeguards should apply when an agent accesses sensitive information, uses privileged tools or attempts an action with a significant business impact.
Organisations must also be able to reconstruct how an outcome was produced. This means maintaining a clear record linking the originating person or business process to the agents involved, the data and tools they used, the actions they took and the resulting outcome. This visibility is essential for oversight, investigation, regulatory assurance and rapid intervention when something goes wrong.
The required approach is therefore an evolution of existing security and governance rather than the creation of a separate control environment for AI agents. By extending established frameworks to govern agent identity, authority, and actions continuously, organisations can scale agentic AI while maintaining coherent enterprise-wide control.

articles.title: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
articles.text:
The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.
- What could China get from Jensen Huang? It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Read Article >
- Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang. Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. Read Article >
- The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women? Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully. Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. (China is denying all this, btw.) Read Article >
- Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below. Read Article >
- Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing. Read Article >

articles.title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 with a price cut and stronger coding scores
articles.text:
Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 with a price cut and stronger coding scores
On Monday, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, the latest versions of its duo of flagship models.
Like before, Fable 5.2 will be available on all platforms today, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, while direct access to Mythos remains limited to organizations in Anthropic’s Cyber and Life Sciences verification programs.
Also like before, Fabe and Mythos share the same underlying model, but Fable ships with stricter cybersecurity and biology safeguards.
It’s maybe a bit of a surprise that Anthropic didn’t designate these models as “5.5,” given that its Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models are now at that version number.
The company stresses that it continues to recommend that users go with Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge tasks, while Fable 5.2 is meant to help users “tackle the most daunting technical challenges.”
And while both models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, according to Anthropic, one feature the company is stressing here is speed. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, the company says, generate output up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, respectively.
Fable Fast mode
For those who want an even faster response, there is now also a Fast mode for both models, which Anthropic says speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times.
It is available in Claude Code, on the Claude Platform, through Claude Models on Google Cloud, and through Anthropic-hosted Microsoft Foundry.
Pricing
As for pricing, Fable still carries a premium over Opus, but Anthropic is cutting the price from $10/$50 per million input/output tokens to $8/$40. Mythos 5.2 gets the same rates.
OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra still costs $10/$50 at its standard rates for prompts of up to 272,000 input tokens, putting Anthropic 20 percent below its rival on those token rates (at least for the time being).
Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens for either model, twice the standard rates.
Even after the price cut, Fable’s standard input and output rates are twice Opus 5.5’s current prices, though Anthropic’s new evaluations suggest that doesn’t necessarily translate into a higher cost per task.
Fable 5.2 targets complex coding
On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 scored 49.1 percent, compared with 32.4 percent for Fable 5.1, 45.5 percent for Opus 5.5, and 42.8 percent for GPT-6 Astra. On FrontierSWE v2, it scored 69.9 percent, ahead of Astra’s 65.5 percent and Opus’s 62.3 percent.
The cost comaprison with Opus may be even more interesting, though. In early FrontierCode 2.0 testing, Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort performed about as well as Opus 5.5 at Max effort for roughly half the cost per task.
Medium is now the default effort level for Fable 5.2 in Claude apps and Claude Code.
It’s worth noting that the results aren’t a clean sweep for Fable 5.2, though.
Gemini 4 Carbon leads Fable on AutomationBench, which tests business workflows, at 53.9 percent versus 51.4 percent. Meanwhile, Opus still retains a small lead on the Elo measure of AA-Briefcase v1.1, a knowledge-work evaluation.
Anthropic says Fable can act as an adviser that smaller models consult on harder problems, or as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to them. In one internal experiment, an engineer asked Fable 5.2 to build a prototype operating system from an empty folder.
The company says it coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced an OS that boots on a laptop, complete with drivers, persistent storage, a graphical interface, and an installer.
Fable promises fewer safety blocks
Anthropic says Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards remain as robust as those in 5.1. In early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, the company observed about 55 percent fewer blocks overall, including about 60 percent fewer in cybersecurity and 40 percent fewer in biology.
That could reduce interruptions to legitimate work, though fewer blocks don’t necessarily mean broader permissions. Fable still blocks high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing and exploit generation, as well as most research biology tasks. When a query is blocked, Anthropic says users instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity or Opus 5 for biology.
Direct Mythos access remains gated, but there is another route for enterprise security work: Claude Enterprise customers can use Claude Security, which now includes Mythos 5.2, even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program.
Anthropic also says it deliberately limited improvements in certain AI-development capabilities during training, including accelerator kernel optimization and work on large language model architectures. In those areas, the models perform at about Opus 5.5’s level, according to the company. It says those limits do not affect agentic coding, hardware development, or traditional machine learning research.
For API developers, Anthropic is expanding preserved thinking to all accounts. The feature restricts changes to Claude’s prior context that could be used to extract its reasoning for distillation.
Enterprise safeguards enter private beta
Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, which the company first announced in September, is also moving into private beta, with Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe among the early customers. Automated safety monitoring runs on prompts and responses stored in customers’ own infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention, Anthropic says.
Eligible customers can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing the system. For other customers, Anthropic retains data for 30 days for safety monitoring.
Fable for physics
Anthropic argues that its models’ coding abilities also apply to scientific research because so much of that work is also based on software, including analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, or controlling instruments.
The company says Fable 5.2 solved two open theoretical-physics problems involving black holes and holographic duality. One involved completing a calculation proposed in 2003 to determine whether black-hole formation remains an abrupt transition in a small-universe quantum description. The other established the limit of a technique used to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe.
The Fermat claim is more specific than the early announcement suggested. Anthropic says a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean in 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Formalization expresses a proof in a language that a computer can check step by step; it is distinct from discovering a new proof.
The agents received a list of intermediate theorem statements to measure progress, but no mathematical references, according to Anthropic. An earlier research version of Claude took 11 days with a purpose-built harness and human guidance. The company’s comparison used a single run per model, with Opus 5.5 reaching 26 percent after 18 hours and making little additional progress by 30 hours.
Anthropic also tested Fable 5.2 on hardware design, working with circuit-board company Diode to produce a voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. The company says Claude selected components, designed the boards and enclosures, and wrote the software. Diode built the boards, and its engineers tested and assembled the devices with Claude’s guidance.
All three worked without electrical modifications, according to Anthropic.

articles.title: France Blames Iran for a Cyberattack That Heated Supermarket Refrigerators
articles.text:
France on Monday blamed Iran for last month’s cyberattack on supermarket refrigerators, summoned the Iranian ambassador and said it would seek European sanctions against those responsible for the attack.
The Oct. 12 attack sent refrigerator temperatures soaring, affecting about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets. In a statement Monday, prosecutors in Paris said they found that Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard was behind the large-scale cyberattack.
The French Foreign Ministry condemned the attack “in the strongest possible terms,” and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, speaking on the sidelines of G7 talks in Paris, said the Iranian ambassador was being summoned to “strongly protest against this extremely serious act.”
“This is an attack of unprecedented scale and aggressiveness,” Barrot said. “It is the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on French soil, and it represents a major threat to our national interests and the security of the French people. That is why it will not go unanswered.”
“We will impose sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack,” he added, vowing to take “any other measures needed” to respond to it and deter future attacks.
Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement that a formal judicial investigation was opened Monday into suspected organized cybercrime with the aggravating circumstance of “having been committed to serve the interests of a foreign power — in this case, Iran.”
France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, attributed the attack to the Shahid Kaveh group, described as a “cyber unit” affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The investigation targets the leader of the group as well as his two deputies and any other individuals who might be identified in connection with the case, Beccuau said.
Investigators found that the attackers had used Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices located in Iran, Beccuau said. The Paris prosecutor’s office is seeking international arrest warrants, she said.
In the early hours of Oct. 12, attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France. Temperatures reached 50 Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) for about six hours, forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen goods. The Intermarché supermarket chain reported losses of “tens of millions of euros” in a single day.
Last week, another cyberattack in France on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples. France’s national cybersecurity agency and Paris prosecutors are investigating the incident.
Also last week, supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia were hit by problems with freezers and fridges that apparently were caused by cyberattacks, forcing some to dispose of ruined food.
The ANSSI cybersecurity agency said it was able to attribute some other cyber attacks carried out against France since 2020 to another group named Shahid Shoostari, also affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. They include attacks targeting satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.

articles.title: Used memory chips are creeping into budget phones, and it could get worse
articles.text:
TL;DR: Desperate times call for desperate measures, and the electronics industry has been there for a while now. After grappling with rising memory costs and inventory shortages, and eventually realizing that the situation may take years to resolve, some device makers are looking for alternative solutions that give old hardware components a new lease on life.
According to a recent report from TrendForce, DRAM contract price hikes are forcing some smartphone brands to consider reballed memory components for their budget lines. In short, reballed memory refers to used memory salvaged from old hardware and fitted with new solder balls so they can be installed on other devices.
TrendForce said most of the reballed memory on the market consists of LPDDR4X 4GB modules, and is ideal for entry-level 4G phones. But with DRAM prices expected to continue on an upward trajectory and little inventory relief in sight, lower-spec components and reballed memory could eventually infiltrate higher-priced devices that have historically been categorized as mainstream.
The use of reballed memory in the smartphone industry is not new, but it isn't terribly common either. TrendForce estimates that "recycled" modules will account for 3-4% of mobile RAM in 2026, and warns that adoption could climb to as high as 7-9% next year.
TeamGroup said earlier this month that the worst of the ongoing memory shortage is still to come. Chen Ching-wen, the Taiwan-based hardware company's CEO, believes prices will keep climbing for months to come. Eventually, however, people won't be able to buy memory no matter how much money they have because there simply won't be any to spare.
SK Hynix's messaging isn't much different. As part of its latest financial results for the third quarter, the South Korean chipmaker said that demand for AI-related products is not slowing down. As such, they expect the memory market to sustain growth over the mid- to long-term. That is great news for those involved in the manufacturing process and their investors, but concerning for virtually everyone else.

articles.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
articles.text:
Sponsored
Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
Connected data, AI, and advanced modeling are helping scientists accelerate research and develop more sustainable materials.
In partnership withInfosys
As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.
Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it's not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”
Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.
"Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they're about to create," Rao says, "things go a lot better." Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.
These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product's life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI's ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.
Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It's not just a single technology. I think it's the combination of all of these, and it'll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data."

articles.title: 'Can it also report how much RAM is sitting in warehouses that OpenAI stockpiled to keep out of the market?': tongue-in-cheek app messages Sam Altman daily about the unused RAM in your PC
articles.text:
Tongue-in-cheek app 'writes to Sam Altman once a day to report the RAM he missed' in your PC, following OpenAI CEO's recent blunder
'Ram Altman' lets the CEO know how much RAM is sitting unused in your PC
- A new Linux script called 'Ram Altman' is a tongue-in-cheek creation
- It emails Sam Altman with a report of the unused RAM in your PC, also known as the RAM he missed out on
- The joke follows a controversial comment Altman made recently about how it's 'quite terrible' that everyone has a load of RAM sitting in their own PC, rather than in data centers
Someone has planted their tongue firmly in cheek and knocked up a little script that reports the amount of RAM being used in your Linux PC via email to Sam Altman.
Okay, so this script on GitHub (spotted by Respawn First) doesn't actually email Sam Altman – though it could be used to message someone (theoretically the OpenAI CEO if you had his private email somehow). However, the creator makes it clear that they don't intend to have this tool used to spam people (as you'd hope).
It's a joke, of course, and one made at the expense of Altman after he recently commented that it's "quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer."
That comment sparked developer Iain Kay to craft this open source script which is called 'Ram Altman' and is: "A bash script that writes to Sam Altman once a day to report the RAM he missed."
The Linux utility is designed to "track total, used and available RAM, plus your standing with the global allocation authorities," with the developer noting that it sends at most one email per day.
As mentioned, you are not supposed to be setting this up to actually spam someone with emails about your RAM usage, not unless it's a willing participant who will enjoy the (daily) joke, such as the "friend who has been waiting for DDR5 prices to come down" as the dev observes.
The email content around the RAM report is rotated with 10 messages, eight different subject lines, and six sign-offs, all to ensure that the "joke gets old at a carefully managed pace."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
No email is sent if you have less than 10% of your system RAM free, incidentally, as the creator judges that your machine has "suffered enough" and doesn't need another task on its memory plate.
Should you not wish to bother with an installation, but want to see the joke messages anyway, they're up on a website here. As ever, run any third-party software on your PC at your own risk.
There's a sample email given on the GitHub page:
"Hi Sam,
Please don't be alarmed, but there is 8.6 GiB of RAM on my desk that isn't in a data center. That's 56.2% of what's installed here, and as far as I can tell it has no plans today.
Hoarding responsibly,
A concerned RAM owner."
Analysis: large language misjudgement
This is a well-observed piece of humorous coding, so full credit to Iain Kay in that respect. Of course, as the developer acknowledges, Sam Altman very quickly walked back his "quite terrible" comment (which it was in a very literal sense, certainly for the OpenAI CEO who has faced monumental amounts of flak for the utterance).
If you recall, Altman was quoted from a podcast, and the CEO has since argued that he was taken out of context. Now, many folks aren't having that and feel this is just his attempt to weasel out of the ensuing controversy, although I can see both sides of the coin here.
Altman's comment was made in a discussion about people running local AI models and using lots of RAM for that, rather than using the likes of ChatGPT or other cloud-based LLMs. The problem is he doesn't specifically say that, and instead uses the term "everybody" having a bunch of RAM sat in their PCs, but I don't think it's a stretch to see that he really meant those using local AIs (the direct competition for his product, as it were) as he later clarified.
Still, he didn't say that, and the way he phrased this, and the lack of understanding of how much anger such a broad and sweeping comment would provoke, remains quite breathtaking. It's the sort of classic and stereotyped blunder out-of-touch-with-reality tech CEOs can typically make, and in that way, the fiery feedback was inevitable in the current climate of ridiculous PC component inflation caused by AI demand.
As one Redditor says: "Can [this script] also report how much unused RAM is sitting in warehouses that OpenAI stockpiled to keep out of the market and can't use yet because they don't have a way to power any of it?" articles.title: LG WOLED TVs suffer from 'edge rot' pixel death — pixels go dark around the edges, similar to a mold pattern; nearly all WOLED test units show clear signs of degradation
articles.text:
LG WOLED TVs suffer from 'edge rot' pixel death — pixels go dark around the edges, similar to a mold pattern; nearly all WOLED test units show clear signs of degradation
User reports of the problem keep mounting, as well, including from RTings staff and our own.
When shopping for an OLED TV, most prospective owners are concerned about burn-in, a problem that's been mostly mitigated, save perhaps for scenarios that involve leaving a TV on 24/7. This has been demonstrated by RTing's famous long-running test, but the site has found a new problem that seemingly pertains to pre-2023 LG WOLED panels: edge rot, where pixels progressively go dark around the edges, similar to a mold pattern.
RTings says that 14 out of the 16 LG televisions in its burn-in test have developed this problem in varying degrees, so 87.5% of a small test sample are affected. Those sets were all made between 2020 and 2022. The site says that several staff members saw the issue pop up on their personal televisions. Some searches indicate similar reports from users everywhere, and coincidentally, I learned about this just last week as a close friend sent photos of his 2019 LG TV.
The site says that the television sets bearing Samsung QDOLED panels in its burn-in test do not exhibit these symptoms, though it notes that it only has three such units in its test run. Additionally, since the test ran between 2022 and 2025, RTings says it can't assess whether LG's newer-generation WOLED panels have this issue, and notes that the manufacturing process for said panels reportedly improved in 2024.
Needless to say, most of the television sets in the study are going to be out of warranty. LG does have five-year panel warranty coverage, but only since 2021, and only covering higher-end units like the G, Z, and M series. It's still worth looking into this, in case you own a set from those lines and within the covered timeframe.
RTings asked for statements on the matter from both LG and Samsung, and interestingly, both firms discussed moisture directly or indirectly. LG stated that the issue "may occur in a very small number of OLED products under prolonged exposure to high-temperature, high-humidity, or other harsh environmental conditions."
It's not likely that RTing's test environment is especially humid, though, and the flurry of user reports with TVs sitting in their own living rooms doesn't lend much credence to LG's argument.
Meanwhile, Samsung is more specific, saying that it's implemented its proprietary Thin Film Encapsulation (TFE), a method for blocking ingress at the panel's edge. The firm says TFE "[eliminates] the root cause of border degradation and [ensures] long-term edge-to-edge uniformity where traditional structures falter."
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
RTings says that according to conversations with industry experts, "contamination during manufacturing, defects in the encapsulation of some OLED displays, or degradation of that encapsulation over time" may be at the source of the problem. The site's investigation also notes that some of its test units are affected by edge delamination.
The publication also believes the pixel-death problem may be related to power-on hours, while edge delamination could be dependent on the unit's age. It's unlikely that all user reports come in from people leaving their TVs on 24/7 or close to it, though. A sample size of one means little, but the TV is used sparingly at my friend's home, only around 30 hours per week — over nearly seven years, he's only seen the pixel refresh function come up twice.
For whatever it's worth, he notes that his set's dark spots mostly reside on the side closest to a portion of the wall with very minor humidity ingress from outside the building. The set is resting on furniture, not wall-mounted, though, so the relation between humidity and the edge rot is inconclusive at best.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: 'It's the idea that coming back or going back to a place that you visited before is fun' — Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director explains how the return of Crusade Mode played a part in its decision to revisit Kronus
articles.text:
Why is Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 going back to Kronus? We asked the real-time strategy game’s creative director to explain why
The fan-favorite mode will offer numerous missions across territories in Kronus
- Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director Jan Theysen explains why the game revisits Kronus
- Theysen says King Art Games wanted to reintroduce Crusade Mode, which opened an opportunity to revisit the planet
- Crusade Mode was first introduced in the first Dawn of War game
King Art Games has explained why Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 will revisit Kronus and how the return of Crusade Mode played a part in the decision.
"It's basically the idea that coming back or going back to a place that you visited before is fun," creative director Jan Theysen shared with TechRadar Gaming when asked what the team's driving force was for Dawn of War 4 to revisit the planet.
"We also knew that we wanted to reintroduce the Crusade Mode, or the crusade-like planetary conquer-the-planet type of mode," he added.
Crusade Mode is a fan-favorite mode that had its origins in the first game's Dark Crusade expansion nearly 20 years ago, and King Art Games describes it as Dawn of War 4's "endless mode."
Players can replay the mode's extended campaigns over and over, featuring numerous territories spread across Kronus, and they’ll always play out differently each time, while also introducing extra gameplay variety to the base game.
"Somebody said, well, if we bring back the mode, wouldn't it be fun that it's on the same planet, right?" Theysen continued. "And you can revisit the territories and the stuff you remember from the first game, and we said, okay, why not? Great idea; it's on the right side of The Great Rift."
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 launches on PC on December 3, and Theysen has also suggested that the game could eventually come to console.

articles.title: Grants aren’t a consolation prize: rethinking non-dilutive capital for early-stage founders - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ask an African founder how they funded their first year and you will often hear a slightly apologetic answer: “We did some grants while we figured out the VC side”. The tone matters. It suggests grants are what you take when the real money says “no” – a holding pattern, a consolation prize for not yet being fundable.
That framing is out of date, and it is costing founders. With venture capital still selective after the funding correction of the last few years, a growing number of early-stage startups across the continent are being built on government grants, foundation programmes, fellowships, cloud credits and small cheques from Web3 ecosystem funds.
The founders who will come out ahead are not the ones who tolerate this capital until a seed round arrives. They are the ones who stack it on purpose.
The recovery didn’t reach the bottom of the funnel
On paper, African tech funding has bounced back. Total investment into the African tech startup ecosystem increased by almost 50 per cent to US$1.64 billion in 2025. Q3 figures for 2026 were up 70 per cent on the corresponding period in 2025, suggesting 2026 will equal or surpass 2025 in terms of funding raised.
That is a healthy sign for scaled fintechs and energy businesses. It is far less comforting for a two-person team in Kigali or Lagos with a prototype and 10 paying customers. Investors are rewarding traction and clear paths to profit, which means the gap between “idea” and “venture-backable” has widened, not narrowed.
Founders have filled that gap with whatever capital doesn’t ask for equity: national innovation agency grants, foundation-backed programmes, fellowships with stipends, prize money from pitch competitions, hyper-scaler cloud credits, and – increasingly – grants and small cheques from blockchain ecosystem funds looking for builders in emerging markets. What began as survival has quietly become a funding layer of its own.
Why “consolation prize” is the wrong frame
The case for taking grants seriously starts with arithmetic. A founder who gives up 10 to 15 per cent of the company in a pre-seed round to buy 12 months of runway has paid for that time with the most expensive currency they own. A founder who buys the same 12 months with three grants and a credits package has paid in paperwork. That is not a lesser outcome. On a cap table, it is a better one.
The second argument is about control. Early VC money arrives with expectations about market size, speed and exit that can push a startup into a shape it isn’t ready for. Grant money gives founders room to do the slow, unglamorous work – regulatory approvals, pilots with public health systems, agri-tech field trials – that many African businesses need before they can scale at all. In sectors such as climate, health and agriculture, the patient capital is often the right capital.
Third, grants are increasingly a signal, not a stigma. Getting through a competitive government or foundation process means a third party has vetted the team, the problem and the budget. Smart investors read that as reduced risk. A startup that walks into a seed conversation with US$150,000 in non-dilutive funding, a pilot and a clean cap table is negotiating from strength, not asking for rescue.
How to stack it on purpose
The difference between a founder who “did some grants” and one who built a non-dilutive capital stack is intent. The second founder treats grants the way a CFO treats a funding plan: mapped, sequenced and tied to milestones. In practice, that looks like five habits.
- Give every source a job. Cloud and software credits cover infrastructure. Research and innovation grants pay for product development and pilots. Fellowships buy founder time and networks. A Web3 ecosystem grant funds a specific integration or open-source component. When each pot has a defined purpose, they complement each other instead of overlapping.
- Sequence from small to large. A US$5,000 competition win or an accelerator stipend is rarely life-changing, but it is evidence. Use the smaller, faster awards to build a track record that makes the larger, slower government or foundation grants easier to win.
- Run it like a pipeline, not a lottery. Keep a calendar of deadlines, eligibility rules and reporting dates across the year. Many founders apply reactively to whatever lands in a WhatsApp group. The ones who win consistently plan 6-12 months ahead and reuse a core application they sharpen each time.
- Tie grants to the milestones investors care about. Work backwards from the seed round you eventually want. If investors will ask for a regulatory licence, a paid pilot or a first 1,000 users, point grant money directly at those proofs. Non-dilutive capital is most powerful when it de-risks the next equity cheque.
- Read the fine print as a stack, not one by one. Matching-fund requirements, IP clauses, exclusivity terms and restrictions on other funding sources can clash. Check how each new award interacts with the ones you already hold before you sign.
Free money isn’t free
None of this means grants are costless. The most common failure is the professional applicant: a startup that becomes very good at winning programmes and much less good at winning customers. African tech has had its fair share of these. If a founder spends more hours on application forms than on sales calls, the stack has become a crutch.
Reporting is the second hidden cost. Several concurrent grants can mean several sets of quarterly reports, audits and site visits, each in a different format. For a team of three, that overhead is real and should be budgeted for, in time and sometimes in a part-time grants manager.
Third is mission drift. Funders have their own priorities, from gender inclusion to climate impact to digital public goods. Those are often worthy, but a founder who bends the product to fit each new call ends up with a company built to satisfy funders rather than a market.
Web3 money deserves its own warning. Ecosystem grants can be generous and fast, but they may be paid in volatile tokens, tied to building on one chain, or come with expectations about promotion and community activity. Convert what you can, understand any lock-ups, and make sure the protocol’s fortunes are not quietly becoming your own.
Stop apologising for it
The ecosystem has a part to play too. Governments and foundations could make stacking easier by harmonising reporting templates and being explicit about which other funding they allow alongside their own. Investors could stop treating a grant-heavy history as a red flag and start asking the more useful question: what did this founder achieve with the money?
But the biggest shift has to come from founders themselves. Non-dilutive capital is not what you settle for when VCs say no. Used well, it is how you get to a VC conversation on your own terms – or, for some businesses, how you avoid needing one at all. Stack it deliberately, point it at real milestones, and stop apologising for it.

articles.title: AMD Confirms Excessive SSD Writes in Radeon Drivers, Fix Coming with Adrenalin 26.11.1
articles.text:
Monday, November 9th 2026
AMD Confirms Excessive SSD Writes in Radeon Drivers, Fix Coming with Adrenalin 26.11.1
AMD has confirmed that the current versions of Radeon drivers, Adrenalin 26.10.1 and Adrenalin 26.10.2, are experiencing an issue that causes excessive SSD writing. This problem results in the SSD writing dozens of gigabytes of data unnecessarily. The culprit appears to be AMD's External Events Client Module, which runs under the name atieclxx.exe on Windows systems. This module is causing some users' system drives to be constantly busy with writes. Reports indicate that the write rate ranges from 0.3 MB/s to 1.5 MB/s, with one Reddit user reporting sustained activity at 5 MB/s. The process is part of AMD's External Events Utility, which manages tasks such as detecting monitors and responding to Radeon software hotkeys. Unfortunately, it has entered an infinite loop of data writing.
While this may seem like a small amount, it's important to remember that systems can run for extended periods, and the writing can accumulate over time, potentially leading to SSD wear and tear. SSD lifespan largely depends on its ability to endure constant random writes, and forcing random writes onto an SSD will undoubtedly shorten its lifecycle. This is particularly concerning given the high cost of NAND Flash, as users are operating expensive SSDs that could undergo unnecessary wear. In response, AMD plans to release an update to its Adrenalin drivers with version 26.11.1, which will address this issue.For users needing an interim workaround, there is an option to disable the AMD External Events Utility or disable Resizable BAR. However, choosing the first option might lead to some display issues, while the second option could cause additional performance issues. Either way, it is best to wait for an official driver update before making a decision.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology. The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia. Historically, China has been a big market for the company. It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China, and some of his persuasion tactics have been successful. Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.
On numerous occasions, Huang has publicly lamented export controls, calling them a “failure” at a conference last year and saying in May that it was “not wise” for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems. He has also warned that shutting Nvidia out of China’s compute market would enable the country to develop its own AI chips to challenge Nvidia internationally.
China is already moving in that direction. Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024. At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
Still, the allegations involving Alice Huang open new scrutiny of the company’s business relationships and could taint any assurances Nvidia offers that it can prevent sensitive technology from reaching unauthorized customers.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned officials close to Trump earlier this year about Huang’s relationship with an alleged spy. Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Google claims its new AI software cuts inference latency by over 90% — but there's a catch
articles.text:
Google claims its new AI software cuts inference latency by over 90% — but there’s a catch
Google’s eighth-generation TPU announcement on Monday included more than new chips, introducing TPU Sync, an open-source system designed to speed up AI inference by tackling a problem that worsens as context windows grow: moving data between different types of memory.
The software is made for developers running large models, particularly ones handling million-token contexts and reinforcement-learning workloads. The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests.
The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests.
Inside the memory hierarchy
Written in C++, the framework moves data between accelerator memory, host DRAM, storage, and the network. It uses zero-copy transfers and native PjRtBuffer hardware descriptors to avoid unnecessary copies.
Combined host-to-device and device-to-host throughput reached 223 GB/s per Ironwood TPU host, approaching the theoretical 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 limit.
Google’s numbers, with caveats
In Google’s benchmarks, moving KV caches for the 235-billion-parameter Qwen3 model went from taking several seconds to about 230 milliseconds. That cut the average time to first token (TTFT) by 60% when relatively few requests were running at once. With a larger 480-billion-parameter model, the reduction reached 90%.
Google saw similar gains when testing prefix caching with 64,000-token contexts. TTFT dropped by as much as 90%, throughput increased by more than 50%, and P99 inter-token latency fell 30%. Developers may see different results depending on what they’re running, how much cached data they can reuse, and how much network bandwidth they have available.
SemiAnalysis, offers some context for the gains. Its analysis suggests that external TPU serving previously lacked the infrastructure needed to separate prefill and decode workloads effectively.
Where Nvidia still leads
Nvidia may still have an advantage in some workloads. SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX data shows its GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems ahead in parts of the disaggregated-serving performance curve, although a direct comparison with a fully tuned TPU v7 setup has yet to be published.
Chipping away at the CUDA moat
Developers can use the new software with the inference tools they already have since the company released the project alongside TorchTPU, with support for vLLM and SGLang, two widely used open-source inference engines. Developers already using those frameworks can run disaggregated workloads on TPUs without rebuilding their serving stack from scratch.
Developers already using those frameworks can run disaggregated workloads on TPUs without rebuilding their serving stack from scratch.
This also fits with Google’s broader effort to make its custom chips more competitive. The company has emphasized reducing inference costs through hardware changes, including reportedly designing chips around Gemini’s architecture.
Now it’s addressing the software problems that can leave those chips waiting for data. Making TPU infrastructure easier to use with familiar frameworks could give developers another reason to consider Google’s hardware instead of defaulting to Nvidia and CUDA; whether it can match Nvidia’s inference performance remains an open question.
Not production-ready yet
The software isn’t production-ready for everyone just yet. Google warns in its GitHub repository that the APIs are still changing and recommends sticking to a verified commit or tagged release. Support is also limited to Cloud TPU v7x and v6e, with specific JAX and PyTorch version requirements.

articles.title: Belib’ augmente ses tarifs : ce que la nouvelle grille va changer pour vos recharges à Paris
articles.text:
Belib’ gère les bornes de recharge installées dans les rues de Paris : TotalEnergies exploite ce réseau pour la Ville depuis mars 2021, et il compte plus de 2 000 bornes réparties sur environ 430 stations.
Dans un e-mail envoyé à ses abonnés le 4 novembre, Belib’ annonce une nouvelle grille de tarifs à partir du 7 décembre 2026, qui sera publiée ce jour-là sur son site et dans son application. L’e-mail promet aux abonnés qu’ils continuent à bénéficier de leurs « conditions préférentielles ». Pourtant, ils paieront eux aussi 2 centimes de plus par kilowattheure sur les bornes lentes.
Environ 1 € de plus pour une recharge de 50 kWh
Sur les bornes Moto, réservées aux deux-roues, et sur les bornes Flex, de 3,7 kW ou 7 kW, prévues pour les longs stationnements, le kilowattheure passe de 0,33 à 0,35 € pour tout le monde. Les visiteurs, ceux qui paient par carte bancaire sans abonnement, versent aussi un centime de plus par quart d’heure branché : ce quart d’heure passe donc à 0,23 € sur une borne Moto et à 0,58 € sur une borne Flex. Les abonnés, eux, gardent les mêmes frais de temps.
Prenons une recharge de 50 kWh sur une borne Flex de 7 kW, soit environ sept heures de branchement. Un visiteur payait 32,46 €, il paiera 33,74 €. Pour un abonné, la même recharge en journée passe de 26,86 € à 27,86 €. Avec une recharge par semaine, la facture annuelle augmente donc d’environ 66 € pour un visiteur et de 52 € pour un abonné.
En revanche, les prix des bornes plus rapides Boost (qui délivre 22 kW) et Boost+ (qui délivre 50 kW) restent les mêmes, tandis que les abonnés résidents paient toujours 0,25 € le kWh la nuit, entre 23h et 8h. Le créneau nuit (20h-23h) des abonnés résidents passe également de 0,33 à 0,35 centimes le kWh. Enfin, le prix de l’abonnement reste le même : 7 € à l’année.
Comment limiter la facture à la borne
Pensez à débrancher dès la fin de la charge : Belib’ continue de facturer le temps passé à la borne, même quand la batterie est pleine. Au-delà de 14 heures de branchement, la borne coûte 10 € de l’heure. Outre le surcoût, c’est également une question de civisme. On ne compte plus le nombre de véhicules 100 % électriques et hybrides rechargeables bloquant des bornes longtemps après que leur recharge soit terminée.
