articles.title: Nous avons accéléré la même IA jusqu’à 72 % sur un PC Nvidia et un Mac : voici ce que change vraiment le MTP — Frandroid
articles.text:
Faire tourner un grand modèle de langage de plus de 120 milliards de paramètres directement sur un ordinateur portable est désormais une réalité dès lors que l’on dispose de 128 Go de mémoire (on aurait peut-être du commencer par ça). En revanche, le regarder rédiger laborieusement une fonction Python à 31 tokens par seconde est nettement moins réjouissant quand des les modèles en cloud comme Claude ou ChatGPT s’exécutent en un clin d’œil.
Pour rappel, un token correspond à une brique de texte (un mot, une syllabe ou un signe de ponctuation) que le modèle génère habituellement une par une : sur une réponse un peu fournie de 1 024 tokens, il faut ainsi patienter plus d’une demi-minute devant son écran.
Cette lenteur n’est pourtant pas une fatalité grâce au MTP (Multi-Token Prediction), une méthode censée réduire drastiquement l’attente sans dégrader le modèle, que nous avons mise à l’épreuve sur deux architectures matérielles radicalement différentes.
Pour ce test, nous avons utilisé Qwen3.8 Flash-Next, un modèle publié fin août par l’équipe Qwen d’Alibaba en guise d’avant-goût de sa future génération Qwen4.
S’il totalise 125 milliards de paramètres accompagnés d’une table annexe de 51 milliards, il n’en sollicite que 6 milliards à chaque étape grâce à une architecture dite MoE (mélange d’experts), qui ne réveille qu’une petite fraction du réseau neuronal par token afin d’économiser du temps de calcul. Sa vraie particularité réside toutefois dans sa « tête MTP » : au lieu d’avancer mot à mot, ce petit module annexe tente de deviner jusqu’à trois tokens d’avance, que le modèle principal valide ou corrige ensuite d’un seul bloc.
Nvidia a justement publié une recette technique permettant d’exploiter cette fonction avec llama.cpp, le moteur open source au cœur de la plupart des outils pour installer un ChatGPT en local. Nous avons donc appliqué ce protocole à la lettre sur un Asus ProArt P16 propulsé par la plateforme RTX Spark de Nvidia (puce N1X et 128 Go de mémoire), ainsi que sur un MacBook Pro M5 Max doté lui aussi de 128 Go de RAM unifiée, à travers une batterie de 495 requêtes.
Jusqu’à 72 % plus rapide sur le code, mais beaucoup moins en français
Premier constat : sur des tâches très structurées, l’accélération est spectaculaire. Lorsqu’on lui demande d’écrire du code Python, l’activation du MTP fait bondir le débit de la plateforme RTX Spark de 31,5 à 50,9 tokens par seconde, et propulse le MacBook Pro de 47,9 à 82,6 tokens/s. Un exercice de calcul d’horaires de train affiche une envolée similaire, avec un gain de vitesse d’environ 68 % sur les deux machines.
En revanche, dès que l’on passe à de la rédaction pure en français, le gain retombe autour de 33 à 36 %. Cet écart s’explique directement par le taux de réussite des prédictions du module MTP : alors que le modèle principal valide plus de 80 % des brouillons anticipés sur du code informatique ou des mathématiques, il n’en retient plus que 58 à 59 % en langue naturelle. Logique : là où une phrase en prose peut être tournée de mille façons différentes, la syntaxe d’une boucle for en Python laisse beaucoup moins de place à l’improvisation.
| Débit médian (tokens/s) | Spark sans MTP | Spark MTP | Gain | M5 Max sans MTP | M5 Max MTP | Gain | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Code Python | 31,5 | 50,9 | +61,6 % | 47,9 | 82,6 | +72,3 % | 
| Explication en français | 30,8 | 42,0 | +36,5 % | 47,9 | 63,7 | +32,8 % | 
| Calcul | 31,5 | 53,1 | +68,5 % | 48,2 | 81,0 | +68,2 % | 
Cette optimisation mise en avant par Nvidia ne suffit d’ailleurs pas à inverser la hiérarchie matérielle. La puce M5 Max d’Apple conserve une large avance dans les trois exercices, au point que la RTX Spark dopée au MTP (50,9 tokens/s en code) dépasse à peine le MacBook Pro dépourvu de cette accélération (47,9 tokens/s).
Excellente surprise en revanche sur l’endurance thermique : les deux ordinateurs portables tiennent parfaitement la cadence sur la durée. Après 30 minutes de génération ininterrompue sur secteur, la plateforme Spark reste d’une stabilité métronomique (de 55,3 à 55,2 tokens/s), tout comme le Mac (de 85,3 à 85,6 tokens/s). Si les sondes internes relèvent un pic à 71 °C sur la puce graphique Nvidia contre 83,7 °C sur le processeur Apple, ces capteurs ne mesurent pas exactement la même zone physique de la puce, ce qui interdit d’en tirer un vainqueur absolu sur le refroidissement.
    Pour aller plus loin
Test du Apple MacBook Pro 16 PROLED XDR : j’ai poussé le premier Mac OLED dans ses derniers retranchements
            
    Pour aller plus loin
On a testé la puce Nvidia RTX Spark qui veut réinventer le PC : les résultats face à Apple, AMD et une RTX 5070
            
Écrire plus vite ne veut pas dire répondre plus vite
C’est ici qu’apparaît le principal angle mort du MTP : s’il accélère l’écriture de la réponse, il n’accélère absolument pas la lecture de vos documents. Pour le vérifier, nous avons soumis aux modèles un rapport PDF de 180 pages (soit 13 753 tokens) en leur demandant d’y dénicher trois références éloignées et d’additionner leurs valeurs. Or, avant même de pouvoir écrire le premier mot de sa réponse, l’IA doit d’abord analyser et « digérer » l’intégralité du texte fourni (la phase dite de prefill), une étape sur laquelle le MTP n’a aucun effet. Résultat : avec ou sans MTP, le mastodonte Qwen3.8 Flash-Next met entre 17 et 21 secondes pour livrer son verdict, là où Qwen3.6 35B, un modèle quatre fois plus léger (22 Go), boucle l’exercice sans faute en moins de 7 secondes.
| Document long | Machine | Premier token | Réponse complète | Résultat exact | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flash-Next sans MTP | RTX Spark | 18,92 s | 20,90 s | 3/3 | 
| Flash-Next MTP | RTX Spark | 20,13 s | 21,30 s | 3/3 | 
| Flash-Next sans MTP | M5 Max | 15,76 s | 17,08 s | 3/3 | 
| Flash-Next MTP | M5 Max | 17,53 s | 18,25 s | 3/3 | 
| Qwen3.6 35B | RTX Spark | 6,16 s | 6,91 s | 3/3 | 
| Qwen3.6 35B | M5 Max | 5,00 s | 5,55 s | 3/3 | 
Un second goulet d’étranglement est du côté de la file d’attente du serveur local. Par défaut, llama.cpp n’ouvre qu’une seule voie de traitement simultanée (un « slot ») : si vous posez une question rapide pendant que l’IA rédige un long bloc de code en arrière-plan, votre demande restera bloquée au feu rouge. Sur le MacBook Pro, un simple calcul « 2+2 » envoyé une demi-seconde après le lancement d’une génération de code a ainsi mis 12,47 secondes à s’afficher, contre à peine 0,31 seconde en configurant deux voies parallèles. Activer ce second canal permet en prime de faire bondir le débit cumulé de Flash-Next (de 79 à 113 tokens/s sur le Mac, et de 52 à 78 sur la Spark), mais exige en contrepartie de doubler la quantité de mémoire vive réservée au contexte.
Reste enfin à vérifier que cette course à la vitesse ne sabote pas la fiabilité des réponses. Sur cinq petits exercices de programmation validés par 30 tests automatisés, Flash-Next réalise un sans-faute (5/5) sur le Mac, mais échoue sur l’une des fonctions (4/5) sur la RTX Spark, sa réponse ayant été tronquée par la limite de longueur maximale. Plus curieux encore : avec un modèle et des consignes strictement identiques, l’IA ne génère pas exactement le même code selon qu’elle tourne sur les librairies CUDA de Nvidia ou Metal d’Apple, même en verrouillant la « température » à zéro (le paramètre censé supprimer le hasard pour garantir des réponses reproductibles). Quant au plus petit Qwen3.6 35B, il s’est illustré sur Mac en livrant une fonction de conversion de prix qui transforme 1 299,95 € en 129 995 €.
Heureusement, nos épreuves pratiques réservent aussi d’excellentes surprises sur le raisonnement logique. Mis face à la fiche d’un casque audio fictif dont le prix passe de 199 à 249 € tout en affichant une fausse pastille promotionnelle « -25 % », Flash-Next déjoue le piège, calcule la hausse réelle (+25,13 %) et dénonce le faux bon plan, là où Qwen3.6 35B repère lui aussi l’arnaque mais arrondit son calcul à 25,0 %. Même efficacité lorsqu’on leur demande de réparer un vrai bug issu de nos scripts de test internes (qui affichait un débit absurde de 12 milliards de tokens/s lorsqu’une durée tombait à zéro) : les deux modèles produisent un correctif fonctionnel validé par nos sept batteries de tests en 7 à 15 secondes, bien que Qwen3.6 35B ait eu besoin d’une seconde tentative sur le Mac.
Faut-il vraiment un monstre de 128 Go pour coder en local ?
Malgré le coup de fouet du MTP, Qwen3.8 Flash-Next reste un poids lourd exigeant qui est loin d’être le plus véloce de notre laboratoire.
Dans notre test de débit brut sans MTP, il plafonne à 25,6 tokens/s sur la Spark et 50,2 sur le Mac, tandis qu’un modèle spécialisé comme Qwen3-Coder 30B s’envole à 104,6 et 154,4 tokens/s tout en occupant cinq fois moins d’espace disque.
Surtout, avec 98 Go de fichiers à charger en mémoire, Flash-Next impose une machine dotée de 128 Go de RAM, soit une facture d’au moins 6 000 euros (si ce n’est plus…).
Si vous possédez déjà une telle station de travail pour générer du code en local, activer le MTP est une évidence absolue : le réglage est gratuit et offre plus de 60 % de vitesse supplémentaire. En revanche, pour résumer ou interroger de longs documents, un modèle plus compact de 20 à 35 Go se montrera tout aussi pertinent et nettement plus réactif sur l’un des mini PC pour l’IA locale autrement plus abordables.
| Modèle (sans MTP) | Poids | Spark | M5 Max | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B | 18,6 Go | 104,6 tok/s | 154,4 tok/s | 
| Qwen3.6 35B-A3B | 22,1 Go | 74,8 tok/s | 109,1 tok/s | 
| gpt-oss-120b | 63,4 Go | 63,3 tok/s | 107,0 tok/s | 
| Qwen3.8 Flash-Next | 93,7 Go | 25,6 tok/s | 50,2 tok/s | 
    Pour aller plus loin
Quel mini PC choisir pour l’IA ? Notre sélection 2026
            
Comment activer le MTP sur son ordinateur
En pratique, l’activation du MTP dans llama-server ne requiert que quelques arguments de ligne de commande, détaillés pas à pas dans la documentation du décodage spéculatif de llama.cpp. 
La seule subtilité consiste à récupérer le fichier de la tête MTP depuis une révision bien précise du dépôt plutôt que sur la branche principale, et à veiller à ce que votre version de llama.cpp soit parfaitement alignée. 
Quant à ceux qui souhaitent d’abord se familiariser avec l’écosystème avant de mettre les mains dans le cambouis, notre guide de l’IA locale sur Windows, Mac et Linux détaille toutes les étapes de base.

articles.title: Ils ont fabriqué un diamant de 20 cm : pourquoi il intéresse l’industrie des puces
articles.text:
Diamond Foundry présente un diamant synthétique monocristallin de 200 mm de diamètre. Ce changement d’échelle pourrait faciliter l’utilisation du matériau dans l’électronique, notamment pour évacuer la chaleur des processeurs d’IA.
Tenu entre deux mains gantées, le disque a les dimensions d’une petite assiette. Sur les photographies publiées le 5 novembre par Diamond Foundry, il apparaît encore brut, sans polissage. L’entreprise américaine revendique une première mondiale : avoir produit un seul cristal de diamant de 20 cm de diamètre.
Un seul cristal, né d’une recherche universitaire
Le mot « monocristallin » compte autant que les dimensions. Il désigne ici un cristal continu, dont l’organisation atomique se prolonge sur toute la surface. Une plaque polycristalline, elle, rassemble des grains aux orientations différentes. L’enjeu consiste donc à conserver cette structure unique en faisant croître le matériau.
Dans un communiqué du 6 novembre 2023, Diamond Foundry présentait déjà un wafer monocristallin de 100 mm. Le nouveau disque double ce diamètre, pour atteindre un format utilisé dans l’industrie des semi-conducteurs.
Comment obtenir un aussi grand cristal sans disposer, au départ, d’un diamant de taille comparable ? Une partie de la réponse porte un nom : l’hétéroépitaxie. Dans une présentation publiée en 2022, Diamond Foundry décrivait la croissance du diamant sur un empilement de couches nanométriques d’iridium et de zircone stabilisée à l’yttrium, le tout déposé sur une plaque de silicium. Ce support permet d’amorcer la formation du cristal sur un autre matériau que le diamant. C’est la voie que l’entreprise décrivait en 2022 ; sa nouvelle annonce ne détaille pas le procédé employé pour ce nouveau disque.
Cette technologie vient d’Augsburg Diamond Technology, ou Audiatec, rachetée en 2022. Fondée en 2015 par Matthias Schreck, Martin Fischer et Stefan Gsell, cette société est issue du département de physique de l’université d’Augsbourg, en Allemagne. C’est dans ces recherches universitaires que le projet trouve ses racines.
Diamond Foundry annonçait d’ailleurs disposer de réacteurs de croissance de 200 mm dès 2022. La taille de la machine ne faisait donc pas tout : encore fallait-il obtenir un cristal unique à cette échelle.
Pourquoi mettre du diamant près d’un processeur ?
Le diamant conduit remarquablement bien la chaleur. Le fabricant spécialisé Diamond Materials indique une conductivité thermique pouvant atteindre environ 2 000 W/m·K, soit près de cinq fois celle du cuivre. Cela ne signifie pas qu’un processeur fonctionnerait à une température cinq fois plus basse. Ce rapport décrit une propriété du matériau, pas les performances d’un système de refroidissement complet.
L’intérêt est de répartir la chaleur concentrée dans une petite zone, puis de faciliter son transfert vers le système chargé de l’évacuer. Cet usage existe déjà : Element Six propose des composants en diamant pour la gestion thermique, avec des applications dans les amplificateurs radiofréquences, les lasers et les accélérateurs d’IA. La qualité du contact entre les matériaux reste essentielle pour que la chaleur circule efficacement.
Les ambitions de Diamond Foundry dépassent aussi le refroidissement. L’entreprise cite l’électronique de puissance, l’optique et les systèmes quantiques parmi les débouchés envisagés pour ses grands cristaux.
Faut-il encore transformer ce disque brut en matériau exploitable à grande échelle. L’annonce ne donne ni coût de production, ni rendement industriel, ni mesure de refroidissement obtenue avec ce spécimen de 200 mm. Qualité après polissage, régularité de fabrication et intégration aux composants seront déterminantes. Le diamant de 20 cm attire les regards ; sa capacité à être produit en quantité, à un coût acceptable, décidera de sa place dans les machines.
Un diamant monocristallin est formé d’un seul cristal continu : son réseau atomique garde la même orientation sur toute la plaque. Un diamant polycristallin rassemble au contraire de nombreux grains séparés par des joints. Ce dernier est déjà utilisé pour dissiper la chaleur de certains composants. Le monocristal offre toutefois une conductivité thermique maximale et homogène, se prête mieux à un collage direct sur une puce et ouvre la voie à des usages comme semi-conducteur. Le difficile est de conserver un cristal unique quand on augmente la taille.
L’hétéroépitaxie consiste à faire croître un cristal sur un matériau différent. Pour le diamant, elle permet d’obtenir un monocristal sans partir d’un « germe » de diamant aussi grand que la plaque visée. Le procédé décrit par Diamond Foundry repose sur un empilement de couches nanométriques déposé sur du silicium : l’iridium oriente la formation du diamant, tandis que la zircone stabilisée à l’yttrium sert de couche intermédiaire entre le silicium et l’iridium. La principale difficulté tient aux défauts et aux contraintes mécaniques, car ces matériaux n’ont ni la même structure ni la même dilatation thermique.
Le 200 mm est un diamètre standard dans une partie de la microélectronique, notamment pour l’électronique de puissance, la radiofréquence ou les capteurs. Les puces les plus avancées, dont les processeurs d’IA, sont en revanche fabriquées sur des plaques de 300 mm. Un format standard permet de s’appuyer sur des outils existants pour manipuler, polir ou découper le matériau. Mais un disque brut n’est pas encore un « wafer » exploitable : épaisseur, planéité, rugosité et densité de défauts doivent être maîtrisées après polissage. Viendront ensuite les critères industriels : rendement, régularité et coût.

articles.title: The climate case for AI has not been made
articles.text:
The climate case for AI has not been made
AI leaders claim their tech will fix the climate. The evidence mostly points in the opposite direction so far.
This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.
But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies.
In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed, the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.
Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles.
But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?
Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress.
The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.
Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study.
The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.
In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe, which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.
But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.
The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours.
There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels. Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy.
Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.
The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.
Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms.
Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast.
Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions. Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint. And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways.
The need has never been more apparent.
Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board.
Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.

articles.title: Russian cloud firm Beget rebuilds from scratch after data wiper attack
articles.text:
A data-wiping malware attack has forced Russian cloud services provider Beget to rebuild its cloud infrastructure from scratch, the company said.
On the night of November 1st, the attacker gained access to the management systems of the company's entire architecture and deployed malware that erased server data.
The Russian cloud provider detected the attack shortly after the malware activated and disconnected all servers from the network to stop the malicious activity from spreading across its infrastructure.
Beget is a major Russian web-hosting, cloud, and domain-registration provider that serves more than 200,000 customers, including online stores, media, and educational services.
More than a week after the destructive attack, Beget says that 60% of shared hosting and 40% of the dedicated servers it manages have been restored, and recovery is still in progress.
In a more detailed announcement on November 3, Beget says that the attacker gained access to the management layer of its entire architecture and then executed data-zeroing scripts.
Beget said all data in its cloud infrastructure, including VPS, S3, and Kubernetes, was lost, along with CDN settings and IP configurations.
The company also said that VPS binary backups were completely lost, and VPS file backups have partially survived. A November 6 assessment specified that these would be available for roughly half of its VPS users.
“Unfortunately, it is impossible to recover all data,” Beget said about VPS data, adding that it "spent a long time looking for solutions, but according to our current assessment, VPS file backups will be available for only half of users."
Even when a backup exists, the company said it would take time to match it to specific users, a task it describes as “technically complex.”
The scale of the recovery effort is massive, with roughly 1,000 servers requiring manual checks for vulnerabilities and hidden scripts before they can be brought back online, said the firm.
Beget is taking a cautious approach, treating all parts of its infrastructure as potentially infected.
“We are therefore cleaning out everything we can and reworking every potentially vulnerable point, including those that previously did not appear to pose a risk.”
Beget said its investigation did not find any evidence that the attacker tried to download or modify any data on the compromised servers, and that the attack appears to have been focused solely on destruction.
The company has notified the police and government agencies and is also working with cybersecurity firms to remediate the incident and recover as soon as possible.

articles.title: Nvidia ouvre une enquête : le patron du géant de la tech aurait eu une liaison avec une espionne chinoise
articles.text:
Nvidia pourrait bien perdre quelques dizaines de milliards de dollars dans cette histoire. L’entreprise vient de lancer une enquête interne après la découverte que son dirigeant Jensen Huang a eu une relation extra-conjugale. Mais le véritable problème se trouve dans l’identité de la femme avec qui il a eu une liaison : elle serait une espionne au service de la Chine.
Une espionne aurait été envoyé par la Chine pour séduire le patron de Nvidia
Tout a commencé le 29 octobre dernier, quand le New York Times a révélé qu’Alice Huang, dirigeante de l’entreprise singapourienne Megaspeed, aurait été recrutée par le ministère chinois de la Sécurité d’État. Cette femme d’affaires, ressortissante chinoise, aurait potentiellement fait passer clandestinement des puces d’IA de Nvidia vers la Chine, comme sont accusées d’autres entreprises d’Asie du Sud-Est. En effet, les puces les plus puissantes de Nvidia font l’objet d’un embargo sur la Chine de la part des États-Unis. Selon le journal, les autorités américaines en seraient convaincues : elle serait bien un agent des services de renseignement chinois.
Alice Huang aurait aussi et surtout entretenu une liaison avec Jensen Huang, comme l’a révélé le Financial Times ce 6 novembre. Le président Donald Trump aurait été informé de ces conclusions, mais n’en aurait pas tenu compte, ne souhaitant pas perturber l’immense croissance de l’entreprise américaine et endommager les relations commerciales avec la Chine.
Nvidia lance une enquête sur la liaison extra-conjugale de Jensen Huang
Ce 8 novembre, Jensen Huang a lui-même envoyé un mail à ses salariés ; un communiqué republié par Nvidia. Il le reconnaît : « J’ai été infidèle à ma femme. […] Rien ne justifie ce que j’ai fait. » L’homme s’excuse auprès de sa famille et de son entreprise : « Je n’ai pas été à la hauteur de cette responsabilité. » Depuis, de nombreuses photos et vidéos montrant Huang en compagnie de cette femme circulent sur les réseaux sociaux.
Le conseil d’administration de Nvidia a lancé une enquête, comme le rapporte Bloomberg. L’objectif est de déterminer si son dirigeant Jensen Huang a été la cible d’une mission d’espionnage. Ce dernier dit vouloir pleinement coopérer pour « protéger Nvidia » et « soutenir la sécurité nationale des États-Unis. » Les États-Unis aussi s’y intéressent : le sénateur démocrate Chris Coons, qui présidera une commission des affaires étrangères en janvier, veut ouvrir une enquête sur cette affaire.
Quid des conséquences financières sur Nvidia, qui a besoin de toujours plus de fonds pour investir dans la fabrication de ses puces ? Alors que l’entreprise va publier ses résultats très bientôt, elle a atteint près de 5 800 milliards de dollars de capitalisation boursière. Une somme qui pourrait s’évaporer : sur un mois, elle a déjà perdu 18,6%, dont 10% des cinq derniers jours. Certains pensent que la bulle de l’intelligence artificielle a déjà éclaté : cet événement conjugué à cette polémique sur Jensen Huang pourrait donc coûter très cher à Nvidia.

articles.title: Jon Hernández, experto en IA: "En un plazo de dos años, el manejo fluido de la inteligencia artificial determinará quién conserva un puesto de trabajo"
articles.text:
El divulgador Jon Hernández, especializado en inteligencia artificial, puso fecha a un cambio en el mercado laboral. En una entrevista en ‘La fórmula del éxito’, el pódcast de Uri Sabat, aseguró que “en dos años, aquella persona que no sea fluida en inteligencia artificial estará fuera del mercado laboral”, dejando claro que en poco tiempo pueden cambiar mucho las cosas.
En otros sitios puede ser antes: Hernández aseguró que con esta afirmación se refiere únicamente a España, porque en otros sitios quizá pueda ser incluso antes. “Yo creo que a día de hoy, la suerte que tienes si sabes poco de inteligencia artificial es que tu jefe sabe menos que tú”, explicó el especialista. “Si tu jefe supiese lo que yo sé, ya te hubiese reemplazado”.
Todavía falta la parte de adopción: El especialista en IA también asegura que actualmente, aunque esta tecnología vaya muy rápido, todavía falta la parte de adopción. Lo explicó con dos paralelismos, como empresas que todavía no usan Excel o repartidores que te hacen firmar en albaranes en vez de PDAs, y asegura que la adopción de la IA también tardará en llegar. “Puede ser por costes, por cultura empresarial, porque tu jefe es un dinosaurio o lo que sea”. Es esta la razón, según dice, por la que la adopción en el mercado laboral está siendo más lenta de lo esperado, algo que puede cambiar en dos años.
A su juicio, esa lentitud da margen para ponerse al día, aunque avisa de que quien no sepa utilizar la IA lo tendrá difícil para que lo contraten, salvo en empleos que no pasan por un ordenador. Eso sí, el plazo de dos años es una previsión personal del divulgador.
Empresas que se suben al carro. Cada vez más empresas incorporan esta tecnología para automatizar tareas, optimizar procesos, analizar grandes volúmenes de información y mejorar la productividad de sus plantillas. Pero esa expansión también abre la puerta a que algunos puestos acaben desapareciendo, algo que el Foro Económico Mundial contempla en sus previsiones hasta 2030, en las que el cambio tecnológico elimina unos empleos aunque crea otros.
Saber usarla ya no basta. Con abrir ChatGPT ya no es suficiente, porque lo que cuenta es utilizar la IA para la tarea adecuada, darle los datos que necesita y revisar lo que te devuelve. Y eso exige criterio y práctica, por eso detectar una respuesta errónea cuenta tanto como conseguirla en segundos. De hecho, el propio ChatGPT avisa de que puede cometer errores y aconseja comprobar la información importante.

articles.title: Kuramo wants to train Nigeria’s next SME fund managers
articles.text:
The Wholesale Impact Investment Fund (WIIF), a naira-denominated vehicle targeting $1 billion for Nigerian small businesses, has begun training the fund managers it may eventually back.
On October 30, the Kuramo Foundation for Sustainable Development launched the WIIF SME Fund Accelerator in Lagos, onboarding 22 first-time and emerging managers selected from 84 applicants across all six of Nigeria’s geopolitical zones.
Established by the Impact Investors Foundation and the National Advisory Board on Impact Investing, the vehicle is managed by Kuramo Capital Management. Alongside its capital commitments, Kuramo is conducting a 12-week accelerator programme for the cohort, covering investment theses, financial modelling, fundraising, pipeline development, legal structuring, and exit strategies.
The fund is working toward a $100 million first close, which it has not yet reached, according to Olamide Adeosun, director at Kuramo Capital, who spoke on behalf of the fund.
Nigeria has about 39.7 million micro, small and medium enterprises, and the International Finance Corporation estimated in 2022 that they face an unmet financing need of $32.2 billion. Adeosun points to the first wave of Nigerian private equity managers, firms such as Verod and CardinalStone, and says a new generation of small business fund managers has not followed. WIIF wants to change that by training and funding the next generation of small business funds.
In June 2025, the Federal Ministry of Finance announced that the government would commit $50 million to the vehicle. Adeosun added that the fund is currently courting domestic pension funds and local development finance institutions as early institutional backers.
Rather than investing directly in small businesses, WIIF operates as a fund of funds, deploying capital into the intermediary vehicles that finance them.
“Capital deployed into managers who are not yet investment-ready does not create durable results,” read a statement shared by Kuramo Capital.
Ijeoma Madueke, the sustainable finance lead of the Kuramo Foundation, says the accelerator’s main test is investment readiness: documents in place, a clear thesis, and a team in sight. For WIIF, Adeosun said success would be two funds from the cohort that WIIF can back or two or more that raise money from outside investors. A 10% hit rate would be “fantastic”, he said.
In this conversation, Adeosun and Madueke explain how WIIF has approached raising money, why the accelerator took in 22 managers, how the programme chose them, what the training covers, and what “investment ready” means.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
WIIF is described as a billion-dollar fund denominated in naira. How much has been committed so far, and what has the process of raising it been like?
Olamide Adeosun: We set out to raise a billion dollars. What we are telling people, and what we are targeting, is $100 million for the first series. We are treating it as a $100 million fund, because a billion dollars is a very large number. That money is for micro, small and medium enterprises.
We chose a fund-of-funds approach because we wanted to reach as many businesses as possible. We invest in other funds, and those funds raise more money and invest in the businesses.
At the moment, we are raising from catalytic investors, meaning investors willing to take early risk, and from pension funds. We are talking to Nigerian development finance institutions and to international foundations that work on the continent. We have not made a first close yet.
In those talks, what investors want to see is a track record. Who are you going to invest in? That is why we use what we call the ABCD approach to building markets, which the Kuramo Foundation developed.
Think about the first wave of private equity managers in Nigeria, firms such as Verod and CardinalStone. We are trying to build the next generation of small business fund managers. When did you last hear of someone launching a new fund to invest in small businesses? You see many new venture funds and many tech founders, but small business funds are rare. That is the problem we are trying to solve. The accelerator will build and identify a pipeline of opportunities, and the Kuramo Foundation runs it.
More than 20 managers are in the accelerator. Why so many, and what was Kuramo trying to achieve?
Ijeoma Madueke: One point to clarify: these are the fund managers in the accelerator, and not all of them will receive money from the fund. In markets that are less developed, you often have to build before you can invest. We are building the bridge as we go. Many of these managers have not finished setting up their funds, so for some we are doing more incubation than acceleration. We have 22.
We wanted variety. If small businesses are the backbone of the economy, the managers who fund them should reflect that. We accepted funds in many sectors, including niche ones such as the creative economy, where we have two managers. One manager has a multi-product strategy built entirely on Islamic financial products. Not everyone will get funded, and not everyone will finish setting up a fund, so we wanted enough managers to give us a real pipeline once capital is ready.
We also spread the managers across the country. A lot of capital concentrates in Lagos, so we have managers from the north, south, east and west. We are looking at markets that capital has not traditionally reached, which we would call Nigeria’s secondary markets, where fund managers are doing exciting things.
The ABCD framework came from Kuramo Capital’s work. After mobilising millions of dollars for funds across the continent, we saw a gap for women-led funds and set up a gender-lens platform under what we call the ABCD framework: Accelerate, Bridge, Catalyze and Develop. If funds do not exist, we need to create them and help them reach investment readiness. That is the accelerate side, and it is what the Kuramo Foundation does.
Bridge and catalyse is about capital. Take the manager building an Islamic products fund. That is niche and untested in fund management. We see a lot of activity in commercial banking, bonds and sukuk, but much less in private equity and venture capital. Can we offer facilities that bridge them? Warehousing and working capital facilities help managers build the track record that investors want and test their ideas.
Development is about support. Emerging managers do not have the depth that a firm like Kuramo Capital has, so we provide shared services such as legal support and fund administration.
We ran earlier cohorts for women-led funds in Cape Town and Nairobi. This is the first time we are doing this in Lagos and the first time for a wholesale impact fund focused on small businesses.
Olamide Adeosun: To add to that, WIIF will invest in about 10 to 12 managers across the country, and we will target a good share of them to be emerging managers. A large part of building that pipeline is the work Ijeoma described and the programme the Kuramo Foundation is running for these managers.
How did you select the managers?
Ijeoma Madueke: Eighty-four applied. We looked first for differentiated strategies.
Even for an emerging manager, we asked, ‘What is your fund targeting?’ What problem are you solving? Are you solving it in a differentiated way, and are you set up to execute? I had first thought we wanted people who had everything in place, but many emerging managers are subject matter experts, such as engineers, who have not done financing before. Structure was one test among several. You can set up an advisory board and an investment committee and do all the supporting things, but the core question is your fund thesis. Why are you the right person to be the general partner of this fund, and what makes you different?
We had about three people on the panel for each interview and a scoring method. We also looked at whether the structure behind a fund could actually come to life. That weeded out quite a few applicants. We widened the cohort in places because we saw potential and wanted a bigger pipeline. We also considered fit with the sector. For example, one manager is working on healthcare financing linked to outcomes, which shows some of the innovative structures coming into the sector.
What would count as success for WIIF and the technical assistance facility?
Ijeoma Madueke: For the technical assistance facility, success means getting a few things right. The ideal measure would be a manager reaching a first close or raising a first cheque, but fundraising cycles are long, so that will take time. We look at clarity: a clear fund thesis, a clear approach and structures that can absorb capital, whether it comes from WIIF or elsewhere. The test is whether a manager is investment-ready by the end of the programme. That depends on how committed a manager is and how ready they are for the journey.
We have also given reality checks. One speaker at the in-person session told the cohort he sold his house to keep fundraising going for around six years. We want managers to know how long and how much work this takes, so they can decide whether to go ahead.
Olamide Adeosun: We also had investors in the room, including a pension fund on the panel, so prospective managers could hear directly what a pension fund wants to see before it gives money. That was invaluable.
For us, success means we can invest in a couple of the funds that come out of the accelerator. If two or more of them go on to raise money from outside investors, that validates the foundation’s work and the selection of managers, because it shows they are investable. One panellist told us that when they look at investments, they examine 100 and fund two, a 2% success rate. Against that, a 10% success rate for managers would be an amazing achievement.
Can you walk me through the training and the timeline?
Ijeoma Madueke: The programme runs 12 weeks and wraps up in December. We take managers through each component of setting up and running a fund. Some of it was in person, and we are now going deeper. We look at the fund thesis and the fund model, and we advise on what to adjust. We look at how managers approach fundraising and what their pitch decks look like. We pair them with mentors who have made a similar journey. We look at building the right team, which is tricky for emerging managers because talent is hard to find and hard to scale up.
We also cover pipeline: how to source deals and how to run diligence. We cover the legal and back-end side, meaning agreements, key terms and the shared service providers that can support a fund as it runs.
On fundraising, we explain which investors to approach. A pension fund is an unlikely investor for an emerging manager at this stage, but we wanted the managers to see what is possible. The right early capital comes from foundations and impact investors, who are willing to take a risk and often give concessional capital, meaning capital on softer terms. We also walk managers through the types of capital available to them: the working capital and warehousing that Kuramo offers, technical assistance, and actual capital through WIIF.
You can imagine the volume of material over such a stretch. That is why we call it a boot camp.
One element gets too little attention: trust. An investor gives money to a manager they trust, and trust comes from communicating your thesis clearly, so the investor does not feel they will lose their money. Fundraising is a long relationship, and we train managers on this too.
How are you thinking about exits?
Ijeoma Madueke: Exits come up in many of our conversations with investors, and a big part of my work at the foundation is raising investors’ confidence to invest in Africa, which depends on exits. For these managers, we bring in specialists who have done exits, and we run masterclasses on exit strategy. That is easier here because these managers have not deployed capital yet, so exit planning can shape their strategy from the beginning. We are building that into the curriculum.
You mentioned managers being “investment ready”. What does that mean?
Ijeoma Madueke: From the accelerator’s side, it means that if an investor wants to look at your fund as an opportunity, they can. You have the documentation in place, you can be shortlisted, and you can go through due diligence. If you lack those things, investors will not put you in their pipeline, and you are not investment-ready.
Olamide Adeosun: That is it. Your documents are ready, your strategy is clear, and you have a strong pipeline of investment opportunities. You also have a line of sight on the team you are trying to build, and your thesis is well thought through.
Why do you think the accelerator matters?
Ijeoma Madueke: There are businesses to fund, and that is why the accelerator matters. We are supporting fund managers who are trying to do something for small businesses in Nigeria. You can always invest in infrastructure or in fintechs, where scale is easy to see. Small businesses need innovation in how aligned capital reaches them. Programmes like this start to bridge the gap in formal and structured financing for what we say is 90% of Nigerian businesses.
What these managers are doing is hard. When we say they need to be investment-ready, we are talking about small businesses that keep their money under the pillow, that do not want to scale or take formal capital, and that do not want to hear the word ‘equity’ or the word ‘debt’. These managers are educating those businesses, setting up structures and investing their money in the effort. I do not want us to breeze past that. It is important to understand the scale of the work, and I hope programmes like this can support them as an extension of their teams as they navigate what is still a new environment.

articles.title: La Tierra tiene una invitada por Navidad: una miniluna de dos metros que vino en abril y se irá después de las fiestas
articles.text:
Estas Navidades, la Tierra tendrá una invitada muy especial. Una miniluna que vino a visitarnos el pasado mes de abril y que ha decidido quedarse hasta que pasen las fiestas. Obviamente, las rocas espaciales no deciden nada, permíteme la licencia literaria. Este objeto fue detectado orbitando a nuestro planeta en agosto de este año, aunque los cálculos de su trayectoria han demostrado que llevaba junto a nosotros cuatro meses. Estos mismos cálculos señalan que seguirá dando vueltas a nuestro alrededor más o menos hasta después de Navidad. Para principios de 2027 ya se habría marchado, aunque posiblemente vuelva a casa dentro de 10 años. Al final, las minilunas siempre nos acaban abandonando.
Una atracción irresistible. Según los cálculos realizados por los científicos, 2026 QQ8 tarda unos 359 días en dar la vuelta al Sol, casi lo mismo que la Tierra. Se acerca a nosotros más o menos cada diez años, por lo que no es su primera visita. Sin embargo, esta vez se acercó tanto y a una velocidad relativa tan baja que la atracción gravitatoria de la Tierra lo capturó y lo introdujo en una órbita a su alrededor. Así, quedó convertido en una miniluna, aunque no estará ahí para siempre.
Lunas que vienen y van. El anuncio sobre este objeto, llamado 2026 QQ8, se hizo el 29 de octubre. Lo ha comunicado el Minor Planet Center, una institución que se encarga de estudiar los cometas, asteroides y otros objetos menores del Sistema Solar. También estudia las minilunas, pequeños objetos que orbitan temporalmente en torno a la Tierra, pero sin llegar a ser satélites fijos. Son tan comunes que, según un estudio reciente, nuestro planeta podría tener normalmente hasta seis minilunas girando a su alrededor. Algunas son fragmentos de nuestro propio satélite, aunque también hay otros tipos de objetos. De media miden unos 75 centímetros y su estancia media es de aproximadamente 9 meses.
No hay nada que temer. Ya hemos visto que este objeto se ha convertido en satélite temporal porque se acercó mucho a nuestro planeta. Podríamos preguntar si dicho acercamiento supone un peligro. Sin embargo, hay varios motivos para estar tranquilos con respecto a eso. Para empezar, aunque 2026 QQ8 es un poco más grande que la media de minilunas, sigue siendo un objeto pequeño, de apenas 2 metros de diámetro. Si se acercase demasiado a la Tierra se quemaría casi por completo al cruzar la atmósfera y se convertiría en una bola de fuego. No caerían restos peligrosos a la superficie. Además, no está tan cerca. Su punto más cercano a la Tierra está a 568.000 km, bastante más lejos que nuestra propia Luna.
Hablando de la Luna… ¿por qué ella sí? Muchísimos objetos se convierten en minilunas temporales y luego siguen su camino. En cambio, la Luna se quedó unida a nuestro planeta para siempre. Hay varios argumentos que explican esto. En primer lugar, 2026 QQ8 y el resto de minilunas son objetos de paso. Circulan alrededor del Sol, no de la Tierra, lo que pasa es que a veces se encuentran con nosotros y son atraídos temporalmente. La Luna, según la hipótesis más aceptada sobre su origen, se formó en la propia Tierra, a partir de los escombros derivados del impacto de un objeto del tamaño de Marte. Por otro lado, la Luna está mucho más cerca que esos objetos, aproximadamente a unos 384.000 kilómetros. Con todo esto, la interacción entre la Tierra y sus minilunas es mucho más débil que la de nuestro planeta con su satélite.
Hay un último factor. Para quedarse con un objeto, un planeta tiene que quitarle energía orbital. En el Sistema Solar primitivo, el gas que rodeaba a los planetas jóvenes podía frenar objetos hasta capturarlos, pero hoy no existe un disco denso así alrededor de la Tierra. Por eso las minilunas pueden escapar con facilidad. La Luna, en cambio, no necesitó ser capturada, porque nació ya ligada a nuestro planeta.
Esta se irá, como lo hacen todas, pero antes de eso se quedará una buena temporada de visita. Y posiblemente volverá dentro de una década. Al final, la Tierra siempre se convierte en un buen lugar al que volver.

articles.title: Starlink impõe preço dinâmico e vai cobrar mais por acesso à internet • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Starlink impõe preço dinâmico e vai cobrar mais por acesso à internet
Starlink começou a aplicar preços dinâmicos para assinaturas de internet via satélite nos Estados Unidos, um sistema de cobrança que lembra o da Uber.
Você contrata um plano de acesso à internet por um valor específico. No mês seguinte, o serviço fica mais caro. No outro, o preço diminui. Soa como algo absurdo, mas que tem se tornado a realidade para muitos assinantes da Starlink. Isso porque o serviço de internet via satélite adotou um sistema de preço dinâmico nos Estados Unidos que lembra o da Uber.
O preço dinâmico significa que a Starlink pode cobrar mais ou menos por seu serviço de acesso à internet de acordo com a demanda (número de clientes ativos) e com a capacidade de rede disponível em determinada região.
É, de fato, um sistema que lembra o da Uber: se há muita demanda, os preços aumentam; se existe capacidade ociosa, os preços caem ou ficam dentro de um eventual valor mínimo para atrair mais clientes.
De acordo com a PCMag, a nova política de cobrança tem gerado um aumento de custo que varia entre 10% e 20% aos clientes afetados. Em outras regiões, os preços caíram nas mesmas proporções. Em todos os casos, os clientes estão sendo avisados por e-mail sobre a mudança de precificação.
As reclamações não demoraram a chegar às redes sociais. Neste tópico no Reddit, por exemplo, há usuários relatando que sua assinatura passou de US$ 130 para US$ 143 com os preços dinâmicos. Outro relatou que o valor cobrado pulou de US$ 85 para US$ 120 e, depois, baixou para US$ 102.
Os preços dinâmicos começaram a ser implementados nas últimas semanas em determinadas regiões dos Estados Unidos, como cidades de estados como Oregon, Washington, Nova York e Colorado.
Mas outros países também podem ser afetados. Já há relatos de aumento dinâmico de preços em Toronto, no Canadá.
Até o momento, não há relatos de cobranças de preços dinâmicos da Starlink no Brasil, e parece pouco provável que isso aconteça.
Para começar, o novo sistema de cobrança tem sido aplicado em regiões onde a infraestrutura da companhia já enfrenta ou está próxima de enfrentar sobrecarga. É possível que, no Brasil, a rede da Starlink ainda tenha margem para crescimento do número de clientes sem que isso gere uma demanda maior do que a capacidade.
Além disso, no Brasil, a regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) aparece como um obstáculo para a adoção do preço dinâmico.
Em linhas gerais, as normas do órgão estabelecem que os preços dos serviços de telecomunicações não podem ser reajustados em intervalos inferiores a 12 meses. Além disso, os critérios dos reajustes precisam estar bem definidos no contrato.
A Starlink até pode cobrar preços diferentes para regiões distintas do país, desde que respeite as regras aplicáveis às ofertas comerciais. Se a alteração de preços for recorrente a ponto de entrar em conflito com essas condições, a empresa poderá ter problemas com a Anatel e, certamente, será questionada por órgãos de defesa do consumidor.

articles.title: Tokio Releases Topcoat: A Batteries-Included Full-Stack Rust Framework
articles.text:
Topcoat, a modular full-stack framework for Rust built by the Tokio team, has moved out of private development with a public GitHub repository, a v0.9 release, and a series of blog posts outlining its direction. The project is positioned as a batteries-included web framework that stays entirely server-rendered, with reactivity added through cross-compiled Rust expressions rather than WebAssembly.
Topcoat introduces several ideas, including a view! macro for mixing HTML with Rust control flow, module-based routing inferred from the project's file tree, an asset pipeline with content-hashed URLs, and a Tailwind integration that works without Node.js. It also announces tighter integration with the Toasty async ORM, which handles migrations and database access in the same Rust workspace.
One of the headline design choices in Topcoat is the $(...) expression. These are ordinary type-checked Rust fragments that Topcoat evaluates on the server for the initial render and also translates to JavaScript, so they re-run instantly in the browser without a WASM bundle or separate client build step.
When an update does need the server, developers can mark a component as a #[shard]. Topcoat re-renders the shard on the server whenever one of its $(...) arguments changes, then swaps the new HTML into the page, giving a similar feel to reactive updates without shipping a client-side router. This positions Topcoat closer to HTMX, Datastar and Phoenix LiveView than to React or SolidJS.
Topcoat also ships Topcoat UI, a component library inspired by shadcn/ui. Components are vendored into the project via the topcoat ui CLI command, so teams can edit their design and functionality rather than wrap a fixed package. The approach has drawn attention on Hacker News, with one commenter excited by the concept:
Oh man I'd love a nice full stack framework in Rust! Django, Laravel, and Rails are very neat. I used to be a micro framework kind of guy, but having everything integrated is more and more appealing over the last few years.
This would take a long time to get feature complete with the core of those big full stack frameworks, but I'm rooting for it! Getting to use the Rust type system with a full stack web framework sounds incredible.
On the same thread, Hobofan worried the project "will possibly gain outsized adoption in the community based on name recognition rather than merit", whilst frio argued the Rust ecosystem still lacks a true Django equivalent with admin, auth and migrations baked in.
Speaking at ScyllaDB's P99 2026 conference, Tokio creator Carl Lerche admitted Topcoat is not aimed at Figma-scale applications, but rather the "run-of-the-mill, browser-based, database-driven applications" that make up most of the web.
Within the Rust ecosystem, Topcoat sits alongside Leptos and Dioxus, both of which compile Rust to WebAssembly and therefore carry an upfront WASM bundle. It overlaps more directly with Loco.rs and Cot, which chase Django-style productivity with ORMs and admin panels, though neither yet matches Topcoat's cross-compiled reactivity model.
Given the rapid 0.x cadence, there is no long-term stability guarantee. The team has committed to release notes for every version and migration guidance where needed, with the roadmap tracking authentication, background jobs, static export and tighter Toasty integration as near-term work on GitHub issue 104. New projects can follow the Getting started guide or the manual setup instructions. Topcoat is published on crates.io under an MIT licence.
Topcoat is an open-source, modular full-stack web framework for Rust, developed and maintained by the Tokio project, the collective behind Rust's most popular asynchronous runtime. It aims to bring Rails or Django-style productivity to Rust developers through server-rendering, declarative reactivity and vendored components, so teams already invested in Rust for infrastructure or performance-critical work can build web applications without adopting a separate language or stack.

articles.title: Chrome Update Patches Exploited XML Zero-Day, Eighth This Year
articles.text:
Google on Monday informed Chrome users of new security updates that patch nine vulnerabilities, including a zero-day exploited in the wild.
The exploited vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated high severity, is a use-after-free in the web browser’s XML component.
A researcher who wants to remain anonymous reported the issue to Google on November 6.
The tech giant has not shared any additional details, and no information appears to be available on the attacks exploiting CVE-2026-125350.
CISA has yet to add CVE-2026-125350 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.
This is the eighth Chrome zero-day exploited this year after CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491.
In addition to the zero-day, the latest Chrome updates patch six high-severity vulnerabilities in the WebGL, FileSystem, Compositing, GPU, V8, and XML components. Google discovered most of the flaws internally.
Two medium-severity bugs described as uninitialized resource issues in the GPU component have also been fixed.
The patches are included in Chrome 157 updates, specifically versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux.

articles.title: Microsoft Showcases Modernized Registry Editor as WinUI 3 Sample
articles.text:
Monday, November 9th 2026
Microsoft Showcases Modernized Registry Editor as WinUI 3 Sample
Microsoft has updated its core component, the Registry Editor, with the latest WinUI framework as a demonstration of what the WinUI 3 framework can offer to existing applications with legacy Win32 components. The Registry Editor, a fundamental Windows application, has remained unchanged across many generations of Windows operating systems, which have relied on it for essential system modifications. According to a report from Windows Latest, Microsoft showcased a modernized version of the Registry Editor built with the WinUI 3 framework as a sample, but it is not intended to replace the current application found in every Windows build.
Initially, Windows Latest did not explicitly state that the application overhaul was just a sample. This led Microsoft's executive Scott Hanselman to clarify on X that the new build is merely a sample application and is not connected to the team maintaining the current Registry Editor. Previously, communities on X criticized the new design for its sparse menus and unfinished look, prompting a response from Microsoft's staff. It is important to note that while a new version might be in development, the current application is only a demonstration and is not related to the team maintaining the existing application. A future update may address this, but for now, we remain with the older version.Since the introduction of WinUI, several versions have been integrated into the operating system. For example, Windows 10 still includes many UI elements from the Windows 7 era and earlier. Microsoft plans to transition the entire user experience to the desktop-only WinUI 3 framework, which is expected to reduce application latency, improve user experience, and provide a noticeably smoother feel. Achieving UI uniformity will enhance dark mode support, ensuring that when users enable dark mode, it will be consistently applied throughout the system, not just on select panels and the home screen. Additionally, once all legacy applications transition to WinUI 3, the OS will finally feel completely new.
Sources:
