articles.text:
Veja os destaques do Olhar Digital News desta segunda-feira (09/11).
IA permite que um único hacker ataque empresas em vários países
O uso de inteligência artificial em ciberataques está permitindo que criminosos coordenem operações mais complexas, atinjam alvos em diferentes países e ampliem o alcance de suas invasões. O alerta faz parte do relatório Acronis TRU Cyber Pulse 2026, divulgado nesta segunda-feira (09).
Novela geopolítica da Nvidia tem China, EUA, espionagem e traição
A semana começou com um furacão na tecnologia. A Nvidia anunciou que abriu uma investigação independente para entender se o CEO e fundador Jensen Huang foi alvo de uma operação de espionagem estrangeira. Ele admitiu ter sido infiel à esposa. Segundo o jornal The New York Times, o CEO teve um relacionamento extraconjugal com uma agente de inteligência da China.
Terra ganha minilua temporária que deve partir em dezembro
A Terra ganhou uma segunda Lua! Ou melhor, uma nova minilua. Trata-se do asteroide 2026 QQ8, capturado temporariamente pela gravidade do planeta. Com apenas 1 metro de diâmetro, o objeto chegou a ser confundido com lixo espacial, mas agora foi identificado por cientistas como um corpo natural.
SpaceX tentará feito inédito em novo lançamento da Starship nesta semana
A SpaceX pretende realizar uma manobra inédita em seu próximo teste da Starship: capturar tanto o propulsor Super Heavy quanto o estágio superior da nave com os braços mecânicos da torre de lançamento. Essa tentativa histórica está prevista para a próxima sexta-feira (13), durante o 15º voo de teste do megafoguete.
Alessandro Di Lorenzo é editor do Olhar Digital e formado em jornalismo pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).
André Milhomem integra a equipe de redes sociais do Olhar Digital e do programa Olhar Digital News.

articles.title: Revolve Puts Data Breach Victim Count at 1.5 Million
articles.text:
Online fashion retailer Revolve has informed the Indiana Attorney General’s Office that 1,515,073 individuals were impacted by the data breach it disclosed in October.
The company revealed the incident on October 29 in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). It started sending notification letters to impacted customers around the same time.
Revolve had not publicly shared a total. Its notices to regulators in Iowa, Massachusetts, South Carolina, Texas, and Vermont covered roughly 197,000 people combined.
The retailer says an unauthorized party broke into some of its systems, including its e-commerce platform, on September 11. Per the Indiana Attorney General’s records, Revolve became aware of the intrusion on September 29.
According to the company, the intruder may have relied on “automated means” to collect customers’ names and contact information, including mailing addresses, along with their card numbers and expiration dates.
The exposure is limited to shoppers who chose to store a payment method in their online accounts.
Revolve reported the attack to federal law enforcement and enlisted external cybersecurity experts to help with its response.
The company has yet to explain how the hackers got into its systems. So far, the attack has not been publicly claimed by any hacker group.
Related: Iris Plaza Breach May Have Exposed Data of 7.7 Million Customers
Related: Amplifon Americas Data Breach Impacts 1.3 Million
Related: Over 3 Million People Hit by Frontline Education Data Breach

articles.title: How skills and agents work in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How skills and agents work in AWS Quick
If you use AI agents, you’ve probably explained the same task more than once. You might describe how to build your weekly status update, write release notes, manage a project, or create tickets. These are all repeatable tasks that you can encode using AWS Quick through agents and skills. AWS Quick is an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research. You work with it in natural language, and Quick uses AI agents to process your requests against your connected data sources and applications.
In this post, we cover how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also show how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use.
Understanding foundational concepts
In this section, we explain the foundational concepts that help you understand AWS Quick in relation to agents, skills, and your data.
The agent sits at the center of Figure 1. It follows its instructions, loads the skills that a task calls for, takes action through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data: spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards.
Working with agents
An agent in AWS Quick is a configurable AI with its own instructions, knowledge sources (spaces), and connectors, which it uses to answer questions and get work done for you. You can work with an agent in chat, or let it run on its own using a routine. Agents can only reach the resources and services that you can, and you decide what each agent is allowed to do.
Quick is the default built-in agent that every user has access to. It has no fixed scope, so in each conversation it works with whatever resources you have access to, such as your spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills. You don’t need to decide in advance which data or tools a request needs, so you can start most work with Quick.
A custom agent is one that you or someone on your team configures for a specific job. An example is a human resources (HR) onboarding assistant that answers new-hire questions from the HR team’s space. You give it its own instructions and limit it to the spaces, connectors, and skills that your use case requires. After you test and publish it, you can share it with other users and groups within your AWS Quick account. For a walkthrough of building one, see Build AI-powered employee onboarding agents with AWS Quick.
Working with data
Agents ground their answers in the data you connect to Quick. A space is a curated collection of documents and AWS Quick resources that an agent uses as a source of information. You can create one for yourself, your team, or another group in your organization. You can upload files and folders to a space, or add assets such as dashboards, knowledge bases, action connectors, and datasets. When you start a conversation with Quick, you can attach a space to narrow the data that Quick uses for that conversation. When you add a space to an agent, the space becomes part of the agent’s configuration, and the agent draws on it when a request needs it.
A knowledge base is an organized, indexed collection of documents or content from data sources, optimized for retrieval and question answering. Quick syncs knowledge bases from sources such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), web crawler, or Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases. Quick keeps them up to date on a sync schedule.
Datasets and dashboards come from AWS Quick Sight, the business intelligence feature in Quick, which is available in accounts provisioned through the AWS Management Console. A dataset is a prepared collection of data ready for use in analyses and dashboards. A dashboard is the published version of an analysis that you share with other Quick users. With datasets, you can build semantically rich metadata over your structured data, such as database tables, so you can accomplish complex analytical use cases with natural language.
Lastly, a connector links AWS Quick to an external application or a native tool, so agents can read data and take action on your behalf. Cloud connectors connect Quick to services such as Microsoft Outlook, Slack, Jira, Asana, and Salesforce, and to remotely hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. They’re available on every device where you use Quick. Local connectors run on your own machine, such as an MCP server that you host yourself, so their tools are available only when that machine is on and connected. For the full list of connector types, see Connectors and Integration-specific guides in the AWS Quick User Guide.
Together, these make your data, documents, and applications available through natural language, so you can ask questions and take actions in your connected sources.
Working with skills
A skill is a reusable set of instructions that teaches an agent how to do a specific task. Skills are also the foundation of how an agent in Quick behaves and completes work. Like other agents, an agent in Quick runs in a harness (a managed agent loop) that follows the reasoning and acting (ReAct) pattern. When you supply AWS Quick with a prompt, the agent uses its available tools and instructions to accomplish its goal and supply you with a response. Agent frameworks such as the Strands Agents SDK are built around the same model-driven loop.
Much of what Quick does by default comes from system skills. For example, you can ask Quick to generate a Word document, a PowerPoint presentation, an Excel spreadsheet, or a PDF. A system skill can then create or edit the document using code with scripts the skill bundles. Other system skills browse the web, run code, execute deep research, transcribe audio and video, and generate images. Some manage Quick itself, such as building AWS Quick Flows, scheduling routines, handing work to a coding agent such as Kiro, managing your memories and knowledge graph, or tracking your to-dos. Within Quick, you can turn system skills on or off, but you can’t edit, duplicate, export, publish, share, or delete them.
Skills can do many kinds of work because of the capabilities and tools that AWS Quick supplies. For example, one skill can produce a deliverable, such as a weekly status update built from your template. Another can automate a workflow across your connectors, such as gathering the week’s Jira updates and posting a summary to Slack. A skill can also run calculations in Python scripts and chart the results with JavaScript.
What is a skill?
Quick skills follow the Agent Skills specification, which Anthropic originally developed and released as an open standard. AWS Quick on desktop, which launched in preview in April 2026 and became generally available in September 2026, uses this specification.
A skill is a folder with a Markdown file SKILL.md at its root, plus any optional scripts or other reference files its instructions use. The file’s frontmatter, the attributes between two --- lines, holds the name, description, and any other metadata relevant to your skill. See the following shortened example of a skill named release-notes-generator.
The description and name are the two most important aspects to triggering a skill. Quick uses progressive disclosure when it loads your skills into the agent’s prompt. The agent reads only each skill’s name and description until a request calls for that skill. It then loads the skill’s full instructions, as How agents load skills describes. This means certain phrases can help trigger the skill, such as “generate my release notes for version 2.3.” The specification caps name at 64 characters and description at 1,024, and recommends instructions within the skill to be under 5,000 tokens.
Build and share a skill in Quick
You can create a skill from chat, from a file (a .md or .zip file), or from a folder that has a SKILL.md file at its root. This post focuses on chat. To start, describe your task to Quick in chat. For example, you can start with this template (replace the content between <> brackets with your requirements):
This is all you need to start building your own skills. Alternatively, you also can take a multi-turn conversation that you previously interacted with to accomplish a task and ask Quick to generate a skill from it. After you are satisfied with the final result, publish and share your skill:
- Choose Customize, and then choose Skills.
- Find your skill in draft, and open its detail panel.
- Choose Publish.
- Choose Share, and then choose the people or groups to share it with.
Publishing and sharing are separate steps, so publishing alone doesn’t give anyone access to the skill. The people you share it with add it from Add to Quick under Shared with me, and their version stays in sync each time you publish again. For the current steps, see Draft and published versions and Sharing your skills in the AWS Quick User Guide.
Improve your skills with best practices
A skill that you build from a quick description or conversation might work consistently for you, but there are many considerations you must take into account when building production skills that you share with your team. Skills are like code, and many engineering best practices can help any knowledge worker build them.
- “It works on my machine” is a common phrase among software engineers. It describes software that runs for the person who built it but breaks when someone else installs or uses it. When building skills, you must consider your environment. Skill instructions can use agents to query data sources or invoke connectors or tools. Software engineers typically work around this limitation by documenting the prerequisites to using software. For example, if you are sharing a skill in isolation, you might want to create a README with your skill documenting these requirements. If you share an agent that uses your skill, also share the sources it connects to, or the people you share it with get answers only from the sources they can already access.
- Plan for failures. Agents use connected sources that depend on third- and first-party services. When engineers write code, they need to understand what to do if a piece of software fails. If you incorporate these scenarios into your skill instructions, your agents can adapt based on concrete instructions. You don’t need to be an expert in the downstream service, because an agent works toward the goal and can retry or try another approach when a step fails. You do need to list what to do when a failure affects your task or business process. Take the following snippet from a workflow in a skill that might have ramifications if it fails.
What should the agent do if sending the email fails? You might want to add instructions on what to do in that scenario.
Handling failure scenarios is even more important when executing agents on a schedule without a human in the loop.
- Test every change. Software engineers write multiple forms of tests, such as unit and integration tests, that help them test software. These tests are run on every change. With skills, it is equally important that you generate your own test cases for various scenarios and continue to add new tests as you make changes. There are multiple ways to do this, but it’s best to test using the environment you expect your downstream users to use.
There are many more aspects to consider when building production skills:
- Add release notes to each change.
- Keep hardcoded values that change, such as /Users/me/notes or #my-team, out of the steps, and declare them as inputs that each person provides.
- Record when the skill changed with human-readable dates.
- Record where each reference file came from, so that if the source changes, you can update your skill instructions too.
- Store a checksum, a fingerprint of the skill’s files that shows when a copy differs from the version that was checked.
- Check the structure after every change, the way a linter catches mistakes before anyone reviews the code.
- Build skills in a consistent way, so your team can contribute changes and review them faster.
For any user, this is a lot to consider. That’s why the AWS Quick official catalog provides pre-built resources, such as skills, built with these best practices in mind.
AWS Quick official catalog
The catalog is a collection of agent resources that you can install and use as they are, or take as a starting point and adapt to your own work. The catalog states that every resource in it is tested and scanned for quality, security, and other factors before it’s published. The skills cover everyday productivity and the work of teams such as sales, marketing, HR, legal, project management, customer success, and software engineering. They also cover industries such as finance, healthcare and life sciences, energy and utilities, hospitality, and supply chain and logistics.
The catalog includes the Skill Architect skill, a pre-built skill that applies these engineering best practices for you, as Build skills with software engineering practices in AWS Quick describes. To install it, choose Customize, Skills, Browse all, and then Official. Enter skill architect in the search box, and then choose Install. For the current steps, see Install skills in AWS Quick on desktop.
Connect skills to your agents
When you create an agent, you configure its name, description, and instructions, and you choose the spaces it reads from, the connectors it can use, and the skills it can load. For details, see Agent configuration in the AWS Quick User Guide. An agent works best when it solves a particular use case, such as answering new-hire questions or preparing a weekly status report, and bounding its world to the spaces, skills, and connectors that use case requires. By default, an agent can use all of your skills, and when you add specific skills, the agent is limited to those. That becomes problematic when you share the agent, because it runs with the access of the person using it. The same request can reach different data and skills for each person, and can return incomplete answers when it needs a source that only you can access.
If you want to tie them all (agents, skills, and spaces) together, try out the personal agent architect module in the linked workshop.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how agents use skills and your data in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also showed how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use.
To learn more, find events, or share your success with AWS Quick, visit the AWS Quick Community. The AWS Quick Community has learning material, feature announcements, events, and examples from other users. You can also ask questions in its Q&A forum.
For a recorded session on the topics in this post, watch Encode Your Enterprise with Agents & Skills on AWS Quick. The session covers how a skill is structured and loaded, how skills work with agents, spaces, and connectors, and best practices for building skills that you share. It ends with a demo of the official catalog and the Skill Architect skill.

articles.title: Auswirkungen von KI auf den Arbeitsmarkt: Berufseinsteiger spüren die Veränderung als Erstes
articles.text:
Auswirkungen von KI auf den Arbeitsmarkt: Berufseinsteiger spüren die Veränderung als Erstes
Der zunehmende Einsatz von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) in vielen Unternehmen geht nach Analyse des Ifo-Instituts mit schlechteren Jobchancen für Berufsanfänger einher. KI-bedingte Stellenstreichungen in großem Maßstab hingegen beobachten die Münchner Ökonomen bislang nicht. Ifo-Präsident Clemens Fuest und seine Mitarbeiter veröffentlichten einen neuen KI-Frühindikator, der die Folgen der zunehmenden Verbreitung von KI für die Arbeitswelt messen soll. Die Wissenschaftler vergleichen dafür die Beschäftigung und Neueinstellungen in 140 Berufen und setzen diese in Relation zur Ersetzbarkeit menschlicher Tätigkeit durch KI.
Nicht nur IT-Arbeitskräfte sind durch KI leicht ersetzbar
Demnach ist die Vollzeitbeschäftigung der 20- bis 24-Jährigen in den am stärksten KI-exponierten Berufen seit 2022 um 14 Prozent zurückgegangen, von rund 279.000 auf 239.000. Vorn auf der Liste der Berufe mit einem hohen Anteil leicht zu automatisierender Tätigkeiten stehen Datenerfassung und Textverarbeitung, gefolgt von Softwareentwicklern, Buchhaltern, Datenbank- und Netzwerktechnikern sowie Autoren und Journalisten. „Von einem breiten Jobabbau durch KI sehen wir bislang nichts“, sagte Fuest. „Aber wer ins Berufsleben startet, spürt die Veränderung als Erstes.“
… doch die KI-Effekte sind keineswegs nur negativ
Die KI-Auswirkungen auf die Arbeitswelt nehmen aber durchaus gegenläufige Richtungen ein, wie Fuest und seine Koautoren betonen: Auf der einen Seite steht die Automatisierung, auf der anderen die „Augmentierung“: Die KI kann menschliche Arbeitskräfte unterstützen und produktiver machen. Was den Arbeitsmarkt insgesamt betrifft, so ist laut Ifo die Beschäftigung in den KI-exponierten Berufen seit 2022 sogar um 1,8 Prozent gewachsen – in den nicht exponierten Berufen hingegen hat sie demnach um 6,4 Prozent abgenommen. Co-Autor Oliver Falck sieht den Jobschwund bei den Berufsanfängern jedoch als Frühwarnzeichen am Arbeitsmarkt.
Manager dürfen sich nicht sicher fühlen
Ein KI-Risiko laufen demnach allerdings keineswegs nur gewöhnliche Arbeitnehmer, sondern auch Führungskräfte bis in die Chefetagen hinein: KI könnte demnach auch einen beträchtlichen Teil der Arbeit von Geschäftsführern und Vorständen erheblich schneller bewältigen. Nicht KI-exponiert sind demnach hauptsächlich handwerkliche und sonstige manuelle Tätigkeiten: An letzter Stelle der Liste stehen Küchenhilfskräfte. Unter den nicht oder kaum durch KI zu ersetzenden Berufen finden sich beispielsweise auch Bauarbeiter und -handwerker, Tischler, Maler, Gebäudereiniger, Bauern und auch Hauswirtschaftsleitungen.
Die Wissenschaftler betonen, dass der neue KI-Indikator des Instituts keine monokausale Erklärung abliefern soll: Demnach lässt sich daraus nicht ableiten, dass allein KI die beobachteten Effekte auslöst. Eine Rolle spielen könnten demnach neben anderen Faktoren der demografische Wandel und längere Ausbildungszeiten.

articles.title: El banco central de Australia advirtió que el auge de la IA empuja los precios al alza
articles.text:
Sarah Hunter, subgobernadora del Banco de la Reserva de Australia, afirmó en Sídney que el auge de la inversión en IA presiona los precios en el corto plazo. También dijo que hay pocas pruebas de que la tecnología haya elevado la productividad o causado despidos masivos.
Según informó Reuters, el aumento de la inversión local en centros de datos es una de las razones por las que el banco central subió la tasa de interés cinco veces este año, hasta 4,85%, el nivel más alto en 18 años.
Hunter habló en una conferencia de UBS y publicó el texto en el sitio del banco. Explicó que la inversión mundial en IA tensiona las cadenas de suministro de productos como los semiconductores, y que esos costos ya se trasladan a los precios de algunos bienes en las economías avanzadas.
Precisó que las subas se concentran en pocos artículos de electrónica de consumo, con poco peso en el índice de precios. Algunas empresas consultadas por el banco también dijeron que la construcción de centros de datos aumenta la demanda de oficios de la construcción que ya escaseaban.
La inversión en centros de datos se multiplicó por 10
Un informe del banco, divulgado el mismo día, estima que la inversión en centros de datos en Australia creció unas 10 veces en tres años, desde una base muy baja. Proyecta otros 115.000 millones de dólares australianos entre mediados de 2026 y fines de 2028, cerca del 2% del PIB por año en términos brutos.
El aporte neto a la economía es menor. Los autores suponen que alrededor del 70% del equipamiento es importado, dentro de un rango externo de entre el 50% y el 80%. Con ese descuento, los centros de datos explicaron hasta 0,2 puntos porcentuales del crecimiento anual del último año.
Hunter dijo que, con el tiempo, la oferta de capacidad alcanzará a la demanda y las presiones iniciales sobre los precios se disiparán. Su conclusión para el largo plazo es que el efecto de la IA sobre la inflación será, en términos generales, neutral, como ocurrió con otras tecnologías de uso general.
La subgobernadora añadió una advertencia financiera. Las acciones de empresas de IA en Estados Unidos se cuadruplicaron aproximadamente desde fines de 2022, y cerca del 5% de la riqueza financiera de los hogares australianos está invertida en ellas, de forma directa o a través de los fondos de jubilación, según estimaciones del personal del banco.
Si los retornos de esa inversión decepcionan, algunos precios de activos, como acciones y deuda de empresas, quedarían expuestos a una corrección brusca y posiblemente desordenada, dijo.
Pocas pruebas de efectos en productividad y empleo
Sobre la productividad, Hunter señaló que las empresas tardan en invertir y reorganizarse para aprovechar la tecnología. Las estimaciones para la próxima década van desde un impacto de más del 2% anual hasta solo 0,1%, según las cifras que citó. Describió un patrón conocido: la productividad medida cae o se estanca antes de subir.
En el empleo, los contactos del programa de consultas a empresas del banco indican que la IA no afectó todavía la dotación de personal de la mayoría de las firmas y que no lo hará en el próximo año. Hay señales tentativas de ajuste: menos avisos de trabajo y peores resultados en ocupaciones muy expuestas, sobre todo entre los jóvenes.
Hunter aclaró que esas diferencias son modestas y que es pronto para saber si responden a la IA u otros factores. Citó estimaciones de la agencia australiana Jobs and Skills Australia: el 4% de los trabajadores está muy expuesto a la automatización y el 31% a que la IA complemente su trabajo.
El banco estima que la tasa neutral, la que equilibra el ahorro y la inversión global, subió en los últimos años. Los rendimientos de los bonos también aumentaron en los últimos meses, con participantes del mercado que citan la fuerte demanda de capital. Hunter reconoció que el alcance es difícil de medir.
El propio banco dijo que todavía es pronto para saber cuán grandes serán los efectos y cuándo aparecerán. Entender su tamaño y su calendario, y qué implica para la política monetaria, es una prioridad de investigación, con un programa de trabajo en marcha.

articles.title: Canadian tech sees promise in federal government’s 500-MW sovereign AI compute pledge | BetaKit
articles.text:
While the Government of Canada’s planned US Qualified Small Business Stock-style tax incentive has hogged much of the post-Budget 2026 spotlight, the feds also announced a notable new sovereign AI computing commitment on Thursday.
“Almost nobody has capacity available at any price.”
Ali Asaria, Transformer Lab
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government has promised to “enable Canadian AI companies to access 500 [megawatts] of sovereign AI compute through new financial tools, such as backstops and offtake agreements, to mobilize private capital and expand compute capacity.” The feds have previously leveraged similar mechanisms to help get carbon capture and mining projects off the ground.
In an interview with BetaKit, Sean Mullin, who previously served as lead economic advisor to the Prime Minister and helped design and launch Canada’s $2-billion sovereign AI compute strategy, said this proposal appears geared towards addressing the “chicken-and-egg, Catch-22 problem” facing smaller domestic AI startups seeking access to compute in Canada.
While the exact nature of this plan appears to still be under development, the feds appear poised to pull together pools of these companies and provide guarantees that the compute they have committed to buy from these data centres will be purchased as a means of de-risking them.
Canadian startups crowded out
Data centre builders require huge commitments to secure the financing they need to break ground on new projects. But demand for the AI computing power these hubs provide is so high that the companies developing them currently have their pick of the litter in terms of buyers.
The feds’ 500-megawatt (MW) target would be a big step up compared to the country’s existing AI processing power. According to a recent Boston Consulting Group report, Canada currently has 300 MW of AI data centre capacity available. Work to drastically boost that number is well underway, including by domestic telecom giant Bell, which aims to build Canada’s largest data centre in Saskatchewan with a 1.2-gigawatt (GW) capacity. Mullin noted that these plans are based on the assumption of a huge increase in AI demand.
“Countries around the world are scrambling to build and attract as much compute as possible … If Canada manages to set the terms on this appropriately, it could be a strong competitive advantage.”
Jaxson Khan, Aperture AI
That 500 MW could be spread across multiple projects over time. “It would be quite a lot right now, but it may be only a small share of demand by 2028, 2029, and so I think it’s a reasonable target,” Mullin said.
At the moment, given the choice between selling future compute to a more established foreign firm with a deep balance sheet and strong credit rating or to a more nascent, cash-strapped domestic startup, many data centre developers look to be choosing the former because they are viewed as less risky by lenders, thus crowding out smaller Canadian AI companies.
“What the [Canadian] government is articulating here is maybe they can help solve this market failure by helping make this market,” said Mullin, who now works as senior fellow at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy.
Demand for AI compute in Canada could soon begin to grow even faster. During the US midterm elections last week, the Democrats seized control of the House and the Senate from Republicans, while voters approved nearly every data centre moratorium on the ballot. This spurred a big tech-stock selloff as experts predicted these shifting political winds to both slow and increase the cost of data centre construction south of the border.
Anthropic, Meta, and Microsoft have already turned to Canada for AI processing power, and these federal election results could lead more major US tech firms to look north.
“If that were to happen … that would make the need for this type of intervention stronger,” Mullin said.
In his budget speech, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne listed AI infrastructure as among the projects “that will power our future.”
“Countries around the world are scrambling to build and attract as much compute as possible … If Canada manages to set the terms on this appropriately, it could be a strong competitive advantage,” Aperture AI CEO Jaxson Khan, who also works at the Munk School as a senior fellow and previously served as a senior policy advisor for Innovation, Science, and Economic Development Canada.
Cautious optimism from Canadian tech
Canadian AI entrepreneurs and investors whom BetaKit spoke with were also happy about the feds’ latest move to expand domestic access, which they think could benefit Canadian AI startups “enormously” if thoughtfully implemented. However, some reserved final judgment until they see what it looks like in practice.
“We’re excited to see the federal government backing sovereign AI compute and the momentum behind a fully Canadian AI stack,” Ideogram co-founder and CEO Mohammad Norouzi said. “Access to compute is one of the biggest challenges for AI companies building in Canada, and this is a significant step toward expanding capacity here at home.”
Norouzi added that Ideogram “would love to bring a meaningful portion” of its compute spending to Canada.
Ali Asaria, co-founder and CEO of Kitchener-Waterloo AI research startup Transformer Lab, said that, at the moment, securing access to the graphics processing units typically used to train and deploy AI models “is close to impossible.”
“Almost nobody has capacity available at any price,” Asaria said. “The vendors who do will only rent to you if you commit to three years or more and pay 25 to sometimes 50 percent up front. Even once you hand over a multimillion-dollar deposit, they tell you they’re going to go buy the hardware and aren’t sure when it’ll be online. It might be six months.”
For startups lacking the balance sheets of major firms, Asaria said that process is simply “a non-starter.” While Transformer Lab is willing to pay for the compute it needs on a monthly or annual basis, he said the company and others like it “can’t finance the hardware on behalf of the data centres and then wait half a year to use it.”
“Ottawa helping data centres finance those purchases might sound crazy, but it might be crazy enough to work,” he added. “Demand is so high that the government’s risk is close to zero.”
More on #Budget2026
Unified.to co-founder and CEO Roy Pereira and Tailscale general manager of sovereign AI Patricia Prewitt also welcome the feds’ plan.
“Making compute more accessible and affordable for smaller Canadian companies through financing new data centres is an excellent public investment,” Prewitt said. “We look forward to seeing who has access as a key metric of success.”
Mullin echoed the latter assertion, noting that “deciding on a fair, transparent way to allocate that compute will be important.”
Allen Lau, co-founder and operating partner at frontier tech-focused Toronto venture capital firm Two Small Fish Ventures, is cautiously optimistic about the proposal, as well. He thinks it could accelerate domestic AI data centre development and improve access for Canadian AI startups “enormously,” but emphasized that “the devil is in the details.”
Lau favours the idea of using financial backstops and offtake agreements to attract private capital rather than relying solely on federal funding. He expects the biggest immediate beneficiaries of such an approach to be the firms developing and operating large-scale AI data centres and the infrastructure and energy providers supporting them.
“To me, the critical question is whether this will actually give Canadian AI companies access to competitively priced compute,” Lau added. “Building 500 MW of capacity in Canada is one thing. Making it accessible and affordable to startups is another. We need both.”
Lau said he is interested to see how the Government of Canada intends to structure these agreements and determine pricing and access, as “those details will ultimately determine how much this initiative moves the needle for Canada’s AI ecosystem.”

articles.title: Los 10 monstruos más icónicos de Godzilla, ordenados
articles.text:
Desde que la primera película de Godzilla viera la luz hace ya más de 70 años, allá por 1954, el mítico monstruo atómico ha recibido todo tipo de adaptaciones. Y en muchas de ellas ha tenido que enfrentarse a otros monstruos absolutamente terribles. Los rivales del Rey de los Monstruos se puede contar por decenas, aunque no todos han gozado de la misma popularidad o de los mismos poderes.
En cualquier caso, está claro que tantas décadas después, el fenómeno sigue muy vivo y atrayendo a los espectadores de todo el mundo. Porque aunque las mejores entregas de Godzilla son las que logran reflexionar sobre temas más profundos y lanzar mensajes y moralejas, lo cierto es que a cualquiera le gusta ver a dos monstruos gigantes pegándose guantazos.
Así las cosas, a continuación ordenamos los 10 kaijus o monstruos más icónicos que se han visto nunca en la franquicia Godzilla. Desde rivales clásicos hasta otros más recientes, pasando por amenazas extraterrestres, robots o criaturas mitológicas.
Gigan
Arrancamos esta lista con Gigan, uno de los monstruos de Godzilla más llamativos y sorprendentes. Este kaiju cibernético fue creado por una raza alienígena para derrotar al lagarto atómico. Y estuvieron a punto de conseguirlo. De hecho, cuenta con el honor de ser el primer personaje que logró hacer sangrar a Godzilla en una película. Se trata de uno de sus adversarios más violentos, brutales y despiadados, en buena parte por sus enormes ganchos metálicos en las manos. Su primera aparición data de 1972.
Rodan
Tras debutar en una película propia en 1956, Rodan se ha visto las caras con Godzilla en varias ocasiones. Aunque en muchas de ellas acaban siendo aliados frente a amenazas mayores como Ghidorah. Este pteranodon mutante se creó originalmente como símbolo de la amenaza atómica de la Unión Soviética y fue muy popular sobre todo en los años 60 y 70, aunque su última aparición es bastante reciente, en Godzilla 2: el rey de los monstruos, de 2019.
Hedorah
Hedorah es, aún a día de hoy, uno de los pocos kajus que han estado a punto de derrotar al mismísimo Godzilla. Se trata de una gigantesca masa de basura y polución que puede disparar rayos y desatar nubes de ácido que desintegran todo a su paso. Su origen es alienígena, es capaz de modificar su cuerpo a voluntad y de adaptarse a entornos terrestres, acuáticos y aéreos. Aunque hace años que no le vemos en ninguna película, sí ha aparecido en varios filmes desde su debut en 1971.
Destoroyah
Alimaña del caos, criatura de los infiernos, Destoroyah siempre podrá presumir de tener uno de los diseños más impresionantes y aterradores de todos los monstruos de Godzilla. Nació por culpa de los humanos, quienes para derrotar al propio Godzilla en la película original de 1954 detonaron el Destructor de oxígeno, un arma masiva que soltaba una violenta sustancia química. Esta sustancia entró en contacto con una colonia de cangrejos prehistóricos, provocando su mutación en diversas formas hasta alcanzar su versión final como este ser del inframundo. Su primera aparición fue en una película de 1995.
Anguirus
Aunque su popularidad ha caído en picado con el paso de las décadas, Anguirus merece estar en esta lista porque fue nada menos que el primer monstruo al que se enfrentó Godzilla. Se trata de un kaiju con forma de dinosaurio mutante, un anquilosaurio con cuernos y un caparazón blindado y con afiladas púas. Su primera aparición fue en 1955 como enemigo pero posteriormente regresaría en múltiples ocasiones como aliado del Rey de los Monstruos.
Mechagodzilla
Acercándonos a los puestos más altos de la lista, tenemos que colocar a Mechagodzilla. Este clon metálico del Rey de los Monstruos ha tenido varios orígenes distintos, desde creación humana hasta alienígena. Apareció por primera vez en 1974 y ya se le ha visto en hasta una decena de películas, la más reciente Godzilla vs Kong de 2021. Lo que siempre se repite es que su poder es casi equiparable al del Titán Alfa, lo que lo convierte en una de las amenazas más temibles de la franquicia.
King Kong
El Rey de las Bestias y de la Isla Calavera. El simio gigante que atemorizó al planeta entero desde lo alto del Empire State. La Octava Maravilla del Mundo. King Kong es uno de los personajes más míticos del cine en general. De hecho, su origen es anterior al de Godzilla, ya que su primera película es aquel legendario filme de 1933. Fue ya en la década de los 60 cuando cruzó caminos con el lagarto. Sus películas se cuentan por decenas, tanto con Godzilla y otros monstruos como también en solitario.
King Ghidorah
Quizá el gran archienemigo de Godzilla, el espeluznante King Ghidorah es conocido como el Rey del Terror por algo. Con un diseño espectacular en forma de dragón amarillo de tres cabezas, apareció por primera vez en 1964 en el cine. Y aún a día de hoy, las nuevas versiones de esta franquicia siguen empleándolo como uno de los kaiju más brutales y poderosos que existen. Su adaptación más reciente es la que puede verse ahora mismo en cines en Godzilla Minus Zero.
Mothra
Mothra es, junto a Godzilla y King Kong, uno de los pocos monstruos que ha sido capaz de liderar sus propias historias tanto en novelas como en varias películas. Es tan popular desde los años 60 que se ganó el apodo de Reina de los Monstruos. Esta gigantesca polilla es, además, uno de los pocos seres de la franquicia que no es resultado de un fallo científico sino que su origen es puro misticismo. Ha aparecido en más de una decena de películas, la última de ellas Godzilla y Kong: El Nuevo Imperio (2024).
Godzilla
Evidentemente, en el número 1 de los monstruos más icónicos de Godzilla solo podía estar él mismo. El Rey de los Monstruos. El lagarto gigante que apareció en cines por primera vez en 1954 y que, desde entonces, lleva aterrorizando a los espectadores durante más de 70 años. De destruir la Tokio de postguerra a salvar a la humanidad, hemos podido verle en todo tipo de aventuras de los más épicas. La última, Godzilla Minus Zero, que acaba de estrenarse en cines.

articles.title: Synaptics sends cease-and-desist order to creator of open-source DisplayLink driver, dares him to publicize its threats — dev reverse-engineers DisplayLink using Claude AI and Rust, Synaptics threatens to bill creator for legal documentation
articles.text:
Synaptics sends cease-and-desist order to creator of open-source DisplayLink driver, dares him to publicize its threats — dev reverse-engineers DisplayLink using Claude AI and Rust, Synaptics threatens to bill creator for legal documentation
The open-source project reportedly violates Synaptics' patents, but its creator begs to differ.
A hobbyist building on open-source driver for DisplayLink hardware received a cease-and-desist from Synaptics, resulting in a lengthy written argument and a threat to sue from the company. According to Phoronix, the Vino driver was “clean-room reverse-engineered” and partly developed using AI and written in Rust. However, even though the person behind the open-source driver, Mike Lothian, did not break the copyright of the code behind the driver, Synaptics argued that his work violates its patent on the DisplayLink technology.
The story began in July 2026, when Lothian reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk, a software engineer working at Synaptics, to help solve a few bugs he’s been encountering. However, Michal Lukaszek, the Strategic Engineering Partnerships Lead at the company, replied a couple of weeks later, saying that the company is concerned that Lothian is attempting to implement the DisplayLink protocol itself, which is a violation of its patents. This resulted in a cease-and-desist letter from Synaptics’ legal department asking him to take down the Vino GitHub repo, among other things.
Synaptics claims that Lothian’s work infringes on two patents: GB2484736 and GB2485613. The former, called Image generation, is about sending screen updates over a general-purpose data network like USB or Ethernet using a specific architecture and compression method, while the latter, called Display control device, details hardware that works with compressed data and only decompresses it as needed. Lothian responded, asking for complete details as to how his work infringes on its patents, but received no response, prompting him to follow up three weeks later.
This was when Synaptics decided to escalate, telling him that it would be billing Lothian “to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts.” Andrew Bateman, the company’s Assistant General Counsel, also added, “By open sourcing our DisplayLink technology for whatever personal reasons you may have as a ‘hobbyist,’ you will be single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology, which we have gone to great lengths and great expense to prevent.”
“If you'd like to notify the media or otherwise publicize our response, I encourage you to do so. We welcome any and all free publicity to let the world (in particular, our competitors and our shareholders) know that Synaptics aggressively defends and protects its DisplayLink IP from all threats of infringement.”
Lothian eventually took the GitHub repo containing the Vino driver offline, but it seems that the fight isn’t over yet. The hobbyist claims that Synaptics’ patents are invalid, saying, “In both cases the independent claims as filed contained no network or transport limitation. The claims were granted only after being amended to add delivery of the display data over a ‘general-purpose data network’ (and, for GB2485613, a ‘transport protocol’ with an ‘unpackaging’ step). That added feature was not new.”
He further argues that even though the company says that DisplayLink isn’t part of the Open Invention Network, Synaptics itself is an OIN licensee. Some say that an OIN license requires that any subsidiary acquired by the original licensee and all its patents would also fall under the company’s OIN license, although Synaptics apparently disagrees with this.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Despite the escalation, Lothian says that he remains open to discussing a sensible resolution. But unless the two parties come to an agreement, it looks like they’re getting ready for a legal face-off. You can see the complete email thread between Lothian and Synaptics in this Linux Kernel Mailing List page and the attached email thread (PDF).
Lothian said that he used a Claude subscription to help out with his cleanroom reverse-engineering efforts, revealing the headache that advanced AI tools pose for tech giants. A user has created a free Adobe Creative Suite clone in Rust using Claude, and was also reportedly working on an open-source office suite and Autodesk tools. Aside from that, we’ve also seen a lot of reverse-engineered games running on platforms they’re not designed for, forcing Anthropic to enforce some limitations on Opus 5.5. There was also concern that the widespread use of AI in chipmaking could result in the inadvertent spread of a copied design or an infringed patent across thousands of chips before anyone catches it.

articles.title: ‘Good luck with that’: Samsung is reportedly testing a paid version of Galaxy AI — but users aren't sold on the proposed benefits
articles.text:
Samsung is reportedly testing a paid version of Galaxy AI — but it promised these 19 features would stay free forever
A trio of new tools and higher usage limits
- Samsung is reportedly testing a paid Galaxy AI Premium service
- It's said to add Gen Video, Bixby Action, and Daily Briefing to Samsung's suite of AI tools
- It will also apparently give you higher usage limits for free tools
It was inevitable that Samsung would start charging for some of its AI tools sooner or later, and lo and behold, the company is reportedly now testing a paid premium version of Galaxy AI.
SammyGuru has found evidence of a Galaxy AI Premium subscription service, which the company looks set to launch into early access soon, and which will seemingly give users access to new AI features, along with four times higher usage limits on existing ones.
Those new features reportedly include Gen Video, which is described as letting you “generate AI videos from your photos,” Bixby Action, which will “automate tasks across your apps,” and Daily Briefing, which doesn’t include a description.
Based on code strings it discovered, SammyGuru expects Galaxy AI Premium to be priced at $4.99 (roughly £3.75 / AU$7.25) per month or $47.99 (around £35 / AU$70) annually, and the service might at least initially be exclusive to the Samsung Galaxy S27 series.
Your existing tools should remain free
The site reports that Browsing Assist, Now Brief, Creative Studio, Smart Capture, Samsung Keyboard, Photo Assist, and Personal Agent are listed within the Galaxy AI Premium interface as tools that will remain free — albeit with usage limits that you’ll have to pay to increase.
But for what it’s worth, Samsung has previously said that all the Galaxy AI features that are "on your phone by default" will always be available for free, and that’s a longer list, which you can find on Samsung’s site. It includes Live Translate, Note Assist, Zoom Nightography, Writing Assist, Chat Assist, Drawing Assist, AI Select, Now Brief, Now Bar, Audio Eraser, Photo Assist, AI Enhanced Wallpaper, Browsing Assist, Voice Recorder, Transcript Assist, Health Assist, Auto Zoom, Auto Framing, and Suggested Replies.
So, assuming Samsung sticks to its word, all of those features will remain free despite the launch of Galaxy AI Premium — though added usage limits could degrade the experience for free users.

Unsurprisingly, this news of a premium subscription hasn’t been met with much fanfare, especially as it sounds like it only adds a few features. On Reddit, comments include “good luck with that,” “not a single one of their AI features [is] worth paying for,” “ewwww, no thanks,” and “dead on arrival,” among other similar sentiments.
Of course, one Reddit thread doesn’t represent the wider world, so it will be interesting to see whether there’s actually much interest in Galaxy AI Premium if and when it launches.

articles.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash.
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.”
Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark (released in April), Spark’s open source twin Glimmer (released in August), and the Wonder frontier model (released in October). The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success, with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.

articles.title: Galaxy AI: Musst Du für deine Samsung-KI bald Geld zahlen?
articles.text:
Galaxy AI: Samsung will für KI-Funktionen offenbar Geld sehen – das steckt im geplanten Abo
Samsung arbeitet offenbar an einem kostenpflichtigen Abo für seine KI-Funktionen auf Galaxy-Handys. Das berichtet das üblicherweise gut informierte Blog SammyGuru. Laut Insiderinfos gibt es bereits ein Angebot namens „Galaxy AI Premium“, das derzeit in einem Early-Access-Programm steckt – also einer frühen Testphase für ausgewählte Nutzer:innen. Laut der zugehörigen App erstattet Samsung derzeit die Beträge, die während des Tests anfallen, nach Programmende noch zurück. Doch dabei wird es wohl kaum bleiben.
Galaxy AI Premium: Was im Test steckt
Eingeführt hatte Samsung sein KI-Paket Galaxy AI mit dem Galaxy S24. Geld verlangt der Hersteller dafür bislang nicht. Wer am Early-Access-Programm teilnimmt, kann bestehende Galaxy-AI-Funktionen wie „Photo Assist“ und „Browsing Assist“ nun in größerem Umfang nutzen. Dazu kommen neue Funktionen, die später in einem Tarif namens „Galaxy AI Max“ landen könnten. Zu diesem Max-Tarif gehört SammyGuru zufolge „Gen Video“: Damit lassen sich aus eigenen Fotos KI-Videos erstellen.
„Bixby Actions“ sollen Aufgaben in anderen Apps automatisieren. Weiterhin gibt’s ein „Daily Briefing“, das der Bericht nicht näher erklärt. Es ist offenbar unabhängig von Samsungs bestehendem „Now Brief“. Möglich ist, dass „Daily Briefing“ ähnlich funktioniert wie Googles Gemini Daily Brief. Googles Funktion liefert jeden Morgen eine persönliche Zusammenfassung.
Galaxy AI: Gratis-Funktionen bekommen wohl ein Limit
Kostenlos bleiben sollen wohl bald nur noch die Standardfunktionen von Galaxy AI: Browsing Assist, Now Brief, Creative Studio, Smart Capture, die Samsung-Tastatur, Photo Assist und der persönliche Assistent. Anders als bisher sollen diese Funktionen aber erstmals ein Nutzungslimit bekommen. Ist das Kontingent aufgebraucht, können Nutzer:innen demnächst ein Guthabenpaket nachkaufen. Das Max-Abo bietet laut Bericht viermal so hohe Limits wie die Gratisvariante. Kosten soll „Max“ rund 5 US-Dollar im Monat oder 48 Dollar im Jahr, umgerechnet etwa 4,50 beziehungsweise 43 Euro. Die Preise stammen allerdings aus Codeleaks in Samsungs App und können sich noch ändern.
Eine Liste kompatibler Geräte gibt es laut SammyGuru bislang nicht. Code in der App deutet aber darauf hin, dass die Nutzung während der Testphase auf die Galaxy-S27-Reihe beschränkt sein könnte. Üblicherweise startet Samsung neue KI-Funktionen auf seinen Topmodellen und bringt sie später per Update der Bedienoberfläche One UI auf weitere Geräte – in diesem Fall vermutlich mit One UI 9.5. Das heißt: Auch Nutzer älterer Geräte müssen gegbeenenfalls ein Abo abschließen, wenn sie alle Features wollen.

articles.title: The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
articles.text:
At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction?
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.
Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.
Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying
The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.
At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom.
And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.
There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.
The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.
When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Koolboks secures credit facility from TLG Capital to fund inventory growth - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian solar-powered cooling startup Koolboks has secured a credit facility from TLG Capital, which it will use to fund inventory and expand its retail and appliance partnerships.
Launched in 2018 by Ayoola Dominic and Deborah Gaël, Koolboks sells solar-powered freezers and appliances to traders, small businesses and corporate customers in Nigeria and beyond. Its products combine solar panels, patented ice-battery technology and connected pay-as-you-go capabilities, allowing them to provide cooling day and night, including during power outages.
Koolboks has sold more than 15,000 units to date and has shipped to over 25 markets. It assembles its products in Lagos and employs around 400 people across Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda. Its Koolbuy platform extends its pay-as-you-go technology to household appliances from major brands.
The new facility combines TLG’s private credit with a guarantee from Cascador, a Nigeria-focused platform for growth-stage founders that recently invested in Koolboks, delivered in partnership with Morgan Stanley. It will give Koolboks the working capital needed to meet growing demand across African markets.
“TLG recognised what our product means for our customers, and found the right kind of financing to back it at the pace that we needed,” said Dominic, who serves as Koolboks’ CEO. “We have serious ambitions to address cold-chain infrastructure across Africa, and this facility gives us the capital and support to chase them.”
The deal takes TLG’s commitments to US$65 million across 16 Nigerian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) over the past two years. It is the second deal TLG and Cascador have completed together in the space of a few weeks, having provided a US$3 million credit facility to Nigeria’s Drive45 Mobility.
“Koolboks has built an incredibly innovative product that addresses critical challenges for individuals and SMEs. Its ability to scale in recent years is a testament to the ingenuity of its cold chain solution,” said Isha Doshi, co-founder and partner at TLG Capital.
Trish Thomas, chief executive officer of Cascador, said her organisation had partnered with Koolboks for several years.
“Their product clearly solves a real problem that exists across countless markets, and they are building at a scale we always believed was possible,” she said. “Cascador finds local champions, but the question is always around positioning them with the right type of financing. With two deals closed in a matter of weeks, TLG and Cascador have identified a scalable product that will allow us to reach the businesses, countries, and sectors that matter most.”

articles.title: Epic Games Store prepara soporte oficial para SteamOS, aunque Fortnite en Steam Deck tendrá que esperar
articles.text:
Epic Games Store prepara soporte oficial para SteamOS, el sistema operativo de Steam Deck y de las nuevas Steam Machine de Valve, dentro del desarrollo de su nuevo launcher multiplataforma. La compañía ya trabaja también en la compatibilidad con otras distribuciones de Linux como Fedora, CachyOS y Omarchy.
Sin embargo, jugar a Fortnite en Steam Deck todavía no tiene fecha, ya que depende de una nueva versión del sistema antitrampas Easy Anti-Cheat que aún está en desarrollo.
Durante años, acceder a los juegos de Epic Games Store en Linux exigía recurrir a herramientas de terceros y soluciones alternativas. Ese panorama empezó a cambiar el mes pasado, cuando la empresa presentó la vista previa de su nuevo launcher y comenzó a dar señales concretas sobre sus planes para 2027.
Soporte de Epic Games para SteamOS y distribuciones Linux
El director de comunicación de Epic Games, Jake Jones, confirmó al medio GamingOnLinux que el nuevo launcher de la compañía será compatible con SteamOS, el sistema que utilizan Steam Deck, Steam Machine y otros PC consolizados portátiles.
Jones explicó que la empresa no se limitará a ese sistema operativo: “El nuevo Epic Games Launcher sigue en fase de vista previa y planeamos dar soporte a tantas distribuciones de Linux como sea posible, incluidas Fedora, SteamOS, CachyOS, Omarchy y más”.
Según indicó el directivo, Epic Games está evaluando distintos métodos de distribución para Linux y contempla volver a ofrecer el launcher en formato AppImage, pensado para facilitar su instalación en diferentes distribuciones de ese sistema.
La vista previa del nuevo launcher se lanzó el 14 de octubre para Windows, macOS y Linux. En este último sistema, por el momento, se descarga como archivo .deb, el formato que utilizan Debian y Ubuntu.
De manera oficial, Epic Games da soporte a Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, Fedora 43 y Debian 12, además de sus versiones posteriores. La compañía aclara que el launcher puede funcionar en otras variantes de Linux, aunque no las ha probado ni garantiza su correcto funcionamiento en ellas.
Para ejecutar títulos desarrollados originalmente para Windows, el programa recurre a GE-Proton, una herramienta que se descarga de forma automática la primera vez que se utiliza y que permite correr esos juegos dentro de Linux.
El medio SteamDeckHQ afirmó haber probado el nuevo launcher de Epic Games en una Steam Deck y señaló mejoras en los tiempos de carga, así como en el diseño general de la aplicación.
Por qué Fortnite no llegará todavía a Steam Deck
Fortnite forma parte de los planes de Epic Games para Linux, aunque la compañía no ha dado una fecha concreta de llegada. Su desembarco en el launcher está condicionado a que esté listo EAC Linux v2, la nueva versión del sistema antitrampas Easy Anti-Cheat.
El objetivo de esta herramienta es frenar a los tramposos de la misma forma en que ya ocurre en Windows, aprovechando los mecanismos de seguridad disponibles en Linux. Para lograrlo, Epic Games necesita coordinarse con los responsables de las distintas distribuciones y conseguir que un número suficiente de ellas sean compatibles con ese nuevo antitrampas.
La estrategia de la compañía contempla probar primero el sistema en Fortnite. Si demuestra eficacia, Epic Games planea ofrecerlo a otros desarrolladores para que puedan integrarlo en sus propios juegos multijugador y así facilitar su llegada a Linux.
Los sistemas antitrampas siguen siendo uno de los principales obstáculos para jugar en Linux. Entre los títulos afectados por esta limitación se encuentran Valorant, Apex Legends, Call of Duty: Warzone, League of Legends, Destiny 2, Escape from Tarkov y Rainbow Six Siege X.
La idea de Epic Games es que su desarrollo sirva como punto de partida para que más estudios lleven sus juegos multijugador a Linux sin renunciar a la protección de sus propios sistemas antitrampas.
Esto no implica que todos los títulos mencionados vayan a volverse compatibles, ya que los que usan otras tecnologías de seguridad necesitarán adaptarlas o migrar a una alternativa compatible.
Las dudas pendientes sobre Fortnite en Steam Deck
Que el nuevo launcher de Epic Games funcione en SteamOS no significa, de forma automática, que también sea posible jugar a Fortnite en Steam Deck. La propia compañía ha reconocido que la portátil de Valve todavía no cumple con los requisitos de seguridad que exige su nuevo sistema antitrampas.
Ambas empresas mantienen conversaciones para intentar resolver esa limitación, aunque no se ha fijado un plazo. Según recoge el medio Videocardz, existen otras incógnitas sin despejar, entre ellas de qué manera se instalará el launcher de Epic Games Store en SteamOS y si contará con una interfaz adaptada a los PC consolizados portátiles.
Tampoco está definido si Fortnite dispondrá de una versión desarrollada de forma específica para Linux o si, en cambio, se apoyará en las herramientas de compatibilidad que permiten ejecutar la versión de Windows dentro de este sistema operativo.

articles.title: « Une partie » de l’argent récupérée : le Crédit Mutuel Arkéa limite la casse après la cyberattaque
articles.text:
Victime d’une cyberattaque d’ampleur la semaine dernière, le Crédit Mutuel Arkéa est parvenu à récupérer une partie de l’argent volé. Sur France 5, Daniel Baal, président de la Confédération nationale du Crédit Mutuel (CNCM), a révélé que le « Crédit Mutuel Arkéa a récupéré aujourd’hui déjà une partie », rapporte l’AFP. Le dirigeant, qui chapeaute les différentes fédérations du Crédit Mutuel, n’a pas précisé le montant récupéré par les équipes d’Arkéa. Il a en revanche confirmé que les pirates avaient bien dérobé plus de 100 millions d’euros. Aux dernières nouvelles, le butin se situe autour des 118 millions d’euros.
À lire aussi : Après les supermarchés, les hackers ciblent les frigos des hôpitaux « pour les vaccins ou les poches de sang »
« Aucun compte de particulier n’a été touché »
Pour rappel, les pirates sont passés par la plateforme d’un prestataire de la banque pour arriver à leurs fins. Ils ont ensuite utilisé le compte propre d’Arkéa pour effectuer des virements vers d’autres banques. L’argent a été promptement converti en cryptomonnaies sur des plateformes spécialisées. Les truands ont surtout converti les fonds en Monero, une crypto qui rend les transactions très complexes à pister. Dès le début de l’affaire, Arkéa a indiqué qu’« une partie des fonds concernés a pu être bloquée ».Certaines plateformes crypto ont en effet réagi à temps pour empêcher les cybercriminels de convertir les fonds et de disparaître dans les limbes de la blockchain. C’est le cas de Crypto.com.
Quelques jours après les faits, Daniel Baal cherche à rassurer les clients de la banque. Le dirigeant a rappelé qu’« aucun compte de particulier n’a été touché ». Même si des comptes de particuliers avaient été piratés, les clients n’auraient rien perdu dans la cyberattaque. En effet, « la banque aurait été largement en mesure de couvrir ce qui serait sorti des comptes des particuliers ».
« C’est effectivement très préjudiciable pour la banque qui est l’objet d’une telle attaque, (…) mais ça ne met en aucune manière en cause la crédibilité, la force du système », martèle Daniel Baal, ajoutant qu’il y a « une telle solidité que cela ne remet absolument rien en cause ». Au-delà, il y aurait « de toute manière la garantie des dépôts ».
Le mystère concernant l’identité des pirates reste entier pour le moment. Daniel Baal se dit dans l’incapacité de « dire si elle est française ou étrangère ». L’attaque n’a d’ailleurs pas été revendiquée à ce stade. Une enquête a été ouverte par le parquet de Paris et confiée à l’Office anti-cybercriminalité (OFAC). Celle-ci doit permettre de remonter jusqu’aux criminels qui ont siphonné les caisses de la banque bretonne. Pour le patron du Crédit Mutuel, l’incident doit néanmoins faire réfléchir tout le secteur : « Ce problème (…) doit servir de leçon. Je suis convaincu que l’ensemble de la place bancaire aujourd’hui regarde ce qui aurait pu éventuellement arriver ».

articles.title: Borja, ingeniero con 10 años de experiencia: “Con una batería de menos de 500 € me puedo desconectar de la red eléctrica”
articles.text:
Borja Pérez prueba una estación de energía portátil de emergencia. En ella mantiene encendidos unos aparatos tras simular un apagón en su vivienda. La unidad principal tiene un coste de menos de 500 euros. Además de esta, hay un módulo adicional. La prueba no demuestra que pueda mantenerse toda la casa siempre encendida.
En este vídeo, Borja - Academia Energía Solar muestra la AFERIY Nomad1800 Pro. Al final aparece el precio de esta unidad principal (479 euros) y con una batería de expansión (849 euros).
Los datos técnicos del fabricante indican que tiene una potencia de salida de 1.800 W. Tiene una capacidad de 1.024 Wh. Utiliza celdas tipo LiFePO4 (litio-ferrofosfato). Anuncian más de 4.000 ciclos de carga/descarga manteniendo el 80 % de capacidad. El peso es de unos 11,6 kg. Sus medidas son de 35 × 22 × 26,3 cm.
Cómo utiliza la batería durante el apagón
Pérez recomienda utilizar las tomas para conectar directamente los equipos clave. Dispone de dos enchufes de CA (220-240 V).
En el primer test se enchufa una lámpara a la batería. Se corta el suministro de la casa. La lámpara sigue funcionando. A continuación, añade un ventilador. El consumo total es de 33 W. Puede usarse una nevera o un microondas, siempre que no se supere la potencia disponible.
En la segunda demostración se conecta la instalación de casa con un cable macho-macho. Borja advierte de los riesgos de este método (las clavijas están en tensión). Es importante aislar la instalación de la red exterior. No debe producirse ninguna realimentación de la batería (por medio de la entrada de carga).
El límite de salida es el mismo (1.800 W). Pérez explica que la estación no aguantaría mayores cargas. No es posible asegurar que pueda abastecer la vivienda durante un tiempo determinado.
La estación puede recargarse con paneles solares (hasta 500 W) y también puede sumarse la entrada de red (hasta 1.500 W en total). Además, es posible cargar en horas valle para luego consumir en horas caras (dependiendo de la tarifa), lo que significa que el gasto no es gratis, pero sí que se puede ahorrar.

articles.title: Cursor and Google join OpenAI in giving coding agents a voice. Claude Code stays silent.
articles.text:
Cursor and Google join OpenAI in giving coding agents a voice. Claude Code stays silent.
Two of the biggest players in the AI coding space are betting that developers want to talk to their agents while they work, with both announcing a two-way voice feature that lets users ask questions and give follow-up instructions without returning to the keyboard.
On Friday, Cursor announced Voice Chat with Agents, a Grok Voice-powered feature that lets developers call an agent and talk through a change. On the very same day, Google announced Voice mode in Antigravity, which uses Gemini Live to bring spoken conversations to its desktop app and command-line tool.
In a blog post announcing the feature, Nick Van der Auwermeulen, developer relations engineer at Google, contrasts the back-and-forth dynamic of human colleagues with the “rhythm” of working with coding agents.
“Some of the best engineering happens out loud,” Van der Auwermeulen writes. “You talk a bug through with a teammate, think out loud in front of a whiteboard, or say ‘wait, try it the other way’ halfway through a pairing session. Working with an agent has mostly had a different rhythm: you type a prompt, the agent works, you read what it did, and you type again.”
“Some of the best engineering happens out loud.”
The longer a job runs, he adds, the more often developers need to check in. A command might be waiting for approval, or a developer might spot a requirement the original instructions missed.
“Each of those moments pulls you back to the keyboard and away from whatever you were looking at,” he continues.
And so Antigravity’s voice mode keeps a live call open while the coding agent works, so the developer can hear an update or approve a command without reaching for the keyboard.
Cursor, for its part, makes a similar pitch for keeping the conversation going.
“Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward,” the company writes.
“Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward.”
Look who’s talking
Antigravity, for the uninitiated, is Google’s agentic software development platform. It debuted alongside Gemini 3 last November, with version 2.0 landing in May replete with a separate desktop app. There’s also a terminal client, Antigravity CLI, and extensions for developers who want to work from editors such as VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and Xcode.
Antigravity is now where Google is consolidating its various coding tools, having moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity in June, while it’s also in the midst of sunsetting Jules, a previously launched background coding agent.
It’s worth noting that Antigravity’s existing dictation feature already turns speech into a written prompt. Now, to start a two-way call in the desktop app, the user clicks the waveform button beside it and tells the agent what they want it to do.
Antigravity replies aloud and keeps the call open while the coding agent works, with the user able to ask how it’s going or give it further instructions. You can also interrupt the agent mid-sentence to ask a question or give it another instruction.
When the agent finishes, its written summary and a button to review the code changes appear in the same chat.
Additionally, voice mode also works in the Antigravity CLI. Users run the /voice live command to start a call, and hear the agent reply while it works away in the terminal.
Coding agents talk back
Cursor, which was acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in August for $60 billion, has followed a similar path toward embracing voice. It added dictation in October 2025, and in release notes last month, the company said it had updated existing voice calls to let agents give short spoken progress updates.
One difference with Cursor’s rollout is where you can call from. Cursor supports voice chat on the web and iOS as well as on desktop, while Google offers it in the Antigravity desktop app and CLI. Cursor’s calls run on Grok Voice, which xAI launched through its API back in April.
“The push now, it seems, is to keep the conversation going after the agent starts work.”
However, Google and Cursor aren’t the first AI companies to bring two-way voice to coding agents. OpenAI launched a Codex desktop app in February with a built-in dictation feature. And as The New Stack reported in July, the company added two-way voice to Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app, letting developers give instructions and check on tasks by speaking. The Codex CLI has offered live voice conversations since the spring, with OpenAI enabling them by default in September.
Anthropic, for what it’s worth, has a voice mode which offers two-way voice functionality inside the Claude app only. In Claude Code, specifically, voice still only goes one way via dictation — the /voice command turns developers’ vocal instructions into prompt text, and the agent replies in writing.
Dictation itself is useful for describing a bug or sketching out a feature aloud, and it’s showing up across the AI coding landscape, from the major AI labs to well-funded startups such as Replit.
The push now, it seems, is to keep the conversation going after the agent starts work, so developers can follow up about a decision, clarify a requirement, or change direction before the work is finished.

Avec le Goat A1600 LiDAR Pro, Ecovacs abandonne l'antenne RTK au profit d'une navigation LiDAR et ajoute un module coupe-bordures. Une formule séduisante pour les grandes pelouses, mais va-t-elle nous débarrasser de la corvée des bords à fignoler ?

articles.title: I tested the Ninja PREPi — a super compact 5-in-1 food processor punches above its weight with brilliant cutting discs, multiple prep bowls, and effortless everyday slicing
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Ninja PREPi comes with several blades and two bowls with lids, so you can slice, chop, puree, shred, and even crinkle cut your foods and then store them away in the bowls.
Reasons to buy
- + Variety of blades for different processing options
- + Quick and easy to use
- + Two bowls with lids included for storage, a smaller and a larger one
- + All parts except motor are dishwasher-safe
- + Fairly compact
Reasons to avoid
- - You may need to run several cycles to fully chop or puree foods
- - Lots of parts to clean
- - Parts don't fully nest for storage
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Ninja PREPi: 30-second review
The Ninja PREPi food processor has power that belies its looks. The 5-in-1 model I tested comes with three different blades for five different food processing options. The included blades include: a chopping/puree blade, a crinkle cut disc, and a reversible slide/shred disc. There is also a six-in-one model that includes a dicing disc, or you can purchase the dicing disc separately if you prefer.
The Ninja PREPi comes with two prep bowls and lids, a five-cup size and a seven-cup size. This allows you to do a big food prep ahead of time and then pop it in the fridge until you need it, without much in the way of extra dishes to wash.
This machine handled all of the tasks we threw at it with ease, including slicing a large bag of potatoes into thin, uniform slices in no time. The one exception was an attempted smoothie, but after all, this isn't a blender.
Like most food processors, the Ninja PREPi has a lot of parts that will need to be taken apart and cleaned after use. Luckily, they can all be cleaned on the top rack of your dishwasher (except for the motor which wouldn't ever need more than a swipe with a damp cloth anyway.)
Ninja PREPi: price and availability
- List price: $179.99 (about £130 / AU$260)
- Available direct from Ninja, and from third-party retailers including Amazon, Target, Walmart, and Best Buy
The Ninja PREPi 5-in-1 Prep System retails for $179.99 and can be found on SharkNinja's website as well as online and brick-and-mortar retailers such as Amazon, Target, Walmart, and Best Buy. That work out at about £130 / AU$260, but at the time of writing it's not yet available in the UK and Australia.
For an extra $50, you can get the 6-in-1 model, which includes a dicing disc. You can also buy the dicing kit separately for $59.99.
The five-in-one model comes in four colorways: Pink Peppercorn (as seen in my photos), Midnight Blue and Mango, Stone and Moss, and Onyx and Apricot. The six-in-one model comes in just one colorway: Copper and Teal.
