- Value score: 4/5
Ninja PREPi: specifications
| Price | $179.99 (about £130 / AU$260) | 
| Prep bowl sizes | 5-cup, 7-cup | 
| Accessories | Two bowls with lids, three multi-purpose blades, 3-part food pusher | 
| Functions | Chop, puree, slice, shred, and crinkle cut | 
| Power | 500 watts | 
| Dishwasher-safe | Yes, all parts except motor | 
Ninja PREPi: design and features
- Three multi-use blades
- Three-part food pusher
- Two bowls with lids for prep and storage
The Ninja PREPi's clever design makes it pretty easy to use. Choose either the larger (seven-cup) or smaller (five-cup) prep bowl, place the spindle inside, and then choose your blade. The blade that sits at the bottom of the bowl is for both chopping and pureeing.
There are also two disc-style blades that sit at the top of the bowl. One disc is for crinkle cutting, the other disc is reversible and can be used for slicing or shredding.
Once you've installed your blade of choice, click the feed chute lid into the bowl and then slide the motor pod into its spot on top of the lid. Turn the dial to your desired mode and press start. It's pretty easy and intuitive to use.
The feed chute lid has a three-part pusher so that you can put in anything from a carrot to a potato and it will be held in place upright for proper slicing or shredding.
Cleanup is pretty easy, just take all of the parts apart. Put the motor pod aside, it doesn't contact food and won't need to be cleaned at all unless you splash something on it, in which case, just wipe it with a very slightly dampened cloth. All of the other parts can be washed on the top rack of the dishwasher (skip the heat dry cycle) or hand-washed very carefully. The blades are sharp!
I couldn't figure out a perfectly neat way to nest and store the Ninja PREPi. I tried a couple of different ways to try and minimize storage space, with the blades all safely enclosed inside the lidded prep bowls.
- Design score: 4.5/5
Ninja PREPi: performance
Crinkle-cut disc
I crinkle cut some carrots with the appropriate disc. I used the narrowest food chute option in order to keep the carrot upright. I turned the dial to the disc setting. The Ninja PREPi took only a few seconds to do the job. I got lots of beautifully cut carrot crinkles, though there were some smaller bits. I planned to make some hummus after so I just left the bits in the bowl to become part of the hummus.
Chop/puree blade
I intended to make hummus, but I accidentally opened a can of white kidney beans, so I made a hummus-like bean dip instead. I incorporated the leftovers from the carrot crinkling I had just done. I started with a chop cycle, which ends automatically. Then I did a low puree cycle, and then a high puree cycle. The result was nice and smooth and so delicious. There were still some chunks in there, but that didn't bother me. I served it with the crinkle-cut carrots and stored the leftovers right in the prep bowl afterwards.

Buy it if
You don't want to dread taking out your food processor
It's easy to put together, use, take apart, and clean. Just pop all the parts in the dishwasher when you're done. I never thought I'd describe a powerful food processor as 'cute' but the Ninja PREPi is just that.
You do food prep
Do you like to prep large batches of food ahead of time? Ninja PREPi makes it easy, since its two prep bowls have lids and double as storage bowls. For example, you could chop up a bunch of veggies in one go and use them for days in your salads, stir-frys, curries, and soups.
You like to entertain
You could easily whip up a party-sized batch of salsa, hummus, or other favorite dip and put it right out in either the five-cup or seven-cup prep bowl. Or put the lid on and bring it to a potluck.

You want a blender/processor combo
This a food processor, full stop. It does offer a lot of flexibility with multi-purpose blades that cover chopping, pureeing, slicing, shredding, and crinkle cuts. Plus the prep bowls that serve as storage. But it's not a blender.
You don't have the space
While it's not overly large, you must have some space designated for the Ninja PREPi motor pod, feed chute lid, three blades, and two large prep bowls.
You don't want to spend the money

articles.title: Security researcher had to jailbreak their car just to update the clock — missing TomTom SD card locked settings menu, custom Linux exploit deployed to adjust daylight saving time
articles.text:
Security researcher had to jailbreak their car just to update the clock — missing TomTom SD card locked settings menu, custom Linux exploit deployed to adjust daylight saving time
By reverse engineering the 2014 Renault Latitude’s firmware and exploiting some vulnerabilities, the researcher fixed their daylight savings time mismatch issue.
A security researcher has revealed how they were forced to update the time on their car infotainment system using reverse engineering techniques. Of course, invasive tech surgery shouldn’t be needed for this kind of basic routine daylight saving time tweaking task. However, Rasmus Moorats’ 2014 Renault Latitude wouldn’t allow him to adjust the time because the original navigation map SD card was missing.
Moorats had been warned. When he bought the used car, the previous owner noted that the SD card would be required to change the time on the in-car display. “I didn't really find that believable,” recalls the security researcher. They seem to have believed it was a skill issue of the prior owner and, because the maps it contained were chronically out of date, they decided to confidently decide they didn’t need the SD card...
The time to adjust non-connected clocks to daylight saving time inevitably came, and Moorats decided to adjust the in-car time display, which had become an hour out of sync. Two settings menus were available via the in-dash system. One allowed the adjustment of Bluetooth and Phonebook settings – clearly no use here. But the second settings menu wouldn’t produce any submenu. Instead, an error message "No maps detected!" popped up every time it was prodded.
With a certain set of skills under his belt, Moorats decided to “just RE it,” where RE = reverse engineer. He found out that the head unit ran a customized Linux-based TomTom operating system on a Samsung SoC. In brief, he extracted and analyzed the firmware, built a QEMU environment for the device, reversed the scripting engine, and uncovered a number of vulnerabilities affecting the system.
The breakthrough came in a brainwave, which seems to stem from experience with kernel exploit techniques during his day job. “Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?” pondered Moorats. The approach worked, rewarding Moorats with root-level access to the infotainment system.
The 2014 Renault Latitude owner subsequently discovered that the date & time settings were in /mnt/flash/settings.dat in a custom binary format. Interestingly, the system “doesn't really have a concept of time zones at all,” observed Moorats in the conclusion of his blog post. “It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180. I changed it to 120.”

articles.title: Binance denies data breach after alleged ShinyHunters claims
articles.text:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has denied claims of a new security breach made by a threat actor using the 'ShinyHunters' handle on a newly emerged underground cybercrime forum.
This follows the threat actor, believed to impersonate the ShinyHunters extortion gang, putting up for sale what they claimed were records of 335 million Binance users.
The allegedly stolen information includes Know Your Customer (KYC) documents, internal infrastructure information, users' account passwords, crypto wallet private keys, transaction history, emails, and phone numbers.
The threat actor also asked for $900,000 for the data, adding that Binance has only "two options left: pay or leak."
However, a Binance spokesperson told BleepingComputer that the company found no evidence of a breach and said that this is likely a scam.
"We have found no evidence that Binance systems, customer KYC data, account credentials, wallet private keys, or internal infrastructure information were compromised in connection with this listing," the Binance spokesperson said.
"Similar past listings have often involved infostealer malware data collected from users' own devices rather than a breach of Binance systems."
Binance also shared some aspects of the breach claim that are inconsistent with how the crypto exchange stores user data. BleepingComputer was told that Binance doesn't hold private keys for users' external wallets, doesn't store user passwords in plaintext, and no longer operates in some of the jurisdictions the threat actor referenced in their cybercrime forum entry.
Other forum users expressed skepticism regarding the threat actor's claims, questioning whether the data they were selling was legitimate and asking: "If you hold the private keys to all the wallets, what would be the justification for selling this?"
While Binance denied these breach claims, it advises customers never to share passwords, 2FA codes, seed phrases, or private keys, and to stay wary of phishing attempts.
This comes after Binance confirmed last week that North Korean hackers tricked an employee into installing malware during a fake job interview, allowing them to steal about $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency after compromising the company's wallet infrastructure.
The FBI has attributed the breach to the TraderTraitor North Korean state-backed hacking group, also tracked as Lazarus Group, Jade Sleet, and APT38.
TraderTraitor was previously linked to other major crypto theft incidents, including the theft of $1.5 billion in the February 2025 Bybit hack.

articles.title: GTA 6 : pas de mode 60 fps, mais une option 40 fps sur PS5 Pro ?
articles.text:
Nous sommes à très exactement 10 jours de la sortie de GTA 6, mais ni Sony, ni Rockstar Games n’ont pris la peine de détailler les différences techniques entre la PS5 et la PS5 Pro. La fiche du jeu sur le PlayStation Store affiche pourtant la mention « PS5 Pro Enhanced », signe que la console la plus puissante de Sony aura droit à des optimisations.
Le pré-téléchargement de GTA 6 ouvre ce mardi 10 novembre 2026 à minuit (heure locale) sur PS5, et les données associées au jeu livrent déjà des détails inédits. Dans un sujet publié sur Reddit ce lundi 9 novembre, un utilisateur partage une capture des métadonnées du jeu. Elles mentionnent une compatibilité HFR (high frame rate, pour haute fréquence d’images) à 120 Hz, qui laisse envisager une option à 40 fps pour la version PS5 Pro de GTA 6.
GTA 6 pourrait tourner à 40 fps sur PS5 Pro
Il faudra sans doute faire une croix sur la possibilité de jouer à GTA 6 en 60 fps, c’est-à-dire avec une meilleure fluidité, même sur PS5 Pro. Si un tel mode existait, Rockstar Games l’aurait vraisemblablement déjà mis en avant. On imagine aussi que le studio n’a pas envie de sacrifier la fidélité visuelle, en dégradant l’image pour gagner en fréquence d’images. Rockstar a ses habitudes. Sur consoles, Red Dead Redemption 2 n’a jamais dépassé les 30 fps. Selon l’analyse de Digital Foundry rapportée par Tom’s Guide, le deuxième trailer de GTA 6 tournait sur une PS5 standard, en 1440p et à 30 fps.
La puissance supplémentaire de la PS5 Pro peut toutefois aider les développeurs à améliorer l’expérience visuelle, avec une bonne optimisation. En cela, un mode 40 fps pourrait être un bon compromis pour GTA 6, à condition, bien sûr, d’avoir un téléviseur compatible avec le 120 Hz. Les métadonnées indiquent par ailleurs que GTA 6 n’est pas compatible avec le VRR (taux de rafraîchissement variable), ce qui n’empêche pas un éventuel mode 40 fps (et que l’on peut forcer sur PS5). Pourquoi 40 fps, et pas 45 ou 50 ? Parce que 40 est un multiple de 120. Un écran 120 Hz affiche donc chaque image trois fois, sans saccade, et le VRR devient inutile.
Les métadonnées montrent aussi que GTA 6 utilisera le PSSR sur PS5 Pro, à savoir la technologie de la console qui s’appuie sur l’IA pour augmenter la définition de l’image. Sur GTAForums, le dataminer Tex2 mentionne une version inédite du PSSR, numérotée 13.60 (contre 13.00A pour des jeux comme Cyberpunk 2077 et Assassin’s Creed Shadows). D’après Tex2, cette version 13.00A correspond au PSSR 2. Sony déploie cette nouvelle version de son outil de mise à l’échelle sur PS5 Pro depuis février 2026, et Resident Evil Requiem a été le premier jeu à en profiter. Le numéro 13.60 laisse penser que GTA 6 utiliserait une version encore plus récente.
Les mêmes métadonnées contiennent enfin une option « High CPU Frequency Mode », qui autorise le processeur de la PS5 Pro à monter en fréquence. Rien de tout cela n’est confirmé. Tex2 rappelle lui-même que proposer un mode 40 fps relève de la décision de Rockstar. De son côté, Sony a promis de détailler les améliorations PS5 Pro de GTA 6 à l’approche de la sortie, le 19 novembre. Il serait temps de clarifier la situation.

articles.title: Switch 2 : Nintendo va enfin laisser offrir des jeux eShop, à quelques semaines de Noël — Frandroid
articles.text:
Jusqu’ici, offrir un jeu dématérialisé à un proche sur Switch tenait du bricolage. Il fallait acheter une carte prépayée eShop ou connaître les identifiants du compte du destinataire, alors que d’autres plateformes comme Steam permettent d’offrir un jeu en cadeau depuis des années. Nintendo s’y met enfin, en deux temps.
Ce lundi 9 novembre, la mise à jour système 23.5.0 a posé les bases sur la Switch 2 comme sur la première Switch. Ensuite, une mise à jour de l’eShop activera la fonction le mardi 17 novembre, « juste à temps pour les fêtes », comme le dit Nintendo lui-même.
Jouez dans les meilleures conditions avec la TV TCL C79L : une expérience gaming fluide en 144 Hz et un son immersif signé Bang & Olufsen, actuellement en promotion !
Dans un billet publié le même jour, Nintendo of America a détaillé le fonctionnement. On pourra offrir des jeux, mais aussi des contenus additionnels (DLC) et des packs de mise à niveau. Il suffit de cocher une case dédiée sur la fiche du produit, puis de choisir le destinataire et la console sur laquelle envoyer le cadeau.
Le cadeau part dès que l’achat est validé, Nintendo ne parle d’aucune option d’envoi programmé. Il s’affiche dans le menu HOME du destinataire, qui peut l’accepter et y jouer aussitôt. Aux États-Unis, la date annoncée est le 16 novembre.
Un cadeau réservé au groupe familial
Le destinataire doit faire partie du groupe familial de votre compte Nintendo. Ce groupe réunit jusqu’à huit comptes et sert déjà à partager l’abonnement familial Nintendo Switch Online. Impossible donc d’envoyer un jeu à un ami qui n’y figure pas. Nintendo ajoute trois limites :
- certains produits ne pourront pas être offerts ;
- les comptes supervisés, c’est-à-dire les comptes enfants gérés par le contrôle parental, ne peuvent pas envoyer de cadeau ;
- le nombre de cadeaux achetés sur une période donnée est plafonné.
Nintendo n’a pas encore donné le plafond exact, la liste des produits exclus ni les pays concernés.
La 23.5.0 apporte aussi autre chose que les cadeaux. Sur Switch 2, les réglages d’accessibilité peuvent désormais être configurés dès la première mise en route de la console. Le portugais du Portugal rejoint également les langues de la synthèse vocale, qui lit l’interface à voix haute, et de la fonction du GameChat qui transforme les messages écrits en voix. Pour le reste, Nintendo évoque des « ajustements et corrections généraux », sans plus de détail.
Comment être prêt pour le 17 novembre
Si votre console est connectée à Internet, la mise à jour 23.5.0 se télécharge toute seule. Sinon, lancez-la depuis les Paramètres de la console, rubrique Console, puis Mise à jour de la console. Si vous n’avez pas encore de groupe familial, créez-le dès maintenant depuis votre compte Nintendo et ajoutez-y les proches à qui vous voulez offrir un jeu.
Un petit geste pour Frandroid ? Abonnez-vous à Frandroid sur Google pour ne manquer aucun de nos articles.
Et le second meilleur moyen de nous donner un coup de pouce, c’est d’ajouter Frandroid à vos sources préférées sur Google.

articles.title: Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
A banking operations employee starts the morning by asking an internal AI assistant which documents are needed to open a business account. The answer is in a single checklist. A few hours later, the same employee asks how those requirements differ across sole proprietorships, LLCs, and partnerships with multiple owners. That answer is spread across several policy guides. One assistant has to handle both questions, quickly and cheaply for the first and thoroughly for the second. Applications need a way to match retrieval effort to each request without building separate systems for simple and complex questions.
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream. With single-shot RAG, the service searches your knowledge bases once and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate an answer from the passages it finds. With retrieval-only requests, the service returns the matching passages without generating an answer, so your application or the user can work with the source text directly. These modes join the existing agentic retrieval, where the service plans and runs multiple searches before answering. You can now use the same API for both of the employee’s questions: single-shot RAG for the checklist lookup and agentic retrieval for the cross-policy comparison.
In this post, we explain how the new settings work and when to use each mode. We use an illustrative internal banking policy assistant to show how single-shot RAG handles direct questions and how agentic retrieval supports comparisons across policy documents. We also show how to configure retrieval-only requests when an employee needs to review source passages rather than a generated answer.
Key benefits
Agentic retrieval helps an assistant answer questions that require more than one search. A foundation model breaks the question into sub-queries, searches the relevant knowledge bases, and evaluates whether the results provide enough information to answer the original question. If it identifies gaps, it can refine the search and retrieve additional evidence, within the configured iteration limit.
For application builders, this provides several benefits:
- Better support for multi-part questions – Targeted searches can find evidence for each part of a question instead of relying on one search to cover everything. In the banking example, the assistant can look up requirements for sole proprietors and LLCs separately before comparing them.
- Follow-up searches when information is missing – The planner can use what it finds to decide what to search for next. It can also retrieve a full document when a passage doesn’t provide enough context, helping address gaps that a single retrieval might leave unresolved.
- Answers with supporting evidence – When response generation is enabled, the service combines retrieved information into an answer with citations. Trace events show the planning and retrieval steps, helping developers inspect how the answer was produced.
- Less custom orchestration – The service manages the planning, retrieval, evaluation, and response-generation workflow through one API. Applications don’t need to implement their own loop to coordinate these steps.
These agentic capabilities remain valuable for complex questions. For straightforward lookups, applications also need a way to retrieve and answer without additional planning. The expanded maxAgentIteration range closes that gap. With one parameter, you can choose one of three modes for each request:
- Retrieval-only returns passages without generating an answer.
- Single-shot RAG retrieves once and generates an answer, with no planning rounds.
- Agentic retrieval plans and runs multiple searches for complex questions.
Single-shot RAG uses one foundation model call to generate the answer, which can reduce latency and model usage compared with agentic retrieval. Retrieval-only requests make no foundation model calls. You can balance speed and answer quality for each request, without integrating a second API or maintaining separate code paths for simple and complex queries.
How retrieval iterations are counted
Before walking through the new values, it helps to anchor on how iterations are counted, because that is what makes the behavior predictable.
One iteration equals one foundation model call. The loop always ends with a single answer-generation call. A value of n buys up to n minus 1 agentic planning rounds, with the last iteration reserved for generating the response. Each planning round is one query rewrite plus a retrieval. More iterations means more planning rounds and better results on hard questions. Fewer iterations means lower latency.
One thing that doesn’t count: speculative retrieval. The initial retrieval that runs ahead of the first planning step is retrieval, not an iteration. It never counts against your maxAgentIteration value, and it only ever makes a request faster. Keep that distinction in mind as you read the following values.
What’s new
The range is now 0–5.
All three modes support multiple knowledge bases, including maxAgentIteration=0 and 1. Single-shot retrieval doesn’t mean a single knowledge base. Agentic mode adds query decomposition, evidence evaluation, and iterative searches, rather than exclusive access to multiple knowledge bases.
maxAgentIteration = 1: Basic RAG (the headline use case)
This is single-shot RAG: one retrieval, then one answer. No agentic planning, no query rewriting. The API retrieves once against your query and generates a response grounded in those passages. This is the retrieve once, then generate a response pattern that previously wasn’t expressible through this API.
Pair it with generateResponse=true to get a generated answer grounded in the retrieved passages. If you only need the passages, use maxAgentIteration=0 instead, as described in the next section.
If most of your traffic is well-scoped, direct questions, this is likely the setting you want as a default.
maxAgentIteration = 0: Passages only, zero LLM calls
This runs one guaranteed retrieval and generates nothing. No foundation model is invoked. It is equivalent to calling the Retrieve API directly. This makes it most useful for callers who are already standardized on AgenticRetrieveStream and would rather change a parameter than switch APIs.
Because no large language model (LLM) is called, there is no answer to generate. Setting generateResponse=true at this value is invalid and returns a 4xx error, because generating an answer requires an LLM call.
maxAgentIteration = 2 to 5: Agentic mode, unchanged
In agentic mode, a foundation model breaks complex questions into focused sub-queries and retrieves evidence in multiple steps, including across multiple knowledge bases. It evaluates the retrieved information and can refine its searches when evidence is missing. This approach can improve retrieval accuracy for multi-part and comparative questions that a single search might not fully address.
With response generation enabled, a value of n allows up to n minus 1 planning rounds before generating an answer grounded in the retrieved evidence. Existing requests using values from 2–5 retain their current behavior.
Choosing a value
One way to reason about it:
| maxAgentIteration | What you get | Best for | 
| 0 | One retrieval, no generation, zero LLM calls | Passage retrieval. Callers standardized on this API who want Retrieve-style behavior | 
| 1 | One retrieval plus one answer | Single-shot RAG for direct, well-scoped questions | 
| 2 to 5 | Up to n minus 1 planning rounds, then an answer | Multi-part, comparative, exploratory, and cross-knowledge-base questions | 
The lower the value, the faster and more predictable the call. The higher the value, the more the planner can decompose and refine on genuinely hard questions. Start low for simple traffic, raise it when accuracy on complex queries matters more than latency.
In practice: An internal banking policy assistant
Consider a fictional bank whose operations team uses an internal assistant backed by a knowledge base of account-opening procedures, documentation checklists, and policy guides. Employees use the assistant to locate and understand the bank’s documented requirements. The following examples illustrate how the application can select a retrieval mode for each workflow. They don’t describe a customer deployment or measured results.
The following diagram shows how the banking assistant selects a retrieval mode for each request.
An employee asks the assistant a question. The application chooses a retrieval mode and sends the request to AgenticRetrieveStream. With single-shot RAG, the service searches the knowledge base once and generates an answer. With agentic retrieval, the service splits the question into parts, searches several times, and then generates an answer with citations. With retrieval-only, the service returns source passages without generating an answer. The following sections explain each mode.
Answer a direct documentation question
An employee asks, “What documents are required to open a business checking account for a sole proprietor?” In this example, the bank maintains a dedicated checklist that contains the answer. The application sets maxAgentIteration=1 and generateResponse=true to retrieve relevant passages and generate a response, without query rewriting or agentic planning.
This is the single-shot RAG pattern: one retrieval, followed by one answer-generation call. It avoids a planning step when the question and supporting content are already well scoped.
Compare requirements across policy documents
Another employee asks, “How do account-opening requirements differ for sole proprietors and LLCs, and what additional checks, if any, apply to nonresident owners under our policy?” Answering this question might require information from separate procedures and ownership-verification guides.
For this workflow, the application can set maxAgentIteration=4 and generateResponse=true, allowing up to three planning rounds before generating an answer. The planner can break the question into sub-queries, retrieve relevant evidence, and refine its search if information is missing. The appropriate iteration limit should be evaluated against representative questions rather than assuming that a higher value always produces a better answer.
Show source passages without generating an answer
An employee reviewing an account-opening procedure might want the relevant policy text instead of a generated summary. The application sets maxAgentIteration=0 and generateResponse=false to return passages with no language model calls. It can then display those passages and their source references for the employee to review.
All three workflows use AgenticRetrieveStream. The application chooses the iteration limit and whether to return a generated answer. Selecting the mode is application logic, not automatic routing provided by this parameter. The assistant supports policy lookup and comparison. It doesn’t approve accounts or replace the bank’s review and authorization processes.
Solution overview
The following example shows a complete agentic request. The sections after it adapt it for single-shot RAG and retrieval-only modes.
Select a retrieval mode for the banking assistant
The sample code demonstrates the three workflows using fictional policy documents.
Example: Single-shot RAG
Setting up basic RAG is a one-line change from an agentic call. Set maxAgentIteration to 1 and keep response generation on.
You consume the stream the same way you always have. The difference is what’s in it: a single retrieval and one grounded answer, with no planning trace events in between.
Example: Passages only
For retrieval with no generation, set maxAgentIteration to 0. Response generation must be off at this value.
This returns the deduplicated source passages with no generated answer. The retrieval behavior matches a direct Retrieve call, but the response format differs: passages arrive in the stream’s result event without score or location fields.
Conclusion
With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can now combine single-shot RAG, agentic retrieval, and retrieval-only requests in one assistant through AgenticRetrieveStream. In the banking example, you can answer the account-opening checklist question with maxAgentIteration=1 and response generation enabled, which produces an answer without planning calls. For the comparison across business structures, you can set maxAgentIteration=4 to allow additional searches before the response is generated. When an employee needs to read the policy text, you can set maxAgentIteration=0 with response generation disabled to return passages without calling a language model. Your application selects the mode, and employees keep using the same assistant.
To adopt the new modes in an existing application, start with a representative set of questions and expected answers from your own documents. Compare single-shot RAG with your current agentic configuration using the same knowledge base. Measure response latency and request cost, and check whether answers are correct and supported by the retrieved passages. Include questions whose answers span several documents, and questions the documents can’t answer, so a faster response doesn’t hide missing evidence or unsupported conclusions.
Use those results to choose the lowest iteration limit that meets each workflow’s quality requirements. Keep agentic retrieval where additional searches improve the answer, use single-shot RAG where one retrieval is sufficient, and disable generation when the task is source review. Existing requests with values from 2–5 remain unchanged, so you can introduce the new modes selectively rather than redesigning the entire application.
To get started, configure maxAgentIteration and generateResponse in your requests using the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference, then evaluate the settings against your application’s questions and response-time targets. To learn more about the service, visit the Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base service page.

articles.title: Black Friday : Amazon fait tomber ce PC portable ASUS de 16 pouces à 549,99€
articles.text:
Pour son Black Friday, Amazon baisse aussi le prix des PC portables du quotidien, ceux qu’on achète pour les cours, le télétravail ou la bureautique familiale. L’ASUS Vivobook 16 avec Core i5-1235U et 512 Go de SSD passe à 549,99 €, une offre solide pour travailler sur grand écran, si vous acceptez une dalle aux couleurs ternes et 8 Go de mémoire.
L’ASUS Vivobook 16 vise la bureautique et les usages courants, pas le jeu ni la création. Il associe un écran de 16 pouces au format 16:10, un processeur Intel Core i5-1235U, 8 Go de mémoire vive et un SSD de 512 Go, sous Windows 11 Famille. Amazon le propose à 549,99 € pour le Black Friday, soit 125,97 € de moins que son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, fixé à 675,96 €.
L’offre vise d’abord les étudiants, les familles et les télétravailleurs qui veulent une grande surface d’affichage sans dépasser 600 €.
Chez Amazon, l’ASUS Vivobook 16 avec Core i5-1235U et 512 Go de SSD tombe à 549,99 € pour le Black Friday, contre 675,96 €.
Pourquoi choisir l’ASUS Vivobook 16 ?
- Un écran 16:10 qui laisse de la place : La dalle IPS de 16 pouces en 1 920 x 1 200 pixels affiche davantage de lignes qu’un écran 16:9 de même largeur, ce qui se remarque dans un tableur ou un long document. Son traitement antireflet limite la gêne sous un éclairage de bureau.
- Un clavier complet : Le grand châssis laisse la place à un pavé numérique, appréciable pour les tableurs, les comptes du foyer ou la saisie de notes. La course de 1,35 mm annoncée par ASUS convient aux longues sessions de frappe.
- Un stockage confortable : Les 512 Go de SSD NVMe laissent de la marge pour Windows, les logiciels et plusieurs années de documents et de photos.
Des cours au télétravail, ce que ce 16 pouces fait bien
Le Core i5-1235U réunit dix cœurs, dont deux performants et huit économes, avec une fréquence qui grimpe jusqu’à 4,4 GHz. C’est une puce de 2022 calibrée pour la navigation, la suite Office, les visioconférences et le multitâche léger, exactement le terrain de ce Vivobook. La webcam 720p dispose d’un cache physique, pratique pour couper l’image entre deux réunions. Deux USB-A, un USB-C, un USB 2.0 et un HDMI 1.4 évitent les adaptateurs.
Le profil idéal est celui d’un étudiant ou d’un parent qui cherche un ordinateur polyvalent, surtout utilisé sur un bureau. Avec 1,88 kg et une batterie de 42 Wh, il se transporte, mais ce n’est pas un compagnon de voyage léger. La partie graphique Intel Iris Xe ne le destine ni aux jeux récents ni au montage vidéo exigeant. Les 8 Go de mémoire deviennent justes quand les onglets et les applications s’accumulent, mais la fiche technique d’ASUS prévoit un emplacement SO-DIMM pour monter jusqu’à 16 Go.
Que vaut-il face aux PC portables plus récents ?
Dans notre comparatif des meilleurs PC portables, nous conseillons 16 Go de mémoire vive pour un ordinateur appelé à durer. Le Vivobook 16 n’en a que la moitié, et sa puce de 12e génération n’embarque pas de NPU, ce qui l’exclut des fonctions Copilot+ de Windows 11. L’Acer Aspire 14 AI, notre choix abordable dans ce guide, coche ces cases avec un écran OLED, mais s’affiche autour de 1 000 €. À 549,99 €, l’ASUS joue une autre carte : la grande diagonale et le pavé numérique pour un budget contenu.
✅ Les points forts
- Écran 16 pouces au format 16:10 en 1 920 x 1 200 pixels
- Pavé numérique et webcam avec cache physique
- SSD de 512 Go et Windows 11 Famille
- 125,97 € sous son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours
- Mémoire extensible jusqu’à 16 Go selon ASUS
❌ Les limites
- Dalle limitée à 45 % NTSC et 300 nits selon ASUS
- 8 Go de mémoire vive seulement à l’achat
- Processeur de 2022, sans NPU pour les fonctions Copilot+
- 1,88 kg et batterie de 42 Wh, peu taillé pour le nomadisme
Avant de commander l’ASUS Vivobook 16 à 549,99 € chez Amazon, vérifiez que la fiche mentionne bien la référence X1605ZA-MB392W.
À 549,99 €, l’ASUS Vivobook 16 offre beaucoup de surface pour le prix : un écran 16:10, un clavier complet et 512 Go de stockage. La baisse de 125,97 € se mesure face à son prix le plus bas du mois écoulé, pas à un prix conseillé gonflé, ce qui lui donne du poids. Pour la bureautique, les cours en ligne et la gestion des papiers de la maison, la configuration répond présent.
Ceux qui retouchent des photos ou regardent beaucoup de vidéos seront moins séduits par une dalle aux couleurs ternes, qu’aucune remise ne corrige. Si vous comptez garder l’ordinateur cinq ans ou plus, prévoyez l’ajout d’une barrette mémoire, ou visez directement 16 Go. Pour un usage sédentaire et un budget serré, c’est en revanche une machine cohérente.
Comment profiter des offres exclusives du Black Friday ?
Durant tout le mois de novembre, Clubic vous propose chaque jour des sélections thématiques regroupant les meilleures offres à saisir en direct.
Retrouvez tous les bons plans du Black Friday 2026 sur la page dédiée à l'événement.
Pour les aficionados de X, n'hésitez pas à suivre notre compte Clubic Bons Plans pour être au courant en direct des meilleures offres.

articles.title: „Bei 42 Grad ist Ende“: Expertin erklärt, wie gut sich Städte an Hitze anpassen können
articles.text:
„Bei 42 Grad ist Ende“: Expertin erklärt, wie gut sich Städte an Hitze anpassen können
Bereits 2008 hat die damalige Bundesregierung eine Klimaanpassungsstrategie entwickelt. Seit zwei Jahren hat sie Gesetzescharakter. Sie schreibt unter anderem Ländern und Kommunen vor, den Klimawandel bei allen Planungen zu berücksichtigen. Was hat das Gesetz bisher bewirkt und wie ließe sich die Klimaanpassung verbessern? Anja Bierwirth beschäftigt diese Frage schon lange. Sie hat Umweltwissenschaften und Architektur studiert und arbeitet seit 2008 am Wuppertal Institut für Klima, Umwelt, Energie – einem renommierten Thinktank für Nachhaltigkeitsforschung. Dort leitet sie den Forschungsbereich Stadtwandel. Ihre Arbeitsschwerpunkte sind kommunale Energie- und Klimaschutzpolitik, Gebäudeenergieeffizienz sowie nachhaltige Stadtentwicklung. Im Interview spricht sie über verpasste Chancen und Möglichkeiten bei der Klimaanpassung.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 8/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns mit den Folgen des Klimawandels und wie wir uns an Hitze, Dürre und Überschwemmungen anpassen sollten. Das Heft ist ab sofort im Zeitschriftenhandel erhältlich und lässt sich in unserem Online-Shop bestellen.
MIT Technology Review: Können Sie sich an einen Zeitpunkt erinnern, bei dem Sie das Gefühl hatten: Jetzt kippt die Diskussion über den Klimawandel von der Minderung der CO₂-Emissionen zur Anpassung?
Anja Bierwirth: Ein recht prägnantes Jahr war der Hitzesommer 2003. Es war das erste Mal, dass man so viele Hitzetote hatte und das Thema eine große mediale Aufmerksamkeit erreichte. Seitdem ist das Interesse immer wieder aufgeflammt, wenn es eine Hitzewelle oder eine Hochwasserkatastrophe gab. Sobald die vorüber waren, war auch das Thema wieder weg.
Lassen sich Anpassungsmaßnahmen leichter durchsetzen als Minderungsmaßnahmen? Schließlich ist der Nutzen konkreter spürbar – zum Beispiel beim Hochwasserschutz.
Ein höherer Deich ist eine sehr griffige Geschichte, die ist noch relativ gut umzusetzen. Aber über die Resilienz von Städten insgesamt zu sprechen, ist schon etwas zäher. Vielleicht liegt das auch daran, dass wir nicht gut darin sind, den Bestand umzubauen. Wir sind besser darin, neue Dinge zu bauen.
Seit 2008 gibt es die Anpassungsstrategie des Bundes, seit 2024 ein Anpassungsgesetz. Dadurch sollte Klimaanpassung bei Planungen eigentlich immer gleich mitgedacht werden.
Das wäre schön.
Aber sie wird wenigstens öfter mitgedacht als früher?
Ja, das würde ich so sagen. Dazu kommen noch Förderprogramme, etwa für die Begrünung von Städten, andere Fruchtfolgen in der Landwirtschaft oder hitzeresiliente Wälder. Die haben schon für Aufmerksamkeit gesorgt. Die Umsetzung ist aber nach wie vor optimierungsbedürftig.

articles.title: Money Fellows took an old savings habit and built a business
articles.text:
The global tech industry likes an old habit best when it can kill it. Cash is going. Brick-and-mortar branches are finished. The informal economy is waiting to be formalised, and all it takes is a platform and a convincing pitch.
That was Ahmed Wadi’s proposition in 2016. Egyptians already had a way to save and borrow. They pooled money, took turns collecting it, and relied on social obligation to keep everyone paying. The arrangement had survived without venture capital funding or a credit engine that powers modern finance.
Perhaps it deserved an upgrade.
Ten years after Wadi began building Money Fellows, an Egyptian fintech, much of its work has involved discovering how difficult that idea becomes when participants no longer know one another.
And, having attracted over one million registrations, the company has only recently taken its model beyond Egypt, into Morocco, with ambitions to explore more markets in the coming years.
Looking at Africa’s fintech ecosystem in the past decade, there are faster ways to grow a company’s operating markets. But Wadi wanted to understand the business first.
“We were very focused on really understanding and cracking the model on a local scale before we start distracting ourselves and launching other countries,” he recalled in an interview with TechCabal.
This sounds sensible. It also sounds considerably easier in retrospect.
An old habit, a new business
Money Fellows began with a problem Wadi encountered while living in Germany: accessing credit without an established local credit history. Back in Egypt, friends and families had long solved similar problems through gameya, the local version of a rotating savings and credit association.
It is very straightforward. Ten people contribute the same amount monthly. One receives the entire amount. The following month, someone else receives it. After ten months, everyone has collected once.
The model is common across Africa, including in East Africa, where savings groups known as chamas use a similar arrangement.
The person paid first has effectively borrowed against future contributions. The person paid last has saved through instalments. Between them are people planning a wedding, paying school fees, or making a purchase that will not wait for their salary to catch up.
He began working on the idea with a close friend alongside their jobs. It was their third startup together. In 2024, an accelerator placement at Startupbootcamp FinTech, a global network of industry-focused accelerators, took Wadi to London; his co-founder could not relocate with him.
London offered Wadi communities familiar with savings circles, something Germany could not. But the approach differed along ethnic lines. African communities organised their circles one way. Indian participants sometimes bid for their turn, while Arab participants agreed the order in advance.
Pooling money was common, but the rules varied.
During a visit home, Wadi took a booth at a startup event in Egypt to introduce Money Fellows to attendees. Describing it as gameya online—an online savings circle—was enough for people to understand the proposition. Their questions concerned trust, regulation, and payment channels, rather than how the savings model worked.
For Wadi, those conversations suggested Egypt offered customers who already understood the arrangement he wanted to digitise.
These were substantial questions. At least they were questions about using the product.
Trust beyond family
Building in Egypt meant working with an existing habit rather than financing the education of an entirely new market. Yet the old system’s most important feature was also the hardest to reproduce.
“People have always been used to do it with friends and family and aunts and uncles and neighbours,” Wadi said. On his platform, “people don’t necessarily need to know each other”.
That change expanded the potential pool of participants. It also transferred responsibility. If a stranger failed to contribute, a customer would have little interest in hearing that the app had successfully connected them.
Money Fellows says it assesses participants’ ability to pay and covers missed contributions to ensure other members receive their payouts. That convenience can sometimes come with an obligation on the company’s own finances.
In the early years, Egypt had no dedicated rules for digital savings circles, according to Wadi. Money Fellows had to work with regulators to develop a framework while persuading customers to entrust their savings to a platform that lacked a clear regulatory stamp of approval.
“You’re building something with so much passion every day that you have the risk of being shut down at any point,” he said.
The company relied on keeping its promises and on satisfied customers recommending it. Referrals could carry reassurance that advertising could only purchase the appearance of. But they took time.
A founder adapting a successful foreign business has a useful opening argument: it works elsewhere. Wadi had a familiar financial practice, but no equivalent company whose success could settle questions about his particular approach.
“No regulations, no benchmark, no success stories,” he said.
At points, Money Fellows struggled to raise enough money to sustain its operations. Investors were wary of backing a business without a clear regulatory framework or successful examples elsewhere to demonstrate that its model could work. Wadi sold personal possessions to keep it going, while the company cut staff to reduce costs.
Outside capital eventually gave the business room to develop. In June 2020, Money Fellows raised $4 million from Partech and Sawari Ventures. The announcement put its verified active user base above 150,000 and already discussed expansion across Africa. In October 2022, a $31 million Series B first close brought backing from CommerzVentures, Middle East Venture Partners and Arzan Venture Capital, among others.
Expansion across Africa and Asia remained the ambition, but Wadi wanted to establish that the model worked in Egypt before taking it elsewhere. Each new market would require Money Fellows to understand local savings habits, find suitable banking partners and establish a regulatory path. Morocco is its first test of that approach.
Making the circles pay
The delay in expanding beyond Egypt explains Money Fellows’ decade. Wadi says the company chose to grow carefully. It also needed to work out how to make each savings circle profitable before taking the model abroad.
More users did not necessarily mean a more profitable business. Early withdrawals attracted fees, while users who waited could receive incentives. If too many chose the later slots, the incentives could eat into the fees.
The breakthrough, Wadi said, was to determine whether each circle made money, rather than looking at each customer individually.
“If you oversell the ones with incentives versus the fee, the economics change,” he said.
The calculation was more important than the founder’s ambition. Money Fellows had to decide which circles to open, which slots to offer, and how to fill them. The fees had to cover incentives, the cost of attracting customers and processing payments, and losses from missed contributions.
Assessing borrowers was another challenge. Wadi said Money Fellows initially lacked access to the credit data other lenders used. It built its own system using information such as browsing behaviour, the type of phone a customer owned, and their location.
Removing the need for participants to know each other created a considerable need for the platform to know them.
By May 2025, another $13 million funding round, co-led by Al Mada Ventures and DPI Venture Capital through the Nclude Fund, brought total investment to more than $60 million, according to investor Partech. The announcement reported more than 8.5 million users.
In October 2025, Money Fellows reported around 350,000 monthly active users, more than $1.5 billion in cumulative transaction value and over two million completed savings groups. The company also says it is profitable.
The test beyond Egypt
After this success, the next question was whether this model could travel across the border.
In April 2026, Money Fellows and Wafacash, a financial services subsidiary of Morocco’s Attijariwafa Bank Group, announced a partnership to digitise the country’s daret savings system, following regulatory approvals from Bank Al-Maghrib. Wafacash brought local infrastructure, distribution and customer relationships. Money Fellows brought the technology developed through its Egyptian operation.
Wadi sees cultural similarity as one attraction. He also wanted to spread the company’s exposure after experiencing currency devaluations in Egypt. An investor with local connections helped make Morocco a practical choice.
The approach reflects a lesson he wishes he had learnt earlier: a banking partner’s quality and incentives matter from the beginning. In Morocco, he said, the company arranged a partnership with financial interests more closely aligned with its own.
He wants the first expansion to yield a method applicable elsewhere. Broader expansion could follow from the end of 2027, he said, once the company is comfortable with the experience.
There is a temptation to make all this a vindication of patience. Wadi’s own assessment is less tidy.
Asked what he would change, he said he would assemble stronger partners earlier. He would pay more attention to banking relationships. And, given the opportunity, he would raise more money than he thought he needed.
The founder who spent years emphasising efficiency now recognises the value of room for experiments to fail.
“With the learnings, it could have been a lot shorter, a lot faster, perhaps,” he said.
Wadi began with an old idea that seemed ready for software. Ten years later, Money Fellows has investors, a second market, and a clearer understanding of what it takes to make that idea work between strangers.
The heaviest task was building the trust friends and relatives bring, while making the economics work for the company organising them. Morocco will test how much of that knowledge travels.

articles.title: School buses are becoming AI-powered ticket machines, generating millions from drivers who fail to stop
articles.text:
A hot potato: AI cameras are turning America's school buses into mobile traffic enforcement systems, and there's plenty of money to be made in this business. Manufacturers say the technology protects children without costing taxpayers, but an investigation questions whether the flood of tickets is delivering the promised safety benefits.
An investigation by Bloomberg and Type Investigations earlier this year reported that BusPatrol equipped around 35,000 buses across 24 states. Its cameras flag suspected illegal passing, with police reviewing evidence before tickets are issued.
In Montgomery County, Maryland, the investigation tallied more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in issued fines. Those are some stunning figures, but the research found little reduction in violations and no evidence of fewer collisions near stopped buses.
Between fiscal years 2019 and 2024, the county retained around $18.5 million from collected fines while setting aside roughly $40 million for manufacturer BusPatrol. The company says its financial arrangements cover installation and operating costs, and that it absorbs shortfalls when camera expenses exceed violation revenue.
The technology itself does more than photograph license plates. Allentown School District describes a process combining footage, GPS coordinates, and timestamps. AI filters incidents before a trained specialist builds an evidence package for police. All parties involved insist that human review remains part of the process, rather than software simply mailing out fines.
Other suppliers are expanding, too. FOX 35 reported in August that Florida's Osceola County school board approved a Verra Mobility contract with no upfront district cost. The company and district will split program revenue equally, with law enforcement confirming suspected violations.
Verra says 98% of cited drivers don't reoffend and citations fall by around 70% over a school year. It's worth remembering that those are the company's claims, and a low repeat-offender rate alone doesn't establish how much safer a bus stop becomes.
The latest example of the technology's use comes from southeast Idaho. Local News 8 reported that Teton Stage Lines is working with AngelTrax on AI detection of drivers passing stopped school buses. The organizations are working with lawmakers to allow the technology statewide.
This is another example of AI cameras being used for more than reading license plates, though other cases can be just as controversial. It was reported in September that Dallas has mounted AI cameras on garbage trucks to flag property violations and assign homes a "blight score," prompting concerns about privacy and unfair fines.
As for Flock and its AI cameras, the list of grievances against the firm is a long one. The most recent example was the company replacing its cameras in a city that rejected them, and it's not the first time this has happened.

articles.title: Brasil recebe a primeira TV com sistema Fire OS, da Amazon • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Brasil recebe a primeira TV com sistema Fire OS, da Amazon
Modelo da Hisense é ofertado em quatro tamanhos de tela: 43, 50, 55 e 65 polegadas.
Um novo sistema de smart TVs começa a desembarcar no Brasil: o Fire OS, da Amazon, que na prática dispensa o uso de dispositivos externos como o Fire TV Stick. A chinesa Hisense iniciou, de forma discreta, as vendas da linha QD6SF. São quatro tamanhos de tela e preços que começam na faixa dos R$ 2 mil.
A novidade amplia o catálogo da fabricante no país. Quando chegou ao mercado, em 2024, a marca apostou nos sistemas Vidaa OS e Google TV. Agora, passa a oferecer também a plataforma da Amazon.
A nova plataforma reúne aplicativos de streaming, recomendações de filmes e séries e integração com a assistente virtual Alexa. Com comandos de voz, os usuários podem pesquisar conteúdos, abrir aplicativos e controlar dispositivos domésticos inteligentes compatíveis, como lâmpadas e câmeras de segurança.
O Fire OS já é utilizado em televisores vendidos em outros países. No Brasil, entretanto, o acesso ao sistema ocorria principalmente por meio dos dispositivos Fire TV Stick, que ficam conectados à entrada HDMI da televisão.
Ainda não há confirmação sobre a compatibilidade da linha QD6SF com o Xbox Cloud Gaming, o serviço de jogos em nuvem da Microsoft. O recurso está disponível em alguns dispositivos Fire TV, mas isso não significa que funcione em qualquer televisor com o sistema da Amazon.
A nova linha conta com resolução 4K e tecnologia Hi-QLED, que utiliza pontos quânticos para ampliar a reprodução de cores. Os televisores também oferecem Dolby Atmos e recursos de aprimoramento de imagem por inteligência artificial.
Para jogos, há suporte ao Game Mode Plus, com taxa de atualização variável (VRR) e modo automático de baixa latência (ALLM). A versão de 43 polegadas tem painel nativo de 60 Hz, segundo a ficha técnica oficial.
Os quatro modelos foram encontrados na Amazon com os seguintes preços, segundo levantamento realizado pelo Tecnoblog nesta segunda-feira (09):
As TVs constam como vendidas e entregues pela Amazon, com indicação de produto sob encomenda. A Hisense ainda não divulgou uma previsão oficial de entrega ou detalhes sobre a distribuição da linha em outras redes varejistas.

articles.title: Plex2Shell Exploited Against QNAP NAS Users
articles.text:
Threat actors are exploiting Plex2Shell to hack into Plex Media Server applications on QNAP NAS devices, Taiwanese storage and networking solutions provider QNAP warns.
Plex2Shell is a chain of four vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656) in Plex Media Server that was patched this summer.
Widespread exploitation of the four-flaw chain started in mid-October, after technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code were published.
Successful exploitation of Plex2Shell does not require valid credentials and could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on exposed servers, with the privileges of the Plex service.
Plex Media Server is available as a third-party application to QNAP NAS users, through the official App Center.
“QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through these vulnerabilities,” the Taiwanese firm warned on Friday.
“The QNAP Technical Support team is assisting affected users and has confirmed that no data loss has occurred. The QNAP Product Security Incident Response Team (QNAP PSIRT) has confirmed that the vulnerabilities exist only in Plex Media Server; QTS, QuTS hero, and other QNAP operating systems are not themselves affected,” it added.
QNAP NAS users are advised to update to Plex Media Server version 1.43.3 or later as soon as possible.
Devices accessible from the internet should be considered potentially compromised and Plex should be reinstalled, QNAP says, adding that the passwords for both Plex and the NAS should be immediately rotated.
“If you do not need remote access to Plex, disable Plex Remote Access and do not forward port 32400. If you do need remote access, use a VPN instead. Also make sure QTS or QuTS hero and all installed apps are up to date,” QNAP says.
The company has published a step-by-step remediation guide to help users identify and respond to potential compromises.
Related: Hackers Exploiting ‘SSHole’ Authentication Bypass in OpenSSH
Related: Chrome 157 Rolls Out With 213 Security Fixes, Seven Rated Critical

articles.title: BYD fecha acordo com a TIM para conectar 200 mil carros no Brasil
articles.text:
A BYD fechou acordo com a TIM para fornecer conexão à internet à frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil. A parceria também prevê a instalação de infraestrutura própria de telecomunicações no complexo industrial da empresa em Camaçari (BA).
Com o contrato, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da operadora. A cobertura será de 4G em todas as cidades brasileiras e de 5G em cerca de 1,1 mil municípios atendidos pela TIM.
A expectativa é que aproximadamente 200 mil veículos da BYD recebam a conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. A iniciativa deve ajudar a montadora a desenvolver novas funcionalidades e ampliar a oferta de serviços conectados nos automóveis.
Leia mais:
- BYD quer produzir 600 mil carros por ano em fábrica no Brasil
- BYD avança na Bahia e quer comprar porto desativado da Ford
- Superesportivo elétrico da BYD atinge 503 km/h e bate recorde
Carros conectados demandam cada vez mais dados
- O avanço de recursos como inteligência artificial (IA), mapas e streaming a bordo tem aumentado a demanda por internet nos veículos. Segundo a CNN, o consumo de dados de um carro já é quase equivalente ao de um plano básico de telefonia pós-pago, na modalidade controle;
- Para a TIM, o acordo representa expansão de sua atuação no setor automotivo. A operadora já fornece conexão para aproximadamente 630 mil veículos no país;
- A empresa também mantém parceria com a antiga Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA), hoje integrante do grupo Stellantis, para oferecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em modelos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram vendidos no Brasil.
Fábrica da BYD em Camaçari terá rede própria
O contrato também prevê a implantação de infraestrutura dedicada de redes 4G e 5G no complexo industrial da BYD em Camaçari. Com 4,6 milhões de metros quadrados, o local é apontado como a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina.
O projeto inclui sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre galpões e áreas operacionais. A estrutura deverá atender às necessidades tecnológicas da fábrica e acompanhar a expansão da produção.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Windows 11 incluye una herramienta de seguridad que muchos ignoran y puede salvar tu ordenador
articles.text:
Cuando se habla de seguridad en Windows 11, la mayoría de las miradas suelen centrarse en Microsoft Defender. Aunque el antivirus gratuito que viene integrado en el sistema operativo puede hacer el trabajo, existe otra herramienta que ayuda a detener amenazas antes de que se ejecuten en tu ordenador. Conocida como Smart App Control, esta función se incluye por defecto en Windows 11 y puede marcar una diferencia frente al malware moderno.
Smart App Control, o Control Inteligente de Aplicaciones, es una nueva función de seguridad que llegó con Windows 11. La herramienta utiliza la inteligencia en la nube de Microsoft para encontrar si una aplicación es segura y se puede ejecutar en tu ordenador. Si vienes de Windows 10, esta función reemplaza a SmartScreen, una función que protegía tu equipo ante programas y descargas de dudosa procedencia.
A diferencia de un antivirus tradicional, que analiza un archivo cuando ya está en el ordenador, el Control Inteligente de Aplicaciones actúa antes. El objetivo es determinar si una aplicación es confiable antes de permitir que se ejecute, lo que reduce el riesgo de que una amenaza comprometa nuestro sistema. A diferencia de su predecesor, Smart App Control bloquea por defecto aplicaciones sin firmar o desconocidas y es necesario desactivarlo por completo si quieres ejecutarlas.
Si bien las protecciones adicionales nunca están de más, el Control Inteligente de Aplicaciones se ha vuelto más útil en estos últimos meses. El lanzamiento de modelos más potentes de IA, como Claude Fable o GPT-6 Astra, ha aumentado el riesgo de ciberataques. Algunos hackers distribuyen programas que parecen legítimos, pero que en el fondo incluyen malware que podría robar tu información.
Aunque el usuario los descargue accidentalmente, Windows 11 puede intervenir antes de que ocurra el daño.
Cómo funciona Smart App Control en Windows 11
El Control Inteligente de Aplicaciones adopta un enfoque distinto al modelo típico de seguridad. En lugar de asumir que todo el software es seguro, salvo que sea detectado como malware, Windows solo ejecutará aplicaciones consideradas como seguras o verificadas.
Cada vez que intentas abrir una aplicación, Windows consulta los servicios de inteligencia de seguridad de Microsoft. Si estos pueden determinar con confianza que el software es seguro, el sistema permitirá la ejecución. En caso de que la aplicación esté identificada como maliciosa o potencialmente no deseada, se bloqueará automáticamente.
En los casos donde el sistema no pueda determinar un valor, Smart App Control revisará si la app cuenta con una firma digital válida de confianza. Si la firma es correcta, Windows la marcará como legítima y permitirá su ejecución. En cambio, si el programa carece de firma o no es válida, el sistema lo tratará como no confiable y lo bloqueará.
Microsoft señala en su web de ayuda que el Control Inteligente de Aplicaciones está diseñado para bloquear malware, aplicaciones inseguras y código desconocido sin firmar. Esta herramienta trabaja en conjunto con Defender y otras medidas de seguridad del sistema.
En pocas palabras, Smart App Control es uno de esos pequeños tesoros ocultos de Windows 11. No suele aparecer en los titulares, pero puede evitar que una descarga peligrosa comprometa tu ordenador. Eso sí, la herramienta no es infalible y la mejor protección siempre será navegar de forma consciente, revisar los sitios y enlaces que te comparten y no hacer caso a esas ofertas que parecen demasiado buenas como para ser verdad.

articles.title: Bridgewater exec Karen Karniol-Tambour to lead Canada’s sovereign wealth fund | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada has found the chief executive to lead its sovereign wealth fund, which aims to pursue more deals like the government’s recent $1.6-billion investment in Cohere.
The news: Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on Monday morning that Karen Karniol-Tambour, co-chief investment officer at US-based hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, will be CEO of the $25-billion Canada Strong Fund. The sovereign wealth fund will provide co-investment in “nation-building projects,” as well as pursue strategic investments in Canadian projects and companies.
The appointment was first reported by Bloomberg, which noted Karniol-Tambour was among the foreign investors Carney brought to Toronto for the inaugural Canada Investment Summit in September.
From the source: Karniol-Tambour, a Canadian citizen, has worked at Bridgewater since she graduated from Princeton University in 2006, according to the Prime Minister’s Office. Starting off as an investment associate, Karniol-Tambour was appointed as head of investment research in 2013 before being promoted to co-chief investment officer for sustainability in 2021; she later took on that role for the firm at large in 2023.
The context: The Canada Strong Fund was announced earlier this year as part of the spring economic update. The 2026 budget, tabled last week, noted the government’s intention to make the fund a Crown corporation that will invest in Canadian companies on a “fully commercial basis” with the private sector. It will be led at arms-length from the government and have its own board of directors. The fund is expected to launch in early 2027 and will include an associated retail investment product called Canada Strong Notes that will allow Canadians to directly benefit from the fund’s growth.
Final thought: Following the government’s hotly debated investment in domestic frontier AI developer Cohere, AI Minister Evan Solomon indicated that Canada will seek to make similar investments in more companies. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne reiterated that point last week, and noted the Canada Strong Fund would be the vehicle to do so. Karniol-Tambour, with experience handling Bridgewater’s more than $100 billion in assets under management, will be its driver.
Feature image courtesy Bridgewater Associates via YouTube.

articles.title: Uber launches parking service following SpotHero acquisition, with an eye on robotaxis | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Uber on Monday said it is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero.
The acquisition, announced back in February, gives Uber access to a network of 13,000 garages, lots, and valet services across more than 400 cities, the company said. And while Uber’s initial plans will focus on human drivers, the company also plans to leverage these parking spots to help the dozens of autonomous vehicle companies it has partnered with.
Uber said the parking spots could be used as staging and waiting locations for autonomous vehicles to help reduce congestion and deadheading, which refers to the miles a vehicle travels without a paying passenger or cargo on board.
For now, the company plans to focus on commuters driving their own vehicles. Uber said it will initially launch in 15 U.S. cities, including Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, DC.
Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi indicated earlier this month that the company wants the app to be more relevant to commuters.
“Commute is one of our largest categories,” he said during Uber’s third-quarter earnings call. “And to be able to offer commuters an Uber to work, a pass to avoid surge, and parking if they want it when they want to drive is a great example of us building out our inventory of services to the commuter who is a top customer for us.”
The parking service is the latest in a series of efforts at Uber to build an ecosystem of products that keep customers engaged with its app for everything from hailing a ride and ordering food and groceries, to package delivery, renting cars, booking hotels, and connecting users with public transit and robotaxis.
Uber’s membership program, called Uber One, is a key part of that strategy. Uber One attracts subscribers by offering rewards and credits, perks that have helped the program grow to more than 55 million members as of September 30. For instance, Uber is offering members a chance to earn 10% back in credits on eligible parking reservations. Those credits can later be used for rides and Uber Eats orders.
Uber Parking can be accessed directly on the app’s homescreen. Users can enter their destination, select the date and time they need parking, and then review options on an interactive map. Users can filter the results to find self-parking, valet, garages, or surface lots. All pricing is shown upfront.
Once a user has found a parking spot, they can book after entering details about their vehicle, and use the payment method in their Uber wallet. Once they arrive at the parking spot, users will either scan a unique QR code or gain entry through license plate recognition. Uber said users will be able to cancel their bookings for free until the start time.

articles.title: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
articles.text:
After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”
Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence.
These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.
For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

articles.title: Meta launches Muse Ember to take on Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna
articles.text:
Meta launches Muse Ember to take on Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna
Meta on Monday debuted Muse Ember, a smaller, more efficient multimodal member of its Muse model family.
The company is clearly taking a similar approach to the other frontier labs, with a family of models that cover everything from focused, high-volume tasks (think OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5) to frontier intelligence like OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, and, most recently, Meta’s Muse Wonder Full. And just like its competitors, Meta is pitching the smaller model for agentic subtasks like reading files, running tests, and making targeted fixes, with a larger model like Muse Wonder doing the planning.
Muse Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API under the model ID muse-ember-1.0. It will likely soon be available on services like OpenRouter and on the neoclouds, too, given that Meta has done the same for its other Muse models in the past. 
Like with previous Muse model releases, Meta is keeping Ember’s model weights private.
Ember is Meta’s take on a small, price-efficient model, and at least when it comes to the benchmarks, it’s a strong entry.
At max reasoning, Meta puts Ember at about $0.14 per task on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, compared with $0.41 for Haiku and $0.15 for Luna. Ember matches Haiku’s rounded score at about a third of the cost and scores higher than Luna for about a cent less per task.
At xhigh, the other Ember setting shown in Meta’s chart, the model scores about 34 at roughly $0.12 per task.
Muse Ember pricing
Ember, which has a 1M-token context window and supports up to 512K output tokens, is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. Those input and output rates match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at their standard short-context prices. Both charge $0.01 per million cached input tokens at those rates, with higher prices for longer prompts. Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0, with support for the Responses API.
How Chinese rivals compare
And while Meta doesn’t directly compare the new model to Chinese competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 Flash, and MiniMax M3.1 Flash in the chart, Ember undercuts the listed uncached input rates for all three. It also undercuts DeepSeek’s direct off-peak and MiniMax’s listed output prices and matches GLM’s. DeepSeek has a slightly lower off-peak cache-hit rate of $0.003 per million tokens.
On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, for example, Ember scores 36 at max reasoning, while DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is at 33, MiniMax at 29, and GLM at 28. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, meanwhile, scores 28 on this same benchmark, while Haiku gets to 36, both at max reasoning.
Muse Ember vs. Muse Spark
Meta’s own Muse Spark 1.3 scores 37 at max reasoning and costs $2.39 per task at the standard API rates used in the comparison. Meta also offers a Spark Contributor tier, where it uses requests to improve its products. That tier matches Ember’s uncached input price and charges $0.20 per million output tokens.
Meta reports a lead over Haiku and Luna on its own Personal Superintelligence Index, a measure of personal and knowledge work. One benchmark where Ember doesn’t fare as well is FrontierCode 2.0, which evaluates whether a repository maintainer would merge an agent’s changes. Ember scores 27.2 percent, compared with 34.9 percent for Haiku and 28.5 percent for DeepSeek. Spark 1.3 scores 23.1 percent.
Computer use on OSWorld
Ember can take text, images, audio, and video as inputs, and Meta says it can operate desktop apps from screenshots.
On OSWorld 2.1, it got nearly the same partial-credit score as Haiku, 69.5 percent versus 68.9 percent, but finished more tasks outright, 33.8 percent versus 27.8 percent for Haiku and 17 percent for Luna. In a separate OSWorld 2.1 run, Spark 1.3 earned nearly identical partial credit to Ember and completed 39.25 percent of tasks.
Meta says the new model is the first it trained using the larger Muse Wonder Full model. That’s similar to what the company did with Muse Wonder to train the specialized models it began rolling out to its Muse personal agent and Meta AI.
