articles.title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
articles.text:
As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them.
Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows.
A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions.
AIM Intelligence, a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments.
On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including Nemotron-Personas-Korea.
Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents.
Learn more about NVIDIA Nemotron open models and get started building secure agents with NVIDIA OpenShell.

articles.title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network.
CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary.
Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production.
Solution overview
ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS.
ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers:
First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge appliances and run locally against existing equipment and controllers. CrossnoKaye reports over 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance also acts as an outbound-only information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) gateway that opens zero inbound firewall ports inside the plant, streaming high-frequency telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). If cloud connectivity drops, the plant continues running safely on the base control narratives on the local edge cluster.
Second, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications run on top of base control using the same shared plant model. In the cloud, CrossnoKaye’s Scheduling system runs two continuous pipelines from versioned Python packages in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), operating on configurable per-instance cadences and event-driven triggers when plant settings change. Synthetic reading algorithms compute derived engineering metrics, such as heat-flow distributions, asset health indices, energy intensity, and mass-balance deviations, and write them back to the historian alongside physical I/O. Closed-loop optimization applications run on top of the base control layer, combining those derived synthetic readings with physics models, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning, utility tariffs, and weather forecasts to compute optimal setpoint schedules. Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues order every schedule and state update by facility before dispatching setpoints to the local base control narrative on the edge cluster, which CrossnoKaye reports runs 650,000 closed-loop control actions per day.
Third, AURA runs inside the platform boundary on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) as microservices and durable Temporal workflows. Under the caller’s enterprise permissions, AURA agents query the internal Atlas Data gateway to read the operational state of a facility or fleet in one consistent model: upstream and downstream equipment topology, the deployed base control narratives and interlocks, physical I/O and synthetic readings, setting change and alarm histories, active optimization schedules, and plant documentation indexed in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Having the equipment layout, the base control logic, and the sensor data in the same system makes a concrete difference when diagnosing plant issues. At an aggregates quarry running primary, secondary, and tertiary rock crushers, the back half of the plant tripped twice in a single shift. From the control room, operators saw the secondary crusher fault, cleared the alarm, and restarted the line, only for it to trip again hours later. In the historian timestamps alone, the secondary crusher faulted seconds after the tertiary crusher, which made it look like a crusher problem. Because AURA also reads the conveyor layout and the deployed base control interlocks, its investigation followed the actual control logic. A recirculating belt beneath the tertiary crusher was slipping, which tripped the tertiary crusher’s overload interlock. That interlock’s upstream safety interlock immediately halted the secondary crusher to prevent burying a stopped downstream crusher in stone. Instead of chasing a phantom crusher fault, the plant manager sent an operator to inspect the recirculating belt, confirming and fixing the slip in minutes.
The numbered flows in Figure 1 trace how an AURA investigation runs on AWS:
- Client and edge ingress: Engineers and Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients connect through AWS WAF and a public Application Load Balancer, where the API gateway validates enterprise single sign-on (SSO) or MCP credentials. Edge telemetry and control schedules flow through Amazon VPC Lattice (authenticated with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Signature Version 4 (SigV4)) and Amazon MSK.
- Context retrieval and guarded inference: AURA workflows read plant state through the Atlas Data gateway and route prompts and organization-scoped Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) queries through the Model Gateway to foundation models, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
- Runtime computation dispatch: For statistical, thermodynamic, or multi-dataset math, the workflow streams input datasets over gRPC to AURA’s internal Sandbox Orchestrator service.
- Session coordination and live streaming: In interactive sessions, the Sandbox Orchestrator tracks active sandbox session IDs and streams live progress through Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey.
- Isolated Python execution: The Sandbox Orchestrator uses the AWS SDK to call the endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, staging datasets and running model-authored Python inside an isolated code interpreter microVM.
- Artifact storage and Brief delivery: Verified Apache Parquet outputs, charts, and cited Briefs are saved to Amazon S3 over AWS PrivateLink, and Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) delivers automated Briefs to plant teams.
Walkthrough
AURA combines foundation models on Amazon Bedrock (for model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide) with isolated Python sandboxes in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, across three operational modes:
- Chats: Interactive, multi-turn engineering conversations spanning a single unit, a process line, or a multi-site portfolio (up to 200 facilities in a single turn).
- Tasks: Repeatable, parameterized investigations bound to immutable version snapshots that produce structured technical Briefs with cited evidence tables and charts.
- Routines: Automated background watchers triggered by schedules, sensor thresholds, rate-of-change windows, alarms, or equipment mode transitions.
The following sections examine four architectural decisions behind these workflows.
Warm conversational sandboxes compared to clean single-run pipelines
Interactive debugging and automated plant reporting have different state requirements:
- In an interactive Chat, an engineer explores hypotheses step by step: loading 24 hours of critical alarms across 94 facilities, filtering out chattering tank-level sensors at one site, and correlating compressor trips against ambient wet-bulb temperatures. Starting a cold sandbox on every turn would wipe in-memory tables and add latency. For Chats, the Sandbox Orchestrator binds one warm Amazon Bedrock AgentCore session to the conversation in Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey with a 15-minute sliding time to live (TTL), transparently provisioning a replacement session if an engineer returns after the idle timeout expires.
- In a scheduled Task or a 2:00 AM Routine, reproducibility comes first. Every run must start in a clean environment with no leftover state from prior runs. For Tasks and Routines, the Sandbox Orchestrator provisions a fresh, single-use AgentCore microVM per run and stops the session with StopCodeInterpreterSession as soon as the calculation finishes, preventing both cross-run contamination and idle sandbox charges.
This warm-session design makes fleet-wide triage practical in a single conversation. When an operations director asks AURA to review all critical alarms across 94 facilities over the past 24 hours and identify the primary mechanical risks, the agent loads the fleet alarm summaries from the Atlas Data gateway into its AgentCore sandbox and groups activations by facility, rule, and inter-arrival time. Rather than ranking sites by raw alarm count, the Python analysis separates a plant where 103 critical activations came from two repeating dump-tank level rules from a plant where 58 activations spanned ammonia detection, evaporator faults, and hot-gas valves within one second of each other, pointing safety and maintenance teams directly to the facility with cascading equipment faults.
Verifiable computation instead of unverified model math
When an engineer asks AURA to analyze a process trend or audit shift performance, the numbers in the response must be exact. Early in AURA’s development, the team found that letting a model write free-form Python scripts that print JSON or text summaries to standard output was too brittle: a model would occasionally misname a column, drop part of a time window, or format output in a way that broke downstream chart rendering.
To make runtime computation verifiable, AURA enforces strict data contracts around every Amazon Bedrock AgentCore run:
- Upfront contract validation and multi-source staging: Before allocating a sandbox session, the Sandbox Orchestrator validates the input contract and stages up to 50 datasets into the microVM workspace, combining physical I/O, derived synthetic readings, setting logs, alarm histories, and utility rate tables.
- In-sandbox DataFrame schema verification: Rather than parsing free-form text from standard output, the service appends a deterministic verification harness to the model’s Python script. Inside the sandbox, the harness verifies that every declared output table exists in memory as a pandas.DataFrame with all required columns and types, and serializes the verified tables directly to binary Apache Parquet files.
- Automated self-correction: If the script raises a Python exception or omits a required column, no unverified numbers reach the user. The Temporal workflow captures the traceback and schema mismatch as a structured retry prompt so the agent fixes its Python logic and re-runs the calculation in a clean sandbox before publishing any conclusion.
Automated night-shift Routines and cited Briefs through Amazon SES
Plant engineers cannot watch dashboards across 100 facilities around the clock, and many equipment issues start as slow drift on the night shift. AURA Routines run in the background, watching for specific process conditions (such as suction-pressure drift on a refrigeration stage, a batch drying curve falling behind specification, or an unscheduled manual setpoint override) and launching an investigation automatically when one triggers.
A night-shift catch on an industrial chiller plant shows how this works end to end:
- Automated detection and sandboxed root-cause analysis (02:00–02:03 AM): At 2:00 AM, a Routine detects low-stage suction-pressure drift and launches its pinned Task in read-only mode. Inside an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore sandbox, the agent correlates condenser approach temperatures against low-stage suction pressure across physical and synthetic readings, rules out sensor drift and low refrigerant charge, and isolates condenser-side fouling.
- Deterministic citation validation (02:04 AM): Before publishing the Brief, AURA parses every inline citation and verifies that each claim links to a saved telemetry window, setting change record, or sandbox output artifact in Amazon S3. No control change is made automatically.
- Brief delivery through Amazon SES and one-click Chat handoff: Within four minutes of the trigger, AURA sends a formatted HTML Brief email through Amazon SES to the plant engineering team with the diagnosis, cited signal traces, and an “Investigate in AURA” button. When the lead engineer selects that button before the morning shift huddle, AURA verifies the engineer’s live facility permissions and opens an interactive Chat pre-loaded with the Brief’s evidence so the team can ask follow-up questions or issue a work order immediately.
Defense in depth industrial safety
In an industrial plant, operational safety cannot depend on an LLM following instructions in a prompt. Because ATLAS and AURA share the same platform from the cloud down to the edge Kubernetes cluster on the plant floor, CrossnoKaye enforces strict boundaries on what AI and optimization workloads can do across four independent layers:
- Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and verifiable provenance (Observe): Every prompt and completion routed through AURA’s Model Gateway is evaluated by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content, topic, and safety policies. Knowledge Base retrieval is isolated by organization, and every Brief requires verified inline citations, noting both which time windows were analyzed and any periods where sensor data was unavailable.
- Air-gapped read-only sandboxes and human-approved proposals (Propose): Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter microVMs run in isolated, AWS managed environments with no network routes, credentials, or API paths to plant equipment. Automated Routines run strictly in read-only mode. When an engineer uses an interactive session to propose a setting change, the platform requires explicit human approval under the operator’s corporate identity and verifies the physical outcome in plant telemetry afterward.
- Non-bypassable deterministic Level 1 base control at the edge (Bounded and Base Control): Cloud optimization applications don’t drive field hardware directly. They run on top of the platform’s base control layer by dispatching setpoint schedules within engineering-approved envelopes. On the plant floor, the edge Kubernetes cluster runs the downloaded base control narratives locally in real time, enforcing deterministic state-machine guards, rate-of-change clamps, operating bounds, and equipment interlocks that cannot be bypassed by cloud services, optimization applications, or AI agents.
- Independent physical hardware protection: Beneath the ATLAS software-defined controller, the plant’s physical machinery and field wiring enforce independent, hardwired protection layers, including safety relays, local programmable trips, and mechanical pressure-relief and over-temperature devices.
Results and lessons learned
Across food processing, industrial refrigeration, aggregates and mining, and manufacturing sites, CrossnoKaye reports that combining software-defined edge control, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA has reduced batch drying-time standard deviation by 34 percent (with 6 percent more product finishing within target yield specification) and identified more than 50,000 tons per year of recoverable production gap in quarry operations. With over 5,000 AI agents monitoring more than 10,000 plant assets across customer facilities (including over 13,000 controlled devices and equipment units across the ATLAS fleet), investigations that previously required hours of exporting historian CSVs, cross-referencing PLC ladder logic, and building spreadsheets now complete in under four minutes, delivering cited technical Briefs through Amazon SES before the morning shift meeting.
Three lessons stood out from building and operating AURA across industrial facilities:
- Unify the plant model and control logic before adding AI: An agent can only diagnose real physical root causes, like distinguishing a slipping downstream recirculating belt from a secondary crusher fault, when it can read the process topology, the deployed base control narratives and interlocks, the setting change history, and the optimizer state in one consistent model rather than stitching together six disconnected plant systems.
- Deliver value inside the operator’s daily workflow, not as a separate tool to go use: Plant teams are busy running equipment. If an AI assistant is a separate destination where engineers must start from a blank prompt, day-to-day adoption stalls. Embedding AURA into the daily shift rhythm (where background Routines catch anomalies overnight, run the Python analysis in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and deliver a cited Brief to the engineer’s inbox with a one-click handoff into a pre-loaded Chat) means operators see the value in their normal routine without having to go use a separate product.
- Enforce data, coverage, and safety contracts in code rather than prompts: In a plant, a missing hour of sensor data isn’t the same as an hour with no events, and an unverified calculation can send a maintenance crew to the wrong machine. Making data-coverage gaps explicit in tool contracts, verifying pandas.DataFrame schemas inside the AgentCore sandbox before extracting binary Apache Parquet outputs, and enforcing deterministic base control bounds on the edge Kubernetes cluster catch probabilistic model errors before they reach an operator or a piece of equipment.
Conclusion
Reliable physical AI in heavy industry requires grounding models in the actual equipment topology and control logic of the plant, and backing every quantitative claim with verifiable Python calculations. Together with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and isolated Python sandboxes in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, ATLAS and AURA allow agents to reason over live facility ontology, base control narratives, setting histories, physical I/O, optimization state, and synthetic readings, delivering checkable engineering answers and cited technical Briefs through Amazon SES while keeping deterministic safety controls firmly on the plant floor.
To learn more about building agents with isolated code execution, refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide or visit CrossnoKaye to see how physical AI is transforming heavy industry.

articles.title: Make a Robot Arm Feel Weightless with NVIDIA Holoscan 5 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Picture guiding a robot arm by hand while its motors supply just enough torque to support its weight and keep the robot upright. This simple interaction, a useful starting point for robots that learn by demonstration, manipulate objects, or work alongside people, depends on a gravity-compensation loop.
Building such a loop is only possible by continuously calculating the inverse dynamics of the system based on precise models of all the links of the robot arm, their dimensions, masses, and moments of inertia. This calculation, which needs to be done rapidly with low jitter, requires knowing the current state of the robot, so gravity-comp demos are an excellent proof of life for both the robot model and the runtime that’s executing these algorithms.
NVIDIA Holoscan 5 introduced robotic control alongside streamlined sensor processing. In this tutorial, we’ll build custom Holoscan SDK operators and wire them into a graph. We’ll test the code on a real robot and use the Holoscan SDK’s built-in Nsight Systems annotations to inspect latency and jitter.
This walkthrough has been tested on Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson Thor, and x86 Ubuntu 24.04 systems.
Why Holoscan?
Holoscan SDK brings low-latency control and high-throughput perception into one programming model, with execution paths designed for CPU- and GPU-based workloads. Its goal is a transparent runtime: minimize avoidable framework overhead while making application execution explicit and inspectable.
Keep the control path focused on the work. Holoscan uses partitions to group chains of operators on a single thread, avoiding cross-thread handoffs and unnecessary syscalls, reducing latency and jitter. Clock and data-arrival triggers express when work should run, while bounded, drop-oldest queues prevent outdated work from accumulating.
Bring existing algorithms and code rather than rewriting them for a framework. Holoscan 5 has a new, lightweight programming model that can be easily integrated into existing code bases, and it’s never been easier to get data into and out of Holoscan graphs.
Add perception without adopting a different programming model. Whether you’re handling 10 kHz CPU-centric motor control loops, heavy-throughput GPU algorithms, or AI inference, Holoscan lets developers and their agents clearly express execution intent using the same operators, ports, and graph APIs, logically splitting their workloads into separate graphs that can coexist, with the ability to pin partitions to dedicated CPU cores, CUDA green contexts, or even execute as a CUDA graph.
Inspect the plan, then measure the result. Operators express their intent with timing contracts, and before the first run, the compiled plan exposes how the application will execute and catches configuration errors before deployment. This means agents and developers can quickly iterate on a design without ever deploying to real hardware. Plus, built-in NVTX annotations make operator execution and message transfers visible in Nsight Systems. Developers can examine host control-path latency and update jitter, then repeat those measurements as the application grows.
An accessible platform for torque-control development
This tutorial is built around the Seeed Studio reBot Arm B601-DM, which is an accessible, affordable platform for getting started with modern robotics control. Most low-cost robot arm development platforms use highly-geared hobby servos, which are only suitable for positional control. The reBot Arm uses quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators that provide high torque bandwidth for both control and sensing — important for haptic, co-bot, or other torque-oriented projects like this one.
Starting off with gravity-comp
Before adding perception pipelines, motion planners, and other higher-level controls, building a basic gravity compensation loop helps provide a useful (and entertaining!) sanity-check for whether your simulation model accurately describes the physical robot. While position-control examples can mask problems with joint axes, offsets, link placements, masses, and moments, all of these affect the required torque in instantly-observable ways; any bugs in DH parameters or mass properties can make the arm sag or push upward as its pose changes.
Even if your end application doesn’t need gravity-comp, torque control lets us shape how the robot responds to forces—a key ingredient in safer interaction between humans and co-bots. Our arm combines gravity feedforward with light stiffness and damping, so it supports its weight while yielding to a person’s hand.
That flexibility makes timing critical. Tracking a position through torque commands requires rapid, consistent feedback at hundreds or thousands of Hz, and runtime overhead and thread handoffs can add phase lag and jitter that cause the robot to become unstable.
This tutorial uses Pinocchio as the inverse-dynamics solver. It loads the robot’s URDF model and provides a Recursive Newton–Euler Algorithm (RNEA) solver, which calculates joint torques for specified positions, velocities, and accelerations. We also use the motorbridge library to read joint feedback and send commands to the arm’s motors.
Set up the Python example
This walkthrough uses Holoscan’s Python API. The tutorial repository also contains a complete C++ implementation, with its own build instructions. Both implement the same three-operator control loop.
Use Python 3.12 or newer on Linux. From the repository root:
python3.12 -m venv build/python-venv
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip install --only-binary=:all: -r requirements-python.txt
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip check
Check the serial device and motor IDs in the arm’s configuration file. The tutorial repository’s technical guide covers configuration, the math, and hardware startup.
Express the control loop as three operators
Holoscan 5 has two programming concepts: Operators and Graphs. To read the robot’s state, calculate the command using the inverse-dynamics solver, and send it to the arm, we can decompose that problem into three operators wired into a graph:
Operators are subclassed from Operator and have three important methods to implement:
| Method | Purpose | 
|---|---|
| setup() | Declare input and output ports. | 
| contract() | Declare when to run and which input data to use. | 
| compute() | Read input(s), do work, and publish output(s). | 
Table 1. Core methods to implement for custom Holoscan operators
Here are outlines of the three operators to build:
1. Read joint state on a clock
JointStateSourceOp declares one output in setup(). Its OnClock contract requests a tick every 2.5 ms (we’re running this demo at 400 Hz). Each compute() reads all seven motors and emits their state:
import holoscan as hsdk
class JointStateSourceOp(hsdk.Operator):
    state = hsdk.Output("state", hsdk.pyobject)
    def setup(self, spec):
        spec.output(self.state)
    def contract(self):
        return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnClock(period=hsdk.time.us(2500)))
    def start(self):
        self.sequence = 0
    def compute(self, ctx):
        self.sequence += 1
        self.state.emit(robot.read_state(self.sequence))
2. Compute gravity compensation when state arrives
PinocchioGravityOp declares a state input and command output. OnEach runs it when state arrives. The hsdk.Param declarations expose gains, torque scaling, and joint direction as operator parameters:
class PinocchioGravityOp(hsdk.Operator):
    state = hsdk.Input("state", hsdk.pyobject)
    command = hsdk.Output("command", hsdk.pyobject)
    kp = hsdk.Param(1.5, range=(0.0, 500.0))
    kd = hsdk.Param(1.0, range=(0.0, 5.0))
    tau_scale = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6)
    joint_direction = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6)
    def setup(self, spec):
        spec.input(self.state, queue_depth=1)
        spec.output(self.command)
    def contract(self):
        return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnEach(self.state))
    def compute(self, ctx):
        state = self.state.receive_data()
        command = controller.compute(
            state, kp=self.kp, kd=self.kd,
            tau_scale=self.tau_scale, joint_direction=self.joint_direction)
        self.command.emit(command)
compute() passes the observed state and current parameters to a helper that maps the six arm angles into the URDF model, checks limits, and obtains gravity torques through Pinocchio:
gravity = pin.computeGeneralizedGravity(self.model, self.data, self.q)[self.v_indices]
Its torques become feedforward in the motors’ commands, alongside position, velocity, stiffness, and damping. The arm uses gravity feedforward and the configured compliant gains from the first command.
3. Send each command to the motors
MotorCommandSinkOp declares one input and runs whenever a command arrives. compute() hands the command to a small robot helper, which rejects expired, out-of-order, or out-of-range commands before sending the batch:
class MotorCommandSinkOp(hsdk.Operator):
    command = hsdk.Input("command", hsdk.pyobject)
    def setup(self, spec):
        spec.input(self.command, queue_depth=1)
    def contract(self):
        return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnEach(self.command))
    def compute(self, ctx):
        robot.send_command(self.command.receive_data())
    def stop(self):
        robot.disable()
After sending all seven motor commands, the helper records the completion time. If no batch completes for 100 ms (the default timeout), the application’s watchdog attempts to disable the motors and stops the graph. The operator’s stop() callback also disables the motors.
Wire, compile, prepare, and run
The application connects the operators through their ports and supplies the gravity parameters when creating the operator:
graph = hsdk.Graph("rebot-gravity", default_clock=hsdk.RealtimeClock)
source = graph.op(JointStateSourceOp, "joint_feedback")
gravity = graph.op(PinocchioGravityOp, "gravity", **controller.parameters.operator_kwargs())
sink = graph.op(MotorCommandSinkOp, "motor_commands")
graph.add_flow(source.state, gravity.state, queue_depth=1, queue_policy=hsdk.QueuePolicy.DROP_OLDEST)
graph.add_flow(gravity.command, sink.command, queue_depth=1, queue_policy=hsdk.QueuePolicy.DROP_OLDEST)
graph.partition("control").add(source).add(gravity).add(sink)
A partition groups operators whose callbacks execute serially on one runtime-owned thread. Keeping all three in control avoids thread handoffs between reading state, calculating torque, and sending commands. The source sets the pace; the other operators follow the data. Depth-one, drop-oldest queues keep old samples from piling up.
Holoscan compiles this description into an inspectable execution plan before we enable the motors:
plan = hsdk.compile(build_graph(robot, controller))
if not plan:
    raise RuntimeError(plan.summary())
prepare_gravity_compensation(robot, controller)
hsdk.run_async(plan)
Model and motor initialization live in prepare_gravity_compensation(), after graph compilation and immediately before execution. The application’s signal handlers set stop_requested on Ctrl+C; the main loop supervises command progress, and the session context manager stops and joins the graph. The control policies cover startup, watchdogs, and shutdown.
See the arm respond
Start with the arm in its power-off-safe home position:
build/python-venv/bin/python python/gravity_compensation.py
When Gravity compensation active appears, guide the arm by hand. Return it home manually before pressing Ctrl+C, which disables the motors.
Measure latency and jitter with Nsight Systems
Holoscan has seamless integration with NVIDIA Nsight Systems, giving you powerful tools for analyzing real-world system behavior for both GPU- and CPU-based workloads. NVIDIA Nsight Systems. No tracing decorators or custom timing code are needed, simply profile the unmodified application:
mkdir -p build/profiles
nsys profile -t nvtx --sample=none --backtrace=none --cpuctxsw=none \
  -o build/profiles/gravity-python \
  build/python-venv/bin/python python/gravity_compensation.py
Open the timeline:
You can also calculate a standard range summary:
nsys stats --report nvtx_sum build/profiles/gravity-python.nsys-rep
Pinning cores
Holoscan’s deployment API lets us pin the control partition to a CPU. For these runs, we put helper and profiler threads on another CPU, then used a temporary Linux cgroup to reserve both physical cores, including their SMT siblings, from other applications. This is a simple setup that needs no kernel rebuild, boot-parameter changes, or reboot, but interrupts, timers, and some kernel threads can still run on those cores.
We compared all four configurations, retaining more than one million cycles per run. Holoscan latency runs from entry into the first operator to entry into the last, excluding motor-command transmission. Solid curves show pinned runs; dotted curves show unpinned runs.
| Implementation | p50 (µs) | p99.99 (µs) | p99.999 (µs) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| HSDK C++ pinned | 7.1 | 17.2 | 20.7 | 
| HSDK C++ unpinned | 15.3 | 86.6 | 133.4 | 
| HSDK Python pinned | 93.0 | 142.6 | 1,014.0 | 
| HSDK Python unpinned | 113.8 | 1,373.5 | 3,134.1 | 
Table 2. Measured latency distributions for C++ and Python Holoscan pipelines in pinned vs. unpinned configurations.
Pinning plus isolation reduced the observed p99.99 latency by roughly 5× for C++ and 9.6× for Python. These sequential, profiled runs exclude the first ten seconds and retain latency outliers.
Both Holoscan versions call Pinocchio’s C++-based solver, but Python adds interpreter execution, object allocation, and GIL coordination around both Pinocchio and the Holoscan runtime. Those costs matter for CPU control loops with microsecond latency budgets. C++ gives us more control over allocations and system calls in the critical path (although this example still allocates memory and is not a zero-syscall pipeline).
For GPU-based perception workloads taking milliseconds or tens of milliseconds—orders of magnitude longer—optimizing small allocations and incidental system calls on the CPU is usually less consequential. Python remains a practical way to compose these pipelines (provided that the pipeline elements are implemented in CUDA).
From gravity compensation to a full control stack
You now have a working gravity-compensation loop built from three Holoscan operators: one reads joint state on a clock, one computes gravity torque with Pinocchio, and one sends commands to the motors. Holoscan compiled and checked the graph before the motors were enabled, and Nsight Systems showed how it ran.
Gravity compensation is the foundation rather than the finished controller. The tutorial repository includes a second Python example that adds kinematics and impedance control as reusable Holoscan operators. It lets you inject a goal position and orientation, for example from a learned policy, while the arm stays compliant to the touch.
From there, you can build toward hand-guided teaching, teleoperation, and manipulation. To add perception, use Holoscan’s vision module, along with components from NVIDIA Isaac ROS, which provides reusable Holoscan operators and reference applications such as GR00T inference.
Next steps
Download the Holoscan 5 SDK and follow the full tutorial here.

articles.title: Mort imminente : 50 témoins ont dessiné leurs visions, quatre formes reviennent sans cesse
articles.text:
Mort imminente : 50 témoins ont dessiné leurs visions, quatre formes reviennent sans cesse
Visio, scans et statistiques en Python : la science cartographie le tunnel de lumière
Le fameux tunnel existe bien dans les souvenirs de ceux qui ont frôlé la mort. Il n’est pourtant qu’un décor parmi d’autres. Des chercheurs ont demandé à 50 personnes de dessiner leur expérience de mort imminente. Dans leurs croquis, quatre architectures reviennent avec une régularité troublante, et la couleur de chaque scène semble dictée par sa forme. Une cartographie de l’invisible qui intrigue jusqu’aux concepteurs de réalité virtuelle.
Une lumière aveuglante, la sensation de flotter au-dessus de son corps, un couloir obscur… Depuis des siècles, les expériences de mort imminente (EMI) se racontent avec les mêmes mots, faute de mieux. France Lerner, chercheuse en neurophénoménologie à l'Université de Haïfa, a choisi le crayon. Avec son équipe, elle a fait dessiner à 50 personnes les espaces qu'elles avaient traversés, dans une étude publiée le 15 octobre par la revue Frontiers in Psychology. Les participants ont décrit 112 scènes, dont 108 se rangent dans quatre familles géométriques.
Le phénomène est loin d'être rare : jusqu'à un survivant d'arrêt cardiaque sur cinq rapporte une EMI, selon une synthèse publiée en 2025.
Quatre formes géométriques au cœur des expériences de mort imminente
Les participants ont été recrutés via le site de l'Association internationale pour l'étude des EMI, puis retenus grâce à deux questionnaires de référence, dont l'échelle de Greyson. Le protocole tient du bureau à distance : des séances en visioconférence sur Google Meet, jamais enregistrées, au cours desquelles chacun découpait son souvenir en étapes chronologiques. Au stylo bleu, il traçait chaque espace en partant d'un catalogue de pictogrammes, marquait sa position d'une croix et ses déplacements de flèches. Les dessins étaient ensuite scannés et envoyés par mail en JPEG, anonymisés et passés en niveaux de gris dans Photoshop. Les statistiques, elles, ont été calculées en Python.
Il en ressort quatre familles. On trouve d'abord des cônes, qui incluent le tunnel classique, puis de larges arches elliptiques, des horizons à la courbure plus douce et, pour finir, des enveloppes à 360 degrés qui entourent entièrement l'observateur. Les cônes surgissent surtout au début ou à la fin du récit, comme une porte d'entrée et de sortie. Quant aux sorties du corps, elles concernent 32 participants sur 50.
Couleur ou noir et blanc : ce que la forme dit du cerveau
La découverte la plus intrigante concerne la palette. Sur 28 espaces coniques, 22 ont été vus en noir, blanc ou gris. À l'inverse, 27 des 31 grandes arches baignaient dans la couleur. Les deux autres familles mêlent couleur et grisaille.
La physiologie de la vision offre des pistes. Quand l'oxygène manque à la rétine ou au cerveau, le champ visuel se rétrécit en commençant par la périphérie, ce qui produit un effet tunnel. Dans la pénombre, les cellules de la vision nocturne prennent le relais et les couleurs s'éteignent. Les enveloppes uniformes évoquent quant à elles l'effet Ganzfeld, où un champ visuel sans relief suffit à déclencher des hallucinations.
Ces cartes mentales intéressent aussi les concepteurs d'expériences immersives. En 2025, une équipe américaine a fait vivre une EMI simulée en réalité virtuelle à 61 adultes, avec l'objectif d'apaiser leur angoisse de la mort, dans une étude parue dans Frontiers in Virtual Reality. Une typologie précise des espaces vécus pourrait un jour nourrir ce genre de dispositif.
L'équipe de Haïfa reste prudente. L'échantillon est modeste et volontaire, certains souvenirs datent de plusieurs années, et les pictogrammes proposés ont pu orienter les tracés. L'étude ne comporte pas non plus de groupe témoin. Les auteurs présentent donc leur grille de lecture comme une approche exploratoire, "plutôt que comme une preuve d'invariants géométriques universels".
	
Le cadre proposé doit être compris comme une approche méthodologique exploratoire […] plutôt que comme une preuve d'invariants géométriques universels.
On ignore donc si ces formes appartiennent en propre aux EMI. L'étude décrit ces paysages intérieurs sans prétendre en livrer la cause, et encore moins prouver un au-delà.
Suivez toute l'actualité des Numériques sur Google Actualités et sur la chaîne WhatsApp des Numériques
Envie de faire encore plus d'économies ? Découvrez nos codes promo sélectionnés pour vous.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: From Chips to Skills, NVIDIA and Korea Expand Sovereign AI Collaboration
articles.text:
NVIDIA and Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) are expanding their collaboration across the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem, from AI semiconductors and data center infrastructure to talent, startups, models, agents and security.
The collaboration lays the groundwork for Korean NPU and XPU companies to explore participation in the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem, and includes NVIDIA training and certification programs, hackathons and technical seminars to strengthen GPU utilization.
Through Korea’s AI for All initiative, NVIDIA will collaborate with three selected consortia and four leading Korean foundation model builders, using NVIDIA Dynamo software to optimize and scale AI inference.
In addition, NVIDIA today announced a collaboration with SK Telecom and Rebellions, supported by MSIT, to advance sovereign AI infrastructure for Korean models and workloads with NVIDIA NVLink Fusion. Read more in the press release.

articles.title: Affaire Jensen Huang : quelles conséquences pour Nvidia, au-delà du scandale ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Lundi 9 novembre, cinq minutes à peine après la clôture de la Bourse américaine, un cabinet d’avocats déposait une plainte en nom collectif (class action) contre Nvidia et son CEO devant le tribunal fédéral de San Jose. Une réactivité millimétrée face au décrochage du titre, qui venait de céder 4,27 % en une journée pour clôturer à 178,67 dollars, à rebours d’un secteur des semi-conducteurs pourtant dans le vert.
La veille, Jensen Huang avait publiquement reconnu une liaison extra-conjugale : une relation nouée avec Alice Huang, cadre chez le client asiatique Megaspeed, que le contre-espionnage américain soupçonne d’agir pour le compte de Pékin.
Depuis cet aveu, la crise a pris une tournure très politique, comme on pouvait s’y attendre. Donald Trump a affirmé lundi avoir échangé par téléphone avec le dirigeant : Jensen Huang lui aurait juré ignorer tout des activités présumées de sa compagne, une version que le président américain dit croire, tout en confirmant que le FBI a ouvert un dossier.
Tandis que Pékin balaie des accusations jugées sans fondement, le conseil d’administration de Nvidia assure n’avoir aucun indice laissant penser que des secrets industriels ont fuité.
Pour autant, aucune date butoir n’a été fixée pour son audit interne, et le patron, qui promettait dans sa lettre d’excuses aux salariés de coopérer pleinement, conserve les rênes du groupe en attendant.
    Pour aller plus loin
« Vous méritez mieux de ma part » : le patron de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, accusé d’avoir entretenu une relation extra-conjugale avec une espionne chinoise
            
Nvidia peut-elle survivre sans Jensen Huang ?
En coulisses, une question taraude les analystes financiers bien plus que la secousse boursière du jour : que se passerait-il si Jensen Huang devait quitter son fauteuil ?
Le cofondateur dirige l’entreprise sans partage depuis sa création en 1993, sans directeur des opérations (COO) pour le seconder, et supervise directement une soixantaine de cadres dirigeants, un mode de gestion ultra-horizontal dont il se félicite régulièrement. Si cette absence de hiérarchie intermédiaire explique l’agilité redoutable de Nvidia, elle a un revers majeur : il n’existe aucun numéro deux identifié, ni aucun plan de succession public.
Un angle mort que l’entreprise reconnaît elle-même dans son rapport annuel, admettant qu’une transition mal préparée pourrait gripper toute sa stratégie.
Le cabinet Bernstein pointe ainsi un « risque homme-clé » maximal (cette dépendance critique d’une société envers un seul dirigeant), tandis que Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, professeur de gouvernance à l’université Yale, estime désormais que Jensen Huang n’a plus qu’une chance sur deux de conserver son poste.
Pour l’analyste Dan Ives, de Yorkville Ives, l’équation est encore plus brutale : le patron à la veste en cuir est tout simplement irremplaçable. Les quelques figures internes citées pour assurer un éventuel intérim, à l’image de la directrice financière Colette Kress, peinent d’ailleurs à rassurer Wall Street sur la vision technologique à long terme.
Or, la stabilité de cette gouvernance dépasse largement le sort des actionnaires de Nvidia, tant ses processeurs constituent aujourd’hui la colonne vertébrale des centres de données mondiaux, comme nous le détaillions dans notre décryptage sur l’onde de choc qui menace tout le secteur de l’IA.
    Pour aller plus loin
Affaire Jensen Huang : pourquoi le scandale d’espionnage chez Nvidia fait trembler tout le secteur de l’IA
            
Un double étau judiciaire et politique à Washington
En parallèle de cette crise de gouvernance, le front judiciaire vient tout juste de s’ouvrir. L’action collective initiée par l’actionnaire Mark Kistenmacher couvre la période d’octobre 2025 à novembre 2026 : elle accuse la direction d’avoir trompé les investisseurs en présentant ses liens commerciaux avec Megaspeed comme parfaitement ordinaires, occultant ainsi un risque majeur pour la réputation du groupe.
Bien que ce genre de recours boursier soit quasi systématique aux États-Unis après un décrochage brutal et aboutisse rarement à des condamnations lourdes, la procédure risque d’obliger Nvidia à déballer ses échanges internes devant un juge fédéral.
La menace la plus immédiate reste toutefois réglementaire. Après des mois de lobbying acharné de Jensen Huang pour conserver un accès au marché chinois, Washington avait fini par autoriser cette année l’exportation sous conditions de la puce H200.
Plusieurs observateurs redoutent désormais que cette licence soit purement et simplement révoquée, et que l’administration verrouille les failles permettant de louer des puces depuis l’Asie du Sud-Est. Le calendrier politique joue d’ailleurs contre Nvidia : non seulement trois présidents républicains de commissions parlementaires exigent déjà d’auditionner le CEO à huis clos, mais les démocrates prendront le contrôle des deux chambres du Congrès dès le mois de janvier.
Un réveil brutal pour des investisseurs qui ont longtemps préféré ignorer ces signaux d’alerte, comme l’illustrait déjà notre article sur l’alerte ignorée de mai dernier.
    Pour aller plus loin
Nvidia trop gros pour être soupçonné ? Cette alerte ignorée de mai en dit long sur l’aveuglement des marchés face à l’IA 
            
Le rendez-vous décisif du 17 novembre
Le premier véritable test grandeur nature aura lieu le 17 novembre lors de la présentation des résultats trimestriels du groupe. Si Nvidia anticipe un chiffre d’affaires colossal d’environ 108 milliards de dollars, les analystes de Wall Street attendront surtout la direction au tournant sur l’avancée de l’enquête interne et sur la sécurisation de l’organigramme. Viendront ensuite le passage devant le Congrès, les conclusions des administrateurs indépendants et, en toile de fond, les investigations du FBI. Si le moindre transfert d’informations sensibles venait à être prouvé, le maintien de Jensen Huang deviendrait intenable, forçant les fonds qui avaient balayé les accusations du rapport Culper à revoir entièrement leur copie.
Pendant plus de trente ans, Nvidia a bâti son hégémonie sur l’omniprésence de son fondateur, une hyper-centralisation du pouvoir saluée comme un coup de génie tant que le dirigeant semblait infaillible. Sans prouver la moindre trahison à ce stade, l’affaire Alice Huang rappelle crûment qu’un mastodonte pesant plus de 4 000 milliards de dollars navigue toujours sans plan B officiel. Pour l’entreprise la plus stratégique de la révolution de l’IA comme pour tout le secteur qui dépend de ses puces, c’est un angle mort devenu impossible à justifier.

articles.title: Ukraine dismantles crypto scam network that stole €4.3 million
articles.text:
Ukrainian law enforcement arrested four suspects in a case involving the theft of more than €4.3 million using a network of cryptocurrency investment scam call centers.
In these fraud schemes (also known as romance baiting or pig butchering scams), criminals lure targets through social media, dating sites, and messaging apps into fake investment schemes, stealing their money instead of investing the funds as promised.
The investigation involved Ukraine's Cyber Police Department, the Main Investigation Department of the National Police of Ukraine, and German law enforcement authorities.
According to Ukraine's Cyber Police, the suspects used phone calls and messaging apps to build victims' trust through social engineering and trick them into investing in cryptocurrency, shares, and other financial instruments through fraudulent online trading platforms.
The crime ring targeted potential victims across the European Union, stealing more than €4.3 million from 135 German victims.
"They assisted victims in opening accounts on cryptocurrency exchanges, purchasing digital assets and transferring them to accounts controlled by the criminal organisation. In some cases, the suspects also gained access to victims' online banking accounts," the Ukrainian Cyber Police said.
"The proceeds of crime were subsequently moved through bank accounts, cryptocurrency exchanges and transit wallets, converted and distributed among members of the criminal organisation."
After two rounds of searches in August and September in the Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, Ukrainian police detained four members of the investment scam ring, including the leader and three accomplices.
During the searches, law enforcement officers also seized over $90,000, nearly 600,000 Ukrainian Hryvnia (roughly $13,000), hardware cryptocurrency wallets, mobile phones, SIM cards, computer equipment, and other evidence.
The four suspects are now held in pre-trial detention and face up to 12 years in prison if found guilty of charges related to fraud and the creation, leadership of, and participation in a criminal organization.
This action comes after European law enforcement authorities dismantled, in December, another fraud network operating call centers in Ukraine that scammed Europeans out of more than 10 million euros.
More recently, in August, Ukrainian authorities also shut down 94 fraudulent call centers that tricked people into investment scams or tried to access their bank accounts.

articles.title: Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick. | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick.
Our first brand campaign celebrates teams who keep business moving and the AI workspace built only for them. Every day, teams at leading enterprises use AWS Quick to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Today we’re launching our first brand campaign to bring that same experience to millions more knowledge workers around the world. The campaign runs across the United States and the United Kingdom on streaming TV, online video, social media, and leading business publications. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work, where teams use AI agents to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Across virtually every industry, leading enterprises including 3M, BMW, Mondelez, New York Life, and Southwest Airlines are using Quick to transform how they work. The campaign celebrates the teams who know that the work they do every day deserves tools built for it.
The work you know
Customers tell us their AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains stay personal. A sales rep still builds territory plans by pulling from the CRM, dashboards, call notes, and email. Because context stays locked inside a single project or one vendor’s suite, productivity never compounds across the team or the company. Most of those tools started as consumer apps and still serve personal and professional use with the same product. AWS Quick took the opposite path: it was built for work from day one, on the same AWS infrastructure that millions of customers use to run their mission-critical applications. These include many of the world’s most complex and security-sensitive workloads.
Built for your business from day one
AWS Quick has no consumer version. Every roadmap decision and every feature we ship starts with one question: does it help individuals, teams, and entire enterprises do their most important work? Quick knows your role, your team, and how your projects, people, and data connect, because it works across the applications and workflows your teams already use. Quick watches for changes, surfaces what matters, and acts on your behalf, which leaves your team free to focus on what moves the business forward. Anyone can build agents, apps, and automations by describing what they need in plain language, without filing an IT ticket. Everything built in a shared space becomes an asset the whole team can use.
Trust built in
Quick is integrated with the security and compliance tools you already use, including Microsoft Purview for data protection, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Microsoft Active Directory for permission-based controls. Quick reads the sensitivity labels already on your files, enforces existing permissions, and flags potentially sensitive data to administrators. Assets including agents, knowledge bases, and skills reach new teams only through approved sharing, and every approval and denial is recorded with who decided, what they shared, and why. Quick also carries the compliance certifications most organizations require, including HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Your data is yours, and your conversations are private. No one else can browse your conversations, and IT admins cannot access your chat transcripts. Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail are built in, giving your organization a full audit trail of what happened, who did it, and when. Your data never leaves your environment and never trains someone else’s models.
That commitment is also why we’re now AWS Quick, a name that signals the enterprise security and governance that have been part of Quick from the start.
Every decision stays yours
IT leaders, account executives, program managers, and finance leads all work differently, and Quick works the way each of them does, on any device and on their schedule. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals.
Ready to transform how your users, teams, and entire enterprise do their best work with an AI built for business? You can download Quick today and get started in minutes, or talk to your AWS account team about options for enterprise pricing plans.

articles.title: Campus Driver : la nouvelle série Prime Vidéo explose tout et elle a une spécificité
articles.text:
Mise en ligne d’un bloc, ses six épisodes ont pris la tête des classements de Prime Video dans des dizaines de pays, de l’Allemagne au Brésil en passant par la Pologne et le Portugal. Dans le classement mondial de FlixPatrol, qui compile les Top 10 publiés par Prime Video dans chaque pays, la série française Campus Drivers totalisait 467 points le 8 novembre 2026, contre 357 pour The Terminal List.
Du phénomène littéraire français au succès international sur Prime Video
Campus Drivers adapte la saga de l’autrice française C.S. Quill, publiée chez Hugo. Ses cinq tomes, devenus un phénomène de la New Romance et de BookTok, se sont vendus à près d’un million d’exemplaires en France. Ils mêlent comédie romantique universitaire, réparties et voitures de collection (oui).
Créée par Thomas Boullé, la série est produite par Campus Entertainment, Carmen Kassovitz (Loïs) et Baptiste Masseline (Lane) tiennent les rôles principaux. La série suit la cohabitation inattendue entre une étudiante au cœur brisé et le créateur de l’application de transport la plus populaire du campus.
Une série française devant The Terminal List
Campus Drivers est la première série française pour jeunes adultes produite par Prime Video, et elle prend la tête du classement mondial dès son premier week-end. Elle passe ainsi devant The Terminal List, la série d’action à gros budget dont la saison 2 est en ligne depuis le 21 octobre. Après Off Campus en juin, la New Romance s’impose de nouveau chez les abonnés de Prime Video. Décidément…
Pour Amazon MGM Studios et l’écosystème audiovisuel français, ce braquage des charts mondiaux marque un tournant. Il confirme non seulement l’incroyable pouvoir d’attraction de la New Romance auprès des abonnés, mais aussi la capacité des séries françaises à s’exporter à une échelle planétaire sans rougir face aux mastodontes américains. Lupin avait pu le prouver sur Netflix. Clairement, Prime Video tient là une franchise majeure qui n’a manifestement pas fini de faire parler d’elle sur les réseaux et de dominer le classement.

articles.title: Google DeepMind’s AI Agents Make 1024-Bit RSA Keys Cheaper to Attack
articles.text:
Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision have found two ways to reduce the cost of attacking 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems.
The research, conducted with cryptographers from UC San Diego and Inria, indicates that attacks on legacy RSA-1024 require less computation than previously assumed.
“In practice, these results only affect obsolete 1024-bit RSA systems, and modern encryption protocols, which almost universally use 2048-bit or larger keys, remain secure,” said Pushmeet Kohli, VP at Google DeepMind and chief scientist at Google Cloud.
The first finding involves digital signatures and padding, the preset data that many signature standards add to a message to bring it to a fixed block size. Padding was known to make forgery harder, but its value against an attacker who can choose what gets signed was unclear.
DeepMind determined that it depends on the share of the signed block the attacker controls. “Once they control roughly half of the block or more, padding adds no protection at all,” Kohli explained.
According to the accompanying paper, this applies to the PKCS#1 v1.5 format used by the PKCS#11 signing interface of cryptographic devices such as hardware security modules (HSMs).
In a sandboxed test, the agents re-ran an earlier academic forgery attack on the same 1024-bit key, cutting CPU time 3.5-fold. The first forgery took 391 CPU core-years, versus 1,380 in the original study.
Two AI agents designed, ran and debugged the forgery computation in under four days, with approximately 20 messages from the human researcher, mostly approvals. The key was not factored; that would take an estimated 500,000 to 1 million core-years.
Forgery is harder when the attacker controls less of the block, such as a 32-byte hash. Even then, DeepMind found an algorithm that by its theoretical estimates is roughly 1,600 times better than the previous best method against 1024-bit keys.
The second finding concerns factoring many RSA keys of the same size, where an attacker can share the cost of one large upfront computation across all of them.
DeepMind’s agents came up with an algorithm that makes factoring each additional 1024-bit key roughly 30 times cheaper on average than the best previous approach. However, this theoretical estimate assumes an initial computation as costly as factoring one key, and the method has not been implemented.
The researchers noted that the signature attack does not recover the private key. It requires roughly 4 billion signing queries made in advance, and does not work against devices that hash messages internally.
“Together, these results show that in a new era of AI-enabled mathematics and computation, we cannot treat cryptographic hardness as a fixed assumption. Using AI to rigorously test our previously held assumptions will ensure that modern encryption stays secure,” Kohli said.
